Source
Open problem. Whether an odd perfect number exists is unknown. This project does not claim a proof; it formalizes necessary conditions.

Every module on the main branch, grouped by topic, with its public theorems. Foundations

Definitions, divisor sums of prime powers, valuations, and the divisor sum network.

OddPerfect.Basic

OddPerfect/Basic.lean · 43 lines · 6 public theorems · imports Seed.Starter

The two definitions everything is read against: OddPerfect N (N is odd and perfect, using mathlib's Nat.Perfect) and OddPerfectConjecture, a statement that is never assumed.

Proof idea. No arguments here: six one line projections such as σ 1 N = 2 * N unpack the definition.

theorem odd (h : OddPerfect N) : Odd N

OddPerfect.perfect

theorem perfect (h : OddPerfect N) : N.Perfect

OddPerfect.pos

theorem pos (h : OddPerfect N) : 0 < N

OddPerfect.ne_zero

theorem ne_zero (h : OddPerfect N) : N ≠ 0

OddPerfect.sigma_eq

theorem sigma_eq (h : OddPerfect N) : σ 1 N = 2 * N

OddPerfect.not_two_dvd

theorem not_two_dvd (h : OddPerfect N) : ¬ 2 ∣ N

OddPerfect.Seed.Starter

OddPerfect/Seed/Starter.lean · 116 lines · 7 public theorems

Exact prime power components of any perfect number: the forcing step and valuation conservation.

Proof idea. By multiplicativity, σ(pe) divides σ(n) = 2n when pe is the full p component of n. So every odd prime dividing σ(pe) divides n (force_prime), and comparing the q exponents of both sides of σ(n) = 2n gives the conservation identity valuation_balance. The examples: σ(3²) = 13 forces 13, σ(13²) = 3·61 forces 61, and the three squares 7², 13², 19² each put a factor 3 into σ(n), which is too many when 3 has exponent exactly 2.

Public theorems

OPNStarter.sigma_eq_two_mul

theorem sigma_eq_two_mul {n : ℕ} (hn : n.Perfect) : σ 1 n = 2 * n

OPNStarter.component_sigma_dvd

theorem component_sigma_dvd {n p e : ℕ} (hn : n.Perfect) (hp : p.Prime)
  (he : n.factorization p = e) : σ 1 (p ^ e) ∣ 2 * n

The divisor sum of an entire prime-power component divides the full divisor sum.

OPNStarter.force_prime

theorem force_prime {n p e q : ℕ} (hn : n.Perfect) (hp : p.Prime)
  (he : n.factorization p = e) (hq : q.Prime) (hodd : q ≠ 2)
  (hdiv : q ∣ σ 1 (p ^ e)) : q ∣ n

Any odd prime dividing the divisor sum of an exact component must divide the number.

OPNStarter.valuation_balance

theorem valuation_balance {n : ℕ} (hn : n.Perfect) (q : ℕ) :
  Nat.factorization 2 q + n.factorization q =
    ∑ p ∈ n.primeFactors, (σ 1 (p ^ n.factorization p)).factorization q

A prime can occur several times among different component sums. This equality counts all incidences, including repeated factors, with the extra factor of two on the left.

OPNStarter.thirteen_dvd_of_three_sq

theorem thirteen_dvd_of_three_sq {n : ℕ} (hn : n.Perfect) (he : n.factorization 3 = 2) :
  13 ∣ n

A certified first link of a factor chain.

OPNStarter.sixty_one_dvd_of_thirteen_sq

theorem sixty_one_dvd_of_thirteen_sq {n : ℕ} (hn : n.Perfect) (he : n.factorization 13 = 2) :
  61 ∣ n

The second link requires its own exact-exponent hypothesis.

OPNStarter.exclude_four_exact_squares

theorem exclude_four_exact_squares {n : ℕ} (hn : n.Perfect)
  (h3 : n.factorization 3 = 2) (h7 : n.factorization 7 = 2)
  (h13 : n.factorization 13 = 2) (h19 : n.factorization 19 = 2) : False

Three distinct exact squares each contribute a factor 3. Together they contradict an exponent of exactly two at 3, regardless of which other primes divide the number.

OddPerfect.Seed.Cut

OddPerfect/Seed/Cut.lean · 68 lines · 2 public theorems

For a perfect number split into two coprime factors a and b, some prime of a divides σ(b).

Proof idea. From σ(a)σ(b) = 2ab: if no prime of a divided σ(b), then a would divide σ(a), so σ(a) = ka with k ≥ 2 because σ(a) > a. Then σ(a)σ(b) ≥ 2aσ(b) > 2ab, a contradiction. Splitting σ(b) over the components of b gives one component of b whose divisor sum is divisible by a prime of a.

Public theorems

OPNCut.exists_crossing_prime

theorem exists_crossing_prime {a b : ℕ} (ha : 1 < a) (hb : 1 < b)
  (hc : a.Coprime b) (hperf : (a * b).Perfect) :
  ∃ r : ℕ, r.Prime ∧ r ∣ a ∧ r ∣ σ 1 b

One prime dividing the first factor also divides the divisor sum of the second. Swapping the factors gives the other direction of the cut.

OPNCut.exists_crossing_component

theorem exists_crossing_component {a b : ℕ} (ha : 1 < a) (hb : 1 < b)
  (hc : a.Coprime b) (hperf : (a * b).Perfect) :
  ∃ r ∈ a.primeFactors, ∃ p ∈ b.primeFactors,
    r ∣ σ 1 (p ^ b.factorization p)

A particular prime-power component on the second side supplies a crossing edge. Here the source exponent is its full exponent in the second factor.

OddPerfect.Seed.Example

OddPerfect/Seed/Example.lean · 90 lines · 3 public theorems · imports Seed.Starter

No perfect number has the exponents of both 3 and 5 congruent to 2 modulo 3; also the divisibility of geometric sums used everywhere.

Proof idea. A geometric sum of length d divides one of length any multiple of d, so σ(pa) divides σ(pe) when a + 1 divides e + 1. With exponents ≡ 2 (mod 3), σ(3²) = 13 and σ(5²) = 31 divide the component sums, so 13 and 31 divide n. If 13 has exponent 1, σ(13) = 14 forces 7 and 3²·5²·13·7 is an abundant divisor; otherwise 3²·5²·13²·31 is abundant.

Public theorems

OPNExample.geom_sum_dvd_geom_sum

theorem geom_sum_dvd_geom_sum {d m : ℕ} (p : ℕ) (hd : d ∣ m) :
  (∑ i ∈ Finset.range d, p ^ i) ∣ ∑ i ∈ Finset.range m, p ^ i

A geometric sum of length d divides every sum whose length is a multiple of d.

OPNExample.sigma_prime_pow_dvd

theorem sigma_prime_pow_dvd {p a e : ℕ} (hp : p.Prime) (h : a + 1 ∣ e + 1) :
  σ 1 (p ^ a) ∣ σ 1 (p ^ e)

If a+1 divides the true component length e+1, the divisor sum of p^a divides that of p^e.

OPNExample.exclude_three_and_five_exponents

theorem exclude_three_and_five_exponents {n : ℕ} (hn : n.Perfect)
  (h3 : n.factorization 3 % 3 = 2) (h5 : n.factorization 5 % 3 = 2) : False

No perfect number has the exponents of both 3 and 5 congruent to 2 modulo 3.

OddPerfect.Abundancy

OddPerfect/Abundancy.lean · 236 lines · 15 public theorems · imports Basic

The abundancy σ(n)/n as an exact rational: multiplicativity, monotonicity, the bound p/(p − 1), and at least three prime factors.

Proof idea. Abundancy is a product over prime power components, each of which is a geometric sum in 1/p and lies strictly below p/(p − 1). A divisor with abundancy above 2 excludes perfection. For three prime factors: odd primes give p/(p − 1) ≤ 3/2 for p = 3 and ≤ 5/4 for every other prime, so with at most two prime factors the product is at most 15/8 < 2.

Public theorems

abundancy_eq_sum_inv

theorem abundancy_eq_sum_inv {n : ℕ} (hn : n ≠ 0) :
  abundancy n = ∑ e ∈ n.divisors, (e : ℚ)⁻¹

For n ≠ 0, the abundancy is the sum of the reciprocals of the divisors.

abundancy_mul_of_coprime

theorem abundancy_mul_of_coprime {a b : ℕ} (h : a.Coprime b) :
  abundancy (a * b) = abundancy a * abundancy b

Abundancy is multiplicative on coprime arguments.

abundancy_prime_pow

theorem abundancy_prime_pow {p : ℕ} (hp : p.Prime) (a : ℕ) :
  abundancy (p ^ a) = ∑ i ∈ Finset.range (a + 1), ((p : ℚ)⁻¹) ^ i

Abundancy of a prime power as a geometric sum in 1/p.

abundancy_prime_pow_lt

theorem abundancy_prime_pow_lt {p : ℕ} (hp : p.Prime) (a : ℕ) :
  abundancy (p ^ a) < (p : ℚ) / (p - 1)

Abundancy of a prime power is strictly below p/(p-1).

abundancy_prime_pow_mono

theorem abundancy_prime_pow_mono {p : ℕ} (hp : p.Prime) {a b : ℕ} (h : a ≤ b) :
  abundancy (p ^ a) ≤ abundancy (p ^ b)

Abundancy of p ^ a is monotone in a.

one_add_inv_le_abundancy_prime_pow

theorem one_add_inv_le_abundancy_prime_pow {p : ℕ} (hp : p.Prime) {a : ℕ} (ha : 0 < a) :
  1 + (p : ℚ)⁻¹ ≤ abundancy (p ^ a)

A positive power of p has abundancy at least 1 + 1/p.

abundancy_le_of_dvd

theorem abundancy_le_of_dvd {d n : ℕ} (hn : n ≠ 0) (hd : d ∣ n) :
  abundancy d ≤ abundancy n

Abundancy is monotone along divisibility.

abundancy_lt_of_dvd_of_ne

theorem abundancy_lt_of_dvd_of_ne {d n : ℕ} (hn : n ≠ 0) (hd : d ∣ n) (hne : d ≠ n) :
  abundancy d < abundancy n

Abundancy is strictly monotone along proper divisibility.

perfect_iff_abundancy_eq_two

theorem perfect_iff_abundancy_eq_two {n : ℕ} (hn : 0 < n) :
  n.Perfect ↔ abundancy n = 2

A positive integer is perfect exactly when its abundancy is two.

abundancy_eq_prod_primeFactors

theorem abundancy_eq_prod_primeFactors {n : ℕ} (hn : n ≠ 0) :
  abundancy n = ∏ p ∈ n.primeFactors, abundancy (p ^ n.factorization p)

Abundancy is the product of the abundancies of the prime power components.

abundancy_lt_prod

theorem abundancy_lt_prod {n : ℕ} (hn : 1 < n) :
  abundancy n < ∏ p ∈ n.primeFactors, ((p : ℚ) / (p - 1))

For n > 1, abundancy is strictly below ∏ p/(p-1) over its prime factors.

not_perfect_of_dvd_of_two_lt_abundancy

theorem not_perfect_of_dvd_of_two_lt_abundancy {d n : ℕ} (hd : d ∣ n)
  (h : 2 < abundancy d) : ¬ n.Perfect

A divisor with abundancy above two excludes perfection.

not_perfect_of_dvd_of_two_le_abundancy

theorem not_perfect_of_dvd_of_two_le_abundancy {d n : ℕ} (hd : d ∣ n) (hne : d ≠ n)
  (h : 2 ≤ abundancy d) : ¬ n.Perfect

A proper divisor with abundancy at least two excludes perfection.

not_perfect_of_prod_le_two

theorem not_perfect_of_prod_le_two {n : ℕ} (hn : 1 < n)
  (h : ∏ p ∈ n.primeFactors, ((p : ℚ) / (p - 1)) ≤ 2) : ¬ n.Perfect

If the full prime support cannot reach abundancy two, the number is not perfect.

OddPerfect.three_le_card_primeFactors

theorem three_le_card_primeFactors {N : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N) : 3 ≤ N.primeFactors.card

An odd perfect number has at least three distinct prime factors.

OddPerfect.Cyclotomic

OddPerfect/Cyclotomic.lean · 180 lines · 7 public theorems · imports Basic

σ(pa) as a product of cyclotomic values, its closed form, and the arithmetic of its prime divisors.

Proof idea. σ(pa)·(p − 1) = pa+1 − 1 and the cyclotomic factorization over the divisors of a + 1 other than 1. A prime q dividing σ(pa) differs from p, and either p ≡ 1 (mod q) with q dividing a + 1, or the order of p modulo q exceeds 1 and divides both a + 1 and q − 1. For an odd prime q dividing p − 1, lifting the exponent gives vq(σ(pa)) = vq(a + 1).

Public theorems

OddPerfect.sigma_prime_pow_eq_prod_cyclotomic

theorem sigma_prime_pow_eq_prod_cyclotomic {p : ℕ} (hp : p.Prime) (a : ℕ) :
  ((σ 1 (p ^ a) : ℕ) : ℤ) =
    ∏ d ∈ (a + 1).divisors.erase 1, (Polynomial.cyclotomic d ℤ).eval (p : ℤ)

The divisor sum of a prime power factors as a product of cyclotomic values.

OddPerfect.sigma_prime_pow_mul_pred

theorem sigma_prime_pow_mul_pred {p : ℕ} (hp : p.Prime) (a : ℕ) :
  σ 1 (p ^ a) * (p - 1) = p ^ (a + 1) - 1

Closed form of the divisor sum of a prime power.

OddPerfect.prime_dvd_sigma_prime_pow

theorem prime_dvd_sigma_prime_pow {p q a : ℕ} (hp : p.Prime) (hq : q.Prime)
  (hdiv : q ∣ σ 1 (p ^ a)) :
  q ≠ p ∧
  ((p % q = 1 ∧ q ∣ a + 1) ∨
   (1 < orderOf (p : ZMod q) ∧ orderOf (p : ZMod q) ∣ a + 1 ∧
     orderOf (p : ZMod q) ∣ q - 1))

A prime divisor q of σ 1 (p ^ a) differs from p, and either p ≡ 1 (mod q) with q ∣ a + 1, or the order of p modulo q exceeds 1 and divides both a + 1 and q - 1.

OddPerfect.prime_dvd_sigma_prime_pow_of_prime_length

theorem prime_dvd_sigma_prime_pow_of_prime_length {p q l : ℕ} (hp : p.Prime) (hq : q.Prime)
  (hl : l.Prime) (hdiv : q ∣ σ 1 (p ^ (l - 1))) : q = l ∨ q % l = 1

Every prime divisor of σ 1 (p ^ (l - 1)), for a prime length l, is l itself or congruent to 1 modulo l.

OddPerfect.dvd_sigma_prime_pow_of_orderOf_dvd

theorem dvd_sigma_prime_pow_of_orderOf_dvd {p q a : ℕ} (hp : p.Prime) (hq : q.Prime)
  (hpq : p ≠ q) (h1 : 1 < orderOf (p : ZMod q)) (hd : orderOf (p : ZMod q) ∣ a + 1) :
  q ∣ σ 1 (p ^ a)

If the order of p modulo a prime q exceeds 1 and divides a + 1, then q divides σ 1 (p ^ a).

OddPerfect.padicValNat_sigma_prime_pow_of_dvd_pred

theorem padicValNat_sigma_prime_pow_of_dvd_pred {p q a : ℕ} (hp : p.Prime) (hq : q.Prime)
  (hq2 : q ≠ 2) (h : q ∣ p - 1) :
  padicValNat q (σ 1 (p ^ a)) = padicValNat q (a + 1)

Lifting the exponent: for an odd prime q dividing p - 1, the q-adic valuation of σ 1 (p ^ a) equals that of a + 1.

OddPerfect.orderOf_eq_of_dvd_cyclotomic_eval

theorem orderOf_eq_of_dvd_cyclotomic_eval {p q d : ℕ} (hq : q.Prime)
  (hdiv : (q : ℤ) ∣ (Polynomial.cyclotomic d ℤ).eval (p : ℤ)) (hqd : ¬ q ∣ d) :
  orderOf (p : ZMod q) = d ∧ d ∣ q - 1

If a prime q not dividing d divides the dth cyclotomic value at p, then the order of p modulo q is exactly d, and hence d ∣ q - 1.

OddPerfect.Valuation

OddPerfect/Valuation.lean · 293 lines · 15 public theorems · imports Cyclotomic, Network

Exact q-adic valuations of σ(pa) for every prime q and every exponent, and the 2-adic and 3-adic ledgers they give.

Proof idea. Through the order d of p modulo q: if d does not divide a + 1 the valuation is 0; otherwise it is vq(pd − 1) + vq((a + 1)/d). Closed forms at q = 2 (zero for even a, v₂(p + 1) + v₂(a + 1) − 1 for odd a) and at q = 3. Applied to the network, the 2-adic ledger shows the special component alone carries the single factor 2, with v₂(s + 1) = v₂(k + 1) = 1.

Public theorems

OddPerfect.padicValNat_sigma_prime_pow_self

theorem padicValNat_sigma_prime_pow_self {p : ℕ} (hp : p.Prime) (a : ℕ) :
  padicValNat p (σ 1 (p ^ a)) = 0

q = p: the prime p never divides σ 1 (p ^ a).

OddPerfect.padicValNat_sigma_prime_pow_of_orderOf_dvd

theorem padicValNat_sigma_prime_pow_of_orderOf_dvd {p q a : ℕ} (hp : p.Prime) (hq : q.Prime)
  (hq2 : q ≠ 2) (hpq : p ≠ q) (h1 : 1 < orderOf (p : ZMod q))
  (hd : orderOf (p : ZMod q) ∣ a + 1) :
  padicValNat q (σ 1 (p ^ a)) =
    padicValNat q (p ^ orderOf (p : ZMod q) - 1) +
      padicValNat q ((a + 1) / orderOf (p : ZMod q))

Odd q, general order: if the order d of p modulo q exceeds 1 and divides a + 1, then v_q(σ(p ^ a)) = v_q(p ^ d - 1) + v_q((a + 1) / d).

OddPerfect.padicValNat_sigma_prime_pow_of_not_orderOf_dvd

theorem padicValNat_sigma_prime_pow_of_not_orderOf_dvd {p q a : ℕ} (hp : p.Prime)
  (hq : q.Prime) (hd : ¬ orderOf (p : ZMod q) ∣ a + 1) :
  padicValNat q (σ 1 (p ^ a)) = 0

If the order of p modulo a prime q does not divide a + 1, then q does not divide σ 1 (p ^ a).

OddPerfect.dvd_sigma_prime_pow_iff

theorem dvd_sigma_prime_pow_iff {p q a : ℕ} (hp : p.Prime) (hq : q.Prime) (hpq : p ≠ q) :
  q ∣ σ 1 (p ^ a) ↔
    (if orderOf (p : ZMod q) = 1 then q ∣ a + 1 else orderOf (p : ZMod q) ∣ a + 1)

Unified divisibility criterion: with d the order of p modulo a prime q ≠ p, q ∣ σ 1 (p ^ a) iff q ∣ a + 1 when d = 1, and iff d ∣ a + 1 otherwise.

OddPerfect.padicValNat_two_sigma_prime_pow

theorem padicValNat_two_sigma_prime_pow {p : ℕ} (hp : p.Prime) (hp2 : p ≠ 2) (a : ℕ) :
  padicValNat 2 (σ 1 (p ^ a)) =
    if Even a then 0 else padicValNat 2 (p + 1) + padicValNat 2 (a + 1) - 1

q = 2: for an odd prime p, σ 1 (p ^ a) is odd for even a, and for odd a its 2-adic valuation is v_2(p + 1) + v_2(a + 1) - 1.

OddPerfect.padicValNat_three_sigma_prime_pow_of_mod_one

theorem padicValNat_three_sigma_prime_pow_of_mod_one {p : ℕ} (hp : p.Prime) (h : p % 3 = 1)
  (a : ℕ) : padicValNat 3 (σ 1 (p ^ a)) = padicValNat 3 (a + 1)

q = 3, p ≡ 1 (mod 3): v_3(σ(p ^ a)) = v_3(a + 1).

OddPerfect.padicValNat_three_sigma_prime_pow_of_mod_two

theorem padicValNat_three_sigma_prime_pow_of_mod_two {p : ℕ} (hp : p.Prime) (h : p % 3 = 2)
  (a : ℕ) : padicValNat 3 (σ 1 (p ^ a)) =
    if Even a then 0 else padicValNat 3 (p + 1) + padicValNat 3 (a + 1)

q = 3, p ≡ 2 (mod 3): v_3(σ(p ^ a)) is 0 for even a and v_3(p + 1) + v_3(a + 1) for odd a.

OddPerfect.padicValNat_three_sigma_three_pow

theorem padicValNat_three_sigma_three_pow (a : ℕ) : padicValNat 3 (σ 1 (3 ^ a)) = 0

q = 3, p = 3: 3 never divides σ 1 (3 ^ a).

OddPerfect.padicValNat_three_sigma_prime_pow

theorem padicValNat_three_sigma_prime_pow {p : ℕ} (hp : p.Prime) (a : ℕ) :
  padicValNat 3 (σ 1 (p ^ a)) = threeWeight p a

v_3(σ(p ^ a)) = threeWeight p a for every prime p and every exponent a.

OddPerfect.sigmaWeight_eq_padicValNat

theorem sigmaWeight_eq_padicValNat (N p : ℕ) {q : ℕ} (hq : q.Prime) :
  sigmaWeight N p q = padicValNat q (σ 1 (p ^ N.factorization p))

The network weight is the q-adic valuation of the component divisor sum.

OddPerfect.padicValNat_two_special

theorem padicValNat_two_special {N s : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N) (hs : s.Prime)
  (hodd : Odd (N.factorization s)) :
  padicValNat 2 (s + 1) = 1 ∧ padicValNat 2 (N.factorization s + 1) = 1

The special prime s of an odd perfect number, with odd exponent k, satisfies v_2(s + 1) = 1 and v_2(k + 1) = 1: the special component alone supplies the single unit of the 2-adic ledger.

OddPerfect.mod_four_special

theorem mod_four_special {N s : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N) (hs : s.Prime)
  (hodd : Odd (N.factorization s)) : s % 4 = 1 ∧ N.factorization s % 4 = 1

Consistency with Euler: the special prime and its exponent are both ≡ 1 (mod 4), derived from the 2-adic ledger.

OddPerfect.factorization_three_eq_sum_threeWeight

theorem factorization_three_eq_sum_threeWeight {N : ℕ} (hN : N.Perfect) :
  N.factorization 3 = ∑ p ∈ N.primeFactors, threeWeight p (N.factorization p)

The 3-adic ledger of a perfect number in closed form.

OddPerfect.factorization_eq_sum_erase

theorem factorization_eq_sum_erase {N q : ℕ} (hN : N.Perfect) (hq : q.Prime) (hq2 : q ≠ 2) :
  N.factorization q =
    ∑ p ∈ N.primeFactors.erase q, padicValNat q (σ 1 (p ^ N.factorization p))

The q-adic ledger of a perfect number at an odd prime q, with the vanishing self term removed.

OddPerfect.padicValNat_pow_orderOf_sub_one_le

theorem padicValNat_pow_orderOf_sub_one_le {N p q : ℕ} (hN : N.Perfect) (hq : q.Prime)
  (hq2 : q ≠ 2) (hp : p ∈ N.primeFactors) (hpq : p ≠ q) (h1 : 1 < orderOf (p : ZMod q))
  (hd : orderOf (p : ZMod q) ∣ N.factorization p + 1) :
  padicValNat q (p ^ orderOf (p : ZMod q) - 1) ≤ N.factorization q

Lower bound: if a prime factor p ≠ q has order d > 1 modulo an odd prime q and d ∣ v_p(N) + 1, then v_q(p ^ d - 1) ≤ v_q(N).

OddPerfect.Phi3

OddPerfect/Phi3.lean · 228 lines · 23 public theorems · imports Network, Seed.ThreeFree, Seed.Collision

Arithmetic of σ(p²) = p² + p + 1: parity, coprimality, the exact power of 3, residues of other prime divisors, and roots modulo a prime.

Proof idea. p² + p + 1 is odd, coprime to p and p + 1, divisible by 3 exactly when p ≡ 1 (mod 3) and never by 9. Any other prime divisor has p of order 3, hence is ≡ 1 (mod 6). It lies strictly between p² and (p + 1)², so it is not a square. Modulo a prime there are at most two roots, and two roots below the prime sum to the prime minus 1. Consequence: each exact square prime ≡ 1 (mod 3) sends exactly one factor 3, so their number is at most v₃(N).

OddPerfect.Network

OddPerfect/Network.lean · 224 lines · 9 public theorems · imports Basic, Seed.Cut

The divisor sum network of a perfect number: weights, conservation, no self loops, and strong connectivity.

Proof idea. Conservation at an odd prime q is valuation_balance with vq(2) = 0, and at 2 the incoming weights sum to 1 because N is odd. A prime never divides σ(pe), so there are no self loops. For connectivity, any nonempty proper set S of prime factors splits N into the coprime parts over S and over its complement, and the cut lemma gives an edge from the complement into S; so the set of primes that reach a given prime cannot be proper.

OddPerfect.Reduction

OddPerfect/Reduction.lean · 263 lines · 10 public theorems · imports Euler, Abundancy, Network

Balanced candidates are exactly the factorizations of odd perfect numbers, so the conjecture is equivalent to their nonexistence.

Proof idea. One direction: an odd perfect number's own factorization is balanced by the conservation laws of Network. The other: for a balanced candidate, compare the q exponent of σ(value) with that of 2·value for every q. Multiplicativity turns the left side into the sum of the weights into q, and balance makes this equal to the exponent of q (or 1 at q = 2, or 0 at non primes). Equal factorizations give σ(value) = 2·value. This is a reformulation, not progress toward a proof.

OddPerfect.NetworkCut

OddPerfect/NetworkCut.lean · 198 lines · 3 public theorems · imports Network

The exact balance across a cut of the prime support. For a set A of prime factors of N with M the product of their full prime powers, σ(M)·In = 2^δ·Out·M, where Out and In collect the divisor sum weights leaving and entering A, and δ is 0 or 1. For a nonempty proper A: In < Out < 2·In when δ = 0, and Out < In < 2·Out when δ = 1.

Proof idea. σ is multiplicative, every prime factor of σ(p^e) is 2 or a prime factor of N, and the weights into each prime of A sum to its exponent, so the weights inside A cancel against M. The inequalities are 1 < σ(M)/M < 2 for the two coprime parts of N. The module restates conservation in a form that certificates can use; it is not a new obstruction.

  σ 1 (cutPart N A) * cutIn N A = 2 ^ cutTwo N A * cutOut N A * cutPart N A

theorem cut_balance {N : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N) {A : Finset ℕ} (hA : A ⊆ N.primeFactors)
  (hne : A.Nonempty) (hpr : A ≠ N.primeFactors) :
  (cutTwo N A = 0 → cutIn N A < cutOut N A ∧ cutOut N A < 2 * cutIn N A) ∧
  (cutTwo N A = 1 → cutOut N A < cutIn N A ∧ cutIn N A < 2 * cutOut N A)

Two sided balance across a nonempty proper cut. With no weight from A into 2, the weight leaving A exceeds the weight entering it by a factor strictly between 1 and 2; with the single unit of weight into 2 inside A, the roles swap.

Euler's form and the special prime

Consequences of the shape N = qkm².

OddPerfect.Euler

OddPerfect/Euler.lean · 199 lines · 7 public theorems · imports Basic

Euler's form N = qkm² with q ≡ k ≡ 1 (mod 4), N ≡ 1 (mod 4), N not a square, and Touchard's congruence.

Proof idea. The 2-adic ledger: the weights into 2 sum to 1, and σ(pe) is even exactly when e is odd, so exactly one prime q has odd exponent k and v₂(σ(qk)) = 1. If q ≡ 3 (mod 4), pairing terms shows 4 divides σ(qk); with q ≡ 1 (mod 4), σ(qk) ≡ k + 1 (mod 4) forces k ≡ 1 (mod 4). Touchard: if 3 divides N then 9 does (3 ≡ 3 mod 4 is not special), giving N ≡ 9 (mod 36); if N ≡ 2 (mod 3) then q ≡ 2 (mod 3), and 3 divides q + 1, which divides σ(qk), so 3 would divide N.

  ∃ q : ℕ, q.Prime ∧ q ∣ N ∧ q % 4 = 1 ∧ N.factorization q % 4 = 1 ∧
    ∀ p : ℕ, p.Prime → p ≠ q → Even (N.factorization p)

Euler: an odd perfect number has a unique prime q of odd exponent, and q ≡ 1 (mod 4) and its exponent is ≡ 1 (mod 4).

  ∃ q k m : ℕ, q.Prime ∧ N = q ^ k * m ^ 2 ∧ ¬ q ∣ m ∧ q % 4 = 1 ∧ k % 4 = 1

Euler form: N = q ^ k * m ^ 2 with q prime, q ∤ m, and q ≡ k ≡ 1 (mod 4).

Proof idea. The 2-adic ledger. N is odd, so σ(N) = 2N has exactly one factor 2, shared among the components σ(pe). For odd p, σ(pe) has e + 1 odd terms, so it is even exactly when e is odd: one prime q has odd exponent k, and v₂(σ(qk)) = 1. If q ≡ 3 (mod 4), pairing consecutive terms puts q + 1, a multiple of 4, into σ(qk). So q ≡ 1 (mod 4), then σ(qk) ≡ k + 1 (mod 4) forces k ≡ 1 (mod 4).

OddPerfect.SpecialPrime

OddPerfect/SpecialPrime.lean · 289 lines · 17 public theorems · imports Euler, Abundancy, Seed.Example

Facts about the special prime: q + 1 divides σ(qk), (q + 1)/2 divides N, abundancy splits, refined Touchard congruence, and small abundant divisors such as 3²·5·7².

Proof idea. Since k is odd, q + 1 divides σ(qk), which divides 2N. The special component has abundancy below q/(q − 1) ≤ 5/4, so the square part m² has abundancy above 2/(5/4) = 8/5. The refinement of Touchard: if v₃(N) = 2 then σ(3²) = 13 divides N, giving N ≡ 117 (mod 468); otherwise 3⁴ divides N, giving N ≡ 81 (mod 324). For 105: the primes 3 and 7 are ≡ 3 (mod 4), hence squared, and 3²·5·7² has σ = 4446 > 4410 = 2·2205.

Proof idea. From N ≡ 1 (mod 4) and Touchard's N ≡ 1 (mod 12) or N ≡ 9 (mod 36). If 3 divides N, its exponent is even. If it is exactly 2, then σ(3²) = 13 divides N, and N is a multiple of 9·13 = 117 that is ≡ 1 (mod 4), so N ≡ 117 (mod 468). Otherwise 3⁴ divides N and N ≡ 81 (mod 324).

OddPerfect.ClassicalSmallTwo

OddPerfect/ClassicalSmallTwo.lean · 138 lines · 4 public theorems · imports SpecialPrime, ExcessSupport, EscapeRowUnique

For a prime q ≡ 1 (mod 4) and an exponent a ≡ 1 (mod 4) with a > 1, σ(qa)/2 is a product of two coprime odd factors above 1, so it is not a prime power, and two distinct primes of an odd perfect number divide the special row.

Proof idea. With a + 1 = 2k: σ(qa) = (1 + q + ⋯ + qk−1)(qk + 1), and a short Bezout identity shows that the first factor and (qk + 1)/2 are coprime. Compare Lemma 2 of Levit (Bull. Amer. Math. Soc. 53, 1947). The module also combines two landed counts: the number of primes of exponent 2 is at most 1 plus the total exponent of the ordinary primes that are 1 modulo 3. No novelty is claimed.

Public theorems

OddPerfect.sigma_special_split

theorem sigma_special_split {q a k : ℕ} (hq : q.Prime) (hq4 : q % 4 = 1) (ha4 : a % 4 = 1)
  (ha : 1 < a) (hk : a + 1 = 2 * k) :
  σ 1 (q ^ a) = 2 * (∑ i ∈ range k, q ^ i) * ((q ^ k + 1) / 2) ∧
    Odd (∑ i ∈ range k, q ^ i) ∧ Odd ((q ^ k + 1) / 2) ∧
    1 < ∑ i ∈ range k, q ^ i ∧ 1 < (q ^ k + 1) / 2 ∧
    Nat.Coprime (∑ i ∈ range k, q ^ i) ((q ^ k + 1) / 2)

The special row splits into two odd coprime factors greater than 1: for a prime q ≡ 1 (mod 4) and a ≡ 1 (mod 4), 1 < a, a + 1 = 2 * k, we have σ(q ^ a) = 2 * d₁ * d₂ with d₁ = ∑_{i < k} q ^ i and d₂ = (q ^ k + 1) / 2. Compare Levit, Bull. Amer. Math. Soc.

OddPerfect.EulerPart

OddPerfect/EulerPart.lean · 469 lines · 22 public theorems · imports SpecialPrime, ClosedLoop, Valuation

Identities and congruences for Euler's form: the index σ(m²)/qk, the deficiency 2m² − σ(m²), congruences modulo 8, and small bounds. The congruence for σ(m²) modulo 4 is equivalent to congruence (2) of Ewell, J. Number Theory 12 (1980), 339 to 342 (p. 340).

Proof idea. Multiplicativity turns σ(N) = 2N into σ(qk)σ(m²) = 2qkm². Since qk is coprime to σ(qk), it divides σ(m²), which defines the index i with σ(m²) = qki and σ(qk)i = 2m². The index is odd because σ(m²) is odd: every exponent in m² is even, so each component sum has an odd number of odd terms. The deficiency identity is algebra: 2m² − σ(m²) = i(σ(qk) − qk) = iσ(qk−1). The congruence N ≡ q (mod 8) uses that m² ≡ 1 and, k being odd, qk ≡ q modulo 8.

OddPerfect.ClosedLoop

OddPerfect/ClosedLoop.lean · 322 lines · 5 public theorems · imports Euler, Network, Cyclotomic

The divisor sums of the ordinary components cannot all be powers of the special prime; consequences σ(m²) ≠ qk and 3qk < 2m².

Proof idea. Suppose σ(rer) = qcr for every ordinary r. Then the ordinary primes receive weight only from q, so rer divides σ(qk), which divides qk+1 − 1. Since qcr = 1 + r·σ(rer−1) is 1 modulo r exactly once, lifting the exponent gives rer−1 dividing k + 1, and with k odd, 2∏ rer−1 divides k + 1. Conservation at q gives k = Σ cr, while a size comparison gives cr < rer−1. With tr = rer−1 this gives k + 1 ≤ 1 + Σ (tr − 1) ≤ ∏ tr ≤ (k + 1)/2, a contradiction.

OddPerfect.Reciprocity

OddPerfect/Reciprocity.lean · 277 lines · 15 public theorems · imports Network, Valuation, Cyclotomic, SpecialPrime contains novelty unverified

Quadratic residue constraints on the network, after Wallace (arXiv 1610.00544): one sign identity per vertex, a reverse edge constraint, and two mutually residual prime factors.

Proof idea. σ(pa) ≡ 1 (mod p), so its Legendre symbol modulo p is 1; expanding over its factorization gives ∏ (r/p)w(p,r) = 1 at an ordinary vertex and (2/q) at the special vertex. In the other direction, if e is even and r divides σ(pe), then pe+1 ≡ 1 (mod r) with e + 1 odd, so p ≡ (pe/2+1)² is a square modulo r. Applied to an edge into the special prime q ≡ 1 (mod 4), reciprocity makes q a square modulo p as well.

Every odd perfect number has two distinct prime factors p and r with p a nonzero square modulo r and r a nonzero square modulo p. One can take r to be the special prime and p any prime factor whose component divisor sum is divisible by r.

Proof idea. The special prime q has positive exponent, so by conservation some prime p ≠ q sends weight to q. Its exponent e is even, so pe+1 ≡ 1 (mod q) with e + 1 odd, which makes p a square modulo q. Since q ≡ 1 (mod 4), quadratic reciprocity makes q a square modulo p.

OddPerfect.SpecialRowResidue

OddPerfect/SpecialRowResidue.lean · 111 lines · 4 public theorems · imports Reciprocity, RestrainedFiveModTwelve

If a ≡ 1 (mod 4) and a prime p ≡ 1 (mod 4) divides 1 + q + ⋯ + qa, then q is a square modulo p. For an odd perfect number with special prime q: every prime p ≡ 1 (mod 4) dividing σ(qa) has q a square modulo p and p a square modulo q. In the restrained family this covers every prime factor p ≡ 5 (mod 12). Necessary conditions only. Novelty not verified.

Proof idea. a + 1 = 2L with L odd, so qL ≡ 1 or −1 modulo p, and q·qL is a square. If qL ≡ −1, use that −1 is a square modulo p. Both congruences are needed: for q = 37 and a = 3 the prime 5 divides σ(qa) and 37 is not a square modulo 5; 7 divides σ(13) and 13 is not a square modulo 7. The second direction is quadratic reciprocity, since q ≡ 1 (mod 4).

OddPerfect.RepunitOrder

OddPerfect/RepunitOrder.lean · 215 lines · 3 public theorems

If 1 + w + … + w^(m−1) = k·p^s with p an odd prime, s ≥ 1 and k < p, then w has order exactly m modulo p.

Proof idea. Lemma 2.1 of Zhao and Chen (Front. Math. 2025). Consequences: p does not divide w − 1 and m divides p − 1. With w a prime and m = e + 1 the sum is σ(w^e), so the lemma describes components that are a small multiple of a prime power. Proof: split the sum along the order d of w; the second factor is a geometric sum in a base that is 1 modulo p, and lifting the exponent shows it cannot divide k·p^s unless it has length 1. Known mathematics.

OddPerfect.SpecialSuccSender

OddPerfect/SpecialSuccSender.lean · 61 lines · 2 public theorems · imports Reciprocity

A prime factor r of q + 1 with r ≡ 3 (mod 4) does not send to the special prime q.

Proof idea. If q ≡ 1 (mod 4) divides the divisor sum of an even power of r, then r is a square modulo q; by quadratic reciprocity q is a square modulo r; and q ≡ −1 (mod r), so −1 is a square modulo r and r ≡ 1 (mod 4). Every prime factor of (q + 1)/2 divides N, so this removes edges of the divisor sum network at the special prime. An elementary remark; whether it is stated in the literature has not been checked.

OddPerfect.SpecialExponentDivisor

OddPerfect/SpecialExponentDivisor.lean · 52 lines · 2 public theorems · imports Basic, SpecialPrime contains novelty unverified

If a + 2 is a prime that does not divide q − 1, where a is the exponent of the special prime q, then (a + 2)² divides N.

Proof idea. By Fermat's little theorem a + 2 divides q^(a+1) − 1 = (q − 1)·σ(q^a), hence σ(q^a), hence N. It is 3 modulo 4, so it is not q, and its exponent in N is even. A statement of this kind is in the literature; the source has not been checked here.

OddPerfect.ParityCount

OddPerfect/ParityCount.lean · 102 lines · 1 public theorem · imports LedgerPrimeThree

The number of prime factors p ≠ q with p ≡ 1 (mod 4) and exponent ≡ 2 (mod 4) is even exactly when q ≡ a (mod 8), where a is the exponent of the special prime q. Known: this is Theorem 2 of Ewell, J. Number Theory 12 (1980), 339 to 342 (p. 340).

Proof idea. For p ≠ q with even exponent e: σ(p^e) ≡ 3 (mod 4) exactly when p ≡ 1 (mod 4) and e ≡ 2 (mod 4), and ≡ 1 otherwise. So the product D of these divisor sums is 1 or 3 modulo 4 according to the parity of the count. Modulo 8, σ(q^a) is 2 when q ≡ a and 6 otherwise, so σ(q^a) = 2s with s ≡ 1 or 3 (mod 4). From s·D = N ≡ 1 (mod 4) the two residues agree.

    q % 8 = N.factorization q % 8

OddPerfect.ThreeFreeParity

OddPerfect/ThreeFreeParity.lean · 155 lines · 3 public theorems · imports Euler

If 3 ∤ N: no prime p ≡ 1 (mod 3) has exponent ≡ 2 (mod 3), every prime p ≡ 2 (mod 3) has an even exponent, and the number of primes p ≡ 1 (mod 3) with exponent ≡ 1 (mod 3) is odd. Known: these are the constraints of Theorem 3 of Ewell, J. Number Theory 12 (1980), 339 to 342 (p. 341), stated there in other variables.

Proof idea. Since 3 ∤ N, N ≡ 1 (mod 3) and σ(N) = 2N ≡ 2 (mod 3). For p ≡ 1 (mod 3), σ(p^e) ≡ e + 1 (mod 3). For p ≡ 2 (mod 3), σ(p^e) is 1 for even e and 0 for odd e. No factor σ(p^e) of σ(N) is divisible by 3, which gives the first two statements. The remaining factors are 2 exactly when p ≡ 1 and e ≡ 1 (mod 3), and 1 otherwise, so the product is a power of 2 that is 2 modulo 3: the count is odd.

OddPerfect.EulerIndexPrimePower

OddPerfect/EulerIndexPrimePower.lean · 213 lines · 4 public theorems · imports EulerPart, Cyclotomic

A normal form for odd perfect numbers N = q·m² with special exponent 1 whose Euler index σ(m²)/q is a prime power rb: then m² = rbM² with M odd, M > 1, prime to r and q, and σ(rb) = q = 2M² − 1, σ(M²) = rb, b even, b + 1 prime. The system is not shown to be impossible here. Results on prime power indices exist in the literature; this normal form is elementary.

Proof idea. The two identities σ(m²) = q·i and (q + 1)·i = 2m² hold for the index i. If i = rb then r divides m. Split off the full power of r from m². The value σ(re) is prime to r, exceeds 1 and divides q·rb, so it equals q. Then q ≡ 1 (mod r), so r does not divide q + 1, and comparing powers of r in the second identity gives b = e. A prime value σ(rb) forces b + 1 prime.

OddPerfect.SpecialBelow

OddPerfect/SpecialBelow.lean · 442 lines · 7 public theorems · imports LargePrimes, EulerPart, Cyclotomic, EulerIndexPrimePower

In Euler's form N = qkm², the special prime satisfies q < m whenever k ≠ 1, and for k = 1 unless N has one exceptional shape: a prime p dividing m with exact power pe in N such that σ(pe) = q and σ((q + 1)/2) = pe. In that shape m < q holds, so q < m for all odd perfect numbers is equivalent to the impossibility of the shape, which is not decided here. The inequality q < m is claimed in the literature (Brown, 2016 preprint); the module does not use that claim, and how the literature treats the shape was not checked. The shape is excluded in SpecialBelowAll, so q < m holds for every odd perfect number.

Proof idea. An extension of the size argument of Acquaah and Konyagin. Some prime p of m has q dividing σ(pe). Write σ(pe) = qu and x = gcd(q + 1, pe); perfection gives exact identities between q, u, x and the divisor sum of the rest of m². They force q² < m² except when x = u = 1 and the rest contributes nothing extra, which is the shape, and in one case with p = 3 that is impossible modulo 5.

OddPerfect.SpecialBelowParity

OddPerfect/SpecialBelowParity.lean · 162 lines · 4 public theorems · imports SpecialBelow, SquareRow

Let N = qkm2 be an odd perfect number with special prime q not dividing m. If m ≤ q, then N has an even number of distinct prime factors. So an odd number of distinct prime factors gives q < m.

Proof idea. The module SpecialBelow leaves one shape: N = q·pe·t2 with σ(pe) = q, q + 1 = 2t2 and σ(t2) = pe, with e even. Each component σ(r2c) for a prime r dividing t is a power pw, and the exponents w add up to e. An even w makes the component a square, which happens only for σ(34) = 112; then p = 11 and 3 divides t, so q ≡ 2 (mod 3), while q = σ(11e) ≡ 1 (mod 3). So every w is odd, t has an even number of prime factors, and N has two more. This does not prove q < m: the parity of the number of prime factors of an odd perfect number is not known.

OddPerfect.SpecialBelowRows

OddPerfect/SpecialBelowRows.lean · 288 lines · 5 public theorems · imports SpecialBelow, PureRows, SpecialBelowParity

In the one open shape of q < m, every prime of (q + 1)/2 has a divisor sum that is a power of p, and one of these powers has an odd exponent at least 3. So q < m follows from one explicit hypothesis on σ(r^g) = p^w.

Proof idea. The shape is N = q·p^e·W with W = (q + 1)/2 an odd square, σ(p^e) = q and σ(W) = p^e. For a prime r dividing W, σ(r^g) divides σ(W) = p^e, so σ(r^g) = p^w, and the exponents w add up to e. A row with w = 1 gives p ≡ 1 (mod r), so q = σ(p^e) ≡ e + 1 (mod r), and r divides q + 1, hence r divides e + 2. If every w were 1, W would have e distinct odd prime factors, all dividing e + 2, so 3^e ≤ e + 2, which is false for e ≥ 2. So some w is at least 2. Such a w is odd, hence at least 3, except for σ(3⁴) = 11², and that case contradicts q = σ(11^e) ≡ 1 (mod 3) with 3 dividing q + 1. The theorem special_lt_of_noHighPureRow takes the absence of such rows as its hypothesis and returns q < m for every odd perfect number.

OddPerfect.ShapeSeries

OddPerfect/ShapeSeries.lean · 192 lines · 2 public theorems

A solution of 2t² = 1 + σ(p^(2h)) in a prime p has p ≤ max(7, 2D), where D comes from a truncated power series certificate.

Proof idea. A certificate is a number D and coefficients c₀ = D, c₁, …, c_h, which are D times the first coefficients of the power series of √((1 − X/2)/(1 − X)). With A = Σ cᵢ pⁱ and U = D·t, the certificate identities give that p^(h + 1) divides (U − A)(U + A). If p > 2D, then p divides at most one factor, so p^(h + 1) divides one of them; but both lie strictly between 0 and p^(h + 1). Hence p ≤ max(7, 2D). The certificate conditions are finitely many integer identities.

  x ^ (h + 1) ∣ 2 * (∑ i ∈ range (h + 1), (c i : ℤ) * x ^ i) ^ 2 -
    (D : ℤ) ^ 2 * (1 + ∑ i ∈ range (h + 1), x ^ i)

The certificate congruence: if c_0 = D and 2 ∑_{i + j = k} c_i c_j = D ^ 2 for 1 ≤ k ≤ h, then x ^ (h + 1) divides 2 A ^ 2 - D ^ 2 (1 + ∑_{i ≤ h} x ^ i) for every integer x, where A = ∑_{i ≤ h} c_i x ^ i.

OddPerfect.ShapeSmall

OddPerfect/ShapeSmall.lean · 412 lines · 29 public theorems · imports ShapeSeries, SpecialBelow

In Euler’s form with m ≤ q, the prime p with σ(p^e) = q has e ≥ 16. The equation 2t² = 1 + σ(p^e) has no solution with e < 16 and e + 1 prime.

Proof idea. For each exponent below 16 with e + 1 prime, a certificate for ShapeSeries bounds p, and the finite range below the bound is checked in the kernel with residue masks and an exact square test. The certificates and masks were produced by a script and each is verified here, so the script is not trusted. The shape with e ≥ 16 is not excluded.

theorem sixteen_le_exponent_of_le_special {N q k m : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N) (hq : q.Prime)

  ∃ p : ℕ, p.Prime ∧ p ∣ m ∧ σ 1 (p ^ N.factorization p) = q ∧ 16 ≤ N.factorization p

In Euler's form N = q ^ k * m ^ 2 of an odd perfect number with q ∤ m, if m ≤ q (the open shape of the inequality q < m), then some prime p ∣ m has σ(p ^ v_p(N)) = q and exponent v_p(N) ≥ 16. Only the equation 2 t ^ 2 = 1 + σ(p ^ e) of the shape is used. The shape is not excluded: exponents e ≥ 16 remain open. Novelty was not verified.

OddPerfect.SpecialBelowOrder

OddPerfect/SpecialBelowOrder.lean · 341 lines · 8 public theorems · imports SpecialBelowRows, EqualExponentsBound

In the open shape of q < m, a row σ(r^g) = p^w has w odd, the order d of p modulo r odd and dividing w, r not dividing w, and r dividing e + 2 when p ≡ 1 (mod r); otherwise d ≥ 3, d does not divide e and w ≥ 3. Derived from a step of Dandapat, Hunsucker and Pomerance (1975).

Proof idea. Reducing σ(r^g) = p^w modulo r gives p^w ≡ 1, so d divides w. The weight w is odd by the earlier parity lemma, hence d is odd. If d = 1 then q = σ(p^e) ≡ e + 1 (mod r) and r divides q + 1, so r divides e + 2. If d divided e, then q ≡ 1 (mod r), against r dividing q + 1. Lifting the exponent, with r² not dividing σ(r^g) − 1, gives that r divides p^d − 1 exactly once and that r does not divide w.

OddPerfect.SpecialBelowRadical

OddPerfect/SpecialBelowRadical.lean · 362 lines · 6 public theorems · imports SpecialBelowOrder

In the open shape of q < m, with W = (q + 1)/2: the product of the primes of W is 1 modulo p, hence at least 2p + 1, and some row prime r ≥ 7 has p not 1 modulo r, order of p modulo r at least 3 and weight at least 3. Hence q < m under the hypothesis NoOrderPureRow, which asks less than NoHighPureRow; neither is proved. Superseded by SpecialBelowAll, which proves q < m with no hypothesis.

Proof idea. Every prime r of W has σ(r^g) = p^w with g the exponent of r in W, and (r − 1)σ(r^g) = r^(g + 1) − 1, so r^(g + 1) ≡ 1 (mod p). Multiplying over the primes of W gives W·rad(W) ≡ 1 (mod p). Also q = σ(p^e) ≡ 1 (mod p) and 2W = q + 1, so W ≡ 1 and rad(W) ≡ 1 (mod p). If every prime r of W had p ≡ 1 (mod r), then rad(W) would divide p − 1 and lie strictly between 1 and p, which is impossible. For a row prime with p not 1 modulo r, the order of p is odd, at least 3, and divides the even number r − 1.

OddPerfect.SquareCycleDigit

OddPerfect/SquareCycleDigit.lean · 470 lines · 3 public theorems

If σ(t²) = p^e and 2t² = 1 + σ(p^e) with t odd, every row σ(r^g) = p^w of t² has g + 1 prime, and an explicit integer J built from the rows of weight one is divisible by p. From a size hypothesis on such rows the configuration is impossible.

Proof idea. Each row gives r^(g+1) = 1 + (r − 1)p^w, so g + 1 is the order of r modulo p, a prime dividing p − 1. Raise 2t² = 1 + σ(p^e) to the power p − 1 and read both sides modulo p²: the right side is 1 + (p − 1)p up to p², and the left side is a product of terms (1 + (r − 1)p^w)^((p−1)·2g/(g+1)) times 2^(p−1)-type factors that cancel through the same identity. Only rows with w = 1 contribute a multiple of p that is not a multiple of p². Comparing the coefficients of p gives p ∣ J, where J = 2·Σ (∏ of the other lengths)·2g·(r − 1) − ∏ lengths.

Prime index lemma. If σ(r ^ g) = p ^ w with r, p prime, p odd, g ≥ 1 and w ≥ 1, then g + 1 is prime, g + 1 ∣ p - 1 and r ^ (g + 1) = 1 + (r - 1) p ^ w.

OddPerfect.square_cycle_digit

theorem square_cycle_digit {p e t : ℕ} (hp : p.Prime) (he : 1 ≤ e) (ht : Odd t)
  (hσ : σ 1 (t ^ 2) = p ^ e) (hc : 2 * t ^ 2 = 1 + σ 1 (p ^ e)) :
  ∃ I : Finset ℕ,
    (∀ r ∈ I, r.Prime ∧ r ≠ 2 ∧ (2 * t.factorization r + 1).Prime ∧
      ∑ i ∈ Finset.range (2 * t.factorization r + 1), r ^ i = p) ∧
    (p : ℤ) ∣ 2 * ∑ r ∈ I, (∏ s ∈ I.erase r, ((2 * t.factorization s + 1 : ℕ) : ℤ)) *
        ((2 * t.factorization r : ℕ) : ℤ) * ((r : ℤ) - 1) -
      ∏ r ∈ I, ((2 * t.factorization r + 1 : ℕ) : ℤ)

The digit congruence. If p is prime, e ≥ 1, t is odd, σ(t ^ 2) = p ^ e and 2 t ^ 2 = 1 + σ(p ^ e), let I be the set of primes r ∣ t with σ(r ^ (2 v_r(t))) = p and ℓ_r = 2 v_r(t) + 1. Then p divides 2 ∑_{r ∈ I} (∏_{s ∈ I, s ≠ r} ℓ_s) (ℓ_r - 1) (r - 1) - ∏_{r ∈ I} ℓ_r.

OddPerfect.square_cycle_false_of_size

theorem square_cycle_false_of_size
  (hsize : ∀ (p : ℕ) (I : Finset ℕ) (ℓ : ℕ → ℕ), I.Nonempty →
    (∀ r ∈ I, r.Prime ∧ r ≠ 2 ∧ (ℓ r).Prime ∧ ℓ r ≠ 2 ∧
      ∑ i ∈ Finset.range (ℓ r), r ^ i = p) →
    2 * (∏ r ∈ I, ℓ r) * (∑ r ∈ I, (r - 1)) < p)
  {p e t : ℕ} (hp : p.Prime) (he : 1 ≤ e) (ht : Odd t)
  (hσ : σ 1 (t ^ 2) = p ^ e) (hc : 2 * t ^ 2 = 1 + σ 1 (p ^ e)) : False

The contradiction, given a size bound for rows with a common value. Under the explicit hypothesis hsize, the setting of square_cycle_digit is impossible.

OddPerfect.RepunitSize

OddPerfect/RepunitSize.lean · 499 lines · 1 public theorem

If a prime p equals the repunit 1 + r + … + r^(ℓ−1) for every base r of a finite nonempty set of odd primes, each with an odd prime length ℓ, then 2·(product of the lengths)·(sum of the r − 1) < p.

Proof idea. Distinct bases give distinct lengths, and a base r with length ℓ has r^(ℓ−1) < p, so many rows force large lengths and a large p. Three regimes by n = log₂ p. For small p two kernel checked certificates do the work: no value below 2^18 is a repunit of odd prime length in two prime bases below 512, and none below 2^1536 in two bases up to 64; both are merge walks over sorted lists that the kernel evaluates. Above that an estimate on the product of the lengths suffices.

OddPerfect.repunit_rows_size

theorem repunit_rows_size (p : ℕ) (I : Finset ℕ) (ℓ : ℕ → ℕ) (hne : I.Nonempty)
  (h : ∀ r ∈ I, r.Prime ∧ r ≠ 2 ∧ (ℓ r).Prime ∧ ℓ r ≠ 2 ∧
    ∑ i ∈ Finset.range (ℓ r), r ^ i = p) :
  2 * (∏ r ∈ I, ℓ r) * (∑ r ∈ I, (r - 1)) < p

If p is the value of the repunit 1 + r + ... + r ^ (ℓ r - 1) for each base r of a finite nonempty set I of odd primes, with odd prime lengths ℓ r, then twice the product of the lengths times the sum of the r - 1 is below p.

OddPerfect.SpecialBelowCycle

OddPerfect/SpecialBelowCycle.lean · 42 lines · 1 public theorem · imports SpecialBelowRows

The reduction: if no prime p, exponent e ≥ 1 and odd t have σ(t²) = p^e and 2t² = 1 + σ(p^e), then q < m for every odd perfect number in Euler’s form.

Proof idea. The shape left by special_lt_or_shape has k = 1, σ(p^e) = q and σ((q + 1)/2) = p^e. The normal form shape_data shows (q + 1)/2 = t² with t odd, which is the configuration named NoSquareCycle.

If NoSquareCycle holds, then every odd perfect number N = q ^ k * m ^ 2 in Euler's form has q < m.

OddPerfect.SpecialBelowAll

OddPerfect/SpecialBelowAll.lean · 49 lines · 2 public theorems · imports SquareCycleDigit, RepunitSize, SpecialBelowCycle

q < m for every odd perfect number N = q^k·m² in Euler’s form, with no further hypothesis (special_lt_root). The configuration σ(t²) = p^e, 2t² = 1 + σ(p^e) does not occur (noSquareCycle). The inequality q < m is stated, or follows from a stated bound, in several places: a 2016 preprint of P. A. Brown (arXiv:1602.01591v1); P. Starni, Notes Number Theory Discrete Math. 24 (2018), 5 to 9 (a stronger bound); J. A. B. Dris, same journal 23 (2017), no. 4, 1 to 13; K. A. P. Dagal and J. A. B. Dris, same journal 27 (2021), no. 2, 12 to 19. As we read them, for special exponent 1 Brown asserts without proof that some component divisor sum has a prime factor other than p, Starni’s Corollary 2.2 leaves the same shape open, and the two papers of Dris conclude from a quantity attached to one number being bounded from above, a step that we could not turn into a proof. These remarks record our reading, are not kernel checked and may be mistaken. No claim of novelty or priority is made.

Proof idea. Three modules joined. SpecialBelow proves q < m outside one shape. SquareCycleDigit obtains in that shape an integer J divisible by p. RepunitSize shows 0 < |J| < p unless J = −1, and J = −1 is excluded by parity of the product of the lengths. So the shape is empty.

OddPerfect.EulerIndexSquare

OddPerfect/EulerIndexSquare.lean · 218 lines · 4 public theorems · imports EulerPart, SquareRow, SpecialPrime

For N = q^k·m² in Euler’s form with k other than 1, the index σ(m²)/q^k is not a square. More generally the index is not d₁²·d₂ with d₂ dividing (q^ℓ + 1)/2, ℓ = (k + 1)/2; and if d₂ is coprime to (q^ℓ + 1)/2, that number is a square and q ≡ 1 (mod 8). Known mathematics (Gallardo 2022; Broughan, Delbourgo and Zhou).

Proof idea. σ(q^k) = 2·R·S with R = σ(q^(ℓ−1)) and S = (q^ℓ + 1)/2 odd and coprime, so m² = d·R·S for the index d. If d₂ divides S, then R times a cofactor coprime to it is a square, so R is a square; by the square rows theorem that forces q = 3, against q ≡ 1 (mod 4), unless ℓ = 1. If d₂ is coprime to S, then S is a square t² with t odd and q^ℓ = 2t² − 1 ≡ 1 (mod 8).

Dichotomy. For an odd perfect number q ^ k * m ^ 2 with special prime q and k ≠ 1, write the index as d₁ ^ 2 * d₂ and put S = (q ^ ℓ + 1) / 2 with ℓ = (k + 1) / 2. Then either d₂ does not divide S but shares a prime factor with it, or q ≡ 1 (mod 8).

OddPerfect.EulerIndexSupport

OddPerfect/EulerIndexSupport.lean · 385 lines · 12 public theorems · imports EulerIndexPrimePower, EulerIndexSquare, SpecialBelowAll

For N = qkm2 the index σ(m2)/qk: at k = 1 it is not a prime power, is at least 2m and is not squarefree; for q ≡ 5 (mod 8) with k > 1, k ≡ 5 (mod 12) or k ≡ 9 (mod 20), two distinct primes have odd valuation in it.

Proof idea. At k = 1 a prime power index gives the normal form of eulerIndex_prime_pow_normal_form, which noSquareCycle excludes; q < m with (q + 1)J = 2m2 gives J ≥ 2m, and J | m2 then shows J is not squarefree. For k > 1 put ℓ = (k + 1)/2, R = σ(qℓ−1), S = (qℓ + 1)/2: m2 = J·R·S with R, S coprime, R is never a square, and S is not a square in the three classes (for 3 | ℓ and 5 | ℓ by squeezing a factor between consecutive squares). A prime of odd valuation in each of R and S has odd valuation in J. The general case is stated under the hypothesis HalfPowerNotSquare; the module OddPerfect.EulerIndexSupportAll proves that hypothesis.

OddPerfect.EulerIndexSupportMore

OddPerfect/EulerIndexSupportMore.lean · 414 lines · 7 public theorems · imports EulerIndexSupport

For U > 1 with U ≡ 1 (mod 4), none of (U7 + 1)/2, (U11 + 1)/2, (U13 + 1)/2 is a square. Hence two distinct primes have odd valuation in the Euler index when k ≡ 13 (mod 28), k ≡ 21 (mod 44) or k ≡ 25 (mod 52). These classes are covered by a published statement (Y. Hirakawa, arXiv 2309.17084); the proof here is elementary.

Proof idea. Write U = 4a + 1 and F = (Up + 1)/(U + 1). The half sum is (2a + 1)·F and F is congruent to p modulo 2a + 1, so a square half sum makes F a square or p times a square. The second is ruled out modulo 8. The first is ruled out by an odd P and an even T with (P − 1)2 < T2·F < (P + 1)2 for large a, and by exhibited integer square roots for the finitely many small a.

OddPerfect.EulerIndexSupportAll

OddPerfect/EulerIndexSupportAll.lean · 144 lines · 2 public theorems · imports SignedRepunit, SignedRepunitJacobi, EulerIndexSupport

For a prime q ≡ 1 (mod 4) and an odd ℓ ≥ 3, the number (qℓ + 1)/2 is not a square: the proposition HalfPowerNotSquare is proved as defined. Consequence: the Euler index of every odd perfect number has at least two distinct prime factors. A lower bound only. Source status: for odd ℓ ≥ 5 this is a case of a published theorem (M. A. Bennett and C. M. Skinner, Canad. J. Math. 56 (2004), Theorem 1.1, page 24, page checked: xn + yn = 2z2 has no solution in nonzero pairwise coprime integers with x > y for n ≥ 4, apart from two listed solutions, both with y = −1). For ℓ = 3 no published source was checked. The proof here is elementary and does not use that theorem. For the corollary on the Euler index no published source was checked. Novelty not verified.

Proof idea. Take a prime p dividing ℓ and u = qℓ/p. Then (qℓ + 1)/2 = ((u + 1)/2)·F with F = (up + 1)/(u + 1) ≡ p modulo u + 1, so the two factors share at most p. If the product is a square, F is a square or p times a square. The first is excluded by the landed theorem on signed repunits of a prime power, the second by alternating_sum_ne_prime_mul_sq.

OddPerfect.halfPowerNotSquare

theorem halfPowerNotSquare : HalfPowerNotSquare

The half power statement. HalfPowerNotSquare holds: for a prime q ≡ 1 (mod 4) and an odd ℓ ≥ 3, (q ^ ℓ + 1) / 2 is not a square. Arithmetic only (no odd perfect number). J. Math. 56, page checked); for ℓ = 3 no published source was checked. The proof is elementary: a coprime split at a prime p ∣ ℓ, then alternating_sum_prime_pow_ne_sq and alternating_sum_ne_prime_mul_sq.

This is the conditional theorem two_le_card_primeFactors_eulerIndex_of_halfPowerNotSquare with its hypothesis discharged by halfPowerNotSquare. It is a lower bound only, for every odd perfect number. OddPerfect.HalfPowerResidue

OddPerfect/HalfPowerResidue.lean · 297 lines · 2 public theorems · imports SignedRepunit, EulerIndexSupport

For a prime q ≡ 1 (mod 4) and odd L ≥ 3: if (qL + 1)/2 is a square then q ≡ 1 (mod 16), every prime factor of L is 1 modulo 8, and the least prime factor of L divides q + 1. Hence two distinct primes have odd valuation in the Euler index whenever one of the three conditions fails for L = (k + 1)/2. These are necessary conditions only; that (qL + 1)/2 is never a square is proved later, in OddPerfect.EulerIndexSupportAll. Y. Hirakawa (arXiv 2309.17084) states the two valuations for every k > 1, so nothing new is claimed.

Proof idea. For a prime p dividing L put u = qL/p and F = (up + 1)/(u + 1). Then ((u + 1)/2)·F is a square and F ≡ p modulo u + 1, so F is a square or p times a square. The first is excluded by SignedRepunit. The second gives p | u + 1 and, modulo 8, p ≡ 1. For the least prime factor p, the order of −q modulo p divides L/p and p − 1, which are coprime.

OddPerfect.OddValuationCount

OddPerfect/OddValuationCount.lean · 581 lines · 1 public theorem

For a prime q ≡ 1 (mod 4) and odd L, at least Ω(L) primes have odd valuation in σ(q2L − 1)/2, where Ω counts prime factors with multiplicity. The two nonsquare statements for the base qh are explicit hypotheses of this module. Novelty not verified.

Proof idea. For a prime p with pd exactly dividing L and each level 1 ≤ j ≤ d, one of the two quotients (up ∓ 1)/(u ∓ 1) with u = qpj − 1 is not divisible by p and is not a square, so some prime t has odd valuation in it; q or −q has order pj modulo t, so different levels and different p give different t. Lifting the exponent shows that the valuation of t in the half sum stays odd.

OddPerfect.OddValuationCountFree

OddPerfect/OddValuationCountFree.lean · 589 lines · 1 public theorem

For a prime q ≡ 1 (mod 4) and odd L, the number σ(q2L − 1)/2 has at least Ω(L) + Ωfree(L) primes of odd valuation, where Ω counts the prime factors of L with multiplicity and Ωfree counts those that do not divide q2 − 1. Two statements on squares are explicit hypotheses. Novelty not verified.

Proof idea. Strong induction on L, removing the least prime factor p last: L = p·L′ and, with X = qL′, the new factors are 1 + X + ⋯ + Xp − 1 and (Xp + 1)/(X + 1). Neither is a square. If p does not divide q − 1 (or q + 1), then p does not divide the first (or second) factor, and a prime r of odd valuation in it has order p (or 2p), so r > p and r divides no earlier factor. Earlier witnesses exceed p, and the new factors are 1 or p modulo each of them, so no witness is lost.

OddPerfect.OddValuationCountSigned

OddPerfect/OddValuationCountSigned.lean · 663 lines · 2 public theorems · imports SignedRepunitJacobi

For a prime q ≡ 1 (mod 4) and odd L, the number σ(q2L − 1)/2 has at least Ω(L) + C(L) primes of odd valuation, where Ω counts the prime factors of L with multiplicity and C counts, with multiplicity, those that do not divide q − 1; and at least Ω(L) + 1 for L ≥ 3. The second bound is sharp at q = 5, L = 3. Arithmetic only. Published context: Y. Hirakawa, arXiv preprint 2309.17084, Theorem 1.1 (2), page checked: for a special exponent above 1 the index is neither a square nor a square times a single prime. The count itself has no checked source. Novelty not verified.

Proof idea. Strong induction on L, removing the least prime factor p last: L = p·L′ and, with X = qL′, the new factors are R = 1 + X + ⋯ + Xp − 1 and A = (Xp + 1)/(X + 1). R is not a square, and A is neither a square nor p times a square (OddPerfect.SignedRepunitJacobi). So A has a prime r ≠ p of odd valuation; −X has order p modulo r, so r does not divide R or the earlier factors. Hence every prime factor of L gives a new prime from A, with no condition on q + 1, and a second one from R when p does not divide q − 1. For L ≥ 3 one more comes from 1 + q + ⋯ + qL − 1, which is not a square and is coprime to qL + 1.

OddPerfect.EulerIndexPair

OddPerfect/EulerIndexPair.lean · 458 lines · 3 public theorems · imports EulerPart, SquareRow

At special exponent 1, if the index is supported on two primes r and s, their valuations in the index are not both odd, and r, s are not both 3 modulo 4.

Proof idea. Exactly one ordinary row is divisible by q, and its base t lies in {r, s}; the other base u has σ(uf) = tj. Then q has odd order modulo t, so t ∤ q + 1 and vt(J) = vt(N) is even. If both primes are 3 modulo 4, the pure row is a square, which forces u = 3 and t = 11 by the square row theorem, and a third row supported on {3, 11} is impossible.

OddPerfect.EulerIndexPairRows

OddPerfect/EulerIndexPairRows.lean · 204 lines · 3 public theorems · imports EulerIndexPair, Zsigmondy, PureRows

At special exponent 1 with the index supported on two primes t, u (labeled as in EulerIndexPair): the pure row σ(uf) = tj has f + 1 prime, u has order f + 1 modulo t and t ≡ 1 (mod 2(f + 1)); the length e + 1 of the sender row σ(te) = q·uv is a prime or the square of a prime.

Proof idea. The pure row: for odd primes u, t with σ(uf) = tj, the length f + 1 is prime by prime_succ_of_sigma_prime_pow_eq_prime_pow (a classical fact), and a primitive prime factor of order f + 1 must be t. The sender row: e + 1 is odd, each divisor d > 1 of e + 1 gives a prime factor of σ(te) in which t has order d (exists_prime_dvd_sigma_orderOf_eq), distinct d give distinct primes, and only q and u are available. So e + 1 has at most two divisors above 1.

Pure row of an odd prime. Let u and t be odd primes, f ≥ 1 and σ(u ^ f) = t ^ j. Then f is even, f + 1 is prime, the order of u modulo t is f + 1, and t ≡ 1 (mod 2 (f + 1)).

OddPerfect.eulerIndex_pair_rows

theorem eulerIndex_pair_rows (h : OddPerfect N) (hq : q.Prime) (hN : N = q * m ^ 2)
  (hqm : ¬ q ∣ m) (hr : r.Prime) (hs : s.Prime) (hrs : r ≠ s)
  (hJ : (eulerIndex q 1 m).primeFactors = {r, s}) :
  ∃ t u, ({t, u} : Finset ℕ) = {r, s} ∧ t ≠ u ∧
    (∃ v, σ 1 (t ^ N.factorization t) = q * u ^ v) ∧
    (∃ j, 0 < j ∧ σ 1 (u ^ N.factorization u) = t ^ j) ∧ ¬ t ∣ q + 1 ∧
    (eulerIndex q 1 m).factorization t = N.factorization t ∧
    (N.factorization u + 1).Prime ∧ orderOf (u : ZMod t) = N.factorization u + 1 ∧
    t % (2 * (N.factorization u + 1)) = 1 ∧
    ((N.factorization t + 1).Prime ∨ ∃ p, p.Prime ∧ N.factorization t + 1 = p ^ 2)

Two prime index, both rows. Let N = q m ^ 2 be an odd perfect number with special prime q of exponent 1, q ∤ m, and suppose the Euler index J = σ(m ^ 2) / q has exactly the two prime factors r ≠ s. For the labeling (t, u) of eulerIndex_pair_sender, with e = v_t(N) and f = v_u(N), all conclusions of that theorem hold, and moreover f + 1 is prime, the order of u modulo t is f + 1, t ≡ 1 (mod 2 (f + 1)), and e + 1 is prime or the square of a prime. This is a restricted result (special exponent 1, index supported on exactly two primes); it does not exclude this case, since infinitely many pairs of prime indices remain possible. Its novelty has not been verified.

OddPerfect.EulerIndexPairAll

OddPerfect/EulerIndexPairAll.lean · 229 lines · 2 public theorems · imports EulerIndexPairRows

At special exponent 1 with the index supported on two primes t, u (labeled as in EulerIndexPairRows): the order of q modulo t is 1 or f + 1, and for every other prime p of N with exponent g the row σ(pg) is a product txuy, pg divides q + 1, and g + 1 is a prime or the square of a prime.

Proof idea. Modulo t we have q·uv ≡ 1 and uf + 1 ≡ 1, so qf + 1 ≡ 1, and f + 1 is prime. For another prime p, the row σ(pg) divides σ(m2) = q·J, and the single factor q sits in the row of t, so the row of p is supported on t and u. Since p does not divide J and J·(q + 1) = 2m2, the power pg divides q + 1. Each divisor d > 1 of g + 1 gives a prime factor of the row in which p has order d (exists_prime_dvd_sigma_orderOf_eq), distinct d give distinct primes, and only t and u are available.

OddPerfect.EulerIndexPairCommon

OddPerfect/EulerIndexPairCommon.lean · 333 lines · 4 public theorems · imports EulerIndexPairAll, KanoldGeneral, OmegaSevenFinal

Let N = q·m2 be an odd perfect number with special exponent 1 whose Euler index has exactly two prime factors. Then no prime l divides the index ep + 1 of every ordinary prime p. Restricted result: the intersection of two restricted families; a special exponent above 1 is not covered, and the two prime index case itself is not excluded. No published source was checked; novelty not verified.

Proof idea. In the labeling (t, u) of EulerIndexPairAll the prime u equals l and every ordinary exponent is l − 1. The column of l gives l − 1 ordinary primes that are 1 modulo l; the column of t then forces every remaining row to equal t·l. An odd perfect number has at least seven prime factors, so two primes share that row.

OddPerfect.HalfSigmaSquare

OddPerfect/HalfSigmaSquare.lean · 167 lines · 2 public theorems

For an odd prime p: σ(p2) + 1 = 2z2 only for p = 5, and σ(p4) + 1 = 2z2 has no solution. Elementary. Novelty not verified.

Proof idea. Modulo p the equation gives z ≡ ±1, so z = kp + 1 after a change of sign. Dividing by p leaves an equation in k and p that is settled by sign arguments, with one more reduction modulo p in the quartic case.

OddPerfect.HalfSigmaSix

OddPerfect/HalfSigmaSix.lean · 181 lines · 2 public theorems

For an odd prime p and every z: σ(p6) + 1 ≠ 2z2. The prime 2 is a true exception (128 = 2·82). Pure arithmetic; it extends the statements of HalfSigmaSquare for exponents 2 and 4. No published source was checked; novelty not verified.

Proof idea. With B = 32 + 8p + 7p2, (32z)2 − B2 = p3·(512p3 + 512p2 + 463p + 400). As p does not divide 2B, p3 divides one factor: 32Z = B + c·p3 with Z = ±z and −36 ≤ c ≤ 31. Substituting and cancelling p3 leaves a cubic in p with constant term 64c − 400, so p divides 4c − 25, which is odd and at most 169 in absolute value. The remaining finite set of pairs (p, c) is checked by the kernel.

OddPerfect.EulerIndexPairOutside

OddPerfect/EulerIndexPairOutside.lean · 207 lines · 4 public theorems · imports EulerIndexPairAll, OmegaSevenFinal

At special exponent 1 with the Euler index supported on two primes r, s: twice the product of the prime powers pvp(N) over the primes of N outside {q, r, s} divides q + 1. Hence every such prime is below q, at most two prime factors of N exceed q, and q ≥ 2668049. Restricted result; the case is not excluded. Novelty not verified.

Proof idea. EulerIndexPairAll gives each prime power dividing q + 1; they are pairwise coprime and odd. By the bound of seven distinct prime factors at least four primes lie outside {q, r, s}, their product is at least 3·5·7·11 = 1155 and every exponent is at least 2, so q + 1 is at least twice the square of 1155.

OddPerfect.EulerIndexPairCofactor

OddPerfect/EulerIndexPairCofactor.lean · 335 lines · 3 public theorems · imports EulerIndexPairPalette, EulerIndexPairOutside

In the same setting, with the two primes labeled t, u (σ(te) = q·uv, σ(uf) = tj) and w the product of pg/2 over the other primes: q + 1 = 2·ud·w2; e = j + A with A the sum of the valuations at t of the other rows, A is odd, and σ(w2) = tA·ub; modulo t, q·uv ≡ 1 and 2·(1 + uv) is a nonzero square. Restricted family result; the family is not excluded. Novelty not verified.

Proof idea. The cofactor (q + 1)/(2w2) divides m2, is prime to t and to the other primes, so it is a power of u. The count at t reads the valuation of σ(N) = 2N at t row by row: the row of q is q + 1, prime to t, the row of t is prime to t, the row of u is tj. Since e is even and j is odd, A is odd. For the last claim multiply q + 1 = 2·ud·w2 by uv; u has odd order modulo t, so u is a square modulo t.

OddPerfect.eulerIndex_pair_cofactor

theorem eulerIndex_pair_cofactor (h : OddPerfect N) (hq : q.Prime) (hN : N = q * m ^ 2)
  (hqm : ¬ q ∣ m) (hr : r.Prime) (hs : s.Prime) (hrs : r ≠ s)
  (hJ : (eulerIndex q 1 m).primeFactors = {r, s}) :
  ∃ t u, ({t, u} : Finset ℕ) = {r, s} ∧ t ≠ u ∧
    (∃ v, σ 1 (t ^ N.factorization t) = q * u ^ v) ∧
    (∃ j, 0 < j ∧ Odd j ∧ σ 1 (u ^ N.factorization u) = t ^ j) ∧ ¬ t ∣ q + 1 ∧
    (eulerIndex q 1 m).factorization t = N.factorization t ∧
    (N.factorization u + 1).Prime ∧ orderOf (u : ZMod t) = N.factorization u + 1 ∧
    t % (2 * (N.factorization u + 1)) = 1 ∧
    ((N.factorization t + 1).Prime ∨ ∃ p, p.Prime ∧ N.factorization t + 1 = p ^ 2) ∧
    (orderOf (q : ZMod t) = 1 ∨ orderOf (q : ZMod t) = N.factorization u + 1) ∧
    (∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ≠ q → p ≠ t → p ≠ u →
      (∃ x y, σ 1 (p ^ N.factorization p) = t ^ x * u ^ y) ∧
      p ^ N.factorization p ∣ q + 1 ∧
      ((N.factorization p + 1).Prime ∨ ∃ P, P.Prime ∧ N.factorization p + 1 = P ^ 2)) ∧
    ∃ d, q + 1 = 2 * u ^ d *
      (∏ p ∈ N.primeFactors \ {q, r, s}, p ^ (N.factorization p / 2)) ^ 2

**Two prime index, the cofactor of q + 1.** Let N = q m ^ 2 be an odd perfect number with special prime q of exponent 1, q ∤ m, and suppose the Euler index J = σ(m ^ 2) / q has exactly the two prime factors r ≠ s. For the labeling (t, u) of eulerIndex_pair_pure_exponent_odd, all of its conclusions hold, and moreover q + 1 = 2 u ^ d w ^ 2 for some d, where w = ∏ p ^ (v_p(N) / 2) over the primes p ∣ N outside {q, r, s}. This is a restricted result (special exponent 1, index supported on exactly two primes); it does not exclude this case. Its novelty has not been verified.

OddPerfect.eulerIndex_pair_t_count

theorem eulerIndex_pair_t_count (h : OddPerfect N) (hq : q.Prime) (hN : N = q * m ^ 2)
  (hqm : ¬ q ∣ m) (hr : r.Prime) (hs : s.Prime) (hrs : r ≠ s)
  (hJ : (eulerIndex q 1 m).primeFactors = {r, s}) :
  ∃ t u, ({t, u} : Finset ℕ) = {r, s} ∧ t ≠ u ∧
    (∃ v, σ 1 (t ^ N.factorization t) = q * u ^ v) ∧ ¬ t ∣ q + 1 ∧
    orderOf (u : ZMod t) = N.factorization u + 1 ∧
    ∃ j, 0 < j ∧ Odd j ∧ σ 1 (u ^ N.factorization u) = t ^ j ∧
    N.factorization t = j + ∑ p ∈ N.primeFactors \ {q, r, s},
      (σ 1 (p ^ N.factorization p)).factorization t ∧
    Odd (∑ p ∈ N.primeFactors \ {q, r, s}, (σ 1 (p ^ N.factorization p)).factorization t) ∧
    (∃ p ∈ N.primeFactors \ {q, r, s}, t ∣ σ 1 (p ^ N.factorization p)) ∧
    t ∣ σ 1 ((∏ p ∈ N.primeFactors \ {q, r, s}, p ^ (N.factorization p / 2)) ^ 2) ∧
    ∃ b, σ 1 ((∏ p ∈ N.primeFactors \ {q, r, s}, p ^ (N.factorization p / 2)) ^ 2) =
      t ^ (∑ p ∈ N.primeFactors \ {q, r, s}, (σ 1 (p ^ N.factorization p)).factorization t) *
        u ^ b

**Two prime index, the valuation count at t.** In the setting of eulerIndex_pair_cofactor, for the same labeling (t, u), with j the exponent in σ(u ^ v_u(N)) = t ^ j and A = Σ v_t(σ(p ^ v_p(N))) over the primes p ∣ N outside {q, r, s}, we have v_t(N) = j + A, A is odd, some outside row is divisible by t, and σ(w ^ 2) = t ^ A u ^ b for some b (so t ∣ σ(w ^ 2)), where w = ∏ p ^ (v_p(N) / 2) over the same primes. This is a restricted result (special exponent 1, index supported on exactly two primes); it does not exclude this case. Its novelty has not been verified.

OddPerfect.eulerIndex_pair_character

theorem eulerIndex_pair_character (h : OddPerfect N) (hq : q.Prime) (hN : N = q * m ^ 2)
  (hqm : ¬ q ∣ m) (hr : r.Prime) (hs : s.Prime) (hrs : r ≠ s)
  (hJ : (eulerIndex q 1 m).primeFactors = {r, s}) :
  ∃ t u, ({t, u} : Finset ℕ) = {r, s} ∧ t ≠ u ∧ ¬ t ∣ q + 1 ∧
    (∃ j, 0 < j ∧ Odd j ∧ σ 1 (u ^ N.factorization u) = t ^ j) ∧
    ∃ v, σ 1 (t ^ N.factorization t) = q * u ^ v ∧ ((q * u ^ v : ℕ) : ZMod t) = 1 ∧
      IsSquare ((2 * (1 + u ^ v) : ℕ) : ZMod t) ∧
      ((2 * (1 + u ^ v) : ℕ) : ZMod t) ≠ 0

Two prime index, a character condition. In the setting of eulerIndex_pair_cofactor, for the same labeling (t, u) with σ(t ^ v_t(N)) = q u ^ v, we have q u ^ v ≡ 1 (mod t), and 2 (1 + u ^ v) is a nonzero square modulo t. This is a restricted result (special exponent 1, index supported on exactly two primes); it does not exclude this case. Its novelty has not been verified.

OddPerfect.EulerIndexPairEmitters

OddPerfect/EulerIndexPairEmitters.lean · 320 lines · 10 public theorems · imports EulerIndexPairPalette

For odd u and odd ℓ the sum 1 + u + ⋯ + uℓ − 1 is 1 modulo 4 if u ≡ 3, and ℓ modulo 4 if u ≡ 1; it is no odd power of 29 for ℓ = 7, of 41 for ℓ = 5, of 23 for ℓ = 11, of 47 for ℓ = 23. Setting: N = q·m2 odd perfect with special exponent 1, and the Euler index σ(m2)/q has exactly two prime factors, labeled t, u with σ(te) = q·uv and σ(uf) = tj, j odd. Then (t, u) = (13, 3), or (31, 5), or t = 43 with f = 6, or t ≥ 53. Restricted family result; the family is not excluded. Novelty not verified.

Proof idea. ℓ = f + 1 is an odd prime and t ≡ 1 modulo 2ℓ, so for t < 53 only finitely many pairs (ℓ, t) occur. ℓ = 3 is settled by the landed lemma that u2 + u + 1 is a prime power only to the first power. An odd power of a prime 3 modulo 4 forces ℓ ≡ 3 modulo 4, which removes t = 11 and t = 31 at ℓ = 5. The other pairs fall to residue certificates: for each odd class of j modulo a period one listed modulus puts tj outside the values of the sum. A checker with one soundness lemma verifies the lists in the kernel. For t = 43 no rational congruence can work, since the sum at u = −2 equals 43.

OddPerfect.eulerIndex_pair_emitter_small

theorem eulerIndex_pair_emitter_small (h : OddPerfect N) (hq : q.Prime)
  (hN : N = q * m ^ 2) (hqm : ¬ q ∣ m) (hr : r.Prime) (hs : s.Prime) (hrs : r ≠ s)
  (hJ : (eulerIndex q 1 m).primeFactors = {r, s}) :
  ∃ t u, ({t, u} : Finset ℕ) = {r, s} ∧ t ≠ u ∧
    (∃ v, σ 1 (t ^ N.factorization t) = q * u ^ v) ∧
    (∃ j, 0 < j ∧ Odd j ∧ σ 1 (u ^ N.factorization u) = t ^ j) ∧ ¬ t ∣ q + 1 ∧
    (N.factorization u + 1).Prime ∧ t % (2 * (N.factorization u + 1)) = 1 ∧
    ((t = 13 ∧ u = 3) ∨ (t = 31 ∧ u = 5) ∨ (t = 43 ∧ N.factorization u = 6) ∨
      53 ≤ t)

Two prime index, small first labels. Let N = q m ^ 2 be an odd perfect number with special prime q of exponent 1, q ∤ m, and suppose the Euler index J = σ(m ^ 2) / q has exactly the two prime factors r ≠ s. For the labeling (t, u) of eulerIndex_pair_pure_exponent_odd (with σ(u ^ v_u(N)) = t ^ j, j odd), either (t, u) = (13, 3), or (t, u) = (31, 5), or t = 43 and v_u(N) = 6, or t ≥ 53. This is a restricted result (special exponent 1, index supported on exactly two primes); it does not exclude this case, and infinitely many values of t remain. Its novelty has not been verified.

OddPerfect.EulerIndexPairSmallPairs

OddPerfect/EulerIndexPairSmallPairs.lean · 341 lines · 2 public theorems · imports EulerIndexPairEmitters, OmegaSevenFinal, Network, Valuation, Cyclotomic, PureRows, SquareRow, NagellPrime

For an odd prime p, even g, t ≡ 3 and u ≡ 1 modulo 4 and odd x, the equation σ(pg) = tx·uy forces p ≡ 1 and g ≡ 2 modulo 4. Setting: N = q·m2 odd perfect with special exponent 1, and the Euler index σ(m2)/q has exactly two prime factors, labeled t, u with σ(te) = q·uv and σ(uf) = tj, j odd. Then t = 43 with f = 6, or t ≥ 53: the pairs (13, 3) and (31, 5) are impossible. Restricted family result; the family is not excluded. Novelty not verified.

Proof idea. For both pairs f ≤ 3. An odd perfect number has at least seven prime factors, so at least four primes p lie outside q, t, u. Each row σ(pg) is tx·uy. A pure power of t has prime length g + 1 dividing t − 1 (order 1 would make the row equal to t). Length 3 gives p2 + p + 1 = t, so p = u. Length 5 at t = 31 fails modulo 4 for odd x, and for even x the row would be a square, which happens only for p = 3 with value 121. So u divides every such row, and the valuation of σ(N) = 2N at u would be at least 4, above f.

If σ(p ^ g) = t ^ x u ^ y, then p ≡ 1 (mod 4) and g ≡ 2 (mod 4): the right side is 3 (mod 4), while σ(p ^ g) ≡ 1 for p ≡ 3 and σ(p ^ g) ≡ g + 1 for p ≡ 1 (mod 4).

OddPerfect.EulerIndexPairSplit

OddPerfect/EulerIndexPairSplit.lean · 169 lines · 2 public theorems · imports EulerIndexPairCofactor, Valuation

Setting: N = q·m2 odd perfect with special exponent 1, and the Euler index σ(m2)/q has exactly two prime factors, labeled t, u with σ(te) = q·uv and σ(uf) = tj, j odd. If e + 1 is prime then v = 0 (so σ(te) = q), or v = 1 with u = e + 1 and t ≡ 1 modulo u. If e + 1 = P2 then v = 2 with u = P and t ≡ 1 modulo u, or v > 0, P divides j and t has order P modulo u. The arithmetic step sigma_row_split is stated for any primes. Restricted family result; the family is not excluded. Novelty not verified.

Proof idea. If u divides the row of t, the order D of t modulo u is 1 and u divides e + 1, or D > 1 divides e + 1. The row of u is tj ≡ 1 modulo u, so D divides j, and j < e. With D = 1 lifting the exponent gives v = vu(e + 1). With e + 1 prime, D = e + 1 cannot divide j. With e + 1 = P2, D = P; and v = 0 is impossible because a row that is a prime has prime length.

theorem sigma_row_split {t u q e v j : ℕ} (ht : t.Prime) (ht2 : t ≠ 2) (hu : u.Prime)
  (hu2 : u ≠ 2) (hq : q.Prime) (htu : t ≠ u) (huq : u ≠ q) (he : Even e)
  (hrow : σ 1 (t ^ e) = q * u ^ v) (hj : 0 < j) (hje : j < e + 1)
  (htj : (t : ZMod u) ^ j = 1) :
  ((e + 1).Prime → v = 0 ∨ (v = 1 ∧ u = e + 1 ∧ t % u = 1)) ∧
  (∀ P, P.Prime → e + 1 = P ^ 2 →
    (v = 2 ∧ u = P ∧ t % u = 1) ∨ (0 < v ∧ P ∣ j ∧ orderOf (t : ZMod u) = P))

**Sender row, the exponent of u.** Let t, u, q be primes, t and u odd, t ≠ u, u ≠ q, e even, σ(t ^ e) = q u ^ v, and t ^ j ≡ 1 (mod u) for some 0 < j < e + 1. If e + 1 is prime, then v = 0, or v = 1, u = e + 1 and t ≡ 1 (mod u). If e + 1 = P ^ 2 with P prime, then either v = 2, u = P and t ≡ 1 (mod u), or v > 0, P ∣ j and the order of t modulo u is P.

OddPerfect.EulerIndexPairPrimeLength

OddPerfect/EulerIndexPairPrimeLength.lean · 366 lines · 3 public theorems · imports EulerIndexPairSplit

Setting: N = q·m2 odd perfect with special exponent 1, and the Euler index σ(m2)/q has exactly two prime factors, labeled t, u with σ(te) = q·uv and σ(uf) = tj, j odd. Then e + 1 is prime, and either σ(te) = q, or v = 1 with u = e + 1, t ≡ 1 and q ≡ 1 modulo u, and q + 1 twice a square. Restricted family result; the family is not excluded. Novelty not verified.

Proof idea. Write Rn(x) = 1 + x + ⋯ + xn − 1, so RP²(t) = RP(t)·RP(tP). If u = P and t ≡ 1 modulo u, both factors are divisible by u and exceed u, so their product is not q·u2. If t has order P modulo u, the second factor is P modulo u, hence equals q, and RP(t) is a power of u; the row of u is 1 + u modulo u2, which forces the power to be u itself, and then u ≡ 1 modulo t, against the order of u. For v = 1 the row of t is u modulo u2, so q ≡ 1 modulo u and u does not divide q + 1.

Setting: N = q·m2 odd perfect with special exponent 1, and the Euler index σ(m2)/q has exactly two prime factors, labeled t, u with σ(te) = q·uv and σ(uf) = tj, j odd. Then every prime factor of N is at most q. Consequence for special exponent 1 in general: a prime factor of N above q forces at least three prime factors of the Euler index. Restricted family result; the family is not excluded. Novelty not verified.

Proof idea. If v = 0 then t < σ(te) = q and u < σ(uf) = tj < te < q. If v = 1 then t ≥ u + 1 and t·u < t2 ≤ te < q·u. Every other prime lies below q by a landed bound. The second statement follows because the index has at least two prime factors at special exponent 1.

OddPerfect.EulerIndexPairShortRows

OddPerfect/EulerIndexPairShortRows.lean · 495 lines · 4 public theorems · imports EulerIndexPairPrimeLength, HalfSigmaSquare, SpecialPrime

Setting: N = q·m2 odd perfect with special exponent 1, and the Euler index σ(m2)/q has exactly two prime factors, labeled t, u with σ(te) = q·uv and σ(uf) = tj, j odd. Then v = 0 forces e ≥ 6, and v = 1 forces u = e + 1 ≥ 5. Three arithmetic lemmas carry the cases e = 2, e = 4 and u = 3. Restricted family result; the family is not excluded. Novelty not verified.

Proof idea. q + 1 = 2·ud·w2 with u prime to w. For e = 2: t ≡ 1 and q + 1 ≡ 4 modulo u, so d = 0 and t2 + t + 2 = 2w2 gives t = 5, q = 31, which is 3 modulo 4. For e = 4: d = 0 is impossible by the landed quartic lemma; otherwise t3 ≡ 1 and q + 1 ≡ 0 modulo u give 18 ≡ 0, so u = 3, and 2tj + 1 = 3f + 1 fails modulo 9 (j = 3) or modulo 243 (j = 1). For u = 3: e = 2, and the count at t leaves one outside prime p with σ(pg) = t·3y and p dividing q + 1; then p divides 6 or 40, or g = 8, and each option fails.

OddPerfect.EulerIndexPairEmitterSix

OddPerfect/EulerIndexPairEmitterSix.lean · 213 lines · 3 public theorems · imports EulerIndexPairShortRows, PureRows, OmegaSevenFinal

At special exponent 1 with the Euler index supported on two primes t, u, labeled with σ(te) = q·uv and σ(uf) = tj: e ≥ 6 in both branches v = 0 and v = 1. Corollary: t and u do not both have exponent 2 or 4 in N. Auxiliary: for an odd prime p and g ≥ 2, σ(pg) is never a power of 5. The two prime index case is not excluded. No published source was checked; novelty not verified.

Proof idea. In the branch v = 1 with e < 6 one has e = 4 and u = 5. No row of another prime is a pure power of 5 (a pure row forces 5 ≡ 1 modulo its length), so each of the at least four other primes of N sends to t, and the count e = j + (sum of these weights) gives e ≥ 5.

OddPerfect.EulerIndexPairSixParity

OddPerfect/EulerIndexPairSixParity.lean · 310 lines · 3 public theorems · imports EulerIndexPairShortRows

At special exponent 1 with the Euler index supported on two primes t, u (σ(te) = q·uv, σ(uf) = tj): in the branch v = 0 with e = 6, the exponent d in q + 1 = 2·ud·w2 is even, so σ(t6) + 1 is twice a square. A second theorem concludes e ≥ 10 in the branch v = 0 from the arithmetic statement of HalfSigmaSix taken as a hypothesis. No published source was checked; novelty not verified.

Proof idea. If d is odd then u divides F(t) = 2 + t + ⋯ + t6 and tj − 1 with j = 1, 3 or 5. Integer polynomial identities give u dividing 8, 8 or 88, so u = 11 and j = 5. Then t5 ≡ 133 modulo 1331, and every such residue t with 11 dividing F(t) has F(t) ≡ 847 modulo 1331, a multiple of 121 but not of 1331, so the exponent of 11 in q + 1 is exactly 2.

At special exponent 1 with the Euler index supported on two primes t, u (σ(te) = q·uv, σ(uf) = tj): the emitter exponent satisfies e ≥ 10 in both branches, and u ≥ 11 when v = 1. Two arithmetic lemmas: no divisor sum of an odd prime power with exponent at least 2 is a power of 7, and 3X ≠ 7Y + 2 for Y ≥ 2. The case is not excluded: e ≥ 10 remains in both branches. Proof idea. In the branch v = 1 with e = 6 one has u = 7. As no row is a power of 7, every other prime of N feeds t, and the count of the exponent of t leaves at most eight prime factors. The landed bound of nine prime factors when 3 does not divide N gives 3 | N. The row of 3 is then t or its square; the square fails, and the remaining equation σ(3g) = σ(7f) has no solution modulo 49 and 29 together.

OddPerfect.EulerIndexPairHigher

OddPerfect/EulerIndexPairHigher.lean · 497 lines · 1 public theorem · imports EulerIndexSupportAll, EulerIndexOmegaSigned

Setting: N = qa·m2 odd perfect with a > 1 and the Euler index has exactly two prime factors. Then L = (a + 1)/2 is prime, both valuations in the index are odd, and the two primes can be labeled t, u with 1 + q + ⋯ + qL − 1 = t·x2, t = L or t ≡ 1 (mod 2L), u ≠ L, u ≡ 1 (mod 2L), and either q + 1 = 2z2 with qL + 1 = (q + 1)·u·w2, or q + 1 = 2L·z2 with qL + 1 = (q + 1)·L·u·w2. Necessary conditions only; the case is not excluded. Novelty not verified.

Proof idea. σ(qa)/2 = R·(q + 1)/2·A with R = 1 + q + ⋯ + qL − 1 and A = (qL + 1)/(q + 1), and it has the same two primes of odd valuation as the index. R is coprime to the other two factors and is not a square, so it carries exactly one of them. A is neither a square nor L times a square and gcd((q + 1)/2, A) divides L, so A carries the other, with or without a factor L shared with (q + 1)/2. Primitive prime factors of R and A are 1 modulo 2L.
