  (hN : N = q * m ^ 2) (hqm : ¬ q ∣ m) (hr : r.Prime) (hs : s.Prime) (hrs : r ≠ s)
  (hJ : (eulerIndex q 1 m).primeFactors = {r, s}) : ¬ 5 ∣ N.factorization 5 + 1

Two prime index, the exponent of 5. Let N = q m ^ 2 be an odd perfect number with special prime q of exponent 1, q ∤ m, and suppose the Euler index J = σ(m ^ 2) / q has exactly the two prime factors r ≠ s. Then 5 ∤ v_5(N) + 1: otherwise 11 and 71 both divide J, and the two primes of J would both be ≡ 3 (mod 4). Restricted result; no published source was checked; novelty not verified.

OddPerfect.EulerIndexPairFrame

OddPerfect/EulerIndexPairFrame.lean · 227 lines · 11 public theorems · imports EulerIndexPairCofactor, EulerIndexPairSmallPairs, EulerIndexPairSeven

Setting: N = q·m2 odd perfect with special exponent 1, and the Euler index σ(m2)/q has exactly two prime factors t, u with σ(te) = q·uv and σ(uf) = tj. The landed results of this family name t and u only by an existential statement. This module fixes the labels: a predicate PairFrame, its existence and uniqueness, and the landed results restated for a fixed frame. No new exclusion. No published source was checked; novelty not verified.

Proof idea. The emitter t is the index prime whose row contains q; the special prime divides only one row, so the labels are unique.

If every ordinary exponent of an odd perfect number is at most 8 (special exponent 1), the Euler index has at least three prime factors. Restricted result. No published source was checked; novelty not verified.

OddPerfect.EulerIndexPairReceiverSieve

OddPerfect/EulerIndexPairReceiverSieve.lean · 499 lines · 23 public theorems

Tools for the branch v = 1 of the two prime Euler index family, without reference to odd perfect numbers: a test that excludes mixed rows of a small prime, a test that excludes its pure rows, a bound for a product of p/(p−1) over a set that avoids listed primes, and a kernel checked table for the receivers 11 to 47. No published source was checked; novelty not verified.

Proof idea. The mixed test finds a divisor of the shortest row that is neither a power of u nor 1 modulo u; the pure test checks roots modulo the small prime; the product is largest for the least primes that remain.

OddPerfect.EulerIndexPairReceiverBound

OddPerfect/EulerIndexPairReceiverBound.lean · 391 lines · 16 public theorems · imports EulerIndexPairFrame, EulerIndexPairEmitters, EulerIndexPairRows, PureRows, NagellPrime, Abundancy, EulerIndexPairReceiverSieve

Setting: N = q·m2 odd perfect with special exponent 1, and the Euler index σ(m2)/q has exactly two prime factors t, u with σ(te) = q·uv and σ(uf) = tj. In the branch v = 1: 3 does not divide N, the number of prime factors is at most u + 1 plus the number of pure outsider rows, and u ≥ 43 with u ≠ 47 (landed before: u ≥ 11). The receiver 43 is not excluded; the family is not excluded. No published source was checked; novelty not verified.

Proof idea. For each receiver in the table the small primes cannot divide N, and with at most u + 1 + z prime factors, all from the remaining primes, the product of p/(p−1) stays below 2.

OddPerfect.OmegaFour

OddPerfect/OmegaFour.lean · 268 lines · 1 public theorem · imports Abundancy, Euler, Cyclotomic, Seed.Example

At least four distinct prime factors.

Proof idea. With exactly three prime factors the bound 2 < ∏ p/(p − 1) forces the support {3, 5, s} with s ∈ {7, 11, 13}. In each case some prime with even exponent has a component sum larger than 1 whose prime factors must lie among the other two primes; multiplicative orders, and in one case the extra prime 3221 or 61, rule out every candidate exponent.

OddPerfect.OmegaFive

OddPerfect/OmegaFive.lean · 515 lines · 1 public theorem · imports Certificate, OmegaFour, SmallestPrime, SpecialPrime, Zsigmondy

At least five distinct prime factors, closed by a kernel computation over 104 explicit supports.

Proof idea. With four prime factors, 3 divides N and the product bound leaves the supports {3, 5, r, s} with 17 ≤ r ≤ 31 and s < 256, {3, 7, r, s} with r ∈ {11, 13} and s ≤ 26, and the families {3, 5, 11, s} and {3, 5, 13, s}, cut to s ≤ 100 and s ≤ 46 ({3, 5, 7, s} is out since 105 does not divide N). That is 70 + 6 + 20 + 8 = 104 supports. For each, a Boolean function lists the candidate exponents of each prime (from Euler's form and primitive divisors: e = 1 for the special prime, or e + 1 dividing y − 1 for some y in the support) and checks that σ(xe) always has a prime factor outside the support and 2; decide +kernel evaluates it.

OddPerfect.SmallestPrime

OddPerfect/SmallestPrime.lean · 288 lines · 9 public theorems · imports Abundancy

Bounds on the smallest prime factor p₁: p₁ ≤ ω and 3p₁ < 2ω + 6, and ω ≥ 7 without 3, ω ≥ 15 without 3 and 5.

Proof idea. Everything rests on 2 < ∏ p/(p − 1) over the prime factors. If all elements of a set are at least m, the product telescopes to at most 1 + |S|/(m − 1), giving p₁ ≤ ω; over odd numbers the squared product is at most 1 + 2|S|/(m − 2), giving 3p₁ < 2ω + 6. The bounds without 3 or 5 compare the product with an explicit set of small primes.

OddPerfect/LeastPrimeSeven.lean · 148 lines · 1 public theorem · imports SmallestPrime contains novelty unverified

The least prime factor p₁ of an odd perfect number with ω distinct prime factors satisfies 7p₁ < 3ω + 21. Published comparison: Zelinsky (INTEGERS 21 (2021), A76, Corollary 4) proves ω ≥ 2p₁ + 2, which is stronger than this bound for p₁ ≤ 23; this bound is stronger from p₁ = 29 on.

Proof idea. The method of the bound 3p₁ < 2ω + 6 with cubes: the prime factors are at least p₁ ≥ 5 and coprime to 6, so the i-th of them is at least p₁ + 3i − 1, and (u/(u − 1))³ < (u + 1)/(u − 2) telescopes to ∏ (p/(p − 1))³ ≤ (p₁ + 3ω − 3)/(p₁ − 3). The left side exceeds 8.

OddPerfect.PerfectRigidity

OddPerfect/PerfectRigidity.lean · 160 lines · 4 public theorems · imports Basic

A unitary divisor B of a perfect number N with 1 < B < N forces a prime into N/B. Two perfect numbers with a common prime factor and equal exponents at all common primes are equal.

Proof idea. Write N = B·C with gcd(B, C) = 1. From σ(B)σ(C) = 2BC and σ(C) > C: B < σ(B) < 2B. So σ(B) does not divide 2B, and some prime r divides σ(B) to a higher power than 2B. Since σ(B) divides 2BC, such a prime divides C. For two perfect numbers N and N′ that agree at their common primes, B = gcd(N, N′) is a unitary divisor of both. If B is smaller than both, a forced prime of B divides both cofactors, hence B: contradiction. If B = N, then N is a proper unitary divisor of N′ with σ(N) = 2N, against σ(B) < 2B.

OddPerfect.PerfectCount

OddPerfect/PerfectCount.lean · 429 lines · 18 public theorems · imports PerfectRigidity, UpperBound, SmallestPrime, UnconditionalSupport contains novelty unverified

At most 4^(k²) odd perfect numbers have at most k distinct prime factors; at most 4^((5T+7)²) have total excess at most T.

Proof idea. Start with the full power of the least prime factor of N. As long as the current unitary divisor B is smaller than N, multiply by the full power of the least forced prime of B, which depends on B alone. The chain gains one prime per step and stops at N, so N is determined by its least prime factor and the exponents along the chain. For ω(N) ≤ k the least prime p₁ satisfies 3p₁ < 2k + 6 and every exponent is below 3·4^(k−1), because 3^e ≤ N < 2^(4^k). Counting the possible data gives 4^(k²). The second bound uses ω(N) ≤ 5T + 7.

OddPerfect.CountBelow

OddPerfect/CountBelow.lean · 67 lines · 2 public theorems · imports EulerPart

At most √(x/5) odd perfect numbers are at most x.

Proof idea. In Euler's form N = q^k·m² the number m determines N (Hornfeck's lemma, in EulerPart). The special prime q is at least 5, so 5m² ≤ N ≤ x and m lies between 1 and the integer square root of x/5. Distinct odd perfect numbers have distinct m.

OddPerfect.Counting

OddPerfect/Counting.lean · 251 lines · 12 public theorems · imports Euler, Network, Seed.ThreeFree

Linear inequalities between Ω and ω: 2ω ≤ Ω + 1 and 12ω ≤ 5Ω + 6v₃(N) + 9.

Proof idea. Every ordinary exponent is even, hence at least 2, which gives 2ω ≤ Ω + 1. Exponent 2 primes ≡ 1 (mod 3) each spend one unit of v₃(N). For the set A₂ of exponent 2 primes not ≡ 1 (mod 3), every prime factor of σ(p²) is ≡ 1 (mod 3) and so outside A₂; conservation at those receivers gives |A₂| ≤ Ω − 2|A₂|. Combining the two counts gives the inequality.

OddPerfect.CountingZelinsky

OddPerfect/CountingZelinsky.lean · 434 lines · 10 public theorems · imports Counting

8ω ≤ 3Ω + 7 when 3 does not divide N, and 21ω ≤ 8Ω + 39 in general, after Zelinsky (arXiv 1706.07009).

Proof idea. A ledger of the exponent 2 primes, split by residue modulo 3, with conservation of the 3-free parts of σ(p²). The new input over Counting is injectivity: when σ(p²) has at most two prime factors its largest prime factor determines p, because a prime shared by σ(a²) and σ(b²) with b < a is at most a; and when the 3-free part of σ(p²) is prime it determines p, using that 3(x² + x + 1) = y² + y + 1 has no solution with x an odd prime (it forces y = 3a + 1 and x(x + 1) = 3a(a + 1)). Linear arithmetic on the resulting relations gives both bounds.

OddPerfect.zelinsky_ledger

theorem zelinsky_ledger {N : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N) :
  ∃ a b x y W ρ F : ℕ,
    (∑ p ∈ N.primeFactors, N.factorization p) = 2 * a + F + N.factorization 3 ∧
    N.primeFactors.card = a + ρ + (if 3 ∣ N then 1 else 0) ∧
    4 * ρ ≤ F + 3 + 2 * b ∧ W ≤ F ∧ 3 * a + 2 * b ≤ W + x + y ∧
    x ≤ a ∧ y ≤ x + b ∧ x ≤ ρ ∧ y ≤ ρ ∧ b ≤ N.factorization 3 ∧
    (3 ∣ N → 2 ≤ N.factorization 3)

With S₂ the exponent 2 primes that are 2 (mod 3) (a of them), S₁ those that are 1 (mod 3) (b of them), R the remaining prime factors other than 3 (ρ of them, total exponent F), W the number of prime factors with multiplicity of the 3-free parts of σ(p ^ 2) over p ∈ S₁ ∪ S₂, X the primes of S₂ whose σ(p ^ 2) has at most two prime factors, and Y the primes of S₁ ∪ S₂ whose 3-free part of σ(p ^ 2) is prime, the listed linear relations hold. The bounds x ≤ ρ and y ≤ ρ are the two injectivity statements (largest prime factor, and the 3-free part itself).

OddPerfect.RadicalBound

OddPerfect/RadicalBound.lean · 662 lines · 18 public theorems · imports Abundancy, SmallestPrime, Euler, SpecialPrime

Identities linking abundancy to the radical R and to φ(R), with consequences such as 2φ(R) < R for perfect numbers and linear bounds on the second, third and fourth smallest prime factors.

Proof idea. Each component contributes σ(pe)/pe = (p/(p − 1))(1 − p−(e+1)), so the abundancy of N is H(N) = R/φ(R) times a product of factors below 1. For a perfect N the abundancy is 2, hence R/φ(R) > 2, and since R and 2φ(R) are integers, R − 2φ(R) ≥ 1, which gives H(N) − 2 ≥ 1/φ(R). Keeping one factor 1 − p−(e+1) and bounding the others by 1 gives the component bound R ≤ pe+1(R − 2φ(R)).

OddPerfect.third_prime_le

OddPerfect.UpperBound

OddPerfect/UpperBound.lean · 773 lines · 6 public theorems · imports Abundancy

N < 24k for an odd perfect number with k distinct prime factors, from the general bound dN < (d + 1)4k for odd N with σ(N)/N = n/d.

Proof idea. The key lemma (cook_lemma in the source): for integers 2 ≤ x₁ < ⋯ < xr with ∏ (1 − 1/xi) ≤ a/b below the same product without xr, one has a∏ xi < (a + 1)2r, proved by strong induction on r with a majorization comparison against the extremal sequence (a + 1)2i + 1. The theorem then grows a set of known primes: the lemma is applied first to new primes and then to prime power components, which splits off a coprime factor V of N; the cofactor N/V is again odd with rational abundancy of denominator dσ(V), and the induction runs on the number of prime factors.

  (hlt : (a : ℚ) / b < ∏ x ∈ G.erase m, (1 - 1 / (x : ℚ))) :
  a * ∏ x ∈ G, x < (a + 1) ^ (2 ^ G.card)

Let G be a finset of integers x ≥ 2 with largest element m, and let a > 0. If ∏_{x ∈ G} (1 - 1/x) ≤ a/b < ∏_{x ∈ G, x ≠ m} (1 - 1/x) then a ∏_{x ∈ G} x < (a + 1)^(2^|G|).

OddPerfect.UpperBoundSharp

OddPerfect/UpperBoundSharp.lean · 639 lines · 5 public theorems · imports UpperBound, RadicalBound

N < 2(2k − 1)² for an odd perfect number with k distinct prime factors (Nielsen 2015).

Proof idea. Two inequalities in power form are combined. First, the Heath-Brown and Nielsen algorithm of OddPerfect.UpperBound is run again with each step keeping the product Π·Π′ of the selected primes p and of the numbers p − 1; this gives 2NΠΠ′ < 24k (Theorem 1.6 of Nielsen, Math. Comp. 84 (2015), second inequality). Second, Cook’s lemma applied to the numbers pe+1 gives 2Π′ΠN < (2Π′ + 1)2k (inequality (19), power form). With c = 2Π′ + 1 ≤ Π, the first is used when c ≥ 22k and the second otherwise. Known mathematics (Corollary 1.7, inequality (18)); no novelty is claimed.

OddPerfect.Zsigmondy

OddPerfect/Zsigmondy.lean · 251 lines · 4 public theorems · imports Cyclotomic

Primitive prime divisors for bases a ≥ 3: for every n ≥ 3 some prime q has a of order exactly n modulo q.

Proof idea. Through the cyclotomic value Φn(a). A prime factor of Φn(a) not dividing n is primitive. Otherwise every prime factor q divides n, the order of a modulo q is the part of n prime to q, which forces a single such prime, and lifting the exponent shows it divides Φn(a) only once. Then Φn(a) = q, contradicting Φn(a) > (a − 1)φ(n) ≥ 2q−1 ≥ q. Consequence: each divisor d ≥ 3 of e + 1 yields a prime factor of N congruent to 1 modulo d.

OddPerfect.ExponentCap

OddPerfect/ExponentCap.lean · 298 lines · 15 public theorems · imports Zsigmondy, Euler, SpecialPrime, UpperBound

Exponents are capped by the largest prime factor (2e + 3 ≤ R), the divisors of e + 1 inject into the prime factors, and finiteness for fixed ω or bounded primes.

Proof idea. For an ordinary prime with exponent e, a primitive prime of order e + 1 divides σ(pe), hence N, and is ≡ 1 (mod 2(e + 1)), so it is at least 2e + 3. For the special prime with exponent k ≥ 5, the primitive primes of orders k + 1 and (k + 1)/2 are distinct and both ≡ 1 (mod k + 1); for k = 1 the special prime itself is at least 5. Distinct divisors d ≥ 3 of e + 1 give distinct primes since p has order exactly d at each. Finiteness for fixed ω uses the bound N < 24ω.

OddPerfect.ValuationBounds

OddPerfect/ValuationBounds.lean · 380 lines · 9 public theorems · imports Valuation, ExponentCap contains novelty unverified

Bounds on the exponent of a prime q in terms of ω(N): the q-adic ledger bounded term by term, with special forms for primes q with q − 1 a power of two and for q = 3. The main formula factorization_le_sq_add_sum_orderWeight is an analogue of a corollary of Thackeray, proved here directly and under different hypotheses: his statement concerns odd squares.

Proof idea. The q-adic ledger vq(N) = Σ vq(σ(pep)) is bounded term by term. A component with p ≡ 1 (mod q) contributes vq(ep + 1), and q, q², …, qj are distinct divisors at least 3 of ep + 1, so the injection of divisors into prime factors gives vq(ep + 1) ≤ ω − 1. A component of order d > 1 contributes vq(pd − 1) + vq((ep + 1)/d), and the second summand is bounded the same way.

Special prime q = 2^k + 1 ≥ 5: (q − 3)/2 · a ≤ T, where a is the special exponent and T the total excess. For q = 5: a ≤ T.

Proof idea. For a prime p ≠ q with even exponent e, the order of p modulo q divides the odd number e + 1 and the power of two q − 1, so q divides σ(p^e) only if p ≡ 1 (mod q), and then v_q(σ(p^e)) = v_q(e + 1). If this valuation is h ≥ 1 then e + 1 ≥ q^h ≥ 3 + h(q − 3), so h·(q − 3)/2 ≤ e/2 − 1. Sum over the ledger for q. Whether this is stated in the literature has not been checked.

OddPerfect.FermatFactor

OddPerfect/FermatFactor.lean · 151 lines · 3 public theorems · imports FermatSpecial contains novelty unverified

A Fermat prime F ≥ 5 that divides N, is not the special prime q, with q ≢ ±1 (mod F): T ≥ (F − 2)·t + (F − 3), where t is the excess of F.

Proof idea. The special component sends nothing to F: the order of q modulo F would divide a + 1 ≡ 2 (mod 4) and a power of two, so it would be 1 or 2. The other components send at most v_F(e + 1) each, as in FermatSpecial, so (F − 3)/2 times the exponent of F is at most the excess of the remaining primes. Whether this is stated in the literature has not been checked.

OddPerfect.LeastOddFactor

OddPerfect/LeastOddFactor.lean · 69 lines · 2 public theorems · imports Valuation, SpecialPrime contains novelty unverified

If L bounds q and every odd prime factor of q − 1 from below, then (L − 3)/2 ≤ T.

Proof idea. Some prime r ≠ q sends to q. The order of r modulo q divides e + 1 (odd) and q − 1, or r ≡ 1 (mod q) and q divides e + 1. So e + 1 has an odd prime factor that divides q − 1 or equals q, and e + 1 ≥ L. Whether this is stated in the literature has not been checked.

OddPerfect.AttackPrimality

OddPerfect/AttackPrimality.lean · 344 lines · 12 public theorems · imports Network, Valuation, Zsigmondy, SpecialPrime, Spoof

Order data on the edges of the network: an edge from a smaller prime to a larger one has order at least 3, and if the largest prime factor P has even exponent e then 2e + 5 ≤ P. The decidable statement MaxReceives asks for a divisor d ≥ 3 of e + 1 with bd ≡ 1 (mod P); it does not require d to be the exact order. Descartes' spoof violates it, while every odd perfect number satisfies it.

Proof idea. For an edge p → r the order d of p modulo r divides both ep + 1 and r − 1. Orders 1 and 2 would force r to divide p − 1 or p + 1, which is impossible for an odd prime r > p, so an upward edge has d ≥ 3. By conservation the largest prime factor receives an edge, necessarily upward.

OddPerfect.OrderRows

OddPerfect/OrderRows.lean · 208 lines · 10 public theorems · imports AttackPrimality, AttackSize, SmallestPrime

Orders modulo a safe prime in the rows σ(p^a): if a safe prime t = 2s + 1 divides σ(p^a) with a even, then s ≤ a + 1. A safe prime factor of an odd perfect number forces a prime power p^(s−1) | N, unless t divides q + 1 for the special prime q. Also a size bound: if every prime factor exceeds L, then N ≥ (L + 1)^(3L − 1).

Proof idea. The order of p modulo t divides a + 1 and t − 1 = 2s, so it is 1, 2, s or 2s; an even a leaves s, or order 1 with t | a + 1. The size bound combines the landed bound p^(2ω+1) ≤ N for the least prime factor p with Grün’s inequality 3p < 2ω + 6. Elementary and standard; no novelty is claimed.

OddPerfect.Phi3Algebra

OddPerfect/Phi3Algebra.lean · 1091 lines · 43 public theorems · imports Phi3

Reusable algebra of φ₃(x) = x² + x + 1, and of x⁴ + x³ + x² + x + 1, for the inequalities between Ω and ω: factorization identities such as φ₃(b²) = φ₃(b)(b² − b + 1) and φ₃((a + 1)²) = φ₃(a)φ₃(a + 1), the solutions of φ₃(x) = m·φ₃(b) when φ₃(b) is prime, and the fact that for a prime c at most two residues x modulo c have c dividing x² + x + 1.

Proof idea. The identities are polynomial identities checked by ring after casting to the integers. For the equation φ₃(x) = m·φ₃(b) with p = φ₃(b) prime and 1 < m ≤ p: x² < φ₃(x) ≤ p² gives x < p, and x ≠ b because m > 1. Then x and b are two distinct roots of t² + t + 1 modulo p below p, and two such roots add up to p − 1, so x + b + 1 = b² + b + 1 and x = b². The counting statement follows because a quadratic has at most two roots modulo a prime.

For 1 ≤ a ≤ b with b ^ 2 + b + 1 prime, x ^ 2 + x + 1 = (a ^ 2 + a + 1)(b ^ 2 + b + 1) holds exactly when b = a + 1 and x = (a + 1) ^ 2. Only the larger factor needs to be prime, and the proof uses no arithmetic of ℤ[ζ₆].

theorem no_double_threat {x a b : ℕ} (hx : x.Prime) (ha : (phi3 a).Prime)
  (hb : (phi3 b).Prime) : phi3 x ≠ phi3 a * phi3 b

No "double threat": if x is prime then x ^ 2 + x + 1 is not the product of two primes of the form a ^ 2 + a + 1.

OddPerfect.phi3_eq_three_mul_phi3_prime

theorem phi3_eq_three_mul_phi3_prime {x b : ℕ} (hp : (phi3 b).Prime)
  (h : phi3 x = 3 * phi3 b) : b = 2 ∧ x = 4

If b ^ 2 + b + 1 is prime and x ^ 2 + x + 1 = 3 (b ^ 2 + b + 1), then b = 2 and x = 4.

OddPerfect.no_phi3_eq_three_mul_phi3

theorem no_phi3_eq_three_mul_phi3 {x a : ℕ} (hx : x.Prime) (ha : (phi3 a).Prime) :
  phi3 x ≠ 3 * phi3 a

There is no prime x with x ^ 2 + x + 1 = 3 (a ^ 2 + a + 1) and a ^ 2 + a + 1 prime (the hypotheses that a is prime and the primes are odd are not needed).

OddPerfect.card_le_two_of_dvd_phi3

theorem card_le_two_of_dvd_phi3 {c : ℕ} (hc : c.Prime) (S : Finset ℕ)
  (hS : ∀ x ∈ S, x < c ∧ c ∣ phi3 x) : S.card ≤ 2

For a prime c, at most two natural numbers below c have c ∣ x ^ 2 + x + 1.

OddPerfect.card_filter_range_dvd_phi3_le_two

theorem card_filter_range_dvd_phi3_le_two {c : ℕ} (hc : c.Prime) :
  ((Finset.range c).filter (fun x => c ∣ phi3 x)).card ≤ 2

The set of x < c with c ∣ x ^ 2 + x + 1 has at most two elements, for a prime c.

OddPerfect.card_image_zmod_le_two_of_dvd_phi3

theorem card_image_zmod_le_two_of_dvd_phi3 {c : ℕ} (hc : c.Prime) (S : Finset ℕ)
  (hS : ∀ x ∈ S, c ∣ phi3 x) : (S.image (fun x : ℕ => (x : ZMod c))).card ≤ 2

Without a size restriction: the inputs x with c ∣ x ^ 2 + x + 1, for a prime c, fall into at most two residue classes modulo c.

OddPerfect.zelinsky_shared_prime_two

theorem zelinsky_shared_prime_two {a b p : ℕ} (hab : a ≠ b) (ha2 : a % 2 = 1)
  (hb2 : b % 2 = 1) (ha3 : a % 3 = 2) (hb3 : b % 3 = 2) (hp : p.Prime)
  (hpa : p ∣ phi3 a) (hpb : p ∣ phi3 b) : 5 * p ≤ a + b + 1

If a ≠ b are odd, a ≡ b ≡ 2 (mod 3), and a prime p divides both a ^ 2 + a + 1 and b ^ 2 + b + 1, then 5 p ≤ a + b + 1. (The paper assumes a, b prime; only oddness is used.)

OddPerfect.zelinsky_shared_prime_one

theorem zelinsky_shared_prime_one {a b p : ℕ} (hab : a ≠ b) (ha2 : a % 2 = 1)
  (hb2 : b % 2 = 1) (ha3 : a % 3 = 1) (hb3 : b % 3 = 1) (hp : p.Prime)
  (hpa : p ∣ phi3 a) (hpb : p ∣ phi3 b) : 3 * p ≤ a + b + 1

If a ≠ b are odd, a ≡ b ≡ 1 (mod 3), and a prime p divides both a ^ 2 + a + 1 and b ^ 2 + b + 1, then 3 p ≤ a + b + 1.

OddPerfect.zelinsky_precursor

theorem zelinsky_precursor {a c : ℕ} (ha : a % 2 = 1) (hc : c.Prime) (hc2 : c % 2 = 1)
  (hp : (phi3 a).Prime) (hac : a ≠ c) (hd : phi3 a ∣ phi3 c) : 2 * phi3 a < c

If a ≠ c are odd, c is prime, a ^ 2 + a + 1 is prime and divides c ^ 2 + c + 1, then 2 (a ^ 2 + a + 1) < c. (The paper assumes a prime; only oddness is used.)

OddPerfect.zelinsky_precursor_of_not_three_dvd

theorem zelinsky_precursor_of_not_three_dvd {a c : ℕ} (ha : a.Prime) (ha2' : a ≠ 2)
  (ha3 : a ≠ 3) (hc : c.Prime) (hc2' : c ≠ 2) (hp : (phi3 a).Prime) (hac : a ≠ c)
  (hd : phi3 a ∣ phi3 c) (h3 : ¬ 3 ∣ phi3 c) : 9 * phi3 a < 2 * c

If a ≠ c are odd primes (a, c ≠ 2), a ≠ 3, a ^ 2 + a + 1 is prime and divides c ^ 2 + c + 1, and 3 ∤ c ^ 2 + c + 1, then 9 (a ^ 2 + a + 1) < 2 c. The paper omits a ≠ 3, and then the statement is false: a = 3, c = 29, 29 ^ 2 + 29 + 1 = 13 · 67.

OddPerfect.no_phi3_eq_three_mul_phi3_mul_phi3

theorem no_phi3_eq_three_mul_phi3_mul_phi3 {a b c : ℕ} (ha : a % 2 = 1) (hb : b % 2 = 1)
  (hc : c.Prime) (hc2 : c % 2 = 1) (hpa : (phi3 a).Prime) (hpb : (phi3 b).Prime) :
  phi3 c ≠ 3 * phi3 a * phi3 b

There are no odd primes a, b, c with a ^ 2 + a + 1, b ^ 2 + b + 1 prime and c ^ 2 + c + 1 = 3 (a ^ 2 + a + 1)(b ^ 2 + b + 1). (Only oddness of a, b is used.)

OddPerfect.phi3_ne_cube_of_prime

theorem phi3_ne_cube_of_prime {x : ℕ} (hx : x.Prime) (k : ℕ) : phi3 x ≠ k ^ 3

If x is prime then x ^ 2 + x + 1 is not a perfect cube. (Primality matters: 18 ^ 2 + 18 + 1 = 7 ^ 3.) An earlier source for the statement is A. Brauer, Bull. Amer. Math. Soc.

OddPerfect.no_phi3_eq_triple_mod_five

theorem no_phi3_eq_triple_mod_five {a b c d : ℕ} (ha : a % 5 = 1) (hb : b % 5 = 1)
  (hc : c % 5 = 1) (hd : d % 5 = 1) : phi3 a ≠ phi3 b * phi3 c * phi3 d

There are no integers a, b, c, d, all ≡ 1 (mod 5), with a ^ 2 + a + 1 = (b ^ 2 + b + 1)(c ^ 2 + c + 1)(d ^ 2 + d + 1) (the left side is 3 and the right side 27 ≡ 2 modulo 5).

OddPerfect.hansen_nielsen_three_family

theorem hansen_nielsen_three_family {a b c x : ℕ} (hc : c * (a + b + 1) = a * b)
  (hx : x = c * (a * b + a + b) + a + b) : phi3 x = phi3 a * phi3 b * phi3 c

If c (a + b + 1) = a b and x = c (a b + a + b) + a + b, then x ^ 2 + x + 1 = (a ^ 2 + a + 1)(b ^ 2 + b + 1)(c ^ 2 + c + 1).

OddPerfect.hansen_nielsen_three_sporadic

theorem hansen_nielsen_three_sporadic :
  phi3 18 = phi3 2 * phi3 2 * phi3 2 ∧ phi3 25 = phi3 1 * phi3 2 * phi3 5 ∧
    phi3 22 = phi3 1 * phi3 3 * phi3 3

F(18) = F(2) ^ 3, F(25) = F(1) F(2) F(5), F(22) = F(1) F(3) ^ 2.

OddPerfect.quadruple_threat_191

theorem quadruple_threat_191 :
  phi3 191 = phi3 2 * phi3 3 * phi3 3 * phi3 5 ∧ Nat.Prime 191 ∧ (phi3 2).Prime ∧
    (phi3 3).Prime ∧ (phi3 5).Prime

191 ^ 2 + 191 + 1 = F(2) F(3) F(3) F(5) = 7 · 13 · 13 · 31, with 191 and the four factors prime.

OddPerfect.phi5_mod

theorem phi5_mod (z m : ℕ) : phi5 z % m = phi5 (z % m) % m

Reduction of phi5 modulo any m.

OddPerfect.phi3_sub_three

theorem phi3_sub_three (z : ℕ) : (phi3 z : ℤ) - 3 = ((z : ℤ) - 1) * (z + 2)

Block identity for Φ₃: F(z) - 3 = (z - 1)(z + 2), over ℤ.

OddPerfect.phi5_sub_five

theorem phi5_sub_five (z : ℕ) :
  (phi5 z : ℤ) - 5 = ((z : ℤ) - 1) * (z ^ 3 + 2 * z ^ 2 + 3 * z + 4)

Block identity for Φ₅: Φ₅(z) - 5 = (z - 1)(z ^ 3 + 2 z ^ 2 + 3 z + 4), over ℤ.

OddPerfect.five_dvd_phi5_iff

theorem five_dvd_phi5_iff (z : ℕ) : 5 ∣ phi5 z ↔ z % 5 = 1

5 ∣ Φ₅(z) exactly when z ≡ 1 (mod 5), for every natural z.

OddPerfect.phi5_mod_twentyfive

theorem phi5_mod_twentyfive {z : ℕ} (hz : z % 5 = 1) : phi5 z % 25 = 5

For z ≡ 1 (mod 5), Φ₅(z) ≡ 5 (mod 25) (from the block identity: 5 ∣ z - 1 and 5 ∣ z ^ 3 + 2 z ^ 2 + 3 z + 4).

OddPerfect.not_twentyfive_dvd_phi5

theorem not_twentyfive_dvd_phi5 (z : ℕ) : ¬ 25 ∣ phi5 z

25 never divides Φ₅(z).

OddPerfect.padicValNat_five_phi5

theorem padicValNat_five_phi5 (z : ℕ) :
  padicValNat 5 (phi5 z) = if z % 5 = 1 then 1 else 0

The exact power of 5 in Φ₅(z) for every natural z: it is 1 if z ≡ 1 (mod 5) and 0 otherwise.

OddPerfect.phi3_phi5

theorem phi3_phi5 (x : ℕ) :
  phi3 (phi5 x) =
    (x ^ 2 - x + 1) * (x ^ 6 + 3 * x ^ 5 + 5 * x ^ 4 + 6 * x ^ 3 + 7 * x ^ 2 + 6 * x + 3)

Φ₃(Φ₅(x)) = (x ^ 2 - x + 1)(x ^ 6 + 3 x ^ 5 + 5 x ^ 4 + 6 x ^ 3 + 7 x ^ 2 + 6 x + 3). Natural subtraction is harmless since x ≤ x ^ 2.

OddPerfect.gcd_phi3_phi5_factors_dvd

theorem gcd_phi3_phi5_factors_dvd (x : ℕ) :
  Nat.gcd (x ^ 2 - x + 1) (x ^ 6 + 3 * x ^ 5 + 5 * x ^ 4 + 6 * x ^ 3 + 7 * x ^ 2 + 6 * x + 3)
    ∣ 31

The gcd of the two factors in phi3_phi5 divides 31, via the explicit combination (5x⁵ + 21x⁴ + 44x³ + 58x² + 55x + 34) A - (5x + 1) B = 31.

OddPerfect.prime_dvd_phi3_phi5_factors

theorem prime_dvd_phi3_phi5_factors {x q : ℕ} (hq : q.Prime) (hA : q ∣ x ^ 2 - x + 1)
  (hB : q ∣ x ^ 6 + 3 * x ^ 5 + 5 * x ^ 4 + 6 * x ^ 3 + 7 * x ^ 2 + 6 * x + 3) : q = 31

The only possible common prime divisor of the two factors in phi3_phi5 is 31.

OddPerfect.ch_factorization3

theorem ch_factorization3 {a b d e f : ℕ} (hd : d.Prime) (hA : phi3 a = 3 * d * e)
  (hB : phi3 b = 3 * d * f) (hde : e ≤ d) (hef : f < e) :
  3 * d = a + b + 1 ∧ a + f = b + e

If d is prime, a ^ 2 + a + 1 = 3 d e, b ^ 2 + b + 1 = 3 d f and d ≥ e > f, then 3 d = a + b + 1 and a - b = e - f (stated as a + f = b + e). The paper also assumes a, b prime; this is not needed.

OddPerfect.ch_factorization2

theorem ch_factorization2 {a b d e f : ℕ} (ha : a.Prime) (hb : b.Prime) (hd : d.Prime)
  (hA : phi3 a = 3 * d * e) (hB : phi3 b = d * f) (hde : e ≤ d) (hef : f < e) :
  d = a + b + 1 ∧ a + f = b + 3 * e

If a, b, d are prime, a ^ 2 + a + 1 = 3 d e, b ^ 2 + b + 1 = d f and d ≥ e > f, then d = a + b + 1 and a - b = 3 e - f (stated as a + f = b + 3 e). The paper assumes d > e; d ≥ e suffices. The paper's mod 3 step tacitly assumes b ≡ 2 (mod 3); the cases b = 3 and b ≡ 1 (mod 3) are handled here separately (the latter by a size argument).

OddPerfect.ch_unique_S1_S31

theorem ch_unique_S1_S31 {a b d e : ℕ} (ha : a.Prime) (hb : b.Prime) (hd : d.Prime)
  (he : 1 < e) (hA : phi3 a = 3 * d * e) (hB : phi3 b = d) (hde : e ≤ d) : False

There are no primes a, b, d and e > 1 with a ^ 2 + a + 1 = 3 d e, b ^ 2 + b + 1 = d and d ≥ e.

OddPerfect.ch_unique_S21_S31

theorem ch_unique_S21_S31 {a b d e : ℕ} (ha : a.Prime) (hd : d.Prime) (he : 1 < e)
  (hA : phi3 a = 3 * d * e) (hB : phi3 b = 3 * d) (hde : e ≤ d) : False

There are no primes a, d and e > 1, and no b, with a ^ 2 + a + 1 = 3 d e, b ^ 2 + b + 1 = 3 d and d ≥ e. (The paper writes d = a + b + 1 where 3 d = a + b + 1 is meant.)

OddPerfect.ch_semilinked_S31

theorem ch_semilinked_S31 {a b c d e f g : ℕ} (hd : d.Prime) (hA : phi3 a = 3 * d * e)
  (hB : phi3 b = 3 * d * f) (hC : phi3 c = 3 * d * g) (hde : e ≤ d) (hef : f < e)
  (hfg : g < f) : False

For a prime d there are no a, b, c and d ≥ e > f > g with a ^ 2 + a + 1 = 3 d e, b ^ 2 + b + 1 = 3 d f and c ^ 2 + c + 1 = 3 d g. (The paper's other primality and distinctness hypotheses are not needed.)

OddPerfect.yamada_gap

theorem yamada_gap {l q x₁ x₂ : ℕ} (hl : Odd l) (hq : q.Prime)
  (h1 : (x₁ : ZMod q) ^ l = 1) (h2 : (x₂ : ZMod q) ^ l = 1)
  (hq1 : x₁ ^ ((l - 1) / 2) < q)
  (hind : ∀ i j : ℕ, x₁ ^ i = x₂ ^ j → i = 0 ∧ j = 0) :
  x₁ ^ ((l + 1) / 6) < x₂

Let q be prime, let x₁, x₂ satisfy x₁ ^ l ≡ x₂ ^ l ≡ 1 (mod q), let x₁ and x₂ be multiplicatively independent (x₁ ^ i = x₂ ^ j only for i = j = 0), and let x₁ ^ ((l - 1) / 2) < q. Then x₂ > x₁ ^ ⌊(l + 1) / 6⌋. In the paper q is the common large prime of Φ_l(x₁) = p ^ {m₁} q and Φ_l(x₂) = p ^ {m₂} q with p ^ {m₁} < q, which gives the size hypothesis. For l = 3 the conclusion is only x₂ > 1; for l = 5 it is x₂ > x₁. The proof counts the l + 1 or more distinct residues x₁ ^ i x₂ ^ j < q that are l-th roots of unity modulo q.

OddPerfect.ch_unique_S1_S2

theorem ch_unique_S1_S2 {a b c d g h : ℕ} (ha : a.Prime) (hb : b.Prime) (hc : c.Prime)
  (hd : d.Prime) (hb2 : b ≠ 2) (hd2 : d ≠ 2) (hd3 : d ≠ 3) (hcd : d < c)
  (hA : phi3 a = c * d) (hB : phi3 b = 3 * c) (hg : g.Prime) (hg2 : g ≠ 2)
  (hG : phi3 g = d * h) (hdh : h < d) (hh : h = 1 ∨ (h.Prime ∧ h ≠ 2)) : False

Let a, b, c, d be odd primes with c > d, d ≠ 3, a ^ 2 + a + 1 = c d and b ^ 2 + b + 1 = 3 c. Then there is no odd prime g with g ^ 2 + g + 1 = d h, d > h, where h = 1 or h is an odd prime.

OddPerfect.LargePrimes

OddPerfect/LargePrimes.lean · 614 lines · 18 public theorems · imports SpecialPrime, Network, Phi3 contains novelty unverified

Upper bounds for prime factors in terms of N. Every prime factor p satisfies p³ < 3N, and p⁴ < 2N when its exponent is at least 2; any two prime factors p < q satisfy p⁴q < 2N; every prime factor other than the largest satisfies p⁵ < 2N; and any two distinct prime factors satisfy (pq)⁴ < 6N². Along the way: no two odd primes satisfy both q | p² + p + 1 and p | q + 1, while 13 divides 3² + 3 + 1 and 3 divides 13² + 13 + 1.

Proof idea. The basic tool: if p has exact exponent e in N, then pe and σ(pe) are coprime divisors of 2N, so their product divides 2N, and pe < σ(pe) gives p2e < 2N. With e ≥ 2 this is p⁴ < 2N. Bounds involving two primes use that the divisor sums of two distinct components together divide 2N, and add a further prime factor q to the product whenever q does not divide σ(pe). For a prime with exponent 1, the cubic bound takes a component rc whose divisor sum is a multiple of p and compares its size with the part of p + 1 that it shares with rc.

Public theorems

OddPerfect.sigma_mul_sigma_dvdnovelty unverified

theorem sigma_mul_sigma_dvd (h : OddPerfect N) {p q : ℕ} (hp : p.Prime) (hq : q.Prime)
  (hpq : p ≠ q) :
  σ 1 (p ^ N.factorization p) * σ 1 (q ^ N.factorization q) ∣ 2 * N

The divisor sums of two distinct full components together divide 2 * N.

OddPerfect.pow_mul_sigma_dvd

theorem pow_mul_sigma_dvd (h : OddPerfect N) {p : ℕ} (hp : p.Prime) :
  p ^ N.factorization p * σ 1 (p ^ N.factorization p) ∣ 2 * N

p ^ e and σ(p ^ e) are coprime divisors of 2 * N, so their product divides 2 * N.

OddPerfect.pow_two_mul_factorization_lt

theorem pow_two_mul_factorization_lt (h : OddPerfect N) {p : ℕ} (hp : p.Prime) (hpN : p ∣ N) :
  p ^ (2 * N.factorization p) < 2 * N

For every prime p with exponent e in N: p ^ (2 * e) < 2 * N, if p ∣ N.

OddPerfect.sq_lt_two_mul

theorem sq_lt_two_mul (h : OddPerfect N) {p : ℕ} (hp : p.Prime) (hpN : p ∣ N) :
  p ^ 2 < 2 * N

Every prime factor p satisfies p ^ 2 < 2 * N.

OddPerfect.pow_four_lt_of_two_le

theorem pow_four_lt_of_two_le (h : OddPerfect N) {p : ℕ} (hp : p.Prime)
  (he : 2 ≤ N.factorization p) : p ^ 4 < 2 * N

A prime with exponent at least two satisfies p ^ 4 < 2 * N.

OddPerfect.pow_four_lt_of_even

theorem pow_four_lt_of_even (h : OddPerfect N) {p : ℕ} (hp : p.Prime) (hpN : p ∣ N)
  (hev : Even (N.factorization p)) : p ^ 4 < 2 * N

Every prime factor with even exponent (every non special prime factor) satisfies p ^ 4 < 2 * N.

OddPerfect.eq_one_or_two_or_four_of_dvd_phi3_of_dvd_succ

theorem eq_one_or_two_or_four_of_dvd_phi3_of_dvd_succ {p q : ℕ} (h1 : q ∣ p ^ 2 + p + 1)
  (h2 : p ∣ q + 1) : p = 1 ∨ p = 2 ∨ p = 4

For all natural numbers: if q ∣ p ^ 2 + p + 1 and p ∣ q + 1, then p ∈ {1, 2, 4}. The complete solution set is (1, 1), (1, 3), (2, 1), (2, 7), (4, 3), (4, 7).

OddPerfect.prime_dvd_phi3_dvd_succ

theorem prime_dvd_phi3_dvd_succ {p q : ℕ} (hp : p.Prime) (hq : q.Prime)
  (h1 : q ∣ phi3 p) (h2 : p ∣ q + 1) : p = 2 ∧ q = 7

For primes, the only solution of q ∣ p ^ 2 + p + 1 and p ∣ q + 1 is (p, q) = (2, 7). So there is no such pair of odd primes (no σ_{1,2} two cycle in an odd perfect number).

OddPerfect.three_thirteen_two_cycle

theorem three_thirteen_two_cycle : 13 ∣ phi3 3 ∧ 3 ∣ phi3 13

The classical σ_{2,2} two cycle: 13 ∣ 3 ^ 2 + 3 + 1 and 3 ∣ 13 ^ 2 + 13 + 1. So the analogue of prime_dvd_phi3_dvd_succ with both exponents two is false.

OddPerfect.prime_two_cycle_succ

theorem prime_two_cycle_succ {p q : ℕ} (hp : p.Prime) (hq : q.Prime) (hpq : p ≠ q)
  (h1 : p ∣ q + 1) (h2 : q ∣ p + 1) : (p = 2 ∧ q = 3) ∨ (p = 3 ∧ q = 2)

The σ_{1,1} two cycle: distinct primes with p ∣ q + 1 and q ∣ p + 1 are 2 and 3.

OddPerfect.phi6_two_cycle

theorem phi6_two_cycle {x y : ℕ} (h1 : x ∣ y ^ 2 - y + 1) (h2 : y ∣ x ^ 2 - x + 1) :
  x = 1 ∧ y = 1

The Φ6 two cycle: positive integers with x ∣ y ^ 2 - y + 1 and y ∣ x ^ 2 - x + 1 are x = y = 1. In contrast the Φ3 version has the infinite family (1, 1), (1, 3), (3, 13), (13, 61), ....

OddPerfect.pow_mul_sigma_mul_sigma_dvd

theorem pow_mul_sigma_mul_sigma_dvd (h : OddPerfect N) {p q : ℕ} (hp : p.Prime) (hq : q.Prime)
  (hpq : p ≠ q) (hnd : ¬ p ∣ σ 1 (q ^ N.factorization q)) :
  p ^ N.factorization p * (σ 1 (p ^ N.factorization p) * σ 1 (q ^ N.factorization q)) ∣
    2 * N

If p ∤ σ(q ^ b), then p ^ a * (σ(p ^ a) * σ(q ^ b)) ∣ 2 * N (exact exponents).

OddPerfect.pow_mul_sigma_mul_prime_dvd

theorem pow_mul_sigma_mul_prime_dvd (h : OddPerfect N) {p q : ℕ} (hp : p.Prime)
  (hq : q.Prime) (hpq : p ≠ q) (hqN : q ∣ N) (hnd : ¬ q ∣ σ 1 (p ^ N.factorization p)) :
  p ^ N.factorization p * σ 1 (p ^ N.factorization p) * q ∣ 2 * N

If a prime factor q ≠ p does not divide σ(p ^ a), then p ^ a * σ(p ^ a) * q ∣ 2 * N.

OddPerfect.pow_four_mul_lt_of_two_one

theorem pow_four_mul_lt_of_two_one (h : OddPerfect N) {p q : ℕ} (hp : p.Prime) (hq : q.Prime)
  (hpq : p ≠ q) (hqN : q ∣ N) (ha : N.factorization p = 2) (hb : N.factorization q = 1) :
  p ^ 4 * q < 2 * N

Exponents two and one: if p ^ 2 ∥ N and q ∥ N with p ≠ q, then p ^ 4 * q < 2 * N. This uses prime_dvd_phi3_dvd_succ.

OddPerfect.pow_four_mul_ltnovelty unverified

theorem pow_four_mul_lt (h : OddPerfect N) {p q : ℕ} (hp : p.Prime) (hq : q.Prime)
  (hpN : p ∣ N) (hqN : q ∣ N) (hpq : p < q) : p ^ 4 * q < 2 * N

Bound for any two prime factors p < q of an odd perfect number: p ^ 4 * q < 2 * N. In particular this holds for the second largest prime Q and the largest prime P: Q ^ 4 * P < 2 * N.

OddPerfect.pow_five_lt_of_lt

theorem pow_five_lt_of_lt (h : OddPerfect N) {p q : ℕ} (hp : p.Prime) (hq : q.Prime)
  (hpN : p ∣ N) (hqN : q ∣ N) (hpq : p < q) : p ^ 5 < 2 * N

Every prime factor p other than the largest one satisfies p ^ 5 < 2 * N; in particular p_{k-1} < (2N)^{1/5}.

OddPerfect.pow_three_lt_three_mul

theorem pow_three_lt_three_mul (h : OddPerfect N) {p : ℕ} (hp : p.Prime) (hpN : p ∣ N) :
  p ^ 3 < 3 * N

Every prime factor p of an odd perfect number satisfies p ^ 3 < 3 * N. For exponent at least two this follows from p ^ 4 < 2 * N. For p ∥ N, take a component r ^ c with p ∣ σ(r ^ c) = p * s, let r ^ e = gcd(p + 1, r ^ c); then r ^ c * σ(r ^ c) * (p + 1) ≤ 2 N r ^ e, and r ^ e ∣ s + (1 + r + ... + r ^ (e - 1)) forces s large enough.

OddPerfect.pow_four_mul_pow_four_lt

theorem pow_four_mul_pow_four_lt (h : OddPerfect N) {p q : ℕ} (hp : p.Prime) (hq : q.Prime)
  (hpN : p ∣ N) (hqN : q ∣ N) (hpq : p ≠ q) : (p * q) ^ 4 < 6 * N ^ 2

For any two distinct prime factors p ≠ q of an odd perfect number: (p * q) ^ 4 < 6 * N ^ 2. For the two largest primes this is p_{k-1} p_k < 6^{1/4} N^{1/2}.

OddPerfect.CountingClaytonHansen

OddPerfect/CountingClaytonHansen.lean · 1478 lines · 58 public theorems · imports CountingZelinsky, Phi3Algebra

99ω ≤ 37Ω + 187 for every odd perfect number, and 51ω ≤ 19Ω + 46 when 3 does not divide N, after Clayton and Hansen (arXiv 2303.11974).

Proof idea. The primes with exponent exactly 2, other than 3, are sorted by the number of prime factors of p² + p + 1 and by p modulo 3. Each class contributes to, and receives from, the others through the factors of p² + p + 1, and each such relation is one linear inequality, proved as its own lemma. A linking map sends a prime of the small classes to a prime factor of its p² + p + 1; it is injective on one union of classes and at most two to one on a larger one. One lemma of the printed argument, whose proof applies an earlier lemma without its size hypotheses, is replaced by two direct lemmas. Some rows of the printed system are used in a merged form with the same optimum. A cited result, that no prime is the largest factor of three values of x² + x + 1 in the required configuration, is proved here by unique factorization in the Eisenstein integers, carried out by hand on integer pairs. The final ledger of linear relations is closed by integer linear arithmetic.

OddPerfect.no_triple_threat

theorem no_triple_threat {x a b c : ℕ} (ha : a.Prime) (hb : b.Prime) (hc : c.Prime)
  (ha2 : a ≠ 2) (hb2 : b ≠ 2) (hc2 : c ≠ 2)
  (ha3 : a % 3 = 2) (hb3 : b % 3 = 2) (hc3 : c % 3 = 2) (hA : (phi3 a).Prime)
  (hB : (phi3 b).Prime) (hC : (phi3 c).Prime) (h : phi3 x = phi3 a * phi3 b * phi3 c) :
  False

No triple threat: for odd primes a, b, c ≡ 2 (mod 3) with a ^ 2 + a + 1, b ^ 2 + b + 1, c ^ 2 + c + 1 prime, no x satisfies x ^ 2 + x + 1 = (a ^ 2 + a + 1)(b ^ 2 + b + 1)(c ^ 2 + c + 1). Repetitions among a, b, c are allowed. The prime 2 has to be excluded: 18 ^ 2 + 18 + 1 = 343 = (2 ^ 2 + 2 + 1) ^ 3. The proof is an explicit descent in ℤ[ω] written on integer pairs.

OddPerfect.ch_ledger

theorem ch_ledger {N : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N) :
  ∃ s t G f s1 a2 b2 a3 b3 a4 b4 s1s s1t xs xt sone : ℕ,
    N.primeFactors.card = s + t + (if 3 ∣ N then 1 else 0) ∧
    ∑ p ∈ N.primeFactors, N.factorization p = 2 * s + G + f ∧
    f = N.factorization 3 ∧ 4 * t ≤ G + 3 ∧
    s = s1 + a2 + b2 + a3 + b3 + a4 + b4 ∧ sone = a2 + a3 + a4 ∧
    s1 ≤ s1s + s1t + 1 ∧ a3 + b3 ≤ xs + xt ∧ sone ≤ f ∧
    s1 + 2 * b2 + 3 * b3 + a4 + 4 * b4 ≤ G + a2 ∧
    s1 + a2 + b2 ≤ sone + t ∧ 2 * (s1 + a2) + b2 + a3 ≤ 2 * (sone + t) ∧
    2 * s1s + xs ≤ 2 * sone ∧ 4 * s1t + xt ≤ G

With s = |S|, t = |T ∪ {p₀}|, G = g₄ + e₀, f = v₃(N), s1 = |S₁|, a2, a3, a4 the sizes of S_{2,1}, S_{3,1}, S_{≥4,1}, b2, b3, b4 those of S_{2,2}, S_{3,2}, S_{≥4,2}, sone = |S_{·,1}|, s1s = |S₁^S|, s1t = |S₁^T|, xs = |X_S|, xt = |X_T|, the listed linear relations hold.

OddPerfect.DivisorCount

OddPerfect/DivisorCount.lean · 222 lines · 8 public theorems · imports ExponentCap, ThreeFreeCert, RadicalBound

For every prime factor p of N with exponent e, the number of divisors of e + 1 is at most ω(N); this includes the special prime. Also two exclusions of exact square patterns without the hypothesis that 3 does not divide N, and identities for the radical R, the product F of p − 1, and the least component pe + 1.

Proof idea. Each divisor d ≥ 3 of e + 1 has a prime factor of N, other than p, modulo which p has order exactly d; different divisors give different primes. The divisor 1 is matched with p itself. For the special prime the divisor 2 is matched with an odd prime factor of (p + 1)/2, which divides N and modulo which p has order at most 2, so it is none of the primes used for d ≥ 3. Counting gives the bound.

theorem card_divisors_succ_factorization_le (h : OddPerfect N) {p : ℕ}

  (N.factorization p + 1).divisors.card ≤ N.primeFactors.card

For every prime factor p of an odd perfect number, the number of divisors of e_p + 1 is at most ω(N). For the special prime, the divisors d ≥ 3 of e + 1 get primitive witnesses of order d, the divisor 2 gets an odd prime r ∣ (p + 1)/2 (in which p has order dividing two), and the divisor 1 is matched with p itself.

OddPerfect.SmallPrimes

OddPerfect/SmallPrimes.lean · 1008 lines · 28 public theorems · imports RadicalBound, ExponentCap

Bounds for the small prime factors. A general inequality bounds the smallest prime outside a set S of prime factors through the exact abundancy of the components in S, with corollaries for the second, third and fourth smallest prime factors. An exchange lemma gives a lower bound on ω(N) for each lower bound on the smallest prime factor: at least 7, 15, 27, 41, 62, 85, 115 prime factors when the smallest is at least 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19, 23. If 3 does not divide N, then ω(N) ≥ 8.

Proof idea. Split the prime factors into S and the rest T, with p the smallest prime of T. From 2 = HS·HT and a telescoped bound for HT over |T| primes that are at least p one gets a linear inequality for p. The exchange lemma compares a set of integers with the primes of an interval: replacing each element by a smaller prime not yet used can only increase the product of s/(s − 1), so if the first k primes from the lower bound on do not reach abundancy 2, no set of k prime factors does. The kernel computes these products. For ω(N) ≥ 8 without 3, only four supports of seven primes pass the product test, and each is excluded with the exponent restrictions that hold when 3 does not divide N.

theorem prod_div_sub_one_le_of_exchange {S T : Finset ℕ} (hS : ∀ s ∈ S, 2 ≤ s)

Exchange lemma. Let S, T be finite sets of integers ≥ 2 with |S| ≤ |T|, such that every element of S outside T is at least every element of T. Then ∏_{s ∈ S} s/(s-1) ≤ ∏_{t ∈ T} t/(t-1). For primes: a set of k primes all ≥ m has product of p/(p-1) at most that of the first k primes ≥ m.

theorem eight_le_card_primeFactors_of_not_three_dvd (h : OddPerfect N) (h3 : ¬ 3 ∣ N) :

If 3 ∤ N for an odd perfect number N, then N has at least eight distinct prime factors. With seven prime factors the support would be {5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19, q} with q ∈ {23, 29, 31, 37} (the only supports with ∏ p/(p-1) > 2); each is excluded by the exponent restrictions for 3 ∤ N (the special prime is ≡ 1 (mod 12), primes ≡ 1 (mod 3) have exponent ≢ 2 (mod 3), all other exponents are even) and a short branch and bound on the exponents of 5, 11, 13, 17, 37 with abundancy bounds only.

OddPerfect.RadicalDefect

OddPerfect/RadicalDefect.lean · 593 lines · 15 public theorems · imports RadicalBound contains novelty unverified

Write R for the product of the prime factors of N and F for the product of p − 1 over them. If every component pe + 1 is at least B³ for an odd B, then 4B³(R − 2F) < (3B + 2)R. Consequences: for every odd perfect number, 3² exactly divides N, or 5 exactly divides N, or 500(R − 2F) < 17R; analogous statements for B = 7, 9, 11; the last inequality whenever 3 does not divide N; and a certificate rule that forces a small component from a subset of the support.

Proof idea. Perfection gives 1 − 2F/R = 1 − ∏(1 − 1/y) ≤ ∑ 1/y over the components y = pe + 1. An ordinary prime above B has e ≥ 2, so its term is at most 1/p³, and the sum of 1/n³ over odd n from B + 2 on telescopes below 1/(4B²). The odd primes up to B number at most (B − 1)/2 and each contributes at most 1/B³ by hypothesis, and the special prime contributes at most 1/B³. The three parts add up to (3B + 2)/(4B³), which bounds the defect uniformly in the unknown primes. The trichotomy then lists the components below B³: for B = 5 these are 3² and 5¹.

OddPerfect.RadicalExponent

OddPerfect/RadicalExponent.lean · 663 lines · 6 public theorems · imports LargePrimes, SpecialBelow, OmegaFive

The radical R of an odd perfect number N (the product of its distinct prime factors) satisfies R < 2 N17/26, stated as R26 < 226 N17: the theorem of Luca and Pomerance (2010) for odd perfect numbers. Also R2 < N when the special exponent is not 1, and R3 < N2 outside one exceptional shape. Known mathematics.

Proof idea. Compare R2 qk with q2 N prime by prime. Then three ranges for the special prime q: small q, large q (with q3 < 3N), and a middle range where the part of N with exponents at least four is small; there the prime p with q dividing σ(p2) and the primes that feed p would make N a product of at most four prime powers, against five distinct prime factors.

OddPerfect/RadicalExponentTwo.lean · 606 lines · 3 public theorems · imports LargePrimes, OmegaFive, Cyclotomic

The radical R of an odd perfect number N satisfies R < 2 N9/14, stated as R14 < 214 N9. The exponent 9/14 is attributed to Klurman (2016); his paper was not read, so the attribution is not page checked. The proof here modifies the argument of Luca and Pomerance.

Proof idea. Same skeleton as RadicalExponent with sharper thresholds. Two new steps: σ(ue) < 2ue for the components of exponent at least four, and, when two primes t > s both feed the prime p, the difference σ(t2) − σ(s2) = (t − s)(t + s + 1) gives p ≤ 2t.

OddPerfect.OmegaSix

OddPerfect/OmegaSix.lean · 946 lines · 6 public theorems · imports Certificate, OmegaFour, SmallestPrime

An odd perfect number has at least six distinct prime factors. The proof is a search over the prime factors in increasing order, run by the kernel, with a soundness theorem for the search.

Proof idea. If 3 does not divide N there are at least seven prime factors, so 3 divides N. A state lists primes with exponents that are exact or bounded below, the number j of further primes, and a lower bound for them. Lower and upper bounds L and U for the abundancy of the listed part use σ(pk)/pk and p/(p − 1). A state closes by an abundant divisor (L > 2), by two exact odd exponents, by a factor chain (the part of an exact σ(pk) coprime to the listed primes needs unlisted prime factors, impossible when none remain or when it is too small), or, with the support fully listed, when 2 is outside the reachable range. Otherwise the smallest unlisted prime lies in a finite window, because the remaining j primes must lift U above 2, and the search tries each prime in it, or it splits one exponent into an exact value and a larger lower bound. Exact exponents force the remaining primes through their divisor sums, which also closes the families where the largest prime is not bounded in advance.

OddPerfect.LargestPrimeOrder

OddPerfect/LargestPrimeOrder.lean · 752 lines · 11 public theorems · imports AttackPrimality, ExponentCap contains novelty unverified

The largest prime factor P and the multiplicative orders of the primes that send a factor P. Results: P is not 3·4t + 1 for any t ≥ 2; P − 1 is not a power of 2; if a prime q = 3·4t + 1 with t ≥ 2 divides N, some prime factor is at least q + 3·2t(2t − 1)/2; and if P − 1 = 3·2j, every sender has order 3 and weight 1, and the exponent of P is 1, or it is 2 and both roots of x² + x + 1 below P are prime factors of N.

Proof idea. A prime p that sends a factor P has an order d modulo P with d ≥ 3, d dividing P − 1 and dividing ep + 1, and ep + 1 is not a multiple of 4. For P = 3·4t + 1 this leaves d = 3 or d = 6. With x = 2t, the two roots of z² + z + 1 modulo P are 3x(x − 1)/2 and 3x(x + 1)/2, both even for t ≥ 2, so no odd prime below P has order 3. An order 6 sender has an odd exponent, so it is the special prime, and its weight is the valuation of P in p² − p + 1, which is 1 by size. Then the exponent of P would be 1, making P special as well, a contradiction. When P − 1 is a power of 2 no order d ≥ 3 that is odd or twice odd exists at all. The exponent t = 1 is a real exception: 3 has order 3 modulo 13.

OddPerfect.SupportBridges

OddPerfect/SupportBridges.lean · 312 lines · 12 public theorems · imports Zsigmondy, ClosedLoop, ValuationBounds, Reciprocity, SpecialPrime, Pratt, Cyclotomic contains novelty unverified

Consequences of existing theorems about the set of prime factors. Call a prime of Fermat type when p − 1 is a power of 2. Every prime with even exponent has a receiver that is not of Fermat type, and at least two prime factors of N are not of Fermat type. Every prime factor has exponent 1 or a receiver modulo which its order is the exponent plus one. If the special prime s divides the component divisor sum of a prime q ≡ 3 (mod 4), then q does not divide s + 1; for q = 3 this bounds the exponent of 3 by (ω − 1)². A control set of six primes shows how small the gap R − 2F can be.

Proof idea. For an even exponent e, a primitive prime factor r of σ(pe) has p of order e + 1 modulo r, an odd number at least 3 dividing r − 1, so r is not of Fermat type. If only one prime t were not of Fermat type, t would be the special prime, and an ordinary p of Fermat type would have odd order above 1 modulo every prime factor r of σ(pe), so r would not be of Fermat type and r = t. Every ordinary component divisor sum would then be a power of t, which the closed loop theorem excludes. For the direct edge: q is a square modulo s, reciprocity with s ≡ 1 (mod 4) makes s a square modulo q, and −1 is not a square modulo q ≡ 3 (mod 4), so s ≢ −1 (mod q).

theorem factorization_eq_one_or_exists_orderOf (h : OddPerfect N) {p : ℕ}
  (hp : p ∈ N.primeFactors) :
  N.factorization p = 1 ∨
    ∃ r ∈ N.primeFactors.erase p, N.factorization p + 1 = orderOf (p : ZMod r)

Order menu: for a prime factor p of an odd perfect number, either v_p(N) = 1 or some other prime factor r has p of exact order v_p(N) + 1 modulo r.

OddPerfect.exists_not_fermatType_of_even

theorem exists_not_fermatType_of_even (h : OddPerfect N) {p : ℕ} (hp : p ∈ N.primeFactors)
  (he : Even (N.factorization p)) :
  ∃ r ∈ N.primeFactors, r ≠ p ∧ ¬ FermatType r

The order v_p(N) + 1 of p modulo r is odd, at least 3, and divides r - 1.

OddPerfect.exists_orderOf_eq_two_special

theorem exists_orderOf_eq_two_special (h : OddPerfect N) {q : ℕ} (hq : q.Prime)
  (hodd : Odd (N.factorization q)) :
  ∃ r ∈ N.primeFactors, r ≠ q ∧ r ∣ (q + 1) / 2 ∧ orderOf (q : ZMod r) = 2

Order two witness for the special prime: if q has odd exponent in an odd perfect number, some prime factor r ≠ q divides (q + 1) / 2 and q has order 2 modulo r.

OddPerfect.two_le_card_not_fermatTypenovelty unverified

theorem two_le_card_not_fermatType (h : OddPerfect N) :
  2 ≤ (N.primeFactors.filter fun r => ¬ FermatType r).card

The filter uses classical decidability.

OddPerfect.not_dvd_succ_special_of_mod_four_eq_threenovelty unverified

theorem not_dvd_succ_special_of_mod_four_eq_three (h : OddPerfect N) {s q : ℕ}
  (hs : s.Prime) (hodd : Odd (N.factorization s)) (hq : q.Prime) (hq4 : q % 4 = 3)
  (hdvd : s ∣ σ 1 (q ^ N.factorization q)) : ¬ q ∣ s + 1

An edge from a prime q ≡ 3 (mod 4) into the special prime s forces q ∤ s + 1. The exponent of q is even, so q is a square modulo s; as s ≡ 1 (mod 4), reciprocity makes s a square modulo q, while -1 is not a square modulo q. No membership or parity hypothesis on q is needed.

OddPerfect.not_three_dvd_succ_special

theorem not_three_dvd_succ_special (h : OddPerfect N) {s : ℕ} (hs : s.Prime)
  (hodd : Odd (N.factorization s)) (hdvd : s ∣ σ 1 (3 ^ N.factorization 3)) :
  ¬ 3 ∣ s + 1

An edge from 3 into the special prime s forces 3 ∤ s + 1.

OddPerfect.special_mod_three_of_dvd_sigma_three

theorem special_mod_three_of_dvd_sigma_three (h : OddPerfect N) {s : ℕ} (hs : s.Prime)
  (hodd : Odd (N.factorization s)) (hdvd : s ∣ σ 1 (3 ^ N.factorization 3)) :

OddPerfect.factorization_three_le_sq_of_dvd_sigma

theorem factorization_three_le_sq_of_dvd_sigma (h : OddPerfect N) {s : ℕ} (hs : s.Prime)
  (hodd : Odd (N.factorization s)) (hdvd : s ∣ σ 1 (3 ^ N.factorization 3)) :
  N.factorization 3 ≤ (N.primeFactors.card - 1) ^ 2

An edge from 3 into the special prime gives v_3(N) ≤ (ω(N) - 1) ^ 2.

OddPerfect.two_mul_factorization_le_of_fermat_of_dvd_sigma

theorem two_mul_factorization_le_of_fermat_of_dvd_sigma (h : OddPerfect N) {s q j : ℕ}
  (hs : s.Prime) (hodd : Odd (N.factorization s)) (hq : q.Prime) (hq2 : q ≠ 2)
  (hqj : q - 1 = 2 ^ j) (hdvd : s ∣ σ 1 (q ^ N.factorization q)) :
  2 * N.factorization q ≤ 3 * (N.primeFactors.card - 1) ^ 2

An edge from an odd Fermat type prime q into the special prime s gives 2 v_q(N) ≤ 3 (ω(N) - 1) ^ 2: with t = v_q(s + 1), the bound for Fermat type primes gives v_q(N) ≤ (ω(N) - 1) ^ 2 + t, and 3 t ≤ v_q(N).

OddPerfect.prime_4294967291

theorem prime_4294967291 : Nat.Prime 4294967291

4294967291 = 2 ^ 32 - 5 is prime, by a Pratt certificate.

OddPerfect.control_support_facts

theorem control_support_facts :
  (∀ p ∈ ({3, 5, 17, 257, 65537, 4294967291} : Finset ℕ), p.Prime) ∧
    (∏ p ∈ ({3, 5, 17, 257, 65537, 4294967291} : Finset ℕ), p) = 18446744047939747845 ∧
    (∏ p ∈ ({3, 5, 17, 257, 65537, 4294967291} : Finset ℕ), p) -
        2 * (∏ p ∈ ({3, 5, 17, 257, 65537, 4294967291} : Finset ℕ), (p - 1)) = 5

Control only. The set {3, 5, 17, 257, 65537, 4294967291} consists of primes, its product R is 18446744047939747845, and with F the product of p - 1 over the set, R - 2 F = 5. This shows that the integrality gap of a squarefree odd radical can be tiny. The set is not the support of an odd perfect number (see primeFactors_ne_control); it is only a control.

OddPerfect.LargestPrimeFactor

OddPerfect/LargestPrimeFactor.lean · 687 lines · 3 public theorems · imports ExponentCap, Abundancy

An odd perfect number has a prime factor above 10000. The proof is a search with a soundness theorem valid for every bound B, run by the kernel for B = 10000.

Proof idea. Suppose every prime factor is at most B. A prime known to divide N branches on its exponent e, which must satisfy 2e + 3 ≤ B and Euler's parity rule, and σ(pe) must have only prime factors up to B that are not excluded. An odd exponent is rejected when another prime already has one. The odd prime factors of σ(pe) are then forced to divide N. When no forced prime is left to treat, the smallest undecided prime is split into dividing and not dividing. A branch closes when the recorded exponents alone give an abundant divisor, or when the product of the abundancy bounds over all primes up to B that are not excluded is below 2, with σ(qe)/qe for a prime with exact exponent and q/(q − 1) otherwise. That product is computed from two fixed products over all primes up to B, corrected at the recorded and the excluded primes.

Public theorems

OddPerfect.LPF.search_sound

theorem search_sound (h : OddPerfect N) (hB : ∀ r ∈ N.primeFactors, r ≤ B)
  {T : List (ℕ × List ℕ)} (hT : ∀ x ∈ T, x.2 = row B (2 * (primesUpTo B).prod) x.1) :
  ∀ fuel ex dv nd, search B (primesUpTo B) (2 * (primesUpTo B).prod)
    ((primesUpTo B).map (· - 1)).prod T fuel ex dv nd = true →
    Holds N ex dv nd → Inv (primesUpTo B) ex dv nd → False

Soundness of the search: an accepted search excludes every odd perfect number with all prime factors at most B that satisfies the state.

OddPerfect.LPF.exists_primeFactor_gt_of_search

theorem exists_primeFactor_gt_of_search {B : ℕ} {P : List ℕ} {M D : ℕ}
  {T : List (ℕ × List ℕ)}
  (hP : primesUpTo B = P) (hM : 2 * P.prod = M) (hD : (P.map (· - 1)).prod = D)
  (hT : T.all (fun x => x.2 == row B M x.1))
  (hs : search B P M D T 1000 [] [] [] = true)
  (h : OddPerfect N) : ∃ p ∈ N.primeFactors, B < p

An accepted search for B gives a prime factor above B. The list P, the numbers M = 2 ∏ P and D = ∏ (q - 1) over P (the odd primes up to B), and the row table T are given explicitly and checked.

OddPerfect.exists_primeFactor_gt

theorem exists_primeFactor_gt {N : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N) : ∃ p ∈ N.primeFactors, 10000 < p

The largest prime factor of an odd perfect number exceeds 10000.

OddPerfect.SpecialFiveCode

OddPerfect/SpecialFiveCode.lean · 108 lines · 0 public theorems · imports DefectTreeCode

A checker for search trees over exact exponents, for odd perfect numbers in which 5 has exponent 1 and every prime power component is at most a bound B. Definitions only.

Proof idea. A node is a list of primes with exact exponents, starting from 5 with exponent 1. Leaves: more factors of a prime sent by the rows than its exponent holds, an abundant divisor, or a forced prime whose square exceeds B. Branches run over the even exponents of a forced prime while its power stays at most B.

OddPerfect.SpecialFiveCheck

OddPerfect/SpecialFiveCheck.lean · 217 lines · 2 public theorems · imports SpecialFiveCode, DefectTreeCheck

Soundness of the checker: an accepted certificate proves that some component of N exceeds B.

Proof idea. Induction over the tree with the invariant that every listed prime divides N with the listed exponent; the fact table and the Pratt certificates are those of the defect tree checker.

  ∀ (c : Cert) (st : List (ℕ × ℕ)) (m : Mode), go B tab c st m = true → Inv N m st →

OddPerfect.SpecialFive.check_sound

theorem check_sound {B : ℕ} {pc : PCert} {tab : Tab} {c : Cert}
  (hc : check B pc tab c = true) {N : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N) (h5 : N.factorization 5 = 1) :
  ∃ p ∈ N.primeFactors, B < p ^ N.factorization p

Soundness of the checker: if check B pc tab c = true, then every odd perfect number N with v_5(N) = 1 has a prime factor p whose component p ^ v_p(N) exceeds B.

OddPerfect.SpecialFiveMore

OddPerfect/SpecialFiveMore.lean · 992 lines · 95 public theorems · imports SpecialFiveCheck, SpecialFiveMoreLemmas, SpecialFiveMoreTree0, SpecialFiveMoreTree1, SpecialFiveMoreTree2

An odd perfect number with v5(N) = 1 has a prime power component above 1033.

Proof idea. Written by scripts/SpecialFiveMore/gen.py. The upper nodes of the search tree are glued to the subtrees of the three tree modules, which gives check_cert, and the landed soundness theorem SpecialFive.check_sound gives the statement. The search is the factor chain method: σ(5) = 6 forces 3, and each component pe below the bound forces the prime factors of σ(pe). A special case of Ochem and Rao (Math. Comp. 81, 2012), who proved a component above 10^62 for every odd perfect number; no novelty is claimed.

OddPerfect.LargestPrimeFactorTwo

OddPerfect/LargestPrimeFactorTwo.lean · 881 lines · 4 public theorems · imports LargestPrimeFactor

A cheaper way for the kernel to accept the table of the largest prime factor search: each row of the table is proved correct from a certificate that passes a cheap check, in place of recomputing the row. Proves that an accepted search with certified rows gives a prime factor above the bound B.

Proof idea. A row lists the exponents e of a prime p for which σ(pe) may have only prime factors up to B. For every other exponent the certificate gives data from which the check shows that σ(pe) has a prime factor above B. The list of odd primes up to B is checked by trial division up to the square root of B.

Public theorems

OddPerfect.LPF2.primesUpTo_eq_filter

theorem primesUpTo_eq_filter {B K : ℕ} (hK : B < (K + 1) * (K + 1)) :
  primesUpTo B = (List.range (B + 1)).filter
    (fun n => !Nat.beq n 2 && primeBy (2 :: primesUpTo K) n)

The odd primes up to B by trial division by 2 and the odd primes up to K, when B < (K + 1) ^ 2.

OddPerfect.LPF2.rowOK_sound

theorem rowOK_sound {B XU : ℕ} {L : List ℕ}
  {c : ℕ × List ℕ × List ℕ × List (ℕ × ℕ) × List (ℕ × ℕ)} (hB : B ≤ 2 ^ 21)
  (hL : listOK XU ((B - 3) / 2) L = true)
  (h : rowOK B (2 * (primesUpTo B).prod) XU (primesUpTo B) L c = true) :
  RowCover B c.1 c.2.1

A row certificate accepted by rowOK gives the meaning RowCover of its row.

OddPerfect.LPF2.search_sound

theorem search_sound (h : OddPerfect N) (hB : ∀ r ∈ N.primeFactors, r ≤ B)
  {T : List (ℕ × List ℕ)} (hT : ∀ x ∈ T, RowCover B x.1 x.2) :
  ∀ fuel ex dv nd, search B (primesUpTo B) (2 * (primesUpTo B).prod)
    ((primesUpTo B).map (· - 1)).prod T fuel ex dv nd = true →
    Holds N ex dv nd → Inv (primesUpTo B) ex dv nd → False

Soundness of the search when the rows of the table cover the admissible exponents.

OddPerfect.LPF2.exists_primeFactor_gt_of_cert

theorem exists_primeFactor_gt_of_cert {B : ℕ} {P : List ℕ} {M D XU : ℕ} {L : List ℕ}
  {T : List (ℕ × List ℕ)} {C : List (ℕ × List ℕ × List ℕ × List (ℕ × ℕ) × List (ℕ × ℕ))}
  (hP : primesUpTo B = P) (hM : 2 * P.prod = M) (hD : (P.map (· - 1)).prod = D)
  (hB : B ≤ 2 ^ 21) (hTC : C.map (fun c => (c.1, c.2.1)) = T)
  (hL : listOK XU ((B - 3) / 2) L = true) (hC : C.all (rowOK B M XU P L) = true)
  (hs : search B P M D T 1000 [] [] [] = true)
  (h : OddPerfect N) : ∃ p ∈ N.primeFactors, B < p

An accepted search with certified rows gives a prime factor above B. The list P of odd primes up to B, the numbers M = 2 ∏ P and D = ∏ (q - 1), the certificates C, from which the table T is read off, and the list L are given explicitly and checked.

OddPerfect.LargestPrimeFactorThree

OddPerfect/LargestPrimeFactorThree.lean · 801 lines · 7 public theorems · imports LargestPrimeFactorTwo

A cheaper row certificate for the largest prime factor search: for each odd prime r a product Mr of the primes q up to the bound with q ≡ 1 (mod 2r) is fixed once, and a row is accepted from σ(pr−1) modulo Mr together with a size bound. Also three step lemmas that join a search from separately checked subtrees.

Proof idea. A prime factor of σ(pr−1) is r or is 1 modulo 2r, so only the primes in Mr matter below the bound; one modular power replaces the full number.

Public theorems

OddPerfect.LPF3.primesUpTo_eq_filterG

theorem primesUpTo_eq_filterG {B K Q : ℕ} (hK2 : 2 ≤ K) (hK : B < (K + 1) * (K + 1))
  (hQ : 2 * (primesUpTo K).prod = Q) :
  primesUpTo B = (List.range (B + 1)).filter (fun n => !Nat.beq n 2 && primeG Q K n)

The odd primes up to B by primeG (trial division up to K, a greatest common divisor with Q = 2 ∏ primesUpTo K above), when B < (K + 1) ^ 2.

OddPerfect.LPF3.drOK_good

theorem drOK_good {B K Q : ℕ} {DR : List (ℕ × ℕ)} (hK2 : 2 ≤ K) (hK : B < (K + 1) * (K + 1))
  (hQ : 2 * (primesUpTo K).prod = Q) (h : drOK B Q K (primesUpTo B) DR = true) :
  DRGood B DR

Soundness of the global check drOK over the odd primes up to B.

OddPerfect.LPF3.rowOK3_sound

theorem rowOK3_sound {B XU : ℕ} {DR : List (ℕ × ℕ)} {L : List ℕ}
  {c : ℕ × List ℕ × List ℕ × List (ℕ × ℕ) × List (ℕ × ℕ)} (hB : B ≤ 2 ^ 21)
  (hDR : DRGood B DR) (hL : listOK XU ((B - 3) / 2) L = true)
  (h : rowOK3 (2 * (primesUpTo B).prod) XU DR L c = true) :
  RowCover B c.1 c.2.1

A row certificate accepted by rowOK3 gives the meaning LPF2.RowCover of its row.

OddPerfect.LPF3.search_nil

theorem search_nil {B : ℕ} {P : List ℕ} {M D : ℕ} {T : List (ℕ × List ℕ)} {fuel : ℕ}
  {ex : List (ℕ × ℕ)} {nd : List ℕ} {q : ℕ}
  (hf : (P.filter (fun q => !memF q ex && !memB q nd)).head? = some q)
  (h1 : search B P M D T fuel ex [q] nd = true)
  (h2 : search B P M D T fuel ex [] (q :: nd) = true) :
  search B P M D T (fuel + 1) ex [] nd = true

One step of LPF.search with no pending divisor: the first undecided prime q either divides N or not.

OddPerfect.LPF3.search_cons_old

theorem search_cons_old {B : ℕ} {P : List ℕ} {M D : ℕ} {T : List (ℕ × List ℕ)} {fuel : ℕ}
  {ex : List (ℕ × ℕ)} {p : ℕ} {rest nd : List ℕ} (hm : memF p ex = true)
  (h : search B P M D T fuel ex rest nd = true) :
  search B P M D T (fuel + 1) ex (p :: rest) nd = true

One step of LPF.search at a pending divisor p whose exponent is already fixed.

OddPerfect.LPF3.search_cons_all

theorem search_cons_all {B : ℕ} {P : List ℕ} {M D : ℕ} {T : List (ℕ × List ℕ)} {fuel : ℕ}
  {ex : List (ℕ × ℕ)} {p : ℕ} {rest nd es : List ℕ} (hm : memF p ex = false)
  (hc : cands nd p (getRow B M T p) = es)
  (h : ∀ e ∈ es, (Nat.beq (e % 2) 1 && ex.any fun x => Nat.beq (x.2 % 2) 1) = true ∨
    search B P M D T fuel ((p, e) :: ex) (newPrimes P (gs p e) ++ rest) nd = true) :
  search B P M D T (fuel + 1) ex (p :: rest) nd = true

It suffices that every e of es is excluded by parity or the search succeeds after it.

OddPerfect.LPF3.exists_primeFactor_gt_of_cert3

theorem exists_primeFactor_gt_of_cert3 {B K Q : ℕ} {P : List ℕ} {M D XU : ℕ} {L : List ℕ}
  {DR : List (ℕ × ℕ)} {T : List (ℕ × List ℕ)}
  {C : List (ℕ × List ℕ × List ℕ × List (ℕ × ℕ) × List (ℕ × ℕ))}
  (hP : primesUpTo B = P) (hM : 2 * P.prod = M) (hD : (P.map (· - 1)).prod = D)
  (hB : B ≤ 2 ^ 21) (hK2 : 2 ≤ K) (hK : B < (K + 1) * (K + 1))
  (hQ : 2 * (primesUpTo K).prod = Q) (hDR : drOK B Q K P DR = true)
  (hTC : C.map (fun c => (c.1, c.2.1)) = T)
  (hL : listOK XU ((B - 3) / 2) L = true) (hC : C.all (rowOK3 M XU DR L) = true)
  (hs : search B P M D T 1000 [] [] [] = true)
  (h : OddPerfect N) : ∃ p ∈ N.primeFactors, B < p

An accepted search with rows certified by rowOK3 gives a prime factor above B. The list P of odd primes up to B, the numbers M = 2 ∏ P, D = ∏ (q - 1) and Q = 2 ∏ primesUpTo K, the global list DR, the certificates C, from which the table T is read off, and the list L are given explicitly and checked.

OddPerfect.LargestPrimeFactorThreeFinal

OddPerfect/LargestPrimeFactorThreeFinal.lean · 67 lines · 2 public theorems · imports LargestPrimeFactorThreeSearch1, LargestPrimeFactorThreeSearch2, LargestPrimeFactorThreeSearch3, LargestPrimeFactorThreeSearch4

An odd perfect number has a prime factor above 200000. Known mathematics: the published bounds are 106 (Hagis and Cohen), 107 (Jenkins) and 108 (Goto and Ohno); they are not proved here.

Proof idea. The search of LargestPrimeFactor for the bound 200000 is assembled from its top steps and the subtrees run by the kernel, on the table read off the certified rows.

OddPerfect.ReciprocalSum

OddPerfect/ReciprocalSum.lean · 538 lines · 16 public theorems · imports Abundancy, SpecialPrime

Bounds for the sum of the reciprocals of the prime factors: 23/40 < ∑ 1/p < 347/500, and log 2 < ∑ 1/(p − 1). The upper bound is the rational form of ∑ 1/p < log 2 + 1/29 − log(30/29).

Proof idea. For the lower bound, 2 = σ(N)/N is below the product of p/(p − 1), so log 2 is below the sum of log(p/(p − 1)). The difference log(p/(p − 1)) − 1/p is bounded explicitly at the primes up to 19 and by a telescoping sum over odd numbers from 23 on, and 3, 5 and 7 cannot all divide N. For the upper bound, an ordinary prime has exponent at least 2, so its component is at least 1 + 1/p + 1/p², whose logarithm exceeds 1/p; the special prime q gives 1 + 1/q. Hence ∑ 1/p is at most log 2 plus 1/q − log(1 + 1/q), minus the slack of the ordinary primes. The term for q decreases in q. For q = 5 and q = 17 the prime 3 divides N and its slack is larger, for q = 13 the prime 7 divides N, and otherwise q ≥ 29.

OddPerfect.LowerBound

OddPerfect/LowerBound.lean · 10585 lines · 43 public theorems · imports Euler, Seed.Example, Seed.Starter, Pratt, OmegaFive, SmallestPrime

Every odd perfect number exceeds 1079. The module defines a proof tree language for lower bounds on N with a soundness theorem, and the kernel checks three trees. A bound that needs no search is also proved: N ≥ 4002075.

Proof idea. A state is a list of facts about N: a prime power divides N, a number divides an exponent plus one, an exponent is exact, or a prime does not divide N. A branch splits the exponent of a prime, forces a prime power qk that divides the product of the known component divisor sums (using σ(N) = 2N and that σ(pa) divides σ(pe) when a + 1 divides e + 1), or passes from an odd exponent to the next even one. A leaf closes when the least common multiple of the recorded prime powers and half the product of the divisor sums, which divides N, exceeds the bound; or by a contradiction: an excluded prime divides N, an exact exponent is exceeded, two primes have odd exponent, or a divisor is abundant. The trees cover the cases 3 divides N; 5 divides N and 3 does not; 7 divides N and 3, 5 do not. If no prime below 11 divides N, the product of t/(t − 1) over the primes from 11 to 127 is below 2, so N has at least 27 prime factors, which gives the bound directly. All primes used for forcing come from one table of primality certificates that is checked once.

OddPerfect.LowerBoundTwoTablePrime

OddPerfect/LowerBoundTwoTablePrime.lean · 796 lines · 129 public theorems · imports LowerBoundTwoTableOk1, LowerBoundTwoTableOk2

Part of the kernel checked lower bound 10150. The statement that every entry of the table is prime, assembled from the two halves.

Proof idea. Combines the chunk checks into one lemma used by the tree runner.

Public theorems

OddPerfect.LowerBoundTwo.allOK_node

theorem allOK_node {T l r : PT} {p a : ℕ} {fs : List (ℕ × ℕ)} (h : entryOK T p a fs = true)
  (hl : PT.allOK T l = true) (hr : PT.allOK T r = true) :
  PT.allOK T (PT.node l p a fs r) = true

A node of the table is valid when its entry and both subtrees are.

OddPerfect.LowerBoundTwo

OddPerfect/LowerBoundTwo.lean · 268 lines · 6 public theorems · imports LowerBoundTwoTree1, LowerBoundTwoTree2, LowerBoundTwoTree3, LowerBoundTwoTree4

Every odd perfect number exceeds 10150. Also: an odd perfect number with no prime factor below 13 has at least 41 distinct prime factors. Known mathematics; the literature reaches 101500 (Ochem and Rao, 2012).

Proof idea. The factor chain method with the proof tree checker of LowerBound: roots 3, 5, 7 and 11 are closed by trees with 40986 instructions in all; an odd perfect number with none of these primes has so many prime factors that it exceeds the bound by counting.

OddPerfect.OmegaSeven

OddPerfect/OmegaSeven.lean · 637 lines · 9 public theorems · imports OmegaSix, SpecialPrime

Partial results for exactly six distinct prime factors, used by the final theorem in OmegaSevenFinal: if an odd perfect number has exactly six distinct prime factors, then 3 and 5 divide it, and its third smallest prime factor is one of 11, 13, 17, 19, 23, 29, 31.

Proof idea. The search of OmegaSix is reused. A state is called closed when no odd perfect number satisfies it. A state is closed when the search closes it, or when every candidate for the next prime in its finite window gives a closed state. This splits one large search into separate leaves, each checked by the kernel on its own. The leaves cover the cases without 5, with 3 and 7, and with 3 and 5 and third prime above 31. The cases with third prime from 11 to 31 need far more search than the kernel can run here, and the case 3, 5, 17 does not close by this search at all, because the abundancy bound for Fermat primes stays below 2 for every exponent.

A state with a bounded next prime is closed when every child in its window is closed.

OddPerfect.exists_prime_dvd_of_card_eq_six

theorem exists_prime_dvd_of_card_eq_six {N : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N)
  (h6 : N.primeFactors.card = 6) :
  3 ∣ N ∧ 5 ∣ N ∧ ∃ p, p.Prime ∧ 11 ≤ p ∧ p ≤ 31 ∧ p ∣ N

An odd perfect number with exactly six distinct prime factors is divisible by 3, by 5, and by a prime p with 11 ≤ p ≤ 31. Equivalently, its third smallest prime factor is one of 11, 13, 17, 19, 23, 29, 31 (it is not 7, since 105 ∤ N).

OddPerfect.OmegaSevenFermat

OddPerfect/OmegaSevenFermat.lean · 111 lines · 3 public theorems · imports OmegaSeven

One more case for exactly six prime factors: if 17 divides N and 11 and 13 do not, some prime factor lies strictly between 17 and 601. So when 3, 5, 17 are the three smallest prime factors, the fourth smallest is below 601. The case is not excluded.

Proof idea. The state with 3, 5, 17 and a fourth prime above 600 has a finite window for that prime, the primes from 601 to 761, because three more primes must lift the abundancy to 2. The kernel checks one search per prime of the window.

theorem exists_prime_dvd_of_card_eq_six_of_seventeen {N : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N)
  (h6 : N.primeFactors.card = 6) (h17 : 17 ∣ N) (h11 : ¬ 11 ∣ N) (h13 : ¬ 13 ∣ N) :
  ∃ p, p.Prime ∧ 17 < p ∧ p < 601 ∧ p ∣ N

If 3, 5, 17 are the three smallest prime factors of an odd perfect number N with exactly six distinct prime factors (that is, 17 ∣ N, 11 ∤ N and 13 ∤ N; then 3, 5 ∣ N by fifteen_dvd_of_card_eq_six and 7 ∤ N since 105 ∤ N), then some prime p with 17 < p < 601 divides N.

OddPerfect.ReciprocalLogTwo

OddPerfect/ReciprocalLogTwo.lean · 157 lines · 6 public theorems · imports ReciprocalSum, SpecialPrime, SupportBridges

The sum of the reciprocals of the prime factors of an odd perfect number is below log 2. This is a classical result. The module proves a sharper form that keeps correction terms: with q the special prime and U any set of ordinary prime factors, the sum is at most log 2 + 1/(2q²) minus a quarter of the sum of 1/p² over U.

Proof idea. Take logarithms in σ(N) = 2N. An ordinary prime p contributes at least log(1 + 1/p + 1/p²), which is at least 1/p + 1/(4p²). The special prime contributes at least log(1 + 1/q), which is at least 1/q minus 1/(2q²). Some ordinary prime r divides (q + 1)/2, so its correction 1/(4r²) is at least 1/(q + 1)², which exceeds the loss 1/(2q²).

OddPerfect.sum_inv_le_log_two_add_sub

theorem sum_inv_le_log_two_add_sub (h : OddPerfect N) {q : ℕ} (hq : q.Prime)
  (hodd : Odd (N.factorization q)) {U : Finset ℕ} (hU : U ⊆ N.primeFactors.erase q) :
  ∑ p ∈ N.primeFactors, 1 / (p : ℝ) ≤
    Real.log 2 + 1 / (2 * (q : ℝ) ^ 2) - (1 / 4) * ∑ p ∈ U, 1 / (p : ℝ) ^ 2

Main lemma: for an odd perfect number with special prime q and any set U of prime factors of N other than q, ∑_{p ∣ N} 1/p ≤ log 2 + 1/(2q²) - (1/4) ∑_{p ∈ U} 1/p².

OddPerfect.sum_inv_le_log_two_add_gap

theorem sum_inv_le_log_two_add_gap (h : OddPerfect N) {q : ℕ} (hq : q.Prime)
  (hodd : Odd (N.factorization q)) :
  ∑ p ∈ N.primeFactors, 1 / (p : ℝ) ≤
    Real.log 2 + 1 / (2 * (q : ℝ) ^ 2) - 1 / ((q : ℝ) + 1) ^ 2

Gap form: for an odd perfect number with special prime q, ∑_{p ∣ N} 1/p ≤ log 2 + 1/(2q²) - 1/(q + 1)².

  ∑ p ∈ N.primeFactors, 1 / (p : ℝ) < Real.log 2

For an odd perfect number N, ∑_{p ∣ N} 1/p < log 2.

OddPerfect.LargestPrimeCapacity

OddPerfect/LargestPrimeCapacity.lean · 414 lines · 8 public theorems · imports LargestPrimeOrder contains novelty unverified

A bound for the exponent of the largest prime factor P in terms of the odd part m of P − 1: the exponent is at most the sum of φ(d)(φ(d) − 1) over the divisors d > 1 of m, and at most m − 1 primes p have P dividing σ(pe). The cases m = 1 and m = 3 recover the two results of LargestPrimeOrder. For large m the bound is weaker than the general exponent cap. Whether this statement is in the literature was not checked.

Proof idea. A prime p that sends a factor P has order t modulo P with t ≥ 3, t not divisible by 4 and t below P. So t is d or 2d with d odd, and p or −p has order exactly d. This signed residue determines p, because two odd numbers below P never add up to P, and there are φ(d) residues of order d. The power of P in σ(pe) equals the power of P in the cyclotomic value Φt(p), which lies below (p + 1)φ(t) ≤ Pφ(t), so it is at most φ(d) − 1.

OddPerfect.padicValNat_pow_orderOf_sub_one_lt_totient

theorem padicValNat_pow_orderOf_sub_one_lt_totient {p P : ℕ} (hp : p.Prime) (hP : P.Prime)
  (hpP : p < P) (ht : 3 ≤ orderOf (p : ZMod P)) :
  padicValNat P (p ^ orderOf (p : ZMod P) - 1) < (orderOf (p : ZMod P)).totient

Weight bound: if p < P are primes and the order t of p modulo P is at least 3, then v_P(p ^ t - 1) < φ(t). Only the factor Φ_t(p) of p ^ t - 1 is divisible by P, and Φ_t(p) < (p + 1) ^ φ(t) ≤ P ^ φ(t).

OddPerfect.sender_largest_data

theorem sender_largest_data (h : OddPerfect N) {P p : ℕ} (hP : P ∈ N.primeFactors)
  (hmax : ∀ r ∈ N.primeFactors, r ≤ P) (hp : p ∈ N.primeFactors) (hpP : p ≠ P)
  (hd : P ∣ σ 1 (p ^ N.factorization p)) :
  p < P ∧ p % 2 = 1 ∧ 3 ≤ orderOf (p : ZMod P) ∧ ¬ 4 ∣ orderOf (p : ZMod P) ∧
    padicValNat P (σ 1 (p ^ N.factorization p)) =
      padicValNat P (p ^ orderOf (p : ZMod P) - 1)

Data of a sender p into the largest prime factor P: p < P, p odd, its order t modulo P satisfies 3 ≤ t, 4 ∤ t, and the weight is v_P(p ^ t - 1).

theorem factorization_largest_le_sum_totient (h : OddPerfect N) {P a m : ℕ}
  (hP : P ∈ N.primeFactors) (hmax : ∀ r ∈ N.primeFactors, r ≤ P)
  (hm : P - 1 = 2 ^ a * m) (hmo : Odd m) :
  N.factorization P ≤ ∑ d ∈ m.divisors.erase 1, d.totient * (d.totient - 1)

Capacity of the largest prime factor. Let P be the largest prime factor of an odd perfect number N and P - 1 = 2 ^ a · m with m odd. Then e_P ≤ Σ_{d ∣ m, d ≠ 1} φ(d) (φ(d) - 1).

theorem card_senders_largest_le (h : OddPerfect N) {P a m : ℕ}
  (hP : P ∈ N.primeFactors) (hmax : ∀ r ∈ N.primeFactors, r ≤ P)
  (hm : P - 1 = 2 ^ a * m) (hmo : Odd m) :
  ((N.primeFactors.erase P).filter (fun p => P ∣ σ 1 (p ^ N.factorization p))).card ≤
    m - 1

Number of senders into the largest prime factor P with P - 1 = 2 ^ a · m, m odd: at most m - 1, since Σ_{d ∣ m, d ≠ 1} φ(d) = m - 1.

OddPerfect.largest_sub_one_odd_part_ne_one

theorem largest_sub_one_odd_part_ne_one (h : OddPerfect N) {P : ℕ}
  (hP : P ∈ N.primeFactors) (hmax : ∀ r ∈ N.primeFactors, r ≤ P) (a : ℕ) :

Regression test, the case m = 1: the largest prime factor P of an odd perfect number does not have P - 1 = 2 ^ a. The capacity sum is empty, so e_P = 0.

  (hP : P ∈ N.primeFactors) (hmax : ∀ r ∈ N.primeFactors, r ≤ P) (ha : P - 1 = 2 ^ a * 3) :
  N.factorization P ≤ 2

Regression test, the case m = 3: if P - 1 = 2 ^ a · 3 for the largest prime factor P, then e_P ≤ φ(3) (φ(3) - 1) = 2.

OddPerfect.SecondLargestPrime

OddPerfect/SecondLargestPrime.lean · 1227 lines · 5 public theorems · imports LargestPrimeFactor

The search engine for two distinct prime factors above a bound B, with its soundness proof. The bounds themselves (72, and 58 as a corollary) are proved in SecondLargestPrimeTwo. Much larger bounds for the second largest prime factor are known in the literature; this is the range the kernel checks here.

Proof idea. Let P₀ be a prime factor above 3000, which exists by LargestPrimeFactor, and suppose every other prime factor is at most B. Each prime up to B is undecided, excluded, has an exponent bounded below, or has an exact exponent. Upper and lower bounds for the abundancy of the small part confine P₀ to a window, since the factor contributed by P₀ lies between 1 + 1/P₀ and P₀/(P₀ − 1). For an exact exponent k of p, the part of σ(pk) coprime to the small primes is a power of P₀, which determines P₀. A short window is enumerated. Once P₀ is fixed, the remaining conditions are finite: every σ(pk) is supported on the small primes and P₀, and σ of the power of P₀ is supported on the small primes. The search is a stack machine with a soundness theorem, and the kernel runs it in nine chunks with the intermediate stacks as literals.
