OddPerfect.OmegaSevenEngine

OddPerfect/OmegaSevenEngine.lean · 1296 lines · 7 public theorems · imports OmegaSeven

A second verified search engine for odd perfect numbers with exactly six distinct prime factors, with a soundness theorem against the same states as OmegaSix. It needs far fewer search nodes than the first engine and each node is cheaper for the kernel. It is the tool for the theorem that an odd perfect number has at least seven distinct prime factors, proved in OmegaSevenFinal.

Proof idea. A state lists some prime factors with exact or minimal exponents and says how many further prime factors there are, all above a bound. New rules: if an exponent is exact, the part of σ(pk) not made of listed primes consists of unlisted prime factors of N, so the state dies when that part has a small prime factor or is itself below the bound, and when that part must be prime it is added to the list; the next unlisted prime is bounded from below for any number of missing primes; small exponents are split before the next prime is enumerated; exact exponents that fail a local test are skipped. The definitions use structural recursors and closed forms for the geometric sums, which the kernel evaluates several times faster.

OddPerfect/OmegaSevenPilot.lean · 26 lines · 1 public theorem · imports OmegaSevenEngine

One kernel run of the new engine: an odd perfect number with exactly six distinct prime factors cannot have 3, 5 and 13 as its three smallest prime factors.

Proof idea. A single decide +kernel on the state with 3, 5, 13 listed and three further primes above 13. The search visits about 4400 nodes.

OddPerfect.OmegaSevenSplit

OddPerfect/OmegaSevenSplit.lean · 152 lines · 5 public theorems · imports OmegaSevenEngine

Lemmas that cut one search of the engine into several smaller kernel runs: a split of an exponent into exactly k or at least the next admissible value, and a cover of the range of the next prime by contiguous intervals, each closed by one kernel run.

Proof idea. Kernel memory grows with the size of a single run, not with the number of runs in a file. Cutting at the split points the engine itself would choose keeps every run below 6000 search nodes.

OddPerfect.OmegaSevenSplit.closed_of_split

theorem closed_of_split {pre post : List Ent} {j m p k k' : ℕ} (hk : nextValid p k = k')
  (h1 : Closed (pre ++ ⟨p, k, true⟩ :: post) j m)
  (h2 : Closed (pre ++ ⟨p, k', false⟩ :: post) j m) :
  Closed (pre ++ ⟨p, k, false⟩ :: post) j m

An exponent split: a state with the inexact entry (p, k) is closed when the state with the exact exponent k and the state with the inexact exponent nextValid p k are closed.

OddPerfect.OmegaSevenRootsA

OddPerfect/OmegaSevenRootsA.lean · 692 lines · 38 public theorems · imports OmegaSevenSplit

Kernel runs of the search engine for exactly six distinct prime factors: the prefixes 3, 5, p for p in 11, 19, 23, 29, 31, 37 to 61 and 3, 5, 17, q for q from 19 to 137. Each statement says that no odd perfect number with exactly six prime factors has the listed primes as its smallest prime factors (with the listed exponent information).

Proof idea. Generated by a script from a cut plan computed with an exact mirror of the engine. The four files hold 280 kernel runs and more than 200,000 search nodes in total.

Kernel runs of the search engine for exactly six distinct prime factors: the prefixes 3, 5, 17, q for q from 139 to 251 and the first part of q = 257. Each statement says that no odd perfect number with exactly six prime factors has the listed primes as its smallest prime factors (with the listed exponent information).

Proof idea. Generated by a script from a cut plan computed with an exact mirror of the engine. The four files hold 280 kernel runs and more than 200,000 search nodes in total.

OddPerfect.OmegaSevenRootsC

OddPerfect/OmegaSevenRootsC.lean · 447 lines · 16 public theorems · imports OmegaSevenRootsB

Kernel runs of the search engine for exactly six distinct prime factors: the rest of the prefix 3, 5, 17, 257 and the prefix 3, 5, 17, 263. Each statement says that no odd perfect number with exactly six prime factors has the listed primes as its smallest prime factors (with the listed exponent information).

Proof idea. Generated by a script from a cut plan computed with an exact mirror of the engine. The four files hold 280 kernel runs and more than 200,000 search nodes in total.

OddPerfect.OmegaSevenFinal

OddPerfect/OmegaSevenFinal.lean · 132 lines · 3 public theorems · imports OmegaSevenRootsD, OmegaSevenPilot

An odd perfect number has at least seven distinct prime factors. This is the theorem of Pomerance (Acta Arith. 25, 1973/74). The bound eight (Chein 1979, Hagis 1980) is not proved here.

Proof idea. By OmegaSix there are at least six. If there are exactly six, then 3 and 5 divide N and 7 does not (105 ∤ N), so the remaining four primes exceed 7. Enumerating the third prime (11 to 61) and, after 3, 5, 17, the fourth prime (19 to 761) reduces everything to the runs in OmegaSevenRootsA to OmegaSevenRootsD and OmegaSevenPilot.

Public theorems

OddPerfect.OmegaSevenFinal.closed_3_5_17

theorem closed_3_5_17 : Closed [⟨3, 2, false⟩, ⟨5, 1, false⟩, ⟨17, 1, false⟩] 3 17

Six prime factors with 3, 5, 17 the three smallest is impossible.

OddPerfect.OmegaSevenFinal.closed_3_5

theorem closed_3_5 : Closed [⟨3, 2, false⟩, ⟨5, 1, false⟩] 4 7

Six prime factors with 3, 5 the two smallest and all others above 7 is impossible.

An odd perfect number has at least seven distinct prime factors.

OddPerfect.OmegaSevenFiveSeven

OddPerfect/OmegaSevenFiveSeven.lean · 148 lines · 6 public theorems · imports OmegaSevenSplit, SmallPrimes

An odd perfect number with exactly seven distinct prime factors is divisible by 5 or by 7. This is a known consequence of the theorem of Chein and Hagis that an odd perfect number has at least eight distinct prime factors, which the library does not prove. The cases where 5 or 7 divides N are not treated.

Proof idea. By the three free theorem 3 divides N. If neither 5 nor 7 divides N, the six further primes all exceed 7, and the abundancy window leaves 11, 13, 17 or 19 for the least of them. Each of the four cases is closed by the verified engine of the seven prime theorem, cut into kernel checks of at most 6000 search nodes; the case 11 needs 6 checks, the others one each.

OddPerfect.NotThreeNine

OddPerfect/NotThreeNine.lean · 170 lines · 2 public theorems · imports OmegaSevenEngine, SmallPrimes

An odd perfect number not divisible by 3 has at least nine distinct prime factors. Known mathematics: Hagis and Kishore (1983) proved eleven and Nielsen (2007) twelve; only nine is proved here.

Proof idea. At least eight is already in SmallPrimes, so only exactly eight prime factors, all above 4, must be excluded. The abundancy window leaves 5, 7 or 11 for the least prime; windows of the next prime are applied until every case is small, and each case is closed by one kernel check of the verified search engine of the seven prime theorem. No fact beyond the cuts of that engine is used.

Public theorems

OddPerfect.NotThreeNine.closed_root

theorem closed_root :
  Closed [] 8 4

Exactly eight prime factors, none of them 3, is impossible.

OddPerfect.nine_le_card_primeFactors_of_not_three_dvd

theorem nine_le_card_primeFactors_of_not_three_dvd {N : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N) (h3 : ¬ 3 ∣ N) :
  9 ≤ N.primeFactors.card

If 3 ∤ N for an odd perfect number N, then N has at least nine distinct prime factors.

OddPerfect.NotThreeTenForce

OddPerfect/NotThreeTenForce.lean · 48 lines · 1 public theorem · imports OmegaSevenSplit

One soundness lemma for the search states of the seven prime theorem: a prime that divides the divisor sum of an exact prime power component may be added to the state.

Proof idea. The divisor sum of an exact component p^k divides 2N, so each of its odd prime factors divides N. The verified engine already uses this step inside a check; stating it as a lemma lets a plan cut a large state at a forced prime.

Public theorems

OddPerfect.NotThreeTenForce.closed_of_force

theorem closed_of_force {l : List Ent} {j m p k c : ℕ} (hj : j ≠ 0) (hc : c.Prime)
  (hc2 : c ≠ 2) (he : (⟨p, k, true⟩ : Ent) ∈ l) (hd : c ∣ geom p k) (hn : c ∉ l.map Ent.p)
  (h : Closed (⟨c, kmin c, false⟩ :: l) (j - 1) m) : Closed l j m

A forced prime: an odd prime c, not listed, dividing the divisor sum geom p k of an exact entry p ^ k, may be added to the state.

OddPerfect.NotFifteenSixteen

OddPerfect/NotFifteenSixteen.lean · 68 lines · 2 public theorems · imports NotFifteenSixteenD, SmallestPrime

An odd perfect number divisible by neither 3 nor 5 has at least sixteen distinct prime factors. Fifteen is classical (Norton 1960); whether sixteen is in the literature was not verified.

Proof idea. At least fifteen is in SmallestPrime, so only exactly fifteen prime factors, all above 6, must be excluded. With fifteen primes from 7 on, the abundancy barely reaches 2, so the small primes are almost forced; the remaining cases are closed by kernel checks of the verified search engine with the forcing step of NotThreeTenForce: 240 checks, 122294 search nodes in all.

  (h3 : ¬ 3 ∣ N) (h5 : ¬ 5 ∣ N) : 16 ≤ N.primeFactors.card

OddPerfect.ReciprocalSumTwo

OddPerfect/ReciprocalSumTwo.lean · 212 lines · 7 public theorems · imports ReciprocalSum

Sharper lower bounds for the sum of the reciprocals of the prime factors: ∑ 1/p > 29/50 and ∑ 1/p > 581/1000. Bounds of this kind are classical (Suryanarayana; Suryanarayana and Hagis; Cohen), and the published constants by cases on 3 and 5 are stronger.

Proof idea. Write c(p) = log(p/(p − 1)) − 1/p, so log 2 < ∑ 1/p + ∑ c(p). The primes at least B contribute at most 1/(4(B − 2)) to ∑ c(p) by a telescoping bound. Each odd prime below B gets an explicit rational bound from the series of −log(1 − 1/p), and one of 3, 5, 7 is absent since 105 ∤ N. The cutoffs B = 101 and B = 1009 give the two constants; the kernel checks the rational inequality and the list of primes below B.

  Real.log ((p : ℝ) / (p - 1)) - 1 / p ≤ (corrBound p : ℝ)

OddPerfect.lt_sum_inv_of_check

theorem lt_sum_inv_of_check {N : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N) (B K : ℕ) (L : List ℕ) (t : ℚ)
  (hB : 9 ≤ B) (hBo : Odd B) (hc : coverCheck B K L = true) (hnd : L.Nodup)
  (hchk : t + ((L.map corrBound).sum - corrBound 7) + 1 / (4 * ((B : ℚ) - 2)) ≤
    6931471803 / 10000000000) :
  (t : ℝ) < ∑ p ∈ N.primeFactors, 1 / (p : ℝ)

The generic transfer: a checked rational inequality for a cutoff B and a list L of the odd primes below B gives the lower bound t < ∑_{p ∣ N} 1/p for every odd perfect N.

OddPerfect.ReciprocalSumThree

OddPerfect/ReciprocalSumThree.lean · 354 lines · 1 public theorem · imports ReciprocalSumTwo

The sum of the reciprocals of the prime factors of an odd perfect number exceeds 59/100. Classical mathematics, and weaker than the published bound near 0.596 (Cohen, 1980).

Proof idea. As in ReciprocalSumTwo, log 2 < ∑ 1/p + ∑ c(p) with c(p) = log(p/(p − 1)) − 1/p. The thirteen smallest odd primes are treated jointly: for the subset of them dividing N, the product of 1 + 1/q at the special prime and 1 + 1/p + 1/p² at the others is at most the abundancy 2. A kernel check over all subsets and all roles of the special prime bounds the total correction weight of any subset that passes this test. The remaining primes below the cutoff are bounded by their weights and the tail by the telescoping bound; the kernel checks each weight against the series bound and the final rational inequality.

OddPerfect.ReciprocalSumFour

The sum of the reciprocals of the prime factors of an odd perfect number exceeds 0.5960631, with separate bounds for the four cases on whether 3 and 5 divide N. Classical mathematics (Cohen, 1980); the constants were not compared digit by digit with the published ones.

Proof idea. The thirteen smallest odd primes are treated exactly: a kernel check runs over every subset of them that can divide N and every role of the special prime. For the remaining prime factors, log 2 < ∑ log(p/(p − 1)) and log(p/(p − 1)) ≤ (1 + 1/(2(m − 2)))/p for p ≥ m give a lower bound for their reciprocal sum; either all of them are at least 257, or one of them is at most 255 and contributes at least 1/255. The extremal case is 3, 5 and 17 together with one prime near 256.

OddPerfect.ReciprocalSumUpper

OddPerfect/ReciprocalSumUpper.lean · 737 lines · 9 public theorems · imports ReciprocalSumFour, ReciprocalLogTwo

Upper bounds for the sum of the reciprocals of the prime factors of an odd perfect number by cases on 3 and 5: below 0.673634, 0.657304 and 0.677637 in the three cases where 3 or 5 divides N. With the lower bounds of ReciprocalSumFour each case has a window. Classical mathematics (Suryanarayana; Suryanarayana and Hagis; Cohen); the constants were not compared digit by digit with the published ones.

Proof idea. For a prime with exact exponent e the factor σ(p^e)/p^e has logarithm above 1/p, and the logarithms add up to log 2, so each small prime known to divide N lowers the bound log 2 by its gap; the special prime costs a little instead. A branch and stop check walks through the small odd primes and decides for each whether it divides N and in which role: exponent exactly 2, exponent at least 4, special with exponent 1, special with larger exponent. Exact components force the odd prime factors of their divisor sums into N, and when 3 has exponent exactly 2 the exact components may carry only two factors 3 in all.

Cohen (1980) proves about 0.66747275 and shows that the bound cannot pass about 0.66747289 without new restrictions; this bound uses none and stays below that limit. OddPerfect.ReciprocalSumSeven

OddPerfect/ReciprocalSumSeven.lean · 410 lines · 7 public theorems · imports ReciprocalSum

Upper bounds in terms of the smallest prime factor p1 of an odd perfect number, for p1 ≥ 7: the sum of the reciprocals of the prime factors is below log 2 − 11/(50 p12), and the product of p/(p − 1) is at most 2 + 9/(4 p12). Known mathematics: Corollary 16 and Proposition 6 of Zelinsky (arXiv 2402.14234), stated there for p1 ≥ 11 and for every odd perfect number respectively; the product bound is proved here only for p1 ≥ 7.

Proof idea. The special prime q satisfies q ≥ 2 p1 − 1 because (q + 1)/2 divides N. The inequality x + 2x2/5 ≤ log(1 + x + x2) is proved for x ≤ 1/7 from truncated logarithm series, independently of the source, and the product bound by a telescoping sum.

OddPerfect.LargestPrimeCapacityTwo

OddPerfect/LargestPrimeCapacityTwo.lean · 256 lines · 4 public theorems · imports LargestPrimeCapacity

Two isolated exclusions: the largest prime factor of an odd perfect number is neither 40961 nor 18433. Both values lie below published lower bounds for the largest prime factor, so the statements are known; they are proved here by the sender argument, not by a search.

Proof idea. A prime p of N whose σ(p^e) is divisible by the largest prime P has order t modulo P with t ≥ 3 and 4 ∤ t. For P = 40961 = 2¹³·5 + 1 this forces p¹⁰ ≡ 1, and the four odd candidates below P are composite, so nothing sends a factor P. For P = 18433 = 2¹¹·9 + 1 the only prime candidate is 4481; its order is even, so it would be the special prime, and it contributes at most one factor P, which contradicts Euler's form. The lists of roots are covered by a kernel check over all residues.

OddPerfect.LargestPrimeSafe

OddPerfect/LargestPrimeSafe.lean · 344 lines · 6 public theorems · imports LargestPrimeCapacity, SignedRepunit, Reciprocity

Case: the largest prime factor of an odd perfect number is P = 2R + 1 with R an odd prime. Call a prime u ≠ P a sender if P divides σ(ue), e the exponent of u. Every sender has e = R − 1, order R modulo P, and 1 + u + ⋯ + uR − 1 = Pj; the special prime is never a sender; j is odd and u ≡ 1 (mod 4) unless u = 3, where j is even; the exponent of P is even; (3R − 1)/2 ≤ Pv with v the exponent of P. These are steps toward OddPerfect.LargestPrimeSafeNone, which shows the case is impossible. Novelty not verified.

Proof idea. The order of u modulo P divides P − 1 = 2R and e + 1 and is at least 3, so R divides e + 1; the landed bound 2e + 3 ≤ P gives e + 1 = R. A prime factor r of the row is R (then u = R + 1, which is even) or has u of order R modulo r, so r ≡ 1 (mod 2R), r ≥ P and r = P. So the row is a power of P. Parity of j: a row of prime length is not a square unless u = 3 (so j is odd), and a Legendre symbol computation for u ≡ 3 (mod 4) forces j even.

P = 2 R + 1 with R an odd prime is not the special prime of an odd perfect number: v_P(N) is even, since P ≡ 3 (mod 4).

theorem largest_safe_sender_row (h : OddPerfect N) (hP : P ∈ N.primeFactors)
  (hmax : ∀ r ∈ N.primeFactors, r ≤ P) (hR : R.Prime) (hR2 : R ≠ 2) (hPR : P = 2 * R + 1)

    1 ≤ padicValNat P (σ 1 (u ^ N.factorization u))

Exact rows. Let the largest prime factor of an odd perfect number N be P = 2 R + 1 with R an odd prime, and let u ≠ P be a prime factor with P ∣ σ(u ^ e_u). Then e_u = R - 1, the order of u modulo P is R, and 1 + u + ⋯ + u ^ (R - 1) = P ^ j with j = v_P(σ(u ^ e_u)) ≥ 1.

  (h3 : ¬ P ∣ σ 1 (3 ^ N.factorization 3)) :
  Even ((N.primeFactors.erase P).filter (fun p => P ∣ σ 1 (p ^ N.factorization p))).card ∧
    2 ≤ ((N.primeFactors.erase P).filter
      (fun p => P ∣ σ 1 (p ^ N.factorization p))).card

Number of senders. If the largest prime factor of an odd perfect number N is P = 2 R + 1 with R an odd prime, and 3 is not a sender (for example 3 ∤ N), then the number of senders into P is even and at least 2: every row exponent is odd and they add up to the even, positive v_P(N).

OddPerfect.LargestPrimeSafeNone

OddPerfect/LargestPrimeSafeNone.lean · 247 lines · 3 public theorems · imports LargestPrimeSafe, LargestPrimeRoots, LargestPrimeSigned, SquareRow

For every odd perfect number: the largest prime factor is never 2R + 1 with R an odd prime. Also, as arithmetic: if n is odd and 3n − 1 = 2y2 then n = 1 or n = 5. This excludes one shape of the largest prime factor; it is not a bound. No published source was checked for the exclusion. Novelty not verified.

Proof idea. Two senders u1, u2 with rows Pj1, Pj2, j1 ≤ j2: the powers u1k, k < R, are all the R-th roots of unity modulo Pj1 and lie below Pj1, and u2 < P is one of them, so the prime u2 equals u1. With one sender the exponent of P is j, which is even, so the sender is 3 and σ(3R − 1) is a square: R = 5, P = 11, j = 2 by the landed theorem on square rows. Then the row of 11, which is 1 + 11 + 121 = 133 = 7·19, divides 2N and 19 > 11.

OddPerfect.LargestPrimeFour

OddPerfect/LargestPrimeFour.lean · 601 lines · 4 public theorems · imports LargestPrimeSafeNone

Case: the largest prime factor of an odd perfect number is P = 4R + 1 with R a prime above 3. Then P is the special prime, its exponent j satisfies j ≡ 1 (mod 4) and 5 ≤ j < R, and exactly one prime u sends to P (P divides the row of u): u has exponent R − 1 and 1 + u + ⋯ + uR − 1 = Pj. Necessary conditions only; this case is not excluded. No published source was checked. Novelty not verified. Superseded as a case description: LargestPrimeFourNone shows that these conditions contradict each other modulo 3, so this shape never occurs.

Proof idea. As 4R + 1 is prime and R > 3, R ≡ 1 (mod 3), so 2R + 1 is divisible by 3 and P is the only prime up to P that is 1 modulo 2R; no odd prime below P is 1 modulo R. So every row of length R that divides 2N is a power of P. A prime of even exponent that sends to P has order R modulo P and exponent R − 1. The other prime q of odd exponent a would need a + 1 = 2R; then 1 + q + ⋯ + qR − 1 is a power of P, so (qR + 1)/(q + 1) is a power of R, and lifting the exponent makes it equal to R, which is too small. Two senders are equal by the lifting argument of OddPerfect.LargestPrimeSafeNone. With one sender the exponent of P is j; an even j makes the row a square, which forces R = 5 and P = 21. So j is odd and P is the special prime; j = 1 is too small.

    1 ≤ padicValNat P (σ 1 (u ^ N.factorization u))

**Largest prime factor 4 R + 1: it is the special prime.** Let the largest prime factor of an odd perfect number N be P = 4 R + 1 with R > 3 prime. Then v_P(N) is odd, v_P(N) ≡ 1 (mod 4), 5 ≤ v_P(N) < R, and there is a prime factor u ≠ P with v_u(N) = R - 1 and 1 + u + ⋯ + u ^ (R - 1) = P ^ v_P(N). These are necessary conditions in a restricted case; the later module LargestPrimeFourNone excludes the case P = 4 R + 1. The odd perfect number conjecture remains open. No published source was checked; novelty not verified.

OddPerfect.LargestPrimeFourNone

OddPerfect/LargestPrimeFourNone.lean · 110 lines · 2 public theorems · imports LargestPrimeFour, OmegaSevenFinal

The largest prime factor of an odd perfect number is never 4R + 1 with R prime (every prime R, no bound). Auxiliary: a geometric sum 1 + u + ⋯ + uR − 1 of length R ≡ 1 (mod 6) is 1 modulo 3 for every u. This excludes one shape of the largest prime factor; other shapes remain. No published source was checked; novelty not verified.

Proof idea. For R > 3, LargestPrimeFour gives a prime u and an odd j with 1 + u + ⋯ + uR − 1 = Pj. Here R ≡ 1 (mod 6) and P ≡ 2 (mod 3), so the left side is 1 and the right side is 2 modulo 3. For R = 2 the number 9 is not prime; for R = 3 at most five primes are available, against seven distinct prime factors.

OddPerfect.LargestPrimeRoots

OddPerfect/LargestPrimeRoots.lean · 197 lines · 6 public theorems · imports LargestPrimeCapacity, Pratt

A root table criterion and two isolated exclusions: 167772161 = 5·2²⁵ + 1 and 12289 = 3·2¹² + 1 can divide an odd perfect number only together with a larger prime factor. The method is elementary and of a known type; 167772161 lies above 10⁸, the published lower bound for the largest prime factor (Goto and Ohno), so that bound does not decide it. The theorems exclude single values and do not bound the largest prime factor in general.

Proof idea. If P = 2am + 1 is the largest prime factor, some smaller prime p of N has σ(pe) divisible by P. The order of p modulo P is not divisible by 4, so p2m ≡ 1 (mod P). In an integral domain, n distinct n-th roots of unity are all of them, so a table of 2m residues lists every candidate. For 167772161 the ten tenth roots are 1, 124765, 2596626, 36505748, 38977608, 128794553, 131266413, 165175535, 167647396 and 167772160; none is prime. For 13 the method rightly declines: 3 is a root and σ(3²) = 13.

OddPerfect.SecondLargestPrimeFast

OddPerfect/SecondLargestPrimeFast.lean · 368 lines · 3 public theorems · imports SecondLargestPrime

A faster form of the step function of the second largest prime search. It computes exactly the same values as the original step, proved by expandF_eq and runF_eq, so a run checked with it certifies its stack exactly as before. No new statement about odd perfect numbers.

Proof idea. Most of the cost of a step was reading the entries of the state in several separate passes. The fast step gathers everything it needs in one pass.

OddPerfect.SecondLargestPrimeTwo

OddPerfect/SecondLargestPrimeTwo.lean · 71 lines · 3 public theorems · imports SecondLargestPrimeFastData1, SecondLargestPrimeFastData2, SecondLargestPrimeFastData3, SecondLargestPrimeFastData4, SecondLargestPrimeFastData5, SecondLargestPrimeFastData6, SecondLargestPrimeFastData7, SecondLargestPrimeFastData8, SecondLargestPrimeFastData9

An odd perfect number has two distinct prime factors above 72. The earlier bound 58 follows as a corollary. Much larger bounds for the second largest prime factor are known in the literature; this is the range the kernel checks here.

Proof idea. The search engine of SecondLargestPrime, unchanged, started from a prime factor above 10000 (from LargestPrimeFactor) in place of 3000. The search for the bound 72 takes 101315 steps, about seven times the search for 58: the number of steps roughly doubles with each new small prime, which is what stops this method well below the bounds in the literature. This module assembles the checks of the nine data modules.

OddPerfect.CycloRootCount

OddPerfect/CycloRootCount.lean · 257 lines · 2 public theorems

Two counting lemmas for rows of prime length l and a prime r ≠ l. At most l − 1 integers in an interval of length rk have rk dividing 1 + x + ⋯ + xl−1. Two primes p1 < p2 whose rows are powers of r satisfy p1l−1 < p2. No published source was checked; novelty not verified.

Proof idea. A root modulo r is a nontrivial l th root of unity, and a simple root lifts uniquely to rk; an interval of length rk holds one integer per class.

OddPerfect.AbundancyTail

OddPerfect/AbundancyTail.lean · 116 lines · 3 public theorems · imports Abundancy, ProductBound

Tail bounds for the product of p/(p−1). A product of 1 + xi is at most 1/(1 − Σxi); an odd perfect number has 2 < ∏ p/(p−1); a set of numbers above B with at most c members per interval (Bj, Bj+1] has Σ 1/(p−1) ≤ c/(B−1). No published source was checked; novelty not verified.

Proof idea. The members are grouped by the integer logarithm of p − 1 to the base B, and each group is bounded by a geometric term.

OddPerfect.FifthOrderReceivers

OddPerfect/FifthOrderReceivers.lean · 257 lines · 8 public theorems · imports SpecialPrime, Cyclotomic

If 5j divides e5 + 1 for an odd perfect number, two distinct prime factors that are 3 modulo 4 have 5 of order 5j. Hence 2·v5(e5 + 1) is at most the number of prime factors that are 3 modulo 4. Trivial when 5 ∤ e5 + 1. No published source was checked; novelty not verified.

Proof idea. Φ5(x) = (x2 + 3x + 1)2 − 5x(x + 1)2. For x = 5z2 this is a difference of squares with two coprime factors, each 3 modulo 4, so each has a prime factor that is 3 modulo 4.

OddPerfect.exists_two_fifth_order_receivers

theorem exists_two_fifth_order_receivers (h : OddPerfect N) {j : ℕ} (hj : 1 ≤ j)
  (hdvd : 5 ^ j ∣ N.factorization 5 + 1) :
  ∃ r₁ r₂, r₁ ≠ r₂ ∧ r₁ ∈ N.primeFactors ∧ r₂ ∈ N.primeFactors ∧ r₁ % 4 = 3 ∧ r₂ % 4 = 3 ∧
    orderOf (5 : ZMod r₁) = 5 ^ j ∧ orderOf (5 : ZMod r₂) = 5 ^ j

**Two receivers of each order 5 ^ j.** Let N be an odd perfect number and j ≥ 1 with 5 ^ j ∣ v_5(N) + 1. Then N has two distinct prime factors r ≡ 3 (mod 4) modulo which 5 has multiplicative order exactly 5 ^ j. Restricted result; no published source was checked; novelty not verified.

OddPerfect.two_mul_padicValNat_le_card_mod_four_eq_three

theorem two_mul_padicValNat_le_card_mod_four_eq_three (h : OddPerfect N) :
  2 * padicValNat 5 (N.factorization 5 + 1) ≤
    (N.primeFactors.filter (fun p => p % 4 = 3)).card

Fifth order receivers. For an odd perfect number N with s = v_5(v_5(N) + 1), at least 2 s distinct prime factors of N are ≡ 3 (mod 4). The statement is trivial when 5 ∤ v_5(N) + 1. Restricted result; no published source was checked; novelty not verified.

OddPerfect.Seed.ThreeFree

OddPerfect/Seed/ThreeFree.lean · 89 lines · 3 public theorems · imports Seed.Starter

When 3 does not divide a perfect number, exact square primes are ≡ 2 (mod 3), and every prime of σ(p²) is ≡ 1 (mod 3) and not itself an exact square.

Proof idea. If p ≡ 1 (mod 3) then 3 divides 1 + p + p², which would force 3. A prime q ≠ 3 dividing 1 + p + p² gives p³ ≡ 1 with p ≢ 1 modulo q, so p has order 3 and 3 divides q − 1.

OddPerfect.SteuerwaldThree

OddPerfect/SteuerwaldThree.lean · 140 lines · 1 public theorem · imports Euler

The ordinary exponents cannot all equal 2 when 3 divides N.

Proof idea. 3 is ≡ 3 (mod 4), so it is ordinary with exponent 2 and the 3-adic ledger has budget exactly 2. A forcing chain starting at σ(3²) = 13 always produces three distinct non special primes p ≡ 1 (mod 3), each contributing a factor 3 through σ(p²) = 1 + p + p², which overflows the budget. The case split follows the primes 13, 61, 97 of the chain and whether each is special.

OddPerfect.Steuerwald

OddPerfect/Steuerwald.lean · 159 lines · 6 public theorems · imports ClosedLoop, SteuerwaldThree, Seed.Example

The ordinary exponents cannot all equal 2; more generally, for an odd prime l not dividing N they cannot all equal l − 1. Hence some prime has an even exponent at least 4.

Proof idea. With l not dividing N and l dividing every ordinary e + 1: no ordinary prime is ≡ 1 (mod l), since such a prime would put a factor l into σ(pl−1). Every prime divisor of σ(pl−1) is l or ≡ 1 (mod l), so it must be the special prime q, and σ(pl−1) is a positive power of q. When all ordinary exponents equal l − 1 this is the situation excluded by ClosedLoop. For l = 3 this is the case where 3 does not divide N; the other case is SteuerwaldThree.

OddPerfect.McDaniel

OddPerfect/McDaniel.lean · 664 lines · 3 public theorems · imports Euler, Abundancy, Seed.Example, Seed.ThreeFree

The ordinary exponents cannot all be ≡ 2 (mod 3).

Proof idea. Case 3 divides N: each ordinary prime t has exponent at least 2 and forces every odd divisor of t² + t + 1, the special prime q forces every odd divisor of q + 1, and primes ≡ 3 (mod 4) are never special. A finite tree starting from 3 and 13 branches on whether each forced prime (13, 61, 97, 3169, 3348577, 3737657091169) is special, and every leaf exhibits an abundant divisor; large primes carry certified primality witnesses. Case 3 does not divide N: every ordinary p has p² + p + 1 = qc with c ≥ 1, q ≥ 13 and p ≥ 5 give 3c < p, distinct p give distinct c, and the abundancy stays below (13/12)·∏ (1 + 3−c) ≤ (13/12)(8/5) < 2.

OddPerfect.KanoldFour

OddPerfect/KanoldFour.lean · 154 lines · 3 public theorems · imports Certificate, Steuerwald, Valuation, SpecialPrime

The ordinary exponents cannot all equal 4.

Proof idea. If 5 does not divide N, the prime length argument of Steuerwald applies with l = 5. If 5 is ordinary, the 5-adic budget is 4, and the chain σ(5⁴) = 11·71, σ(11⁴) = 5·3221, σ(71⁴) = 5·11·211·2221, σ(211⁴) = 5·1361·292661 yields 11, 71, 211 (all ≡ 3 mod 4, so ordinary) and 1361, 2221, 3221, at most one of which is special; five ordinary primes ≡ 1 (mod 5) each contribute a factor 5, which overflows. If 5 is special with exponent k, then 6 divides σ(5k), so 3 divides N; no σ(p⁴) is divisible by 3, and the 3-adic ledger gives 6 dividing k + 1, so σ(5⁵) = 2·3²·7·31 divides σ(5k), 7 divides N, and 3⁴·5·7⁴ is abundant.

OddPerfect.ExponentSix

OddPerfect/ExponentSix.lean · 206 lines · 4 public theorems · imports Certificate, Steuerwald, SpecialPrime

The ordinary exponents cannot all equal 6.

Proof idea. If 7 does not divide N, the prime length argument applies with l = 7. If 7 divides N, it is ordinary (7 ≡ 3 mod 4) with 7-adic budget 6, and each ordinary prime p ≡ 1 (mod 7) puts a factor 7 into σ(p⁶), so seven such primes overflow. Forcing chains supply them: σ(7⁶) = 29·4733, then 4733 → 70001 → 50359 → 71 → 883 → 379 → 43 when neither 4733 nor 70001 is special. If 4733 is special, 4734 = 2·3²·263 forces 3 and 263, with chains 3 → 1093 → 14939 → 197, 263 → 239, 7211, and 7 → 29 → 88009573. If 70001 is special, 70002 = 2·3²·3889 forces 3, with chains through 1093, 14939, 197, then 29, 88009573 and 4733, 69655517.

OddPerfect.EqualExponents

OddPerfect/EqualExponents.lean · 537 lines · 20 public theorems · imports Steuerwald, Valuation, McDaniel, SpecialPrime

Odd perfect numbers whose ordinary exponents all equal 2β, and general forms: an l-adic counting bound, divisibility by l when every ordinary e + 1 is a power of l, and l⁴ dividing N. The count near the end of the module bounds only the ordinary primes whose σ(p2β) is not a power of the special prime; it does not bound the total number of prime factors.

Proof idea. The counting bound is the l-adic ledger: a prime factor p ≡ 1 (mod l) with exponent e has vl(σ(pe)) = vl(e + 1) by lifting the exponent, and these contributions add up to at most vl(N). Residue avoidance is the forcing step: if p has order l modulo a prime r and l divides e + 1, then r divides σ(pl−1), which divides σ(pe) and hence N.

OddPerfect.EqualExponentsBound

OddPerfect/EqualExponentsBound.lean · 474 lines · 9 public theorems · imports KanoldGeneral

If every ordinary exponent of an odd perfect number equals 2β, the number has at most 4β2 + 2β + 3 distinct prime factors. Known mathematics: Theorem 1.1, part (1), of Yamada, Colloq. Math. 103 (2005). Part (2) of that theorem (a bound for the size of N) and the later improvement of the bound are not proved here.

Proof idea. When 2β + 1 = l is prime, l is an ordinary prime factor; at most 2β(2β + 1) ordinary primes p have σ(p2β) not a power of the special prime q. For any other p ≠ l the whole power p2β divides σ of the special component, which forces p2β − 1 to divide the special exponent plus one; the divisors of that number each give a different prime factor of N, so at most one such p exists. When 2β + 1 is not prime, every ordinary prime sends to a prime that is 1 modulo a prime divisor l of 2β + 1, and there are at most 2β of those.

OddPerfect.ClassicalSmall

OddPerfect/ClassicalSmall.lean · 231 lines · 9 public theorems · imports SupportBridges, EqualExponentsBound, Phi3

Five small classical lemmas: two primes cannot feed each other through rows of prime index ℓ unless each divides ℓℓ − 1 (no solution for ℓ = 3); p divides σ(pa) − 1 exactly once; a unitary divisor bound; a congruence form of ℓ | 1 + r + ⋯ + rj; and a special prime dividing σ(3e) is 1 modulo 12.

Proof idea. Mutual rows: if 1 + p + ⋯ + pℓ−1 = ℓqα and 1 + q + ⋯ + qℓ−1 = ℓpβ, reduce the second equation modulo p to get qℓ ≡ 1, and the first to get ℓqα ≡ 1, so p divides ℓℓ − 1. The argument, for ℓ = 5, is in the proof of Proposition 6.2 of Hagis (Math. Comp. 35, 1980). The valuation lemma compares with Lemma 3 of Pomerance (Math. Comp. 29, 1975). Textbook facts; no novelty is claimed.

Proof idea. Both primes divide ℓℓ − 1, and 5^5 − 1 = 2² · 11 · 71 and 7^7 − 1 = 2 · 3 · 29 · 4733, so a finite check of the first equation remains: a numeral comparison for α = 1, and for α ≥ 2 the square q² does not divide the left side. Known mathematics (the case ℓ = 5 is in Hagis 1980); no novelty is claimed.

OddPerfect.ClassicalSmallThree

OddPerfect/ClassicalSmallThree.lean · 126 lines · 3 public theorems · imports McDaniel, Valuation, SpecialPrime

Three known lemmas: with equal ordinary exponents 2β and 3 | N the special row sends the whole exponent of 3; a special exponent k with k + 2 prime and q ≢ 1 (mod k + 2) forces (k + 2)² | N; and a special prime 5 has exponent 1 or 9 modulo 12.

Proof idea. First: an ordinary prime that is 2 modulo 3 sends nothing to 3 (even exponent), and one that is 1 modulo 3 sends v3(2β + 1), which is 0 by the landed theorem of McDaniel; so v3(σ(qa)) = 2β (Starni, J. Number Theory 116 (2006), p. 484). Second: by Fermat k + 2 divides qk+1 − 1 = σ(qk)(q − 1) and not q − 1 (Starni, J. Number Theory 44 (1993), 58 to 59, statement (ii)). Third: the order of 5 modulo 7 is 6, so 7 would divide σ(5k) when 6 divides k + 1, and 3, 5, 7 cannot all divide N (Bërdëllima, Elem. Math. 81 (2026), Proposition 2). Known mathematics; no novelty is claimed.

  padicValNat 3 (σ 1 (q ^ N.factorization q)) = 2 * β

Starni, J. Number Theory 116, Theorem, p. 484; no novelty is claimed. Let N be an odd perfect number with special prime q, let every other prime factor of N have exponent 2 * β, and let 3 ∣ N. Then the special component sends the whole exponent of 3: v_3(σ(q ^ a)) = 2 * β. The ordinary components send nothing to 3: a prime 2 (mod 3) has even exponent, and a prime 1 (mod 3) sends v_3(2 β + 1), which is 0 by McDaniel's theorem (mcdaniel). For 2 β + 1 prime the same statement for every ordinary prime in place of 3 is padicValNat_sigma_special_eq.

OddPerfect.PrimePowerIndexBound

OddPerfect/PrimePowerIndexBound.lean · 329 lines · 4 public theorems · imports EqualExponentsBound, UpperBound

Let l be an odd prime. If every ordinary exponent e of an odd perfect number N has e + 1 a power of l and e ≤ E, then N has at most E2 + 2E + 3 distinct prime factors, so N < 24E² + 2E + 3 and the family is finite for each E. Also: l is then not the special prime, for any exponents. The family is empty for l = 3 (McDaniel) and l = 5 (Fletcher, Nielsen and Ochem); the statement has content for l ≥ 7. Whether it is new was not verified.

Proof idea. The argument for equal exponents (Yamada) run with varying exponents. Every prime factor of an ordinary divisor sum is l or 1 modulo l; at most E ordinary primes are 1 modulo l and each receives from at most E senders; every other prime p has σ of its component a power of the special prime q, which forces pl − 2 to divide the special exponent plus one, and the divisors of that number each give a different prime factor.

Every prime factor of X = ∏ σ(p ^ e_p) is l or ≡ 1 (mod l), so the part U of X prime to l is ≡ 1 (mod l); removing the powers of l from σ(l ^ k) X = 2 l ^ k Y gives σ(l ^ k) U = 2 Y, which reads 1 = 2 modulo l since p ^ (l ^ γ) ≡ p.

OddPerfect.CommonIndexCapacity

OddPerfect/CommonIndexCapacity.lean · 123 lines · 3 public theorems · imports EqualExponentsBound, UpperBound

Let an odd prime l divide every ordinary index e + 1 of an odd perfect number N, with arbitrary other factors in the indices. Then N has at most 1 + S distinct prime factors, where S is the sum of the exponents of the prime factors that are 1 modulo l. If also the special prime is not 1 modulo l, and the exponents of l and of those prime factors are at most E, then N has at most E2 + 1 distinct prime factors and N < 2^(4^(E2 + 1)).

Proof idea. For an ordinary prime p the value 1 + p + … + p^(l−1) divides σ(p^e), and by Bang's theorem it has a prime factor r that is 1 modulo l. That prime divides N and is not p. A receiver r takes at most e_r senders, by the exact count of the factors r in σ(N) = 2N. So the ordinary primes are counted by the exponents of the receivers. When the special prime is not 1 modulo l every such receiver is ordinary, so each sends one factor l, and there are at most e_l of them. The result bounds the number of prime factors and excludes nothing; the case where the special prime is 1 modulo l is open here.

OddPerfect.PrimePowerIndexCapacity

OddPerfect/PrimePowerIndexCapacity.lean · 266 lines · 4 public theorems · imports PrimePowerIndexBound

Let every ordinary index of an odd perfect number N be a power of one odd prime l. If the exponent of l and the exponents of the ordinary prime factors that are 1 modulo l are at most B, then N has at most B2 + 2B + 2 distinct prime factors and N < 2^(4^(B2 + 2B + 2)). No condition on the special prime modulo l and no cap on the other exponents.

Proof idea. Let S be the ordinary prime factors that are 1 modulo l and C the exponent of l plus the sum of the exponents over S. An ordinary prime outside S and different from l sends only to primes that are 1 modulo l. So either its σ value is a power of the special prime q (call these sources U), or it sends to a member of S, and a receiver s takes at most e_s senders. Also |S| ≤ e_l. This gives ω(N) ≤ C + |U| + 2. No ordinary row feeds a member of U, so its whole exponent comes from σ(qα), and the lemma of Dandapat, Hunsucker and Pomerance puts pl−2 into α + 1 for each p in U. Bang's theorem at q bounds the number of divisors of α + 1 by ω(N) + 1, so 2(l − 1)|U| ≤ C + |U| + 3, and |U| ≤ B under the caps. The cap B is a hypothesis; nothing is excluded.

OddPerfect.ThreeFreeException

OddPerfect/ThreeFreeException.lean · 617 lines · 1 public theorem · imports Abundancy, Euler, Seed.ThreeFree, Seed.Example contains novelty unverified

If every prime other than q and one further prime r has exponent exactly 2, then 3 divides N.

Proof idea. Assume 3 does not divide N. Then q ≡ 1 (mod 12), so q ≥ 13, and for every other ordinary p, σ(p²) = qarb with a, b not both even, since 1 + p + p² lies strictly between consecutive squares. If r divides no σ(p²), the σ(p²) are odd powers of q, consecutive ordinary primes grow by a factor at least 13, and the abundancy is below (13/12)(5/4)(7/5) = 91/48 < 2. Otherwise r ≡ 1 (mod 3), the map p ↦ (a, b) is injective with (p + 1)² > 13arb, and a box count for small (a, b) plus a geometric tail bound the abundancy below 2. The argument uses only elementary size bounds.

A restrained odd perfect number is divisible by 3.

Proof idea. Assume 3 does not divide N. Then q ≡ 1 (mod 12), and for every other ordinary p, σ(p²) = qarb. Size comparisons on these values, split by whether r divides some σ(p²), bound the abundancy below 2. No computer search is used.

OddPerfect.ThreeFreeCert

OddPerfect/ThreeFreeCert.lean · 159 lines · 8 public theorems · imports Certificate

Certificates excluding exponent 2 at 5, 11, 29 and a fourth prime x: outright for x ∈ {17, 23, 47}, and for x ∈ {41, 53} when 3 does not divide N.

Proof idea. Each certificate forces primes from the exact squares (σ(5²) = 31, σ(11²) = 7·19, σ(29²) = 13·67, and for example σ(17²) = 307 or σ(23²) = 7·79) and closes with an abundant divisor that takes every forced prime to the first power. The certificates were produced by an untrusted program and are accepted by check through decide +kernel.

OddPerfect.AttackSize

OddPerfect/AttackSize.lean · 542 lines · 6 public theorems · imports Abundancy, Euler, Network, ExponentCap, Steuerwald, Seed.ThreeFree contains novelty unverified

Results that mix exact arithmetic with size. When 3 does not divide N, primes p with p² exactly dividing N and σ(p²) a power of the special prime carry little abundancy, so 3 divides N if every ordinary exponent is 2 except for at most twelve primes ≡ 2 (mod 3), or except for at most four primes that divide no σ(p²) of the exponent two primes. For every odd perfect number, a proper set S of prime factors that are all at least p gives 2p2|S| < 3N, and if every prime factor is at least p then p2ω(N)+1 ≤ N.

Proof idea. For the first part, call p a pure square when p² exactly divides N and 1 + p + p² is a power qa of the special prime. Then q ≡ 1 (mod 12), and p ≡ 2 (mod 3) and p ≡ 3 (mod 4), so p ≡ 11 (mod 12); 11, 23 and 47 fail because 133 = 7·19, 553 = 7·79 and 2257 = 37·61, so p ≥ 59. The exponent a is odd since 1 + p + p² lies strictly between two squares, so two pure squares p < p' satisfy 13p ≤ p'. The pure squares therefore contribute at most 61/59 to the abundancy, and the remaining primes must have ∏ p/(p − 1) > 1416/793. For the second part, the components over S multiply to at least p2|S|−1, because at most one exponent is odd. Strong connectivity of the network gives an edge from some component lb outside S into S, so σ(lb) ≥ p, while σ(lb) < (3/2)lb. Multiplying gives 2p2|S| < 3N.

OddPerfect.ExponentTenTwelve

OddPerfect/ExponentTenTwelve.lean · 660 lines · 4 public theorems · imports Certificate, Steuerwald, Valuation, SpecialPrime, Pratt contains novelty unverified

The ordinary exponents cannot all equal 10 and cannot all equal 12. Also, for every prime l, the special prime cannot be l when every ordinary exponent equals l − 1.

Proof idea. Write l for 11 or 13. If l does not divide N, the prime length argument of Steuerwald applies. If l is the special prime, write N = lkRl − 1; every prime factor of the product of the ordinary component divisor sums is l or ≡ 1 (mod l), and removing the powers of l from σ(N) = 2N leaves an identity that reads 1 = 2 modulo l. If l is ordinary, its budget is l − 1, and every ordinary prime ≡ 1 (mod l) spends one unit, so at most l such primes divide N. Forcing chains then exhibit l + 1 of them, starting from σ(11¹⁰) = 15797·1806113 and σ(13¹²) = 53·264031·1803647, after a case split on which forced prime ≡ 1 (mod 4) is special. Large primes carry certificates checked by Pratt.

OddPerfect.UniformExponents

OddPerfect/UniformExponents.lean · 822 lines · 21 public theorems · imports EqualExponents, SmallestPrime contains novelty unverified

Structure of a hypothetical odd perfect number whose ordinary exponents all equal l − 1, for every odd prime l at once. The ordinary primes split into S (those ≡ 1 mod l) and W (the others, apart from l). Results: every prime of W receives its whole budget from the special component, so 2(∏W)l − 1 divides σ(qk); the size of S is bounded; W is nonempty, with at least two elements for l ≥ 53; and the exact l-adic ledger |S| + vl(k + 1) = l − 1 holds when l is ordinary.

Proof idea. No ordinary component divisor sum is divisible by a prime w of W, because an ordinary σ(pl − 1) only has prime factors equal to l or ≡ 1 (mod l). So the w-adic ledger has a single term, vw(σ(qk)) = l − 1. Each prime of S spends one unit of the budget of l, which bounds |S| and hence the product of s/(s − 1) over S. Abundancy 2 must then be supplied by q, l and the primes of W, which forces W to be nonempty and gives the lower bounds on |W|. Lifting the exponent turns vw(σ(qk)) = l − 1 into exact statements about vw(k + 1) and the order of q modulo w. For w = 3 the single term statement is the theorem of Starni, J. Number Theory 116 (2006), 483 to 486 (p. 484), who proves it for every common exponent.

Interface theorems for the family in which every ordinary exponent equals l − 1 for an odd prime l: the prime l divides N and is not the special prime; at most l prime factors of N are 1 modulo l; σ(pl−1) divides N for every ordinary prime p. Restricted family statements. No published source was checked; novelty not verified.

Proof idea. No new argument: the three statements join theorems already in the library (l divides N; the congruence that keeps l from being special; the count of primes 1 modulo l) in the form a counting checker needs.

OddPerfect.KanoldGeneral

OddPerfect/KanoldGeneral.lean · 503 lines · 10 public theorems · imports EqualExponents, Zsigmondy, Abundancy contains novelty unverified

If t divides e + 1 for every ordinary exponent e, then t⁴ divides N. Also: if an odd prime l divides every e + 1 then l divides N, the prime power form l4a | N, and two cases of the stronger fifth power statement.

Proof idea. Suppose an odd prime l divides every ordinary e + 1 but not N. Then every Φl(p) = 1 + p + … + pl − 1 with p ordinary is a power of the special prime q. A growth lemma shows that such primes are sparse: for ordinary p < p′, both are l-th roots of unity modulo M = Φl(p), the unit group modulo a power of q is cyclic, so p′ is congruent to a power pj with j < l, and p′ < M would force p′ = pj. Hence Φl(p) < p′, the ordinary primes grow faster than squaring, and the abundancy stays below 2. For the fourth power: if l is ordinary its exponent is at least la − 1; if l = q, primitive prime factors of the cyclotomic values at q, q², …, qa of one ordinary prime give a + 1 primes ≡ 1 (mod q), each of which spends a units, and the residue of the special exponent modulo 4 finishes.

OddPerfect.ForcingClosed

OddPerfect/ForcingClosed.lean · 527 lines · 15 public theorems · imports Euler, Abundancy, Zsigmondy, Pratt contains novelty unverified

A relaxation of the problem. A forcing closed configuration is a finite set of odd primes with exponents that satisfies Euler's parity pattern, closure (every odd prime factor of a component divisor sum is in the set), and total abundancy at most 2. The exact valuation ledger is dropped. Every odd perfect number gives a configuration, so nonexistence of configurations (the statement C1, a definition that is never assumed and may be false) would imply the conjecture. Proved for configurations: every exponent is below the largest prime of the set, the exponents can be reduced to 1 for the special prime and l − 1 with l prime for the others, and the ordinary exponents e cannot all satisfy 3 | e + 1.

Proof idea. Closure and a primitive prime factor give, for each exponent e ≥ 2, a prime r ≡ 1 (mod e + 1) in the set, so e + 2 ≤ r. Reduction uses that σ(pa) divides σ(pb) when a + 1 divides b + 1, so closure and the size bound survive when exponents shrink. If every ordinary e has 3 | e + 1, then p² + p + 1 divides every ordinary component divisor sum; closure and parity force 3 into the set, and a finite forcing tree starting at 3 produces a subset whose abundancy already exceeds 2. No valuation count is used, only closure, parity and size.

theorem reduce (hF : ForcingClosed S e) :
  ∃ q ∈ S, q % 4 = 1 ∧ e q % 4 = 1 ∧ (∀ s ∈ S, s ≠ q → e s % 2 = 0) ∧
    ForcingClosed S (reduceExp q e) ∧ reduceExp q e q = 1 ∧
    ∀ s ∈ S, s ≠ q → (reduceExp q e s + 1).Prime ∧ reduceExp q e s + 1 ≠ 2

Reduction: every forcing closed configuration has a reduced one on the same support, with special exponent 1 and every ordinary exponent of the form l - 1, l an odd prime. It also returns the special node q of the original configuration with its parity data. So C1 is equivalent to C1 for reduced configurations.

OddPerfect.ForcingClosed.three_mem

theorem three_mem (hF : ForcingClosed S e) (h3 : ∀ s ∈ S, e s % 2 = 0 → 3 ∣ e s + 1) :
  3 ∈ S

Closure and parity alone (no size): if every ordinary exponent e s has 3 ∣ e s + 1 (for example all ordinary exponents equal 2), then 3 is a node. Proof: otherwise every ordinary node is ≢ 1 (mod 3), so every prime factor of s ^ 2 + s + 1 is the special node q; an odd prime s ∣ q + 1 then gives s ^ 2 + s + 1 = q, so s ∣ 2.

McDaniel and Steuerwald for forcing closed configurations. In every forcing closed configuration some ordinary exponent e s (even) has 3 ∤ e s + 1. In particular the ordinary exponents cannot all equal 2 (Steuerwald) and cannot all be ≡ 2 (mod 3) (McDaniel). The proof uses only closure, parity and size: no valuation ledger.

OddPerfect.ExceptionCount

OddPerfect/ExceptionCount.lean · 827 lines · 4 public theorems · imports AttackSize contains novelty unverified

Let E be a finite set such that every prime factor outside E and other than the special prime q has exponent exactly 2. Then 3 divides N if E has at most 29 elements, all ≡ 2 (mod 3), or if E has at most 5 elements, none of which divides a σ(p²) with p outside E. With q ≠ 109 the first count rises to 31, and with q ≥ 61 the second rises to 6. These sharpen the counts 12 and 4 of AttackSize.

Proof idea. Assume 3 does not divide N. Then every exponent 2 prime p outside E has σ(p²) equal to a power of q, is ≡ 11 (mod 12), is at least 59, and two such primes s < t satisfy 13s ≤ t. So their abundancies multiply to little more than that of the smallest one. The abundancy 2 must then come from q and the primes of E, and the product of r/(r − 1) over the smallest admissible primes is compared with the bound. Small values of q are removed by forcing through the odd prime factors of q + 1, which must divide N and must lie in the allowed residue class. The module docstring records the values of q at which the comparison stops, which is why the counts 29 and 5 are the limits of this method without a condition on q.

OddPerfect.ExceptSmallThree

OddPerfect/ExceptSmallThree.lean · 104 lines · 1 public theorem · imports Phi3, SpecialPrime

If 3 divides an odd perfect number N, some prime factor with an even exponent at least 4 is at most 331.

Proof idea. Call a prime factor exceptional when its exponent is even and at least 4. Suppose every exceptional prime exceeds 331. Then every prime factor up to 331 other than the special prime has exponent 2. The exponent of 3 is 2, so at most two primes of exponent 2 are 1 modulo 3. The row of 3 has the value 13, which forces 13 | N, and four cases on the special prime (13, 61, 97, or none of these) each force three such primes.

OddPerfect.ExceptSmallBound

OddPerfect/ExceptSmallBound.lean · 509 lines · 4 public theorems · imports ExceptSmallThree

Some prime factor with an even exponent at least 4 is at most max(331, 9h2), where h is the number of such primes; when h ≤ 6 it is at most 331.

Proof idea. The case 3 | N is exceptSmall_three. Otherwise suppose every exceptional prime exceeds the bound. Every prime s of exponent 2 is 2 modulo 3, so every prime factor of s2 + s + 1 is the special prime q or exceptional. These numbers are distinct, so a finite Euler product over q and the exceptional primes, with weights ⌊√t⌋, bounds the sum of their reciprocal weights (exceptSmall_euler, exceptSmall_weight_sq_le). Together with 2 < ∏ p/(p − 1) this contradicts a numeric bound on log 2.

OddPerfect.ExceptRoots

OddPerfect/ExceptRoots.lean · 183 lines · 4 public theorems · imports Phi3, SpecialPrime, LedgerReceiver

If 3 divides N, one of the primes 3, 7, 13, 19, 31, 61, 97, 127, 331 has an even exponent at least 4. If every prime of even exponent at least 4 is 2 modulo 3, then 3 ∤ N and there are at least 32 such primes.

Proof idea. The proof of exceptSmall_three uses the hypothesis "exponent exactly 2" only at nine primes: 3 itself, the forced factors 7, 13, 19, 31, 61 and the primes of the two closing triples. So one of the nine is exceptional. The nine primes other than 3 are 1 modulo 3. If all exceptional primes are 2 modulo 3, none of the nine can be one, so 3 ∤ N. Then every prime factor that is 1 modulo 3 is the special prime, and receiver_three_free gives at least 32 primes whose exponent e has 3 ∤ e + 1; these have exponent at least 4.

OddPerfect.thirtytwo_le_card_exceptions_of_mod_three

theorem thirtytwo_le_card_exceptions_of_mod_three {N q : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N)
  (hq : q.Prime) (hodd : Odd (N.factorization q))
  (hmod : ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, Even (N.factorization p) → 4 ≤ N.factorization p →
    p % 3 = 2) :
  32 ≤ ((N.primeFactors.erase q).filter (fun p => 4 ≤ N.factorization p)).card ∧
    33 ≤ ω N ∧ 2 * ω N + 63 ≤ Ω N

Let N be an odd perfect number with special prime q (odd exponent), and suppose every prime factor with even exponent at least 4 is 2 modulo 3. Then at least 32 prime factors p ≠ q have exponent at least 4, ω(N) ≥ 33 and Ω(N) ≥ 2 ω(N) + 63. Proof: 3 ∤ N by not_three_dvd_of_exceptions_mod_three. A prime factor t ≠ q with t ≡ 1 (mod 3) has even exponent; exponent at least 4 is excluded by the hypothesis, and exponent 2 gives 3 ∣ t ^ 2 + t + 1 = σ(t ^ 2), so 3 ∣ N. Hence every prime factor ≡ 1 (mod 3) is q, and receiver_three_free applies; a prime p ≠ q with 3 ∤ e_p + 1 has even exponent other than 2, hence at least 4. The hypothesis is the hypothesis hH of five_le_card_budgetExceptions in OddPerfect/ExcessBudget.lean (the prime factors r ≠ q with exponent other than 2 are exactly those with even exponent at least 4). Both other hypotheses of that theorem are dropped: hA (no exception r divides e_q + 1) and hW (no exception r has r ^ 2 ∣ p ^ (r - 1) - 1 for p in the exceptions or q, p ≠ r). The count rises from 5 to 32. Conditional family result; novelty was not verified.

OddPerfect.ExceptRootsCases

OddPerfect/ExceptRootsCases.lean · 226 lines · 7 public theorems · imports Phi3, SpecialPrime

For an odd perfect number divisible by 3 with special prime q, a prime of even exponent at least 4 lies in {3, 7, 19, 127} if q = 13, in {3, 13, 31, 331} if q = 61, in {3, 7, 13, 61} if q = 97, and in {3, 13, 61, 97} otherwise. So such a prime is at most 97 unless q is 13 or 61, and at most 127 unless q is 61. Novelty not verified.

Proof idea. These are the four branches of the proof of exceptRoots_three, which states the union of the four sets. If no prime of the set has exponent at least 4, then 3 has exponent 2 and three primes that are 1 modulo 3 have exponent 2, which the count at 3 forbids.

OddPerfect.ExceptSmallTwoTail

OddPerfect/ExceptSmallTwoTail.lean · 473 lines · 10 public theorems · imports ExceptSmallBound

Estimates for the bound max(331, 2h2): a tail bound for sums over products of at least three primes, a bound for reciprocal sums in a residue class, and the numeric inequality for every h.

Proof idea. The primes s of exponent 2 are split by the shape of F(s) = s2 + s + 1: a single exceptional prime, a product of two distinct exceptional primes, a multiple of the special prime q, or a product of at least three exceptional primes. The first two classes lie in a residue class modulo 6 above an explicit point, and their sums of 1/(s − 1) are bounded by logarithms (exceptSmallTwo_ap). The third class is bounded through the Euler product, and the fourth by a tail of it (exceptSmallTwo_tail). The total stays below log 2 (exceptSmallTwo_numeric): for h below 81 by one rational computation, above it by a uniform estimate.

theorem exceptSmallTwo_numeric (h : ℕ) :
  ∃ z : ℝ, ∃ d : ℕ, 0 ≤ z ∧ z < 1 ∧
    (∀ t, exceptSmallTwoM h < t → ((Nat.sqrt t : ℕ) : ℝ)⁻¹ ≤ z) ∧ 7 ≤ d ∧
    (∀ s, 41 ≤ s → exceptSmallTwoM h < phi3 s → d + 1 ≤ s) ∧
    Real.log (1 + 6 * h / ((d : ℝ) - 6)) / 6 + Real.log (5 / 2) / 6 +
      (1 / 672 + h / (exceptSmallTwoM h : ℝ) + 41 / 40 *
        (((1 - z) ^ h)⁻¹ / 24 + exceptSmallTwoTau z h 3)) ≤ Real.log 2

The numerical part of the estimate, for every h: parameters z and d that bound the weights of the primes above M and the exact square primes s with s ^ 2 + s + 1 > M, and for which the total of the estimate is at most log 2.

OddPerfect.ExceptSmallTwo

OddPerfect/ExceptSmallTwo.lean · 595 lines · 3 public theorems · imports ExceptSmallTwoTail

Some prime factor with an even exponent at least 4 is at most max(331, 2h2), where h is the number of such primes; when h ≤ 12 it is at most 331.

Proof idea. The case 3 | N is exceptSmall_three. Otherwise suppose every exceptional prime exceeds M = max(331, 2h2). Then q ≡ 1 modulo 12, each prime s of exponent 2 is 5 modulo 6 and at least 41, q ≥ 673, and every prime factor of s2 + s + 1 is q or exceptional. The four class sums of ExceptSmallTwoTail, with 1/(q − 1) ≤ 1/672 and h/M for the exceptional primes, keep the sum of 1/(p − 1) below log 2, against 2 < ∏ p/(p − 1).

OddPerfect.EqualExponentChain

OddPerfect/EqualExponentChain.lean · 2053 lines · 25 public theorems · imports Pratt, Steuerwald, SpecialPrime, Valuation, Cyclotomic contains novelty unverified

A certificate checker for the case where every ordinary exponent equals l − 1 with l an odd prime, with a soundness theorem, and certificates checked by the kernel that exclude the common exponents 4, 6, 10, 12, 16, 18, 22 and 28. The exponents 4, 6, 10, 12, 16, 22 and 28 are known results. For the exponent 18 we did not find a published proof; an independent computer assisted claim by another author exists and is not peer reviewed. The case l = 31 is not covered.

Proof idea. If l does not divide N the prime length argument applies. Otherwise l is ordinary or special, and a certificate tree is checked in each case. A state records primes proved to be ordinary prime factors, primes proved to differ from q, the value of q once fixed, and a number M proved to divide k + 1 for the special exponent k. Steps: a prime factor r of σ(pl − 1) for a known p divides N, and is ordinary when it is not ≡ 1 (mod 4) or is known to differ from q; a prime factor of σ(qm − 1) with m | M is ordinary; a branch decides whether a given prime is q; and for a known prime s with s ≠ l and s ≢ 1 (mod l), the whole budget l − 1 of s comes from σ(qk), so lifting the exponent forces a new divisor of k + 1. A branch closes when a prime receives more than l − 1 factors or when the fixed q is not ≡ 1 (mod 4). Divisibility is checked by Horner evaluation modulo the divisor and primality by Pratt certificates.

OddPerfect.Restrained

OddPerfect/Restrained.lean · 1508 lines · 3 public theorems · imports ThreeFreeException, Steuerwald, Phi3, Valuation, ValuationBounds, SpecialPrime, Reciprocity, Certificate

The restrained case: every prime factor other than the special prime q and one further prime r has exponent exactly 2. The module proves a case map and excludes nothing outright. If r ≠ 3, then 3² exactly divides N and only four explicit cases remain: r = 13; q = 13 with r = 7; r = 61 with 13² exactly dividing N; r = 97 with 13² and 61² exactly dividing N. If r = 3, the exponent of 3 is even and at least 4, q ≡ 1 (mod 3), and neither 5 nor 7 divides N. The four cases with r ≠ 3 are excluded in the modules RestrainedTwo to RestrainedFive, so r = 3.

Proof idea. With 3² exactly dividing N, each ordinary prime ≡ 1 (mod 3) spends one unit of the budget 2 of the prime 3. Forcing from σ(3²) = 13 gives nine leaves according to which forced primes equal q or r; every other branch has three ordinary primes ≡ 1 (mod 3). In five leaves the budget is spent or nearly spent, so every further ordinary prime t has σ(t²) supported on known primes. An exact search checked by the kernel lists the t with σ(t²) below a bound, the small survivors are removed by abundant divisors, and for the rest a weighted sum bound keeps the abundancy below 2. For r = 3, quadratic reciprocity gives q ≡ 1 (mod 3), and factor chains from 5 and from 7 end in abundant divisors or in an overflow of a budget.

OddPerfect.ThreeFreeTwo

OddPerfect/ThreeFreeTwo.lean · 1698 lines · 2 public theorems · imports Abundancy, Euler, Seed.ThreeFree, Seed.Example, ThreeFreeException contains novelty unverified

If every prime factor other than the special prime q and two further primes r₁, r₂ has exponent exactly 2, then 3 divides N. No condition is placed on r₁ and r₂. This extends the one exception theorem.

Proof idea. Assume 3 does not divide N. Every ordinary prime s then has σ(s²) = qar₁br₂c, and s determines the exponent vector. For s ≥ 300 the excess σ(s²)/s² − 1 is bounded by a weight that decays geometrically in (a, b, c), so the sum over all vectors is a small box evaluated exactly plus a geometric tail. For s < 300 a table of the prime factors of 1 + s + s² confines the ordinary primes to an explicit finite set once the classes of r₁ and r₂ are fixed. For each of 41 pairs of classes the resulting upper bound for the abundancy is below 2.

OddPerfect.ForcingClosedBound

OddPerfect/ForcingClosedBound.lean · 275 lines · 7 public theorems · imports ForcingClosed, Pratt, Cyclotomic

Every forcing closed configuration has a node above 1000. In particular this holds for the set of prime factors of an odd perfect number, where it is weaker than the bound in LargestPrimeFactor; the point is that it uses only parity and closure under forcing, and none of the size information.

Proof idea. A greatest fixed point computation. Start from the odd primes up to 1000 and delete every prime p that has no move inside the current list: a special move (p ≡ 1 (mod 4) and every prime factor of p + 1 in the list, apart from 2) or an ordinary move (an odd prime l with 2l + 1 ≤ 1000 such that every prime factor of σ(pl−1) is in the list). By the reduction theorem of ForcingClosed, the special exponent may be taken to be 1 and each ordinary exponent to be l − 1 for a prime l, so the nodes of a configuration with all nodes at most 1000 survive every round. Smoothness of n over the list is tested exactly as n dividing a power of the product of the list. The kernel checks nine rounds, one lemma per round, and the list becomes empty.

OddPerfect.EqualExponentChainMore

OddPerfect/EqualExponentChainMore.lean · 2656 lines · 8 public theorems · imports EqualExponentChain contains novelty unverified

Four more excluded patterns: the ordinary prime factors of an odd perfect number cannot all have exponent 30, 36, 40 or 42. These are the instances l = 31, 37, 41, 43 of the checker in EqualExponentChain. The exponent 36 is a known result (Cohen and Williams, 1985). For 30, 40 and 42 we did not find a published proof; the surveys we read list the equal exponent case as settled only for other values, so these three carry the tag novelty unverified. The cases l = 47, 53, 59 and 67 are in EqualExponentChainFar and the modules after it.

Proof idea. Same method as EqualExponentChain: a search outside Lean builds a tree of forced prime factors, with Pratt certificates for every prime used, and the kernel checks the tree with the checker and its soundness theorem. The largest prime in these certificates has 121 digits.

OddPerfect.EqualExponentChainFarCut

OddPerfect/EqualExponentChainFarCut.lean · 182 lines · 4 public theorems · imports EqualExponentChain

A variant runC of the chain checker for certificates too large for one module: a leaf may stop at a listed cut state, and a separate tree refutes that state. The soundness theorems runC_sound_cuts and split_sound chain the pieces. A tool; it states nothing about odd perfect numbers by itself.

Proof idea. Same induction as the soundness proof of the original checker, with one more leaf case: the current state equals a cut state, and the hypothesis for that cut state applies. Equality of states is decided by a boolean test proved sound.

OddPerfect.EqChain.runC_sound

theorem runC_sound (hpc : Pratt.check pc = true) (hl : l.Prime) (hl2 : l ≠ 2)
  (h : OddPerfect N) (hq : q.Prime) (hodd : Odd (N.factorization q))
  (hexp : ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ≠ q → N.factorization p = l - 1) {cuts : List St}
  (hcuts : ∀ s ∈ cuts, Holds l N q s → False) :
  ∀ (c : Node) (st : St), runC l pc cuts st c = true → Holds l N q st → False

OddPerfect.EqualExponentCount

OddPerfect/EqualExponentCount.lean · 377 lines · 10 public theorems · imports EqualExponentChain, EqualExponents

A certificate checker for the family in which every ordinary exponent equals l − 1, for an odd prime l different from the special prime. It needs no complete factorization: it counts pairwise coprime divisors of σ(pl−1). Soundness is proved once; the theorems for single values of l are instances. Restricted family result. No published source was checked; novelty not verified. The counting method follows the approach described in a repository outside this project (mathdiscoveries/odd-perfect-equal-exponents), read as text only. That repository states the cases l ≤ 73 in Lean; its proof was not compiled or verified here, and no priority is claimed.

Proof idea. Every prime factor of σ(pl−1) other than l is 1 modulo l, and for an ordinary prime factor p of N it divides N. At most l prime factors of N are 1 modulo l. The checker walks a list of primes p already known to divide N and to differ from the special prime, with a divisor m of σ(pl−1) for each. The numbers m are pairwise coprime, so each adds at least one new prime factor; a witness a with gcd(am − a, m) = 1 shows by Fermat that m is not a prime power, and then m adds two. More than l such prime factors is a contradiction. A prime p is known to differ from the special prime when it is 3 modulo 4, or when the case in which it is the special prime is closed separately.

Public theorems

OddPerfect.EqCount.two_le_card_of_witness

theorem two_le_card_of_witness {m a : ℕ} (hm : 1 < m) (ha : a < m)
  (h : Nat.gcd (fermatRes a m) m = 1) : 2 ≤ m.primeFactors.card

A prime power m has gcd(a ^ m - a mod m, m) ≠ 1; so a witness shows that m > 1 has at least two distinct prime factors.

theorem card_filter_le (h : OddPerfect N) (hl : l.Prime) (hl2 : l ≠ 2)
  (hexp : ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ≠ q → N.factorization p = l - 1)
  (hlN : l ∈ N.primeFactors) (hlq : l ≠ q) :
  (N.primeFactors.filter (fun p => p % l = 1)).card ≤ l ∧
    (N.primeFactors.filter (fun p => p ≠ q ∧ p % l = 1)).card ≤ l - 1

OddPerfect.EqualExponentCountDivisible

OddPerfect/EqualExponentCountDivisible.lean · 248 lines · 6 public theorems · imports EqualExponentCount

The counting checker under a weaker hypothesis. An accepted certificate also excludes: l divides the index ep + 1 of every ordinary prime p, l divides N, l is not the special prime, and the exponent of l is l − 1. Consequence: under the divisibility hypothesis with l | N, the exponent of l is at least 3l − 1. No certificate is checked again. Restricted result; the case l ∤ N is not treated here. No published source was checked; novelty not verified.

Proof idea. A counted number m divides σ(pl−1), and σ(pl−1) divides σ(pe) when l divides e + 1. The count of prime factors that are 1 modulo l comes from the exponent of l alone. For the floor: el + 1 = l·t with el even, so t is odd, and t = 1 is the excluded case.

Public theorems

OddPerfect.EqCount.card_filter_le_div

theorem card_filter_le_div (h : OddPerfect N) (hl : l.Prime) (hl2 : l ≠ 2)
  (hdiv : ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ≠ q → l ∣ N.factorization p + 1)
  (hE : N.factorization l = l - 1) :
  (N.primeFactors.filter (fun p => p % l = 1)).card ≤ l ∧
    (N.primeFactors.filter (fun p => p ≠ q ∧ p % l = 1)).card ≤ l - 1

At most v_l(N) = l - 1 ordinary prime factors are 1 modulo l when every ordinary index is divisible by l; so at most l prime factors of N are 1 modulo l.

OddPerfect.EqCount.run_sound_div

theorem run_sound_div {pc : List (ℕ × ℕ × List ℕ)} (hpc : Pratt.check pc = true)
  (hl : l.Prime) (hl2 : l ≠ 2) (h : OddPerfect N) (hq : q.Prime)
  (hodd : Odd (N.factorization q))
  (hdiv : ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ≠ q → l ∣ N.factorization p + 1)
  (hE : N.factorization l = l - 1)
  (hlN : l ∈ N.primeFactors) (hlq : l ≠ q) {qs : Option ℕ} {ex : List ℕ}
  (hc : Ctx q qs ex) :
  ∀ (c : List (ℕ × ℕ × ℕ)) (P k : ℕ), run l pc qs ex P k c = true → Holds l N P k → False

Soundness of run under divisible indices: an accepted walk refutes every state that holds.

OddPerfect.EqCount.checkCert_sound_div

theorem checkCert_sound_div {l : ℕ} {pc : List (ℕ × ℕ × List ℕ)}
  {main : List (ℕ × ℕ × ℕ)} {cases : List (ℕ × List (ℕ × ℕ × ℕ))}
  (hc : checkCert l pc main cases = true) {N q : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N) (hq : q.Prime)
  (hodd : Odd (N.factorization q))
  (hdiv : ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ≠ q → l ∣ N.factorization p + 1)
  (hlN : l ∣ N) (hlq : l ≠ q) (hE : N.factorization l = l - 1) : False

Soundness of an accepted certificate under divisible indices: if l ∣ N, l ≠ q, every ordinary index v_p(N) + 1 is divisible by l and v_l(N) = l - 1, there is no odd perfect number N with special prime q.

Exponent floors for l = 61, 71, 73, 79: if l divides the index of every ordinary prime and l divides N, the exponent of l is at least 3l − 1 (182, 212, 218, 236). OddPerfect.EqualExponentDivisorFan

OddPerfect/EqualExponentDivisorFan.lean · 194 lines · 5 public theorems · imports UniformExponents, Zsigmondy, EqualExponentNotSpecial

For an odd perfect number with special exponent a and an odd prime l, the divisors of a + 1 that are multiples of l inject into the prime factors that are 1 modulo l. In the equal exponent family with a + 1 = lc·B, l ∤ B, this gives c·(τ(B) + 1) ≤ l − 1, hence 3c ≤ l − 1. Trivial when c = 0; the family is not excluded. No published source was checked; novelty not verified.

Proof idea. For each divisor d of a + 1 that is a multiple of l, Zsigmondy gives a prime factor of N for which q has order d. Such a prime is 1 modulo l, and different d give different primes. There are c·τ(B) such divisors, and in the family the number of such primes plus c is at most l − 1 (landed in UniformExponents).

  ((N.factorization q + 1).divisors.filter (l ∣ ·)).card ≤ (congrPrimes N q l).card

The fan. For an odd perfect number N with special prime q and an odd prime l, the divisors d of v_q(N) + 1 with l ∣ d are at most as many as the prime factors s ≠ q of N with s ≡ 1 (mod l).

theorem padicValNat_mul_succ_card_divisors_le {N q l : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N) (hq : q.Prime)
  (hodd : Odd (N.factorization q)) (hl : l.Prime) (hl2 : l ≠ 2)
  (hexp : ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ≠ q → N.factorization p = l - 1) :
  padicValNat l (N.factorization q + 1) *
      (((N.factorization q + 1) / l ^ padicValNat l (N.factorization q + 1)).divisors.card
        + 1) ≤ l - 1

The divisor fan inequality. Let N be an odd perfect number with special prime q, and let l be an odd prime such that every prime factor p ≠ q of N has exponent l - 1. With c = v_l(v_q(N) + 1) and B = (v_q(N) + 1) / l ^ c, c (τ(B) + 1) ≤ l - 1.

OddPerfect.TwoExceptionsNinetySevenData

OddPerfect/TwoExceptionsNinetySevenData.lean · 181 lines · 13 public theorems · imports EqualExponentCount

Kernel checked data for TwoExceptionsNinetySeven: for each odd prime p below 100 other than 97, the number 1 + p + ⋯ + p96 has at least three distinct prime factors, or two for seven listed primes whose rows are pairwise coprime; lists of the primes up to 1600; one whole number inequality for the final product. It proves nothing about odd perfect numbers alone. No published source was checked; novelty not verified.

Proof idea. Each statement is closed and proved by decide +kernel.

OddPerfect.TwoExceptionsNinetySevenCore

OddPerfect/TwoExceptionsNinetySevenCore.lean · 666 lines · 30 public theorems · imports TwoExceptionsNinetySevenData, Seed.Example, Seed.Starter, Cyclotomic

The argument of TwoExceptionsNinetySeven with its five analytic inputs as hypotheses. No published source was checked; novelty not verified.

Proof idea. Every prime factor of a row of length 97 is 97 or 1 modulo 97, so all compatible rows are built from the at most two exceptions. With fewer than two receivers the rows are powers of one prime, the compatible primes grow like p2 > p196, and the product of p/(p−1) stays below 2. With two receivers (both at least 389) each block (1600j, 1600j+1] holds at most 192 compatible primes, and the product again stays below 2.

OddPerfect.TwoExceptionsNinetySeven

OddPerfect/TwoExceptionsNinetySeven.lean · 38 lines · 1 public theorem · imports TwoExceptionsNinetySevenCore, CycloRootCount, AbundancyTail

If every prime factor p of an odd perfect number N, apart from two arbitrary numbers, has index ep + 1 divisible by 97, then 97 divides N. With the special prime as one of the two: an odd perfect number not divisible by 97 has at least two ordinary prime factors whose index is not divisible by 97. Restricted result: it says nothing when three prime factors have an index not divisible by 97. No published source was checked; novelty not verified.

Proof idea. Supplies the five inputs of the core module from CycloRootCount and AbundancyTail.

Let a and b be arbitrary natural numbers. An odd perfect number all of whose prime factors other than a and b have an index divisible by 97 is divisible by 97. Restricted result; no published source was checked; novelty not verified.

OddPerfect.TwoExceptionsGeneralCore

OddPerfect/TwoExceptionsGeneralCore.lean · 712 lines · 27 public theorems · imports EqualExponentCount, Seed.Example, Seed.Starter, Cyclotomic, CycloRootCount, AbundancyTail

The argument of the 97 modules for a general prime l. Its hypotheses are the block base, the least small compatible prime, the least receiver and the finite row facts; its conclusion is that l divides N when all prime factors but two have an index divisible by l. A conditional statement: the modules for 67 and 89 supply the hypotheses. No published source was checked; novelty not verified.

Proof idea. Two receivers, at most l − 1 roots of the row polynomial modulo each receiver power, so at most 2(l − 1) compatible primes in each block; the product of p/(p − 1) then stays below 2.

OddPerfect.ThreeComponentGap

OddPerfect/ThreeComponentGap.lean · 312 lines · 10 public theorems · imports SpecialPrime, TwoExceptionsGeneralCore

For an odd perfect number N and any set of at most three prime factors, the product of σ(ce)/ce over the set is at most 52514/26325. A statement on every odd perfect number, used for three exceptions. No published source was checked; novelty not verified.

Proof idea. Cases on the set: without 3, without 5, with 3 and 5 and a third prime that is at least 17, and exponent cases for the third prime 7, 11 or 13, where a divisor of abundancy above 2 contradicts perfection. One explicit triple of prime powers attains the bound.

OddPerfect.PrimeMonomialCount

OddPerfect/PrimeMonomialCount.lean · 181 lines · 5 public theorems · imports CycloRootCount

A statement on primes; no odd perfect number appears. If powers of one prime d (other than l) divide the rows 1 + p + ⋯ + pl−1 of two primes p < p′, both powers exceed pA, and more than l pairs (i, j) satisfy i + Gj ≤ A, then pG < p′. Published method: the counting argument is that of Lemma 3.1 of T. Yamada, On finiteness of odd superperfect numbers (arXiv 0803.0437v7); the statement here uses another region of exponents.

Proof idea. The products of powers of p and p′ below the common modulus are distinct roots of xl = 1 modulo a power of d, and there are at most l such residues.

Let l and d ≠ l be primes and p < p' primes with d ^ x ∣ R(p), d ^ x' ∣ R(p'), where R(y) = ∑ i < l, y ^ i, and p ^ A below both powers. OddPerfect.TwoExceptionsUniform

OddPerfect/TwoExceptionsUniform.lean · 303 lines · 4 public theorems · imports TwoExceptionsGeneralCore, PrimeMonomialCount

If every prime factor p of an odd perfect number N, apart from two arbitrary numbers, has index ep + 1 divisible by a prime l ≥ 23, then l divides N. No data module is needed, and the theorems at 67, 89 and 97 are special cases. Restricted result: three exceptions and primes below 23 are not covered by this module. The counting method is published: Lemmas 3.1 to 3.3 of T. Yamada, On finiteness of odd superperfect numbers (arXiv 0803.0437v7). That paper does not state this result; no other source was checked; novelty not verified.

Proof idea. Each compatible prime has a dominant receiver among the exceptions. Two primes with the same receiver are far apart by the monomial count, so each block of base 81 holds at most one per receiver, and the product of p/(p − 1) stays below 2.

OddPerfect.AbundancyGapGeneral

OddPerfect/AbundancyGapGeneral.lean · 418 lines · 11 public theorems · imports AbundancyGap

A statement on finite sets of odd prime powers; no odd perfect number appears. For every s there is a rational ε > 0 such that the product of σ(ce)/ce over at most s odd primes, with even exponents except for one prime that is 1 modulo 4 with an exponent that is 1 modulo 4, is below 2 − ε as soon as it is below 2. The exponents are arbitrary; ε is not explicit. No published source was checked; novelty not verified.

Proof idea. Induction over states: each known prime carries either an exact exponent or a large one. With a large exponent present the limit value is never 2, by a count modulo 4. A new least prime is either large, and the product stays away from 2, or one of finitely many small primes, which joins the state with a large or an exact exponent.

That paper does not state this result; no other source was checked; novelty not verified.

If every prime factor p of an odd perfect number N outside a set of at most s numbers has index ep + 1 divisible by a prime l with 16s < l, and some prime factor lies outside the set, then l divides N. OddPerfect.DivisorRichExceptions

OddPerfect/DivisorRichExceptions.lean · 179 lines · 5 public theorems · imports KanoldSquare, EqualExponents

Let a number D divide the index ep + 1 of every prime factor p of an odd perfect number N outside a set of at most s numbers, with some prime factor outside the set, and let l be an odd prime. Write F for the set of divisors of D that l divides. Then vl(D)·(|F| − s) ≤ vl(N). So l divides N when l divides D and s < |F|, when l divides D and 2s < τ(D), and when lb divides every index outside the set with s < b. There is no size condition on l. Restricted results: nothing is said once s reaches |F|; for D = l only s = 0 is covered, and there the theorem of KanoldGeneral is stronger. No published source was checked; novelty not verified.

Proof idea. Each divisor of D that l divides gives, for every prime outside the set, a prime factor of its row that is 1 modulo that divisor. These primes are distinct, at most s of them are exceptions, and each of the others feeds the full power of l in D into N.
