OddPerfect.ReceiverSqueeze

OddPerfect/ReceiverSqueeze.lean · 433 lines · 10 public theorems · imports ExceptionsExplicit, EulerPart

Let T be a set of prime factors of an odd perfect number N with at most c prime factors outside it, l a prime that divides the index of every p in T, and X a set of at most b numbers that contains every prime factor other than l of the rows 1 + p + ⋯ + pl−1, p in T. Then 4c+b < l and 16b24b < l cannot both hold. Consequences: if l divides every ordinary index, then l ≤ 16t24t with t the number of prime factors that are 1 modulo l, and the same with t = ω(J) + 1 for the Euler index J. Restricted results: with the exceptions as receivers this returns the threshold of ExceptionsExplicit and nothing better; the common index family is not excluded. The counting method is published: Lemmas 3.1 to 3.3 of T. Yamada, On finiteness of odd superperfect numbers (arXiv 0803.0437v7). That paper does not state this result; no other source was checked; novelty not verified.

Proof idea. Each source has a dominant receiver in X. Sources with one receiver form a chain in which each is above a power of the one before, so few sources fit below the landed upper bound for N; the sources and the primes outside T then leave too few prime factors for that bound.

OddPerfect.KanoldFive

OddPerfect/KanoldFive.lean · 427 lines · 10 public theorems · imports KanoldGeneral

Boundary cases of the fifth power form of Kanold's theorem. If a prime power la divides e + 1 for every ordinary exponent e, then l5a divides N whenever l is an ordinary prime. For the special prime q the same holds when a is not 2. The case a = 2 with the exponent of q equal to 9 stays open here in general; it is excluded for q = 5. These are known results; the general statement t⁵ divides N for every t is in the literature and is not fully proved here.

Proof idea. Count the power of q through the exact ledger: the exponent of q is the sum of the powers of q in σ(pe) over the other primes p. Primes p ≡ 1 (mod q) contribute the power of q in e + 1, at least a each, and a prime of this class with qb dividing e + 1 brings b more primes of the class through primitive prime factors. Primes outside the class contribute nothing or at least a + 1. The exponent a(a + 1) + 1 fits neither count. For the ordinary prime 5 with exponent 4, the factors forced by σ(5⁴) = 11 · 71 give at least five ordinary primes ≡ 1 (mod 5), more than the exponent 4 allows.

OddPerfect.KanoldSquare

OddPerfect/KanoldSquare.lean · 318 lines · 3 public theorems · imports KanoldFive

The last case of the fifth power theorem, reduced to a normal form; the normal form is excluded in KanoldSquareFinal. Let q be the special prime and let q² divide e + 1 for every ordinary exponent e. Then q¹⁰ divides N, or the exponent of q is 9 and: only primes ≡ 1 (mod q) contribute to the power of q, exactly four prime factors are ≡ 1 (mod q), three of them have e + 1 = q² and one has e + 1 = q³. The known proof excludes this configuration with a further Diophantine argument, which is not formalized here.

Proof idea. The exponent 9 of q is the sum of the powers of q in σ(pe) over the other primes. A contributing prime outside the class ≡ 1 (mod q) would bring four primes of the class through the orders q, q², dq, dq², for a total of at least 11. So the class carries all 9, with at least 2 from each member. A member with qb dividing e + 1 forces b + 1 members, which leaves only four members with powers 3, 2, 2, 2. A further prime factor of a length e + 1 would bring a fifth member.

theorem kanold_square_normal_form {N q : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N) (hq : q.Prime)
  (hodd : Odd (N.factorization q))

The normal form of the square case with exponent 9. Let N be an odd perfect number with special prime q, suppose q ^ 2 ∣ e_p + 1 for every ordinary prime p, and v_q(N) = 9. Let S be the set of prime factors ≡ 1 (mod q). Then (a) every ordinary prime p with q ∣ σ(p ^ e_p) lies in S; (b) |S| = 4; (c) one member r of S has e_r + 1 = q ^ 3 and every other member s has e_s + 1 = q ^ 2. This is the normal form preceding the last step of the known proof of the fifth power theorem q ^ 10 ∣ N; that last step is not formalized here.

OddPerfect.ExponentTwentyFour

OddPerfect/ExponentTwentyFour.lean · 181 lines · 1 public theorem · imports KanoldFive

The ordinary prime factors of an odd perfect number cannot all have exponent 24. This is a known result (Hagis and McDaniel, 1975). The checker of EqualExponentChain needs a prime length and 25 is not prime, so this case has its own short proof.

Proof idea. Since 25 divides every ordinary e + 1, the fourth power theorem gives 5 ∣ N. If 5 is ordinary, σ(5²⁴) has the prime factors 11, 71, 101, 251, 401 and 9384251, and the values 1 + p + p² + p³ + p⁴ at 11, 71, 251, 9384251 and 211 give eight more, fourteen primes ≡ 1 (mod 5) in all. At most one is special, and each ordinary one contributes exactly 2 to the power of 5 in σ(N), so that power is at least 26, above 24. If 5 is special, its exponent is at least 13, 3 divides 5 + 1 and 11 divides σ(3²⁴), and 3⁴·5⁵·11² is an abundant divisor of N.

OddPerfect/CommonPrimeChain.lean · 1395 lines · 31 public theorems · imports KanoldFive, EqualExponentChain contains novelty unverified

Families where one prime divides every ordinary e + 1. If 5 divides every ordinary e + 1, then 5 is not the special prime and 5186 divides N. If 7 divides every ordinary e + 1, then 7124 divides N. So the ordinary exponents cannot all equal E when 5 divides E + 1 and E < 186, or 7 divides E + 1 and E < 124; this includes 34, 48, 54, 64, 76, 84, 90 and 94. The method is the classical one of forced prime chains. Of the excluded exponents, 34 and 48 are results of Hagis and McDaniel (1975). The family of 5 is empty by published results: the Main Theorem of Fletcher, Nielsen and Ochem (Math. Comp. 81, 2012) excludes the prime factor 5 when 3 or 5 divides every ordinary e + 1, and Kanold's theorem forces it; a preprint of 2015 also claims this, by a computation with about 960 thousand forced primes. Both are far beyond the tables checked here, and the library does not prove the general statement. For the family of 7 we did not find published statements of this kind (novelty unverified). The families themselves are not excluded here.

Proof idea. Let r divide every ordinary e + 1. For an ordinary prime p, every odd prime factor of 1 + p + … + pr−1 divides N, and it is r or ≡ 1 (mod r). Each ordinary prime ≡ 1 (mod r) contributes at least 1 to the exponent of r. A table of forced primes, starting from r, is checked by the kernel. The special prime is unknown and cannot be used as a source, so the checker removes each possible node in turn and counts the primes that are still forced; the smallest count is the bound. For r = 5 the special case is excluded first: 5 special would force 3 and 11 and the abundant divisor 3⁴·5⁵·11².

OddPerfect.CommonFamily

OddPerfect/CommonFamily.lean · 375 lines · 16 public theorems · imports CommonPrimeChain

A whole family excluded: if 35 divides e + 1 for every ordinary exponent e, then N is not an odd perfect number. This is a theorem of Hagis and McDaniel (1975). In particular the ordinary exponents cannot all equal E when 35 divides E + 1, with no bound on E. The module also proves two facts of Evans and Pearlman (2007) for the family where 5 divides every ordinary e + 1: 3 does not divide N, and the special prime is ≡ 1 (mod 12).

Proof idea. In the family of 35, the primes 5 and 7 divide N and are ordinary, and for an ordinary prime s every odd prime factor of 1 + s + … + s³⁴ divides N. A kernel checked table forces the 22 primes 5, 7, 11, 29, 31, 41, 43, 61, 71, 101, 113, 127, 131, 151, 181, 191, 197, 211, 239, 241, 251 and 271, whichever prime is special: the special prime is ≡ 1 (mod 12), and the checker never uses such a node as a source. Every ordinary exponent is at least 4, so the fourth powers of these primes divide N; if one of 61, 181, 241 is the special prime, only its first power is used. In each of the four cases the divisor is abundant, which is impossible. For 3 ∤ N in the family of 5: otherwise 3⁴·5⁴·11⁴ would be an abundant divisor.

OddPerfect.not_three_dvd_of_common_five

  (hodd : Odd (N.factorization q))
  (hexp : ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ≠ q → 5 ∣ N.factorization p + 1) : ¬ 3 ∣ N

In the common 5 family, 3 ∤ N (known; Evans and Pearlman). Let N be an odd perfect number with special prime q and 5 ∣ v_p(N) + 1 for every ordinary prime p. If 3 ∣ N, then 3 and 11 ∣ σ(3 ^ 4) = 121 are ordinary, as is 5, all with exponent at least 4, and 3 ^ 4 · 5 ^ 4 · 11 ^ 4 is abundant.

OddPerfect.ForcingClosedBoundTwo

OddPerfect/ForcingClosedBoundTwo.lean · 285 lines · 3 public theorems · imports ForcingClosedBound

Every forcing closed configuration has a node above 2000, up from 1000 in ForcingClosedBound. As there, this uses only parity and closure under forcing, and none of the size information of an odd perfect number.

Proof idea. The same greatest fixed point iteration: start from the odd numbers up to 2000 that pass a cheap sieve and repeatedly delete every entry with no move inside the current list. The step is faster: an ordinary move of length l at p needs a node r with r ≡ 1 (mod l) and pl ≡ 1 (mod r), so the expensive smoothness test of a row runs only when such an r is present. The list empties in ten rounds, one kernel check per round.

OddPerfect.CommonFiveSeven

OddPerfect/CommonFiveSeven.lean · 1272 lines · 39 public theorems · imports CommonFamily

In the family where 5 divides e + 1 for every ordinary exponent e, 7 does not divide N. This is a theorem of Evans and Pearlman (2007). With 3 ∤ N from CommonFamily it gives gcd(N, 21) = 1 in that family. The module also holds the general tools used for the larger tables: a reach checker with an arbitrary test for the special prime, primality by trial division to the square root, and an abundancy check for all cases at once.

Proof idea. Suppose 7 ∣ N. Then 7 is ordinary with exponent at least 4, and the forcing table starts from 5 and 7: for an ordinary prime s, every odd prime factor of 1 + s + s² + s³ + s⁴ divides N. A table of 358 rows, checked by the kernel, forces 110 primes up to 3911 whichever prime is special (the special prime is ≡ 1 (mod 12), and each such source is switched off in turn). The fourth powers of these primes, with only the first power for the special one, form an abundant divisor in every case; the smallest margin is 2.00048, when 61 is special.

  (hstep : ∀ x ∈ nodes.take rows.length, x ∣ N → x ≠ b → ∀ t ∈ nodes, gm x t r = 0 → t ∣ N)
  (hgm0 : ∀ x ∈ nodes, gm x 0 r ≠ 0)
  (hz : ∀ e ∈ nodes.zip rows, ∀ j ∈ e.2, gm e.1 (nodes.getD j 0) r = 0) :
  ∀ (n M : ℕ), (∀ k, M.testBit k = true → nodes.getD k 0 ∣ N) →
    ∀ k, (fiter b nodes rows tm n M).testBit k = true → nodes.getD k 0 ∣ N

fiter preserves the same property.

OddPerfect.FamInst.pPow_pSig_split

theorem pPow_pSig_split : ∀ {S : List ℕ} {b : ℕ}, (∀ t ∈ S, t ≠ 0) → S.Nodup → b ∈ S →
  pPow (expL S 0) = pPow (expL S b) * b ^ 3 ∧
    pSig (expL S 0) * (b + 1) = pSig (expL S b) * geomS b 4

Splitting off one element: with b ∈ S, distinct nonzero elements, the full products pPow (expL S 0) and pSig (expL S 0) relate to those with b to the first power.

OddPerfect.dvd_of_reach

theorem dvd_of_reach {N q d ns passes tm : ℕ} {cand : ℕ → Bool} {nodes : List ℕ}
  {rows : List (List ℕ)} (h : OddPerfect N)
  (hexp : ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ≠ q → d ∣ N.factorization p + 1) (hd : 1 ≤ d)
  (hcq : cand q = true) (hP : ∀ t ∈ nodes, t.Prime) (h2 : ∀ t ∈ nodes, t ≠ 2)
  (hseed : ∀ t ∈ nodes.take ns, t ∣ N) (hns : ns ≤ nodes.length)
  (hrows : ∀ e ∈ nodes.zip rows, rowChk d nodes e = true)
  (hcand : ∀ b ∈ nodes.take rows.length, cand b = true →
    reach nodes rows ns tm passes b = true)
  (h0 : reach nodes rows ns tm passes 0 = true) :
  ∀ k, tm.testBit k = true → nodes.getD k 0 ∣ N

Soundness of the reach checks. Let N be an odd perfect number and q a number such that d ∣ v_p(N) + 1 for every prime factor p ≠ q, where d ≥ 1, with cand q. Take a table with odd prime nodes nodes, whose first ns nodes divide N (with ns at most the number of nodes), and whose rows pass rowChk. If all bits of tm are reached for every blocked source node b (one of the first rows.length nodes) with cand b, and for the blocked value 0, then every node whose index is a bit of tm divides N.

OddPerfect.FamInst.abOK2_sound

theorem FamInst.abOK2_sound {N q P G : ℕ} {cand : ℕ → Bool} (hN : N.Perfect) {S : List ℕ}
  (hP : ∀ t ∈ S, t.Prime) (hnd : S.Nodup) (hS : ∀ t ∈ S, t ∣ N)
  (h4 : ∀ t ∈ S, t ≠ q → t ^ 4 ∣ N) (hcq : cand q = true)
  (hPG : pPow (expL S 0) = P ∧ pSig (expL S 0) = G) (hab : abOK2 S cand P G = true) :
  False

Soundness of abOK2. Let N be perfect, S a list of distinct primes dividing N with t ^ 4 ∣ N for every t ∈ S other than q, and cand q. If P and G are the products of t ^ 4 and of 1 + t + ... + t ^ 4 over S, then abOK2 S cand P G fails.

OddPerfect.false_of_reach

theorem false_of_reach {N q d ns passes tm P G : ℕ} {cand cand' : ℕ → Bool}
  {nodes vals : List ℕ} {rows : List (List ℕ)} (h : OddPerfect N)
  (hexp : ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ≠ q → d ∣ N.factorization p + 1) (hd : 5 ≤ d)
  (hcq : cand q = true) (hcq' : cand' q = true) (hP : ∀ t ∈ nodes, t.Prime)
  (h2 : ∀ t ∈ nodes, t ≠ 2) (hseed : ∀ t ∈ nodes.take ns, t ∣ N) (hns : ns ≤ nodes.length)
  (hrows : ∀ e ∈ nodes.zip rows, rowChk d nodes e = true)
  (hcand : ∀ b ∈ nodes.take rows.length, cand b = true →
    reach nodes rows ns tm passes b = true)
  (h0 : reach nodes rows ns tm passes 0 = true) (hv : sel 0 tm 0 nodes = vals)
  (hnd : vals.Nodup) (hPG : pPow (expL vals 0) = P ∧ pSig (expL vals 0) = G)
  (hab : abOK2 vals cand' P G = true) : False

The combined closer. Let N be an odd perfect number and q a number with cand q and cand' q, such that d ∣ v_p(N) + 1 for every prime factor p ≠ q, where d ≥ 5. A table as in dvd_of_reach, whose selected target primes vals (the nodes whose index is a bit of tm) pass abOK2 with cand', gives a contradiction.

OddPerfect.not_seven_dvd_of_common_five

theorem not_seven_dvd_of_common_five {N q : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N) (hq : q.Prime)
  (hodd : Odd (N.factorization q))
  (hexp : ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ≠ q → 5 ∣ N.factorization p + 1) : ¬ 7 ∣ N

In the common 5 family, 7 ∤ N. Let N be an odd perfect number with special prime q and 5 ∣ v_p(N) + 1 for every ordinary prime p. Then 5 ∣ N and q ≡ 1 (mod 12); if 7 ∣ N, the forcing table from the seeds 5, 7 reaches all target primes whichever source node ≡ 1 (mod 12) is special, and they give an abundant divisor.

OddPerfect.CommonSixtyFive

OddPerfect/CommonSixtyFive.lean · 696 lines · 33 public theorems · imports CommonFiveSeven

A second family excluded as a whole: if 65 divides e + 1 for every ordinary exponent e, then N is not an odd perfect number. This is a theorem of Evans and Pearlman (2007). In particular the ordinary exponents cannot all equal E when 65 divides E + 1.

Proof idea. The seeds are 5 and 13, which divide N. For an ordinary prime s every odd prime factor of 1 + s + … + s⁶⁴ divides N. The prime 13 is ≡ 1 (mod 12) and may itself be special, so the proof splits. If 13 is special, 7 = (13 + 1)/2 divides N and joins the seeds, and the rows of 13 are not used. Otherwise 13 is ordinary and every other source ≡ 1 (mod 12) is switched off in turn. In both branches a kernel checked table of 361 rows forces 315 primes, and their fourth powers (first power for the special prime) form an abundant divisor; the smallest margin is 2.0000666.

OddPerfect.not_common_sixty_five

theorem not_common_sixty_five {N q : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N) (hq : q.Prime)
  (hodd : Odd (N.factorization q))
  (hexp : ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ≠ q → 65 ∣ N.factorization p + 1) : False

The common 65 family is impossible. Let N be an odd perfect number with special prime q. Then 65 ∣ v_p(N) + 1 cannot hold for every ordinary prime p. Here 5 ∣ N, 13 ∣ N and q ≡ 1 (mod 12). If q = 13, then 7 ∣ 13 + 1 divides N and the seeds are 5, 13, 7 with the rows of 13 blocked; otherwise 13 is ordinary, the seeds are 5, 13, and every source node ≡ 1 (mod 12) other than 13 is blocked in turn. In both cases the target primes give an abundant divisor.

OddPerfect.CommonFiftyFive

OddPerfect/CommonFiftyFive.lean · 1364 lines · 44 public theorems · imports CommonFastChecks

A third family excluded as a whole: if 55 divides e + 1 for every ordinary exponent e, then N is not an odd perfect number. Known mathematics: every family whose common divisor is a multiple of 5 follows from the Main Theorem of Fletcher, Nielsen and Ochem (Math. Comp. 81, 2012) together with Kanold's theorem that a common prime divisor of all ordinary e + 1 divides N. The module gives an independent certificate checked by the kernel.

Proof idea. The same method as for 35 and 65, with a larger table. The seeds are 5 and 11, both ordinary. A kernel checked table of 911 rows forces 936 primes whichever source ≡ 1 (mod 12) is special (186 sources are switched off in turn), and their fourth powers, with the first power for the special prime, form an abundant divisor in every case. The smallest margin is 2.0000034, when 61 is special. The table was found by a search outside Lean; the kernel rechecks every primality, every divisibility, every reach computation and every inequality.

OddPerfect.not_common_fifty_five

theorem not_common_fifty_five {N q : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N) (hq : q.Prime)
  (hodd : Odd (N.factorization q))
  (hexp : ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ≠ q → 55 ∣ N.factorization p + 1) : False

The common 55 family is impossible. Let N be an odd perfect number with special prime q. Then 55 ∣ v_p(N) + 1 cannot hold for every ordinary prime p. Here 5 ∣ N, 11 ∣ N and q ≡ 1 (mod 12); the forcing table from the seeds 5, 11 reaches all target primes whichever source node ≡ 1 (mod 12) is special, and they give an abundant divisor.

OddPerfect.not_all_exponents_eq_of_fifty_five_dvd_succ

theorem not_all_exponents_eq_of_fifty_five_dvd_succ {N q E : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N)
  (hq : q.Prime) (hodd : Odd (N.factorization q)) (hE : 55 ∣ E + 1)
  (hexp : ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ≠ q → N.factorization p = E) : False

The ordinary exponents of an odd perfect number cannot all equal one E with 55 ∣ E + 1.

OddPerfect.CommonEightyFive

OddPerfect/CommonEightyFive.lean · 1649 lines · 49 public theorems · imports CommonFastChecks

A fourth family excluded as a whole: if 85 divides e + 1 for every ordinary exponent e, then N is not an odd perfect number. Known mathematics: every family whose common divisor is a multiple of 5 follows from the Main Theorem of Fletcher, Nielsen and Ochem (Math. Comp. 81, 2012) together with Kanold's theorem that a common prime divisor of all ordinary e + 1 divides N. The module gives an independent certificate checked by the kernel.

Proof idea. The method of CommonFiftyFive with the seeds 5 and 17; 17 is ≡ 5 (mod 12), so it is not the special prime. A kernel checked table of 1147 rows forces 1059 primes whichever source ≡ 1 (mod 12) is special (215 cases), and their fourth powers, with the first power for the special prime, form an abundant divisor in every case. The smallest margin is 2.0000027.

OddPerfect.CommonOneFifteenData

OddPerfect/CommonOneFifteenData.lean · 2540 lines · 48 public theorems · imports CommonFastChecks

Data for the family of 115: the forcing table of 1958 rows on 2728 primes, the kernel checks that every listed receiver divides 1 + s + … + s¹¹⁴ for its source s, the 1521 targets, and the two full products used in the abundance check.

Proof idea. The divisibility checks are split into 40 kernel runs to keep memory low. The table was found by a search outside Lean and is fully rechecked here.

OddPerfect.CommonOneFifteenPrime

OddPerfect/CommonOneFifteenPrime.lean · 157 lines · 29 public theorems · imports CommonOneFifteenData

Proof idea. The largest node is 15352501, below 4201², so trial division by the odd primes up to 4201 suffices for each node.

OddPerfect.CommonOneFifteen

OddPerfect/CommonOneFifteen.lean · 163 lines · 11 public theorems · imports CommonOneFifteenPrime

A fifth family excluded as a whole: if 115 divides e + 1 for every ordinary exponent e, then N is not an odd perfect number. Known mathematics: every family whose common divisor is a multiple of 5 follows from the Main Theorem of Fletcher, Nielsen and Ochem (Math. Comp. 81, 2012) together with Kanold's theorem that a common prime divisor of all ordinary e + 1 divides N. The module gives an independent certificate checked by the kernel.

Proof idea. The method of CommonFiftyFive with the seeds 5 and 23. A kernel checked table of 1958 rows forces 1521 primes whichever source ≡ 1 (mod 12) is special (391 cases), and their fourth powers, with the first power for the special prime, form an abundant divisor in every case. The smallest margin is 2.0000023. This module holds the reach checks, the abundance check and the final theorem; the table and the primality proofs are in the two modules it imports.

The common 115 family is impossible. Let N be an odd perfect number with special prime q. Then 115 ∣ v_p(N) + 1 cannot hold for every ordinary prime p. OddPerfect.KanoldObstruction

OddPerfect/KanoldObstruction.lean · 614 lines · 17 public theorems

Kanold's obstruction: for an odd prime p, primes r, s and positive a, b, the equations G(r^(p^u)) = p·s^a and G(s^(p^v)) = p·r^b cannot both hold, where G(X) = 1 + X + … + X^(p−1). A special case of a theorem of H.-J. Kanold (J. reine angew. Math. 189, pages 243 to 245).

Proof idea. Both equations force r ≡ s ≡ 1 (mod p). If one exponent is small (a ≤ p^v), a size comparison forces v = 0, a = 1 and then s < r^(p^u), against p·s = G(r^(p^u)). Otherwise u = v, and with r < s the residue of b modulo p·p^u is pinned down, which forces u = 0, a = 2 and p(s − 1) = s² − r², impossible since p divides s − r. The lemma is the Diophantine input for the last case of the fifth power divisibility theorem, proved in KanoldSquareFinal.

OddPerfect.KanoldSquareFinal

OddPerfect/KanoldSquareFinal.lean · 1159 lines · 24 public theorems · imports KanoldSquare, KanoldObstruction

The fifth power theorem in full: if t divides e + 1 for every ordinary exponent e, then t⁵ divides N. The theorem is due to Kanold (fourth power) and Yamada (fifth power). This module settles the last case, the special prime q ≥ 13 with q² dividing every ordinary e + 1 and exponent 9 at q.

Proof idea. In the last case exactly four primes ≡ 1 (mod q) carry all of q⁹: three with e + 1 = q² and one with e + 1 = q³. The cyclotomic blocks 1 + Y + … + Y^(q−1) of these primes are q times products of powers of the other three, and blocks at different levels share no prime. Kanold's obstruction rules out two blocks that are q times a prime power of each other; order arguments force one prime above q², and size comparisons with real logarithms then contradict q ≥ 13.

  (hD0 : ∃ k, 0 < k ∧ (kC q 0 D = q * B ^ k ∨ kC q 0 D = q * E ^ k))
  {γ e2 e3 e4 : ℕ} (hγ : γ ≤ 1) (he3 : 0 < e3) (he4 : 0 < e4)

  KanoldObstructionAt p

OddPerfect.pow_ten_dvd_of_special_sq

theorem pow_ten_dvd_of_special_sq {N q : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N) (hq : q.Prime)
  (hodd : Odd (N.factorization q))
  (hexp : ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ≠ q → q ^ 2 ∣ N.factorization p + 1) : q ^ 10 ∣ N

The fifth power at the special prime with exponent 2: if q ^ 2 ∣ e_p + 1 for every ordinary prime p of the odd perfect number N with special prime q, then q ^ 10 ∣ N.

OddPerfect.pow_five_dvd_of_forall_dvd_succ

  (hodd : Odd (N.factorization q))
  (ht : ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ≠ q → t ∣ N.factorization p + 1) : t ^ 5 ∣ N

If t ∣ e_p + 1 for every ordinary prime p of the odd perfect number N with special prime q, then t ^ 5 ∣ N.

OddPerfect.CommonFastChecks

OddPerfect/CommonFastChecks.lean · 358 lines · 15 public theorems · imports CommonFiveSeven

Three cheaper forms of the forcing table checks, each with a proof that it implies the original check: primality by trial division over a fixed list of odd primes, row checks through a node list cut into parts, and reach checks with a whole set of source nodes blocked at once.

Proof idea. The kernel evaluates the same facts with far less work. Each fast check comes with a soundness lemma, so the theorems that use them state exactly what they stated before.

Public theorems

OddPerfect.FamInst.tdl_sound

theorem tdl_sound {q : ℕ} : ∀ {L : List ℕ}, L.Pairwise (· < ·) → tdl q L = true →
  (∃ a ∈ L, q < a * a) ∧ ∀ p ∈ L, p * p ≤ q → q % p ≠ 0

Soundness of tdl on an increasing list: the walk stops at some element a with q < a * a, and no element p with p * p ≤ q divides q.

OddPerfect.FamInst.pairwise_of_incr

theorem pairwise_of_incr : ∀ {L : List ℕ}, incr L = true → L.Pairwise (· < ·)

Soundness of incr.

OddPerfect.FamInst.not_prime_of_hasDiv

theorem not_prime_of_hasDiv {m : ℕ} (h : hasDiv m = true) : ¬ m.Prime

A number with a divisor d with 2 ≤ d < m is not prime.

OddPerfect.FamInst.cover_sound

theorem cover_sound : ∀ (f m : ℕ) (L : List ℕ), cover f m L = true →
  ∀ p, p.Prime → m ≤ p → (∃ a ∈ L, p ≤ a) → p ∈ L

Soundness of cover: every prime p ≥ m that is at most some element of L is in L.

OddPerfect.FamInst.fastPrime_sound

theorem fastPrime_sound {L : List ℕ} {f : ℕ} (hi : incr L = true) (hc : cover f 3 L = true)
  {q : ℕ} (h : fastPrime L q = true) : q.Prime

Soundness of fastPrime for an increasing list that contains every odd prime up to its elements.

OddPerfect.FamInst.oddP_incr

theorem oddP_incr : incr oddP = true

oddP is increasing.

OddPerfect.FamInst.oddP_cover

theorem oddP_cover : cover 5000 3 oddP = true

oddP contains every odd prime up to 4201.

OddPerfect.FamInst.prime_of_fastPrime

theorem prime_of_fastPrime {q : ℕ} (h : fastPrime oddP q = true) : q.Prime

Primality by trial division over oddP, for odd numbers below 4201 ^ 2.

OddPerfect.FamInst.getD_flatten

theorem getD_flatten {K : ℕ} (hK : 0 < K) : ∀ (parts : List (List ℕ)), lensOK K parts = true →
  ∀ j, parts.flatten.getD j 0 = ptD K parts j

Reading the flattening of parts of length K.

OddPerfect.FamInst.rowChk_of_rowChkP

theorem rowChk_of_rowChkP {K d : ℕ} {nodes : List ℕ} {parts : List (List ℕ)} (hK : 0 < K)
  (hn : nodes = parts.flatten) (hl : lensOK K parts = true) {e : ℕ × List ℕ}
  (h : rowChkP K parts d e = true) : rowChk d nodes e = true

rowChkP agrees with rowChk on the flattened node list.

OddPerfect.FamInst.land_eq_iff

theorem land_eq_iff {X tm : ℕ} : X &&& tm = tm ↔ ∀ k, tm.testBit k = true → X.testBit k = true

X &&& tm = tm means that every bit of tm is set in X.

OddPerfect.FamInst.fpassS_sub

theorem fpassS_sub {bl : ℕ → Bool} {b : ℕ} (hb : bl b = true) :
  ∀ (i : ℕ) (xs : List ℕ) (rs : List (List ℕ)) (M M' : ℕ),
    (∀ k, M.testBit k = true → M'.testBit k = true) →
    ∀ k, (fpassS bl i xs rs M).testBit k = true → (fpass b i xs rs M').testBit k = true

A pass with a blocked set gives a submask of a pass with one blocked node of the set, from a submask.

OddPerfect.FamInst.fiterS_sub

theorem fiterS_sub {bl : ℕ → Bool} {b : ℕ} (hb : bl b = true) {nodes : List ℕ}
  {rows : List (List ℕ)} {tm : ℕ} : ∀ (n M M' : ℕ),
    (∀ k, M.testBit k = true → M'.testBit k = true) →
    fiterS bl nodes rows tm n M &&& tm = tm → fiter b nodes rows tm n M' &&& tm = tm

The passes with a blocked set reach the target mask only if the passes with one blocked node of the set do, from a submask.

OddPerfect.FamInst.reach_of_reachS

theorem reach_of_reachS {nodes : List ℕ} {rows : List (List ℕ)} {ns tm passes : ℕ}
  {bl : ℕ → Bool} (h : reachS nodes rows ns tm passes bl = true) {b : ℕ} (hb : bl b = true) :
  reach nodes rows ns tm passes b = true

A reach check with a blocked set implies the reach check for every blocked node of the set.

OddPerfect.FamInst.hcand_of_groups

theorem hcand_of_groups {nodes : List ℕ} {rows : List (List ℕ)} {ns tm passes : ℕ}
  {cand : ℕ → Bool} (bls : List (ℕ → Bool))
  (hg : ∀ f ∈ bls, reachS nodes rows ns tm passes f = true)
  (hc : (nodes.take rows.length).all (fun b => !cand b || bls.any fun f => f b) = true) :
  ∀ b ∈ nodes.take rows.length, cand b = true → reach nodes rows ns tm passes b = true

Reach checks for all blocked candidates from a few blocked sets: every source node b with cand b lies in one of the sets of bls, and each set passes the reach check.

OddPerfect.CommonNinetyFiveData

OddPerfect/CommonNinetyFiveData.lean · 4296 lines · 0 public theorems · imports CommonFastChecks

Data for the family of 95: the forcing table of 3200 rows on 4480 primes (largest 17607871), and the 2700 targets.

Proof idea. The table was found by a search outside Lean and is fully rechecked by the kernel in the modules that import this one. The node list is defined as the concatenation of its parts so that the parts can be checked separately.

OddPerfect.CommonNinetyFiveFacts

OddPerfect/CommonNinetyFiveFacts.lean · 104 lines · 9 public theorems · imports CommonNinetyFiveData

List facts for the family of 95: the equations between the table and its parts, no node is 2, the target primes are selected and distinct, and the two full products of the abundance check.

Proof idea. Kept apart from the heavy check modules so that each of those needs only the data.

Reach checks for the family of 95: four kernel checks, each with a whole set of candidate special primes blocked at once, which together cover every candidate.

Proof idea. One closure computation per candidate, run in the kernel; 639 candidates in all.

OddPerfect.CommonNinetyFive

OddPerfect/CommonNinetyFive.lean · 218 lines · 6 public theorems · imports CommonNinetyFiveFacts, CommonNinetyFiveRows1, CommonNinetyFiveRows2, CommonNinetyFiveRows3, CommonNinetyFiveRows4, CommonNinetyFiveRows5, CommonNinetyFivePrime1, CommonNinetyFivePrime2, CommonNinetyFivePrime3, CommonNinetyFivePrime4, CommonNinetyFiveReach1

A sixth family excluded as a whole: if 95 divides e + 1 for every ordinary exponent e, then N is not an odd perfect number. Known mathematics: every family whose common divisor is a multiple of 5 follows from the Main Theorem of Fletcher, Nielsen and Ochem (Math. Comp. 81, 2012) together with Kanold's theorem that a common prime divisor of all ordinary e + 1 divides N. The module gives an independent certificate checked by the kernel.

Proof idea. The method of CommonFiftyFive with the seeds 5 and 19; 19 is ≡ 3 (mod 4), so it is not the special prime. A kernel checked table of 3200 rows on 4480 primes forces 2700 primes whichever source ≡ 1 (mod 12) is special (639 cases), and their fourth powers, with the first power for the special prime, form an abundant divisor in every case. The smallest margin is 2.0000015. This module assembles the checks of the modules it imports and states the final theorem.

theorem not_common_ninety_five {N q : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N) (hq : q.Prime)
  (hodd : Odd (N.factorization q))

The common 95 family is impossible. Let N be an odd perfect number with special prime q. Then 95 ∣ v_p(N) + 1 cannot hold for every ordinary prime p. Here 5 ∣ N, 19 ∣ N and q ≡ 1 (mod 12); the forcing table from the seeds 5, 19 reaches all target primes whichever source node ≡ 1 (mod 12) is special, and they give an abundant divisor.

OddPerfect.ThreeFreeThreeCore

OddPerfect/ThreeFreeThreeCore.lean · 908 lines · 21 public theorems · imports ThreeFreeTwo, OmegaFour

The setting for three exceptional primes: the core configuration of an odd perfect number not divisible by 3 with special prime q and three exceptional primes, the facts about its ordinary primes, whose exponents e satisfy 3 ∣ e + 1, and the closing inequality with an abstract bound per exponent vector.

Proof idea. For an ordinary prime s with exponent e, 3 ∣ e + 1 makes 1 + s + s² divide σ(se), so s ≡ 2 (mod 3) and 1 + s + s² = qar₁br₂cr₃d, and s determines the vector (a, b, c, d). Each ordinary component is below s/(s − 1), which is the bound for exponent 2 times s³/(s³ − 1); the product of these factors over all s from a cap on is bounded by a constant close to 1, which the checker fixes. The excess σ(s²)/s² − 1 is bounded by the product of four weights raised to these exponents, so the sum over all ordinary primes is a finite box sum plus a geometric tail. Labels that are not distinct prime factors of N are replaced by three distinct prime factors other than q, which only weakens the hypothesis.

  (hγ0 : 0 ≤ γ) (hγ1 : γ < 1) (hδ0 : 0 ≤ δ) (hδ1 : δ < 1)
  (hα : 1 ≤ α ^ 2 * q ∨ q % 3 = 2) (hβ : 1 ≤ β ^ 2 * r₁ ∨ r₁ % 3 = 2)
  (hγ : 1 ≤ γ ^ 2 * r₂ ∨ r₂ % 3 = 2) (hδ : 1 ≤ δ ^ 2 * r₃ ∨ r₃ % 3 = 2)
  (hρ₀ : (q : ℚ) / (q - 1) ≤ ρ₀) (hρ₁ : (r₁ : ℚ) / (r₁ - 1) ≤ ρ₁)
  (hρ₂ : (r₂ : ℚ) / (r₂ - 1) ≤ ρ₂) (hρ₃ : (r₃ : ℚ) / (r₃ - 1) ≤ ρ₃)
  (C : Finset ℕ) (hC : ∀ x ∈ C, 2 ≤ x)
  (hsmall : ∀ s ∈ ord4 N q r₁ r₂ r₃, s < cap → s ∈ C)
  (g : ℕ × ℕ × ℕ × ℕ → ℚ) (hg0 : ∀ v, 0 ≤ g v)

OddPerfect.ThreeFreeThreeChecker

OddPerfect/ThreeFreeThreeChecker.lean · 1114 lines · 9 public theorems · imports ThreeFreeThreeCore

A Boolean certificate checker for the three exception theorem, in natural number arithmetic, with its soundness proof, and the proof that 102 sorted class triples cover every configuration. It contains no certificate data.

Proof idea. A node constrains each of q, r₁, r₂, r₃ to a pinned value or to a residue class with a lower bound and a list of excluded values. A leaf check computes the least possible values, the small ordinary primes that the constraints allow (from a table of the prime factors of 1 + s + s² for s below 300), the box sum, the tail and the closing inequality, which carries the factor s/(s − 1) for each small ordinary prime and the tail factor 178802/178801. Exponent vectors supported on pinned primes are decided exactly: 4n − 3 must be an odd square for a prime s with 1 + s + s² = n to exist, and the checker tests a computed integer square root. A tree is sound by induction: a split pins a free slot to a value or excludes that value.

This theorem proves nothing by itself: the three exception statement is proved only once a data module supplies trees and establishes the check. If N is an odd perfect number, q its special prime, and every prime factor p of N other than q, r₁, r₂, r₃ has an exponent e with 3 ∣ e + 1, then 3 ∣ N.

OddPerfect.ThreeFreeThreeData01

OddPerfect/ThreeFreeThreeData01.lean · 495 lines · 6 public theorems · imports ThreeFreeThreeChecker

Case data for the three exception theorem, part 1 of 11: 77 leaves of the case trees, each rechecked by the kernel.

Proof idea. The leaves were found by a search outside Lean. Each group of five leaf checks is one kernel evaluation of the checker, and the subtree lemmas combine them with the split rule. Grouping by five keeps the memory of the module below 10 GB.

OddPerfect.ThreeFreeThreeData11

OddPerfect/ThreeFreeThreeData11.lean · 606 lines · 13 public theorems · imports ThreeFreeThreeChecker

Case data for the three exception theorem, part 11 of 11: 85 leaves of the case trees, each rechecked by the kernel.

Proof idea. The leaves were found by a search outside Lean. Each group of five leaf checks is one kernel evaluation of the checker, and the subtree lemmas combine them with the split rule. Grouping by five keeps the memory of the module below 10 GB.

OddPerfect.ThreeFreeThree

OddPerfect/ThreeFreeThree.lean · 1031 lines · 106 public theorems · imports ThreeFreeThreeData01, ThreeFreeThreeData02, ThreeFreeThreeData03, ThreeFreeThreeData04, ThreeFreeThreeData05, ThreeFreeThreeData06, ThreeFreeThreeData07, ThreeFreeThreeData08, ThreeFreeThreeData09, ThreeFreeThreeData10, ThreeFreeThreeData11 contains novelty unverified

If every prime factor other than the special prime q and three further primes r₁, r₂, r₃ has an exponent e with 3 dividing e + 1 (for example e = 2), then 3 divides N. No condition is placed on r₁, r₂, r₃. Counting form: if 3 does not divide N, at least four prime factors other than q have an exponent e with 3 not dividing e + 1. This extends the two exception theorem and the earlier version for exponents exactly 2. Whether the statement is new has not been checked (novelty unverified, literature not screened).

Proof idea. The method of ThreeFreeTwo with four target primes. Assume 3 does not divide N. The three exceptional primes are sorted into classes (the fixed primes 5, 7, 13, 19, 31, 37, 43, other primes ≡ 2 (mod 3), and primes ≡ 1 (mod 3) from 61 on), which gives 102 class triples. For each triple a tree of cases pins the special prime or an exceptional prime to explicit values or excludes them, and at each of the 1223 leaves the abundancy is bounded below 2: an exact part of the box sum is decided by an integer square root test, the rest by geometric weights and a tail. This module assembles the checks of the data modules and states the final theorem.

OddPerfect.three_dvd_of_three_mod_exceptionsnovelty unverified

theorem three_dvd_of_three_mod_exceptions {N q r₁ r₂ r₃ : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N) (hq : q.Prime)
  (hodd : Odd (N.factorization q))
  (hmod : ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ≠ q → p ≠ r₁ → p ≠ r₂ → p ≠ r₃ → 3 ∣ N.factorization p + 1) :
  3 ∣ N

An odd perfect number N with special prime q, in which every prime factor p other than q and three further numbers r₁, r₂, r₃ has an exponent e = N.factorization p with 3 ∣ e + 1, is divisible by 3. Here r₁, r₂, r₃ are arbitrary natural numbers: they need not be distinct, prime, or divisors of N, so the cases of fewer exceptional primes are included. The case analysis behind the proof was found by a search outside Lean and is rechecked by the kernel.

OddPerfect.three_dvd_of_three_exceptionsnovelty unverified

theorem three_dvd_of_three_exceptions {N q r₁ r₂ r₃ : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N) (hq : q.Prime)
  (hodd : Odd (N.factorization q))
  (hsq : ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ≠ q → p ≠ r₁ → p ≠ r₂ → p ≠ r₃ → N.factorization p = 2) :
  3 ∣ N

An odd perfect number in which every prime factor other than the special prime q and three further primes r₁, r₂, r₃ has exponent exactly 2 is divisible by 3. Here r₁, r₂, r₃ are arbitrary natural numbers: they need not be distinct, prime, or divisors of N, so the cases of fewer exceptional primes are included. This is the case e = 2 of three_dvd_of_three_mod_exceptions.

OddPerfect.four_le_card_mod_exceptionsnovelty unverified

theorem four_le_card_mod_exceptions {N q : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N) (hq : q.Prime)
  (hodd : Odd (N.factorization q)) (h3 : ¬ 3 ∣ N) :
  4 ≤ ((N.primeFactors.erase q).filter fun p => ¬ 3 ∣ N.factorization p + 1).card

The counting form of three_dvd_of_three_mod_exceptions: if N is an odd perfect number with special prime q and 3 ∤ N, then at least four prime factors p ≠ q of N have an exponent e = N.factorization p with 3 ∤ e + 1.

OddPerfect.ThreeFreeCount

OddPerfect/ThreeFreeCount.lean · 95 lines · 3 public theorems · imports ThreeFreeThree, Counting, SpecialPrime

Counting corollaries of the modular three exception theorem: if 3 does not divide N, at least four prime factors other than the special prime have exponent at least 4, and 2 ω(N) + 7 ≤ Ω(N). Formal consequences inside this library; the literature has much stronger results when 3 does not divide N.

Proof idea. The modular theorem gives four ordinary primes whose exponent e has 3 not dividing e + 1. Such an exponent is even, positive and not 2, so it is at least 4. Summing the exponents (at least 1 for the special prime, at least 4 for these four, at least 2 for the rest) gives the count.

Public theorems

OddPerfect.four_le_factorization_of_mem_mod_exceptions

theorem four_le_factorization_of_mem_mod_exceptions {N q p : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N)
  (hq : q.Prime) (hodd : Odd (N.factorization q))
  (hp : p ∈ (N.primeFactors.erase q).filter fun p => ¬ 3 ∣ N.factorization p + 1) :
  4 ≤ N.factorization p

A prime factor p ≠ q of an odd perfect number with special prime q whose exponent e has 3 ∤ e + 1 has 4 ≤ e: the exponent is even and positive, and e = 2 gives 3 ∣ e + 1.

OddPerfect.four_le_card_ne_two

theorem four_le_card_ne_two {N q : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N) (hq : q.Prime)
  (hodd : Odd (N.factorization q)) (h3 : ¬ 3 ∣ N) :
  4 ≤ ((N.primeFactors.erase q).filter fun p => N.factorization p ≠ 2).card

If 3 ∤ N, at least four prime factors other than the special prime q have exponent different from 2. A superset of the set in four_le_card_mod_exceptions.

OddPerfect.two_mul_omega_add_seven_le

theorem two_mul_omega_add_seven_le {N : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N) (h3 : ¬ 3 ∣ N) :
  2 * ω N + 7 ≤ Ω N

If 3 ∤ N, then 2 ω(N) + 7 ≤ Ω(N): the special prime has exponent at least 1, four further prime factors have exponent at least 4 by four_le_card_mod_exceptions, and the rest have exponent at least 2. A formal consequence inside this library; the literature has much stronger results when 3 ∤ N, which are not proved here.

OddPerfect.FiveExceptionCore

OddPerfect/FiveExceptionCore.lean · 870 lines · 47 public theorems · imports ThreeFreeCount

Setting of the five exception result: N odd perfect, 3 not dividing N, special prime 13, and 19 and 31 dividing N. Proves the facts that need no computation: if at most four ordinary primes have an exponent e with 3 not dividing e + 1, they are 7, 19, 31 and one more prime t; for every other prime s, 1 + s + s2 is a product of powers of 7, 13, 19, 31 and t; exponent classes; the abundancy identity.

Proof idea. σ(13) = 14 forces 7, and 3 not dividing N makes 7, 19 and 31 exceptional, since σ(p2) is divisible by 3 for them. A good prime s has σ(s2) dividing σ(N) = 2N with prime factors that are 1 modulo 3, so they lie among 7, 13, 19, 31 and t, and the exponent vector determines s.

Public theorems

OddPerfect.FiveException.mem_good

theorem mem_good {N t s : ℕ} :
  s ∈ good N t ↔ s ∈ N.primeFactors ∧ s ≠ 13 ∧ s ≠ 7 ∧ s ≠ 19 ∧ s ≠ 31 ∧ s ≠ t

OddPerfect.FiveException.not_dvd_of_one_mod

  (h1 : p % 3 = 1) : ¬ 3 ∣ N.factorization p + 1

A prime factor p ≡ 1 (mod 3) of N with 3 ∤ N has 3 ∤ e + 1.

OddPerfect.FiveException.Inst.good_facts

theorem Inst.good_facts (c : Inst N t) {s : ℕ} (hs : s ∈ good N t) :
  s.Prime ∧ 3 ∣ N.factorization s + 1 ∧ 1 + s + s ^ 2 ∣ N ∧ s % 3 = 2

Facts about a good prime.

theorem Inst.tgt (c : Inst N t) {s : ℕ} (hs : s ∈ good N t) {d : ℕ} (hd : d.Prime)
  (hdd : d ∣ 1 + s + s ^ 2) :
  (d = 7 ∨ d = 13 ∨ d = 19 ∨ d = 31 ∨ d = t) ∧ d % 3 = 1

Every prime factor of 1 + s + s^2, for a good s, is one of 7, 13, 19, 31, t and is 1 modulo 3.

  abundancy (13 ^ N.factorization 13) * abundancy (7 ^ N.factorization 7) *

OddPerfect.FiveException.inv_le_of_w4

theorem inv_le_of_w4 {s : ℕ} (hs : 2 ≤ s) {W F K κ : ℚ} (hW : 0 ≤ W) (hWF : 1 ≤ W ^ 4 * F)
  (hK : 0 < K) (hFK : K ^ 4 ≤ F) (hκ : 0 ≤ κ) (hκF : F ≤ κ ^ 2 * ((s : ℚ) - 1) ^ 2) :

OddPerfect.FiveExceptionThirteen

OddPerfect/FiveExceptionThirteen.lean · 909 lines · 44 public theorems · imports FiveExceptionData0, FiveExceptionData79, FiveExceptionDataT, FiveExceptionScan

If 3 does not divide N, the special prime is 13, and 19 and 31 divide N, then at least five ordinary primes have an exponent e with 3 not dividing e + 1. This is one case; the same count for every special prime is not proved. Whether the statement is new was not verified.

Proof idea. With only four such primes, 2 ≤ ∏ p/(p − 1) over 13, 7, 19, 31, t and the good primes. The good primes are so sparse (their 1 + s + s2 has at most five prime factors) that the product stays below 2 for every t: by the sender scan for 37 ≤ t < 24500, a square root tail above, and interval tables for t = 17, 67, 79, 307.

OddPerfect.RestrainedTwo

OddPerfect/RestrainedTwo.lean · 796 lines · 4 public theorems · imports Restrained

Two more steps in the restrained case (every prime factor other than the special prime q and one further prime r has exponent exactly 2, and 3² exactly divides N): the case r = 97 with 13² and 61² exactly dividing N is impossible, and the case r = 61 with 13² exactly dividing N forces q ≡ 1 (mod 3). Three explicit cases remain when r ≠ 3: r = 13; q = 13 with r = 7; r = 61 with 13² exactly dividing N and q ≡ 1 (mod 3). Known mathematics: see RestrainedFive for the published source. The remaining cases with r ≠ 3 are closed in the later modules, up to RestrainedFive.

Proof idea. For r = 97, σ(13²) = 3·61 and σ(61²) = 3·13·97 spend the budget of the prime 3, so q ≡ 1 (mod 3) and every other prime t is ≡ 2 (mod 3) with σ(t²) = 61a97bqc and a ≤ 1. The primes q below 100 are 37 and 73, and both overflow the budget. For q ≥ 100 an exact check of the values 61a97b with b < 6 shows b ≥ 6 when c = 0; then 1/(t + 1) is at most (13/100)a(11/100)b(1/10)c, t determines (a, b, c), and the sum of these weights keeps the abundancy below 2. For r = 61 with q ≡ 2 (mod 3) the same argument runs on the primes 13 and 61.

OddPerfect.RestrainedThree

OddPerfect/RestrainedThree.lean · 910 lines · 2 public theorems · imports RestrainedTwo

In the restrained case with 3² exactly dividing N, the configuration q = 13 with r = 7 is impossible. Two explicit cases remain when r ≠ 3: r = 13; r = 61 with 13² exactly dividing N and q ≡ 1 (mod 3). Known mathematics: see RestrainedFive for the published source. The remaining cases with r ≠ 3 are closed in the later modules, up to RestrainedFive.

Proof idea. At most two further primes are ≡ 1 (mod 3), since each sends one factor 3 into σ(N). A kernel check over every z below 10000 with z ≡ 1 (mod 3) shows that such a prime is at least 10000: otherwise the part of σ(z²)/3 coprime to 7 and 13 would have to be the other such prime or its square, and that prime in turn would need σ of its square supported on 7, 13 and z. Every other prime t is ≡ 2 (mod 3) with σ(t²) = 7a13bxcyd, where x and y are the two large primes. If c = d = 0, an exact check of the values 7a13b below 1016 shows σ(t²) ≥ 1016; otherwise 1/(t + 1) is at most 0.378a0.2774b(1/100)c+d. The sum over all t is at most 0.0559, and the known factors give at most 13/9 · 7/6 · 13/12, so the abundancy stays below 2.

OddPerfect.RestrainedFour

OddPerfect/RestrainedFour.lean · 1048 lines · 4 public theorems · imports RestrainedThree

In the restrained case with 3² exactly dividing N, the configuration r = 61 with 13² exactly dividing N is impossible. One explicit case remains when r ≠ 3: r = 13. Known mathematics: see RestrainedFive for the published source. The remaining cases with r ≠ 3 are closed in the later modules, up to RestrainedFive.

Proof idea. By RestrainedTwo, q ≡ 1 (mod 12). The budget of the prime 3 leaves room for at most one further prime x ≡ 1 (mod 3), and σ(x²) = 3·13d61aqb. For each q below 9465 a kernel check lists every such value below a bound and shows that it is not of the form x² + x + 1 with x an admissible prime, so x is large; for q from 9465 on, either q divides σ(x²), which makes x large, or the same check applies. Eight small special primes (37, 73, 97, 109, 181, 1801, 3169, 8269) are refuted by forcing through q + 1, which divides σ(qe): each produces two different primes ≡ 1 (mod 3). For every other prime t, σ(t²) = 61a13bqcxd, and a weighted sum over the exponent vectors keeps the abundancy below 2. The tail lemma is stated for four arbitrary generators.

OddPerfect.RestrainedFive

OddPerfect/RestrainedFive.lean · 1266 lines · 3 public theorems · imports RestrainedFour, Pratt

The last case with r ≠ 3: in the restrained setting with 3² exactly dividing N, r is not 13. Together with the earlier modules this gives restrained_exception_eq_three: if every prime factor other than the special prime q and one further prime r has exponent exactly 2, then r = 3, the exponent of 3 is even and at least 4, q ≡ 1 (mod 3), and neither 5 nor 7 divides N. The case r = 3 itself is not excluded. The conclusion r = 3 is the first half of Theorem 1 of Ochem and Zelinsky (arXiv 2607.19746), who also state that the exponent of 3 is at least 23,000,000,000; their proof of this half uses searches to 1010, Nielsen's bound of ten distinct prime factors and results on the Nagell-Ljunggren equation, which the Lean proof does not need. Known mathematics; whether the route is new has not been checked.

Proof idea. Here 13 = σ(3²) divides N with a free exponent. The budget of the prime 3 allows at most two further primes ≡ 1 (mod 3), and at most one when q ≡ 2 (mod 3). If q ≡ 2 (mod 3), such a prime x has σ(x²) = 3·13a, a kernel check makes x at least 106, and the known factors give at most 13/9 · 13/12 · 5/4 < 1.957, so the abundancy stays below 2. If q ≡ 1 (mod 12), forcing trees refute every prime q below 337 and, for larger q, every prime ≡ 1 (mod 3) below 1225: each tree follows the prime factors of σ(p²) and of q + 1 until a third prime ≡ 1 (mod 3) appears. A checker for these trees is proved sound once, and the primes in them are certified by Pratt certificates. A tail lemma with one fixed generator (13) and three split generators (q and the two large primes) closes the bound.

    (α₂ + α₃ + α₄) * (1 / (1 - α₁) * (1 / (1 - α₂) * (1 / (1 - α₃) * (1 / (1 - α₄))))))

Rankin bound for a set of exact squares t ≡ 2 (mod 3) with one floor generator: σ(t^2) is supported on {g₁, g₂, g₃, g₄}, and when none of the primes g₂, g₃, g₄ divides it, σ(t^2) ≥ B.

OddPerfect.RankinTailGeneral

OddPerfect/RankinTailGeneral.lean · 462 lines · 3 public theorems · imports RestrainedFour

A general tail bound: for a finite set of numbers t at least x whose rows t2 + t + 1 have all prime factors in a finite set of generators, the sum of σ(t2)/t2 − 1 is bounded by an explicit rational expression.

Proof idea. Rankin's trick with a general exponent 1/k and rational witnesses only. Each known generator g gets a weight a with ak·g ≥ 1; the further generators, known only to be at least x, share one weight. A row n = t2 + t + 1 satisfies n < (t + 1)2, so 1/(t + 1) is below n−1/2, which is at most B−(1/2 − 1/k)·n−1/k for n ≥ B; raising to the power 2k removes every root. Distinct t give distinct exponent vectors, so the weights add up to at most a product of geometric series. The earlier lemmas rankin_tail and rankin_tail3 cover four generators and the exponents 1/2 and 1/4; this one takes any number of generators and any exponent. It is a tool lemma and says nothing about odd perfect numbers by itself.

Public theorems

OddPerfect.rankin_tail_general

theorem rankin_tail_general (T K U : Finset ℕ) {x k M u : ℕ} {α : ℕ → ℚ} {αx mL mM : ℚ}
  (hx : 2 ≤ x) (hk : 3 ≤ k) (hKU : Disjoint K U) (hU : U.card ≤ u)
  (hα0 : ∀ g ∈ K, 0 ≤ α g) (hα1 : ∀ g ∈ K, α g < 1) (hαw : ∀ g ∈ K, 1 ≤ α g ^ k * g)
  (hax0 : 0 ≤ αx) (hax1 : αx < 1) (haxw : 1 ≤ αx ^ k * x) (hUx : ∀ g ∈ U, x ≤ g)
  (hmL0 : 0 ≤ mL) (hmL : 1 ≤ mL ^ (2 * k) * ((x ^ 2 + x + 1 : ℕ) : ℚ) ^ (k - 2))
  (hmM0 : 0 ≤ mM) (hmM : 1 ≤ mM ^ (2 * k) * (M : ℚ) ^ (k - 2))
  (hT : ∀ t ∈ T, x ≤ t ∧ (phi3 t).primeFactors ⊆ K ∪ U ∧
    ((∀ g ∈ U, ¬ g ∣ phi3 t) → M ≤ phi3 t)) :
  ∑ t ∈ T, (fv t - 1) ≤ ((x + 1 : ℚ) / x) ^ 2 *
    (mL * (∏ g ∈ K, 1 / (1 - α g)) * ((1 / (1 - αx)) ^ u - 1) +
      mM * ∏ g ∈ K, 1 / (1 - α g))

General Rankin tail bound with exponent 1/k. Let every t ∈ T satisfy t ≥ x ≥ 2, let the prime factors of phi3 t lie in K ∪ U, and let phi3 t ≥ M whenever no element of U divides phi3 t. Known generators g ∈ K carry weights 0 ≤ α g < 1 with α g ^ k * g ≥ 1; the at most u unknown generators in U are at least x and share the weight 0 ≤ αx < 1 with αx ^ k * x ≥ 1. With mL^(2k) (x^2 + x + 1)^(k - 2) ≥ 1 and mM^(2k) M^(k - 2) ≥ 1, ∑ (σ(t^2)/t^2 - 1) ≤ ((x + 1)/x)^2 (mL G ((1/(1 - αx))^u - 1) + mM G), where G = ∏_{g ∈ K} 1/(1 - α g). This is Rankin's trick; the elements of K and U need not be prime.

OddPerfect.prod_fv_le_of_rankin_tail_general

theorem prod_fv_le_of_rankin_tail_general (T K U : Finset ℕ) {x k M u : ℕ} {α : ℕ → ℚ}
  {αx mL mM : ℚ}
  (hx : 2 ≤ x) (hk : 3 ≤ k) (hKU : Disjoint K U) (hU : U.card ≤ u)
  (hα0 : ∀ g ∈ K, 0 ≤ α g) (hα1 : ∀ g ∈ K, α g < 1) (hαw : ∀ g ∈ K, 1 ≤ α g ^ k * g)
  (hax0 : 0 ≤ αx) (hax1 : αx < 1) (haxw : 1 ≤ αx ^ k * x) (hUx : ∀ g ∈ U, x ≤ g)
  (hmL0 : 0 ≤ mL) (hmL : 1 ≤ mL ^ (2 * k) * ((x ^ 2 + x + 1 : ℕ) : ℚ) ^ (k - 2))
  (hmM0 : 0 ≤ mM) (hmM : 1 ≤ mM ^ (2 * k) * (M : ℚ) ^ (k - 2))
  (hT : ∀ t ∈ T, x ≤ t ∧ (phi3 t).primeFactors ⊆ K ∪ U ∧
    ((∀ g ∈ U, ¬ g ∣ phi3 t) → M ≤ phi3 t)) {S : ℚ}
  (hS : ((x + 1 : ℚ) / x) ^ 2 *
    (mL * (∏ g ∈ K, 1 / (1 - α g)) * ((1 / (1 - αx)) ^ u - 1) +
      mM * ∏ g ∈ K, 1 / (1 - α g)) ≤ S) (hS1 : S < 1) :
  ∏ t ∈ T, fv t ≤ 1 / (1 - S)

Product form of rankin_tail_general: under the same hypotheses, if the bound is at most S < 1, then ∏ σ(t^2)/t^2 ≤ 1/(1 - S) over T.

OddPerfect.rankin_tail_general_example

theorem rankin_tail_general_example (T : Finset ℕ) {q : ℕ} (hq : q.Prime) (hq53 : 53 ≤ q)
  (hT : ∀ t ∈ T, 53 ≤ t ∧ (phi3 t).primeFactors ⊆ {97, q} ∧
    (¬ q ∣ phi3 t → 10 ^ 30 ≤ phi3 t)) :
  ∑ t ∈ T, (fv t - 1) ≤ 3 / 20

A numerical instance with K = {97}, one unknown prime q ≥ 53, x = 53, k = 4, M = 10^30: if every t ∈ T is at least 53, phi3 t has prime factors in {97, q}, and phi3 t ≥ 10^30 when q ∤ phi3 t, then ∑ (σ(t^2)/t^2 - 1) ≤ 3/20. The witnesses are α 97 = 10^6/3138288, αx = 10^6/2698167, mL = 8/53 and mM = 31622777/10^15; the resulting bound is about 0.13542. When q = 97 the lemma is applied with K empty.

OddPerfect/ProductBound.lean · 139 lines · 7 public theorems

Two rational upper bounds for a finite product of factors 1 + x with a bounded sum, sharper than 1/(1 − S).

Proof idea. Induction on the finite set with a one step inequality for each rational function; no exponential and no real numbers.

theorem prod_one_add_le_of_step (R : ℚ → ℚ) {D : ℚ} (h1 : ∀ S, 0 ≤ S → S < D → 1 ≤ R S)
  (hstep : ∀ x y, 0 ≤ x → 0 ≤ y → x + y < D → (1 + x) * R y ≤ R (x + y))
  {ι : Type*} (s : Finset ι) (x : ι → ℚ) (hx : ∀ i ∈ s, 0 ≤ x i)
  {S : ℚ} (hS : ∑ i ∈ s, x i ≤ S) (hSD : S < D) :
  ∏ i ∈ s, (1 + x i) ≤ R S

A generic product bound: if 1 ≤ R S for 0 ≤ S < D and (1 + x) R y ≤ R (x + y) for 0 ≤ x, 0 ≤ y, x + y < D, then ∏ (1 + x i) ≤ R S whenever the x i are nonnegative and ∑ x i ≤ S < D.

OddPerfect.pade11_nat_eq

theorem pade11_nat_eq {n d : ℕ} (hd : 0 < d) (hn : n < 2 * d) :
  ((2 * d + n : ℕ) : ℚ) / ((2 * d - n : ℕ) : ℚ) =
    (2 + (n : ℚ) / d) / (2 - (n : ℚ) / d)

Natural number form of the (1,1) bound at S = n/d: for 0 < d and n < 2 d, the quotient (2 d + n)/(2 d - n) of naturals (the subtraction does not truncate) equals (2 + S)/(2 - S).

    (((n : ℚ) / d) ^ 2 + 4 * ((n : ℚ) / d) + 6) / (6 - 2 * ((n : ℚ) / d))

OddPerfect.RankinTailPade

OddPerfect/RankinTailPade.lean · 56 lines · 1 public theorem · imports RankinTailGeneral, ProductBound

Product bound for a tail: ∏(1 + xᵢ) ≤ (S² + 4S + 6)/(6 − 2S) when the sum of the xᵢ is at most S < 3.

Proof idea. Same hypotheses as the general tail lemma, with a sharper conclusion: the product of the abundancy factors of the unknown primes is at most (S² + 4S + 6)/(6 − 2S), which is below the older bound 1/(1 − S) for every S in (0, 1) and still finite up to S = 3. The certificate engine tries the older test first and this one second.

OddPerfect.RestrainedSix

OddPerfect/RestrainedSix.lean · 160 lines · 5 public theorems · imports RestrainedFive, ForcingClosed

In the restrained family (every prime factor other than the special prime and one further prime has exponent exactly 2), the exponent e of 3 has 3, 5, 11 and 17 not dividing e + 1, hence e is at least 6. Known mathematics and far weaker than the published bound of Ochem and Zelinsky (2026) for this exponent.

Proof idea. If d divides e + 1 then σ(3^(d − 1)) divides σ(3^e), which divides 2N. For d = 5, 11, 17 this number has a prime factor p ≡ 3 (mod 4): 11, 23 and 1871. Such a prime is not the special prime, so its exponent is 2, and 7 divides σ(p²); but 7 does not divide N by the earlier restrained modules. The case d = 3 follows from the theorem that some ordinary exponent f has 3 not dividing f + 1: all others equal 2. These exclude infinite arithmetic classes of e but leave infinitely many values.

OddPerfect.RestrainedSevenCheck

OddPerfect/RestrainedSevenCheck.lean · 178 lines · 8 public theorems · imports Pratt

The checker for exclusion trees in the restrained family: definitions of the tree check, the row check and the coverage check, with only light imports so that the data modules load quickly.

Proof idea. A tree for a prime p follows primes forced to divide N: a prime t with exponent 2 forces every prime factor of t² + t + 1, and the special prime q forces the odd prime factors of q + 1. A branch ends at a prime already known not to divide N.

OddPerfect.RestrainedSeven

OddPerfect/RestrainedSeven.lean · 174 lines · 7 public theorems · imports RestrainedSix, RestrainedSevenData2, Phi3, SpecialPrime, ForcingClosed

In the restrained family (every prime factor other than the special prime and one further prime has exponent exactly 2), no prime p with 5 ≤ p < 132257 divides N. No novelty is claimed: Ochem and Zelinsky (2026) treat this family in depth and state that the exponent of 3 is at least 23,000,000,000, which is not proved here.

Proof idea. The exceptional prime is 3 and the special prime is 1 modulo 12 (earlier modules). Each prime below the bound is excluded by a tree of forced primes that ends in a prime already excluded; this module proves the tree checker sound and applies it to the 12342 rows.

An odd divisor of 2N divides N.

OddPerfect.RestrainedSeven.at_sound

theorem at_sound {N q : ℕ} (F : Fam N q) {M : ℕ} {t qv : ℕ} {qb ob : Br} (htp : t.Prime)
  (htN : t ∣ N) (ht3 : t ≠ 3) (hqv : qv = 0 ∨ qv = q)
  (hqb : t = q → chk M t (t + 1) qb = true) (hob : chk M qv (t * t + t + 1) ob = true)
  (ihq : ∀ qv src, chk M qv src qb = true → src ∣ 2 * N → (qv = 0 ∨ qv = q) → False)
  (iho : ∀ qv src, chk M qv src ob = true → src ∣ 2 * N → (qv = 0 ∨ qv = q) → False) :
  False

The step at a prime t ∣ N, t ≠ 3: either t = q, and the branch qb closes the source t + 1; or the exponent of t is 2, and the branch ob closes the source t * t + t + 1.

OddPerfect.restrained_not_dvd_of_lt

theorem restrained_not_dvd_of_lt {N q r p : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N) (hq : q.Prime)
  (hodd : Odd (N.factorization q)) (hr : r.Prime) (hrq : r ≠ q)
  (hsq : ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ≠ q → p ≠ r → N.factorization p = 2)
  (hp : p.Prime) (h5 : 5 ≤ p) (hlt : p < 132257) : ¬ p ∣ N

**Restrained odd perfect numbers have no prime factor 5 ≤ p < 132257.** With the hypotheses of restrained_exception_eq_three (special prime q, a further prime r ≠ q, every other prime factor with exponent exactly 2), no prime 5 ≤ p < 132257 divides N; together with r = 3 this says that the smallest prime factor of N other than 3 is at least 132257. Each prime is excluded by a kernel checked exclusion tree. No novelty is claimed: Ochem and Zelinsky prove that the exponent of 3 in such N is at least 23,000,000,000, which is not proved here.

OddPerfect.RestrainedEight

OddPerfect/RestrainedEight.lean · 404 lines · 21 public theorems · imports RestrainedSeven, RestrainedSix, Counting, Network, Valuation

Restrained family (every prime other than the special prime and one prime has exponent exactly 2): at least 38049 distinct prime factors; a prime factor that is 2 modulo 3 receives exactly two units, from the components of 3 and of the special prime only; the exponent of 3 is at least 12; Ω ≥ 76107. No novelty: Ochem and Zelinsky prove much more about this family.

Proof idea. Every prime factor other than 3 is at least 132257, so 2 < (3/2)(B/(B − 1))ω − 1 with B = 132257; the comparison of two powers with about 195000 digits is one kernel evaluation. A prime below the cutoff that divides σ(3d − 1) would divide N, so d cannot divide the index of 3.

OddPerfect.restrained_two_sources

theorem restrained_two_sources {N q r t : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N) (hq : q.Prime)
  (hodd : Odd (N.factorization q)) (hr : r.Prime) (hrq : r ≠ q)
  (hsq : ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ≠ q → p ≠ r → N.factorization p = 2)

Two sources. In the restrained family, a prime factor t ≡ 2 (mod 3) of N receives its two units only from the components of 3 and of q: v_t(σ(3 ^ E)) + v_t(σ(q ^ α)) = 2 with E = v_3(N) and α = v_q(N). Conditional family result; whether this is in the literature was not verified.

OddPerfect.restrained_two_sources_cor

theorem restrained_two_sources_cor {N q r t : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N) (hq : q.Prime)
  (hodd : Odd (N.factorization q)) (hr : r.Prime) (hrq : r ≠ q)
  (hsq : ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ≠ q → p ≠ r → N.factorization p = 2)

    padicValNat t (σ 1 (q ^ N.factorization q)) ≤ 2 ∧
    (padicValNat t (σ 1 (3 ^ N.factorization 3)) = 1 →
      padicValNat t (σ 1 (q ^ N.factorization q)) = 1) ∧
    ¬ t ^ 3 ∣ σ 1 (3 ^ N.factorization 3)

In the restrained family, for a prime factor t ≡ 2 (mod 3), each of the two source valuations is at most 2, a simple factor t of σ(3 ^ E) is matched by a simple factor of σ(q ^ α), and t ^ 3 ∤ σ(3 ^ E). Conditional family result; whether this is in the literature was not verified.

OddPerfect.RestrainedNine

OddPerfect/RestrainedNine.lean · 175 lines · 9 public theorems · imports RestrainedNineData, RestrainedSeven, RestrainedEight

In the restrained family the exponent of 3 is at least 198, and Ω(N) ≥ 76293.

Proof idea. If a prime d divides E + 1 then (3^d − 1)/2 divides σ(3^E), which divides 2N; the branch of d shows that this is impossible, so the least prime factor of the odd number E + 1 is at least 199. Ochem and Zelinsky (2026) state the bound 23,000,000,000, which is not proved here.

  (hodd : Odd (N.factorization q)) (hr : r.Prime) (hrq : r ≠ q)
  (hsq : ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ≠ q → p ≠ r → N.factorization p = 2) :
  198 ≤ N.factorization 3

**Restrained family: 198 ≤ v_3(N).** The exponent E = v_3(N) is even and at least 6, so the least prime factor p of E + 1 is odd; every prime 3 ≤ p < 199 is in dList and does not divide E + 1, so 199 ≤ p ≤ E + 1. Conditional family result; no novelty is claimed: the bound stated by Ochem and Zelinsky, 23,000,000,000, is far stronger and is not proved here.

OddPerfect.RestrainedTen

OddPerfect/RestrainedTen.lean · 130 lines · 4 public theorems · imports RestrainedEight, ExcessSupport, EscapeRowUnique

In the restrained family ω(N) ≤ 2E + 3, where E is the exponent of 3; hence E ≥ 19024 and Ω(N) ≥ 95119.

Proof idea. Each prime s of exponent 2 either is an escape row (every prime factor of s² + s + 1 is 3 or the special prime) or sends a prime factor of s² + s + 1 to a prime t ≡ 1 (mod 3) of exponent 2. Such a t receives at most 2, there is at most one escape row, and the primes t number at most E. With ω(N) ≥ 38049 and E even this gives the bound. The counting follows a lemma of Ochem and Zelinsky (arXiv 2607.19746), who state E ≥ ω(N)/2 − 2 and a far larger bound for E, which is not proved here.

Public theorems

OddPerfect.restrained_card_squarePrimes_le

theorem restrained_card_squarePrimes_le {N q r : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N) (hq : q.Prime)
  (hodd : Odd (N.factorization q)) (hr : r.Prime) (hrq : r ≠ q)
  (hsq : ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ≠ q → p ≠ r → N.factorization p = 2) :
  (squarePrimes N q).card ≤
    2 * {p ∈ N.primeFactors | N.factorization p = 2 ∧ p % 3 = 1}.card + 1

Restrained family: the square primes against the square primes that are 1 modulo 3. #squarePrimes N q ≤ 2 * #{p ∣ N : v_p(N) = 2, p ≡ 1 (mod 3)} + 1: every square prime that is not an escape row sends weight to an ordinary prime t ≡ 1 (mod 3), which has exponent 2 and so receives weight at most 2, and there is at most one escape row. Proved inside the restrained family only: in general the receivers may have exponent larger than 2. Conditional family result; no novelty is claimed.

OddPerfect.restrained_omega_le

theorem restrained_omega_le {N q r : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N) (hq : q.Prime)
  (hodd : Odd (N.factorization q)) (hr : r.Prime) (hrq : r ≠ q)
  (hsq : ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ≠ q → p ≠ r → N.factorization p = 2) :
  ω N ≤ 2 * N.factorization 3 + 3

**Restrained family: ω(N) ≤ 2 * v_3(N) + 3.** The prime factors are q, 3 and the square primes, and #squarePrimes ≤ 2 * #O1 + 1 ≤ 2 * v_3(N) + 1. Conditional family result; no novelty is claimed.

OddPerfect.restrained_nineteen_thousand_le_three

  (hodd : Odd (N.factorization q)) (hr : r.Prime) (hrq : r ≠ q)
  (hsq : ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ≠ q → p ≠ r → N.factorization p = 2) :

**Restrained family: 19024 ≤ v_3(N).** From 38049 ≤ ω(N) ≤ 2 * v_3(N) + 3 we get v_3(N) ≥ 19023, and v_3(N) is even. Ochem and Zelinsky (arXiv 2607.19746) state a much larger bound for this exponent, obtained by a long computation; it is not proved here. Conditional family result checked by the kernel; no novelty is claimed.

OddPerfect.RestrainedElevenCheck

OddPerfect/RestrainedElevenCheck.lean · 202 lines · 9 public theorems

A certified sieve over the odd numbers of a range, with a fixed point bound for the product of n/(n − 1) over the numbers it cannot remove.

Proof idea. The certificate Cert X lo hi a b says: there is a finite set T inside [lo, hi) that contains every prime n of the range for which n² + n + 1 has no divisor below 132257 prime to 6, and a times the product over T of nX/((n − 1)(X + 1)) is at most b. The checker walks the odd numbers, checks each witness, and multiplies an integer accumulator, rounding up, for each number without a witness. It is sound (runL_sound), certificates of adjacent ranges combine (cert_trans), and the module has a positive and a negative control.

Public theorems

OddPerfect.RestrainedElevenCheck.cert_trans

theorem cert_trans {X lo mid hi a b c : ℕ} (h₁ : Cert X lo mid a b) (h₂ : Cert X mid hi b c) :
  Cert X lo hi a c

Certificates of adjacent ranges combine.

theorem fac_step {X n acc : ℕ} (hn : 3 ≤ n) :
  (acc : ℚ) * fac X n ≤ (cdiv (acc * n * X) ((n - 1) * (X + 1)) : ℕ)

OddPerfect.RestrainedElevenCheck.runLimb_sound

theorem runLimb_sound {X : ℕ} : ∀ (c n W acc a : ℕ), runLimb X c n W acc = some a →
  n % 2 = 1 → 3 ≤ n → Cert X n (n + 2 * c) acc a

OddPerfect.RestrainedElevenCheck.runL_sound

  Cert X n hi acc b

Soundness of the checker.

OddPerfect.RestrainedElevenCheck.runL_accept

theorem runL_accept : runL 1000000 [19] 132259 1 132291 (2 ^ 64) = true

Positive twin of runL_reject: the odd number 132259 is 19 * 6961, and a limb with the witness 19 for it (and no witness for the next fifteen odd numbers) is accepted.

OddPerfect.RestrainedElevenCheck.runL_reject

theorem runL_reject : runL 1000000 [5] 132259 1 132291 (2 ^ 64) = false

Negative control: the same limb with the witness 5, which divides neither 132259 nor 132259 ^ 2 + 132259 + 1, is rejected.

OddPerfect.RestrainedElevenData7

OddPerfect/RestrainedElevenData7.lean · 2626 lines · 6 public theorems · imports RestrainedElevenCheck

Certificate data: sieve witnesses for the odd numbers 918689 to 1000000. Each block is accepted by the checker in the kernel.

Proof idea. Written by scripts/RestrainedSieve/gen.py. Each odd number of the range carries a witness below 218, sixteen witnesses to a numeral: a proper divisor (the number is not prime), or a divisor of n² + n + 1 that is prime to 6 and below the bound of the family (the number cannot be a prime of exponent 2 in the family), or 0 (the number stays). The module only evaluates the checker RestrainedElevenCheck.runL by decide +kernel; what an accepted block means is the soundness theorem runL_sound.

OddPerfect.RestrainedEleven

OddPerfect/RestrainedEleven.lean · 276 lines · 10 public theorems · imports RestrainedTen, RestrainedElevenData1, RestrainedElevenData2, RestrainedElevenData3, RestrainedElevenData4, RestrainedElevenData5, RestrainedElevenData6, RestrainedElevenData7

In the restrained family ω(N) ≥ 275251, the exponent E of 3 is at least 137624, and Ω(N) ≥ 688123.

Proof idea. Every prime of exponent 2 in the family passes the sieve: a divisor w below 132257 of s² + s + 1 would give a prime 5 ≤ p < 132257 dividing N, which the landed results exclude. The seven data modules leave a set T of 9063 numbers in [132257, 10^6]. The abundancy 4/3 < ∏ σ(pe)/pe over the primes other than 3 is then compared with (132257/132256) · y#R · ∏T, where y = (10^6 + 1)/10^6 and R is the set of primes other than 3 and q: a prime above 10^6 contributes at most y. One kernel comparison of two integers of about 1,650,000 digits gives #R ≥ 275249. Then E ≥ 137624 follows from ω(N) ≤ 2E + 3. Ochem and Zelinsky (arXiv 2607.19746) state a far larger bound for this exponent, by a long computation that this library does not check. A conditional family result; no novelty is claimed.

OddPerfect.RestrainedTwelve

OddPerfect/RestrainedTwelve.lean · 117 lines · 4 public theorems · imports RestrainedEight

In the restrained family a prime factor t ≡ 2 (mod 3) divides σ(qa), or divides E + 1, or satisfies 3t−1 ≡ 1 (mod t²), where E is the exponent of 3.

Proof idea. A prime t ≡ 2 (mod 3) receives nothing from the rows of exponent 2, so its two units come from the special row or from σ(3E) = (3E+1 − 1)/2. If t² divides 3E+1 − 1 and t does not divide E + 1, then the element 3t−1 of the integers modulo t² has order dividing both t and E + 1, so it is 1 (pow_pred_modEq_one_of_sq_dvd, stated for a general base). A conditional family result; whether it is in the literature was not verified.

OddPerfect.RestrainedThirteen

OddPerfect/RestrainedThirteen.lean · 519 lines · 22 public theorems · imports RestrainedEight, Phi3Algebra

In the restrained family: vt(3d − 1) + vt(E + 1) ≤ 2 for a prime t other than 2, 3, q whose order d of 3 divides E + 1; and if every prime factor p has 2p + 1 ≤ 3q, then E + 1 < q, a ≤ 2 + vq(3E+1 − 1), and a > 1 forces 3q−1 ≡ 1 (mod q³).

Proof idea. Lifting the exponent (padicValNat_pow_sub_one_eq, for a general base): vt(bm − 1) = vt(bd − 1) + vt(m) when the order d of b modulo an odd prime t divides m. The row of 3 sends vt(3E+1 − 1) to t, and an ordinary prime t ≠ 3 has exponent 2. For the special prime: a row s² + s + 1 with s below 3q/2 is below 3q² and is not a square, so it sends at most 1 to q, and at most two odd numbers below 2q are roots of x² + x + 1 modulo q. Counting the primes that feed the column of 3 then gives q ≥ 2E + 1. The cube condition is stronger than the Wieferich condition to the base 3. Conditional family results; whether they are in the literature was not verified.

OddPerfect.restrained_big_special

theorem restrained_big_special {N q r : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N) (hq : q.Prime)
  (hodd : Odd (N.factorization q)) (hr : r.Prime) (hrq : r ≠ q)
  (hsq : ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ≠ q → p ≠ r → N.factorization p = 2)
  (hbig : ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, 2 * p + 1 ≤ 3 * q) :
  N.factorization q ≤ 2 + padicValNat q (3 ^ (N.factorization 3 + 1) - 1)

The special prime against the other primes. In the restrained family, if every prime factor p of N satisfies 2 p + 1 ≤ 3 q, then a ≤ 2 + v_q(3 ^ (E + 1) - 1). The row of 3 sends v_q(σ(3 ^ E)) = v_q(3 ^ (E + 1) - 1). Every other row is a square prime s, with s ^ 2 + s + 1 < 3 q ^ 2; an odd quotient below 3 would give s ^ 2 + s + 1 = q ^ 2, which is not a square, so the row sends at most 1. The senders are odd and below 2 q, so distinct senders have distinct residues modulo q, and at most two residues are roots of x ^ 2 + x + 1. Conditional family result; whether this is in the literature was not verified.

OddPerfect.restrained_big_succ_lt

theorem restrained_big_succ_lt {N q r : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N) (hq : q.Prime)
  (hodd : Odd (N.factorization q)) (hr : r.Prime) (hrq : r ≠ q)
  (hsq : ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ≠ q → p ≠ r → N.factorization p = 2)
  (hbig : ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, 2 * p + 1 ≤ 3 * q) :
  N.factorization 3 + 1 < q

The exponent of 3 is below the special prime. In the restrained family, if every prime factor p of N satisfies 2 p + 1 ≤ 3 q, then E + 1 < q. With E = 2 m: v_q(3 ^ (E + 1) - 1) ≤ E as q > 3, so a + 1 ≤ 2 m + 3 < 3 ^ (m + 1) and v_3(a + 1) ≤ m. The column of 3 gives E ≤ v_3(a + 1) + #T, where T is the set of square primes s ≡ 1 (mod 3); these are 1 modulo 6 and at most (3 q - 1) / 2, so #T ≤ (3 q - 1) / 12, and m ≤ #T gives q ≥ 4 m + 1 = 2 E + 1. Conditional family result; whether this is in the literature was not verified.

OddPerfect.RestrainedFourteen

OddPerfect/RestrainedFourteen.lean · 519 lines · 20 public theorems · imports RestrainedEight, DefectRules

In the restrained family, the rows s² + s + 1 that contain at most one ordinary prime carry a fixed share of the reciprocal sum: S(R) ≤ (433/183) · S(O1 ∩ K1) + S(O2 ∩ K1).

Proof idea. R is the set of primes of exponent 2, O1 and O2 its classes modulo 3, K1 the members whose row contains at most one member of R (with multiplicity), S the sum of 1/s. Each t in R has exponent 2, so the rows feed it at most twice; weighting by 1/t gives a total of at most 2 · S(O1). A row with two members t₁, t₂ of R costs 1/t₁ + 1/t₂, and t₁t₂ (times 3 when s ≡ 1 mod 3) is below (s + 1)², so the cost exceeds 2/(s + 1), and by a factor close to the square root of 3 more when s ≡ 1 (mod 3); squares are compared, no square root is used. Summing over the rows outside K1 gives (183/250) · S(O1 \ K1) + (132257/132258) · S(O2 \ K1) ≤ S(O1 ∩ K1). A row in K1 that q does not divide is t or 3t with t a prime of O1. The inequality does not close the family: the reciprocal sum over K1 is not bounded here. A conditional family result; whether it is in the literature was not verified.

OddPerfect.RestrainedFifteen

OddPerfect/RestrainedFifteen.lean · 241 lines · 7 public theorems · imports RestrainedTen

In the restrained family the count is exact: v3(N) = #O1 + v3(a + 1), so ω(N) + v3(a + 1) = v3(N) + 2 + #O2, and the product of t² over O2 divides σ(3E) · σ(qa)/2.

Proof idea. O1 and O2 are the primes other than 3 and q that are 1, respectively 2, modulo 3. A member of O1 sends exactly one factor 3, a member of O2 none, and the special row sends v3(a + 1) because q ≡ 1 (mod 3). A member of O2 divides no row s² + s + 1, so its exponent 2 comes from the rows of 3 and q only. As every member of O2 is at least 132257, this bounds #O2 by the size of σ(3E) · σ(qa)/2. The counting is of the type of a lemma of Ochem and Zelinsky (arXiv 2607.19746). A conditional family result; no novelty is claimed.

  (hodd : Odd (N.factorization q)) (hr : r.Prime) (hrq : r ≠ q)

Conditional family result; no novelty is claimed.

OddPerfect.RestrainedSixteen

OddPerfect/RestrainedSixteen.lean · 710 lines · 66 public theorems · imports RestrainedEleven

In the restrained family, ω(N) ≥ 360549, v3(N) ≥ 180274 and Ω(N) ≥ 901369, from the landed sieve data read again with a count and a packing bound for the prime factors above 106.

Proof idea. The sieve certificate hides how many numbers below one million are left without a witness. A counted certificate (CertC, runL_soundC) reads the same witness lists and counts the zero digits: at most 9063 are left (certC_all); no witness is checked again. So all but 9063 of the ordinary primes exceed one million. The earlier proof bounded the factor of each of these by 1. They are distinct odd numbers, and for a set S of distinct odd numbers t ≥ x the square of the product of t/(t − 1) is at most 1 + 4·#S/(2x − 3) (prod_sq_le), by a telescoping product. One kernel comparison of integers (final_ineqC) then shows that fewer than 360547 ordinary primes cannot bring the abundancy of the part prime to 3 above 4/3. The exponent of 3 follows from ω ≤ 2 v3(N) + 3 and its evenness. Lower bounds only; the family is not excluded. Ochem and Zelinsky (arXiv 2607.19746) state a far larger bound from a long computation, which is not proved here.

The counted certificate of the whole range 132257 ≤ n ≤ 10 ^ 6: the leftover set has at most 9063 members (the zero digits of the landed limb lists).

OddPerfect.RestrainedSixteen.step_le

theorem step_le {x m : ℚ} (hx : 3 ≤ x) (hm : 0 ≤ m) :
  (x / (x - 1)) ^ 2 * (1 + 4 * m / (2 * (x + 2) - 3)) ≤ 1 + 4 * (m + 1) / (2 * x - 3)

The step of prod_sq_le: (x/(x - 1)) ^ 2 (1 + 4 m/(2 (x + 2) - 3)) ≤ 1 + 4 (m + 1)/(2 x - 3) for x ≥ 3.

OddPerfect.RestrainedSixteen.prod_sq_le

theorem prod_sq_le (S : Finset ℕ) : ∀ x₀ : ℕ, 3 ≤ x₀ → (∀ t ∈ S, x₀ ≤ t ∧ t % 2 = 1) →
  (∏ t ∈ S, (t : ℚ) / (t - 1)) ^ 2 ≤ 1 + 4 * (S.card : ℚ) / (2 * x₀ - 3)

Packing of distinct odd numbers. A set S of odd numbers, each at least x₀ ≥ 3, has (∏_S t/(t - 1)) ^ 2 ≤ 1 + 4 #S/(2 x₀ - 3).

OddPerfect.RestrainedSixteen.card_gt_of_certC

theorem card_gt_of_certC {N q X X₁ X₂ B c a b d M : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N) (h3 : 3 ∣ N)
  (hqN : q ∈ N.primeFactors) (hq3 : q ≠ 3) (hBc : B = c + 1) (hc : 1 ≤ c) (hqB : B ≤ q)
  (hR : ∀ r ∈ (N.primeFactors.erase 3).erase q, Good r ∧ B ≤ r) (hX : 2 ≤ X)
  (hX₁ : X₁ = X + 1) (hX₂ : X₂ + 1 = 2 * X) (hcert : CertC X B X₁ a b d) (ha : 0 < a)
  (hineq : 9 * B ^ 2 * b ^ 2 * (X₁ ^ d) ^ 2 * (X₂ + 4 * M) ≤
    16 * c ^ 2 * a ^ 2 * (X ^ d) ^ 2 * X₂) :
  M + d < ((N.primeFactors.erase 3).erase q).card

The counting step with the tail. Setting of card_gt_of_cert, with a counted certificate CertC X B X₁ a b d and the comparison 9 B ^ 2 b ^ 2 (X₁ ^ d) ^ 2 (X₂ + 4 M) ≤ 16 c ^ 2 a ^ 2 (X ^ d) ^ 2 X₂, where B = c + 1, X₁ = X + 1 and X₂ = 2 X - 1. Then M + d < #R.

OddPerfect.restrained_omega_ge_tail

theorem restrained_omega_ge_tail {N q r : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N) (hq : q.Prime)
  (hodd : Odd (N.factorization q)) (hr : r.Prime) (hrq : r ≠ q)
  (hsq : ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ≠ q → p ≠ r → N.factorization p = 2) :
  360549 ≤ ω N

**Restrained family: ω(N) ≥ 360549.** With the hypotheses of restrained_not_dvd_of_lt, the landed sieve certificate counted (at most 9063 leftovers up to 10 ^ 6) and the packing of the prime factors above 10 ^ 6 force at least 360547 prime factors other than 3 and q. Conditional family result checked by the kernel; no novelty is claimed.

OddPerfect.restrained_tail_le_three

theorem restrained_tail_le_three {N q r : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N) (hq : q.Prime)
  (hodd : Odd (N.factorization q)) (hr : r.Prime) (hrq : r ≠ q)
  (hsq : ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ≠ q → p ≠ r → N.factorization p = 2) :

**Restrained family: v_3(N) ≥ 180274.** From ω(N) ≥ 360549, ω(N) ≤ 2 v_3(N) + 3 (restrained_omega_le) and the evenness of v_3(N) (restrained_exception_eq_three). Ochem and Zelinsky (arXiv 2607.19746) state a far larger bound for this exponent, obtained by a long computation; it is not proved here. OddPerfect.RestrainedSeventeen

OddPerfect/RestrainedSeventeen.lean · 227 lines · 9 public theorems · imports RestrainedThirteen

In the restrained family with every prime factor p satisfying 2p + 1 ≤ 3q: a ≤ 2 + vq(3q−1 − 1), and qa−2 divides 3q−1 − 1. Also: a prime whose exponent is already supplied by the row of 3 divides no other row.

Proof idea. Write m = v3(N) + 1. The landed bound is a ≤ 2 + vq(3m − 1), with m < q. If a > 2 then q divides 3m − 1, so the order d of 3 modulo q divides m and q − 1; q divides neither, and lifting the exponent gives vq(3m − 1) = vq(3d − 1) = vq(3q−1 − 1) (restrained_big_special_fermat). The bound holds for each fixed q and is not uniform in a; the size hypothesis is not proved for the family. Saturated receiver (saturated_receiver): the valuations at a prime t of all rows add up to vt(N); if the row of 3 alone reaches vt(N), every other row is prime to t. In the family this applies to a prime t whose clock is tight (restrained_tight_square, restrained_tight_special).

Public theorems

OddPerfect.restrained_big_special_fermat

theorem restrained_big_special_fermat {N q r : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N) (hq : q.Prime)
  (hodd : Odd (N.factorization q)) (hr : r.Prime) (hrq : r ≠ q)
  (hsq : ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ≠ q → p ≠ r → N.factorization p = 2)
  (hbig : ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, 2 * p + 1 ≤ 3 * q) :
  N.factorization q ≤ 2 + padicValNat q (3 ^ (q - 1) - 1)

The order d of 3 modulo q divides E + 1 (when a > 2) and q - 1; since E + 1 < q, lifting the exponent gives v_q(3 ^ (E + 1) - 1) = v_q(3 ^ d - 1) = v_q(3 ^ (q - 1) - 1). The hypothesis 2 p + 1 ≤ 3 q is not proved for every member of the family, and the bound depends on q. Conditional family result; whether this is in the literature was not verified.
