OddPerfect.saturated_receiver_sigmaWeight

theorem saturated_receiver_sigmaWeight {N t : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N) (h3 : 3 ∣ N)
  (ht : t.Prime) (ht2 : t ≠ 2) (ht3 : t ≠ 3)
  (hd : orderOf (3 : ZMod t) ∣ N.factorization 3 + 1)
  (hsat : padicValNat t (3 ^ orderOf (3 : ZMod t) - 1) +
    padicValNat t (N.factorization 3 + 1) = N.factorization t) :
  ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ≠ 3 → sigmaWeight N p t = 0

Saturated receiver, weight form. Let N be an odd perfect number with 3 ∣ N, and t a prime other than 2 and 3 whose order of 3 divides E + 1. If the row of 3 already sends the full exponent, v_t(3 ^ ord_t(3) - 1) + v_t(E + 1) = v_t(N), then every other prime factor sends nothing to t: the weights over all prime factors sum to v_t(N).

OddPerfect.saturated_receiver

theorem saturated_receiver {N t : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N) (h3 : 3 ∣ N) (ht : t.Prime)
  (ht2 : t ≠ 2) (ht3 : t ≠ 3)
  (hd : orderOf (3 : ZMod t) ∣ N.factorization 3 + 1)
  (hsat : padicValNat t (3 ^ orderOf (3 : ZMod t) - 1) +
    padicValNat t (N.factorization 3 + 1) = N.factorization t) :
  ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ≠ 3 → ¬ t ∣ σ 1 (p ^ N.factorization p)

Saturated receiver. Let N be an odd perfect number with 3 ∣ N, and t a prime other than 2 and 3 whose order of 3 divides E + 1. If v_t(3 ^ ord_t(3) - 1) + v_t(E + 1) = v_t(N), then t divides σ(p ^ v_p(N)) for no prime factor p ≠ 3.

OddPerfect.restrained_tight_factorization

theorem restrained_tight_factorization {N q r t : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N) (hq : q.Prime)
  (hodd : Odd (N.factorization q)) (hr : r.Prime) (hrq : r ≠ q)
  (hsq : ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ≠ q → p ≠ r → N.factorization p = 2)
  (ht : t.Prime) (ht2 : t ≠ 2) (ht3 : t ≠ 3) (htq : t ≠ q)
  (hd : orderOf (3 : ZMod t) ∣ N.factorization 3 + 1)
  (htight : padicValNat t (3 ^ orderOf (3 : ZMod t) - 1) +
    padicValNat t (N.factorization 3 + 1) = 2) :
  N.factorization t = 2

Tight clock. In the restrained family, if a prime t ∉ {2, 3, q} has order of 3 dividing E + 1 and v_t(3 ^ ord_t(3) - 1) + v_t(E + 1) = 2, then t divides N with exponent exactly 2. Conditional family result; whether this is in the literature was not verified.

OddPerfect.restrained_tight_square

theorem restrained_tight_square {N q r t : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N) (hq : q.Prime)
  (hodd : Odd (N.factorization q)) (hr : r.Prime) (hrq : r ≠ q)
  (hsq : ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ≠ q → p ≠ r → N.factorization p = 2)
  (ht : t.Prime) (ht2 : t ≠ 2) (ht3 : t ≠ 3) (htq : t ≠ q)
  (hd : orderOf (3 : ZMod t) ∣ N.factorization 3 + 1)
  (htight : padicValNat t (3 ^ orderOf (3 : ZMod t) - 1) +
    padicValNat t (N.factorization 3 + 1) = 2) :
  ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ≠ q → p ≠ 3 → ¬ t ∣ p ^ 2 + p + 1

Tight clock, square rows. In the restrained family, if a prime t ∉ {2, 3, q} has order of 3 dividing E + 1 and v_t(3 ^ ord_t(3) - 1) + v_t(E + 1) = 2, then t ∤ p ^ 2 + p + 1 for every prime factor p ∉ {3, q} (all of these have exponent 2). Conditional family result; whether this is in the literature was not verified.

Tight clock, special row. In the restrained family, if a prime t ∉ {2, 3, q} has order of 3 dividing E + 1 and v_t(3 ^ ord_t(3) - 1) + v_t(E + 1) = 2, then t ∤ σ(q ^ a). Conditional family result; whether this is in the literature was not verified.

OddPerfect.RestrainedEighteenWheel

OddPerfect/RestrainedEighteenWheel.lean · 199 lines · 6 public theorems

Packing inequality with a wheel: for distinct numbers t ≥ x0 prime to W, the W-th power of the product of t/(t − 1) is at most (1 + 2W·#S/(φ(W)(2x0 − W − 1)))φ(W). No data.

Proof idea. Members of one residue class modulo W are spaced by at least W. For rational x > 1 and 2x > n + 1, (x/(x − 1))n ≤ (2x + n − 1)/(2x − n − 1) (ratio_pow_le), and with n = W these bounds telescope along a class (class_pow_le): the W-th power of the product over a class A is at most 1 + 2W·#A/(2x0 − W − 1). The inequality of the arithmetic and geometric means (prod_le_mean_pow) joins the φ(W) classes prime to W (wheel_pow_le). totient_30030 evaluates φ(30030) = 5760 in the kernel.

Public theorems

OddPerfect.RestrainedEighteen.ratio_pow_le_aux

theorem ratio_pow_le_aux (c : ℚ) : ∀ n : ℕ, (n : ℚ) < c →
  ((c + 1) / (c - 1)) ^ n ≤ (c + n) / (c - n)

((c + 1)/(c - 1)) ^ n ≤ (c + n)/(c - n) for rational c > n.

OddPerfect.RestrainedEighteen.ratio_pow_le

theorem ratio_pow_le {x : ℚ} {n : ℕ} (hx : 1 < x) (h : (n : ℚ) + 1 < 2 * x) :
  (x / (x - 1)) ^ n ≤ (2 * x + n - 1) / (2 * x - n - 1)

Ratio bound. For rational x > 1 and natural n with n + 1 < 2 x, (x/(x - 1)) ^ n ≤ (2 x + n - 1)/(2 x - n - 1).

OddPerfect.RestrainedEighteen.class_pow_le

theorem class_pow_le {W r : ℕ} (hW : 0 < W) (A : Finset ℕ) : ∀ x₀ : ℕ, W + 1 < 2 * x₀ →
  (∀ t ∈ A, x₀ ≤ t ∧ t % W = r) →
  (∏ t ∈ A, (t : ℚ) / (t - 1)) ^ W ≤
    1 + 2 * (W : ℚ) * A.card / (2 * (x₀ : ℚ) - W - 1)

One residue class. If the members of A are congruent modulo W ≥ 1 and each at least x₀, with W + 1 < 2 x₀, then (∏_A t/(t - 1)) ^ W ≤ 1 + 2 W #A/(2 x₀ - W - 1).

OddPerfect.RestrainedEighteen.prod_le_mean_pow

theorem prod_le_mean_pow {ι : Type*} (s : Finset ι) (z : ι → ℚ) (hz : ∀ i ∈ s, 0 ≤ z i) :
  ∏ i ∈ s, z i ≤ ((∑ i ∈ s, z i) / s.card) ^ s.card

Arithmetic and geometric means, natural exponent: for nonnegative rationals, ∏_s z ≤ ((∑_s z)/#s) ^ #s.

OddPerfect.RestrainedEighteen.wheel_pow_le

theorem wheel_pow_le {W x₀ : ℕ} (hW : 0 < W) (hx₀ : W + 1 < 2 * x₀) (S : Finset ℕ)
  (hS : ∀ t ∈ S, x₀ ≤ t ∧ W.Coprime t) :
  (∏ t ∈ S, (t : ℚ) / (t - 1)) ^ W ≤
    (1 + 2 * (W : ℚ) * S.card / (W.totient * (2 * (x₀ : ℚ) - W - 1))) ^ W.totient

Wheel packing. Let W ≥ 1 and let every member of S be at least x₀ and prime to W, with W + 1 < 2 x₀. Then (∏_S t/(t - 1)) ^ W ≤ (1 + 2 W #S/(φ(W) (2 x₀ - W - 1))) ^ φ(W).

φ(30030) = 5760.

OddPerfect.RestrainedEighteen

OddPerfect/RestrainedEighteen.lean · 287 lines · 5 public theorems · imports RestrainedSixteen, RestrainedEighteenWheel

In the restrained family, ω(N) ≥ 576967, v3(N) ≥ 288482 and Ω(N) ≥ 1442413, by packing the prime factors above one million in the residue classes prime to 30030.

Proof idea. The counted certificate of RestrainedSixteen leaves at most 9063 ordinary primes below one million. The others are distinct, exceed one million and are prime to 30030 (the family has no prime factor below 132257 other than 3), so wheel_pow_le bounds their product of t/(t − 1). The factor of the at most 9063 primes below one million is bounded by a single ratio (ratio_pow_le), which keeps the integers small. One kernel comparison of integers (final_ineqW) shows that 567901 large primes cannot bring the abundancy of the part prime to 3 above 4/3; 567901 is the largest count for which this comparison holds. The exponent of 3 follows from ω ≤ 2 v3(N) + 3 and its evenness. Lower bounds only; the family is not excluded. Ochem and Zelinsky (arXiv 2607.19746) state a far larger bound from a long computation, which is not proved here.

theorem card_gt_of_wheel {N q X B c a b d M W φ D Ep Em : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N) (h3 : 3 ∣ N)
  (hqN : q ∈ N.primeFactors) (hq3 : q ≠ 3) (hBc : B = c + 1) (hc : 1 ≤ c) (hqB : B ≤ q)
  (hR : ∀ r ∈ (N.primeFactors.erase 3).erase q, Good r ∧ B ≤ r) (hW : 0 < W) (hWX : W ≤ X)
  (hφ : W.totient = φ) (hD : D + W = 2 * X + 1) (hEp : Ep = 2 * X + 1 + d)
  (hEm : Em + d = 2 * X + 1) (hEm0 : 0 < Em) (hcert : CertC X B (X + 1) a b d) (ha : 0 < a)
  (hineq : (3 * B * b * Ep) ^ W * (φ * D + 2 * W * M) ^ φ ≤
    (4 * c * a * Em) ^ W * (φ * D) ^ φ) :
  M + d < ((N.primeFactors.erase 3).erase q).card

The counting step with the wheel. Setting of card_gt_of_certC, with a wheel modulus 0 < W ≤ X, φ = φ(W), D + W = 2 X + 1, E₊ = 2 X + 1 + d, E₋ + d = 2 X + 1 with E₋ > 0, a counted certificate CertC X B (X + 1) a b d and the comparison (3 B b E₊) ^ W (φ D + 2 W M) ^ φ ≤ (4 c a E₋) ^ W (φ D) ^ φ, where B = c + 1. Then M + d < #R.

OddPerfect.RestrainedNineteen

OddPerfect/RestrainedNineteen.lean · 379 lines · 16 public theorems · imports RestrainedFourteen, RestrainedFifteen, RestrainedEighteen

Restrained family: 2ω(N) ≤ 3v3(N) + 2vq(N) + 4 and 8ω(N) ≤ 3Ω(N) + 15.

Proof idea. Let R be the prime factors other than 3 and q, with A of them 1 modulo 3. A member s of R is light when its row count is at most 1 and heavy otherwise. The row of a light member free of q is t or 3t with t in R and t ≡ 1 modulo 3, and s ↦ t is injective, because x2 + x + 1 is increasing and x2 + x + 1 = 3(w2 + w + 1) has no solution with w a prime above 3. So these number at most A. Each receiver takes at most two rows, which gives #L + 2#H ≤ 2A. The light members whose row is divisible by q number at most vq(N), and A ≤ v3(N). Counting gives the two inequalities.

Public theorems

OddPerfect.RestrainedNineteen.phi3_ne_three_mul_phi3

theorem phi3_ne_three_mul_phi3 {x w : ℕ} (hw : w.Prime) (hw3 : 3 < w) :
  x ^ 2 + x + 1 ≠ 3 * (w ^ 2 + w + 1)

Step 1. x ^ 2 + x + 1 ≠ 3 (w ^ 2 + w + 1) for a prime w > 3. Equality forces x = 3 u + 1 and 3 u (u + 1) = w (w + 1); then w divides u or u + 1, so w ≤ u + 1, which leaves only u ≤ 1, and neither u = 0 nor u = 1 fits.

OddPerfect.RestrainedTwentyWheel

OddPerfect/RestrainedTwentyWheel.lean · 75 lines · 1 public theorem · imports RestrainedEighteenWheel

Wheel packing on a set J of residues modulo W: for primes t ≥ x₀ with t mod W in J, the product of t/(t − 1) to the power W is at most (1 + 2W·#S/(#J(2x₀ − W − 1)))#J.

Proof idea. The set S is split into the residue classes of J. Each class is bounded by the class lemma of RestrainedEighteenWheel, and the classes are combined by the inequality between the arithmetic and geometric means.

Public theorems

OddPerfect.RestrainedTwenty.wheel_pow_le_on

theorem wheel_pow_le_on {W x₀ : ℕ} (hW : 0 < W) (hx₀ : W + 1 < 2 * x₀) (J : Finset ℕ)
  (hJ : J.Nonempty) (S : Finset ℕ) (hS : ∀ t ∈ S, x₀ ≤ t ∧ t % W ∈ J) :
  (∏ t ∈ S, (t : ℚ) / (t - 1)) ^ W ≤
    (1 + 2 * (W : ℚ) * S.card / (J.card * (2 * (x₀ : ℚ) - W - 1))) ^ J.card

Wheel packing on a residue set. Let W ≥ 1, let J be a nonempty set of residues and let every member of S be at least x₀ with its residue modulo W in J, where W + 1 < 2 x₀. Then (∏_S t/(t - 1)) ^ W ≤ (1 + 2 W #S/(#J (2 x₀ - W - 1))) ^ #J.

Proof idea. A prime factor t other than 3 and q has t2 + t + 1 free of small primes, so modulo W = 51870 = 2·3·5·7·13·19 its residue is prime to W and is not a root of x2 + x + 1 modulo 7, 13 or 19: 5120 classes (card_J20). OddPerfect.RestrainedCountThree

OddPerfect/RestrainedCountThree.lean · 125 lines · 6 public theorems · imports RestrainedNineteen, RestrainedTwenty

Restrained family, with a the special exponent and c = v3(a + 1): 2ω + 3c ≤ 3·v3(N) + 2a + 4 and 8ω + a + 3c ≤ 3Ω + 16. With the landed lower bound on ω: 3Ω ≥ 10710800 + a + 3c and 3·v3(N) + 2a ≥ 2677700 + 3c. Restricted family result; the family is not excluded. Novelty not verified.

Proof idea. The landed count proves twice the number of ordinary primes ≤ three times the number of those that are 1 modulo 3, plus 2a, and then bounds that number by v3(N). The exact value is v3(N) − c. Keeping the term c gives the sharper inequalities.

OddPerfect.RestrainedFiveModTwelve

OddPerfect/RestrainedFiveModTwelve.lean · 141 lines · 5 public theorems · imports RestrainedFifteen, RestrainedFive, ClassicalSmall

A prime p ≡ 5 (mod 12) does not divide 3n − 1 for odd n. In the restrained family (special prime q of exponent a) a prime factor p ≡ 5 (mod 12) has p2 dividing σ(qa)/2, and the product of these squares divides σ(qa)/2. At a = 1 twice the product divides q + 1, so 2·p2 ≤ q + 1. Restricted family result; the family is not excluded. Novelty not verified.

Proof idea. In the restrained family a prime 2 modulo 3 receives its exponent 2 from the rows of 3 and q only. The row of 3 is (3E + 1 − 1)/2 with E even. Modulo p ≡ 5 (mod 12) the number 3 is not a square, so its order is even and cannot divide the odd number E + 1.

  ¬ p ∣ 3 ^ n - 1

A prime p ≡ 5 (mod 12) does not divide 3 ^ n - 1 for odd n: otherwise it divides σ(3 ^ (n - 1)) with n - 1 even, and mod_three_eq_one_of_dvd_geom_sum_three gives p ≡ 1 (mod 3). No odd perfect number is involved.

OddPerfect.ReturnReach

OddPerfect/ReturnReach.lean · 690 lines · 36 public theorems · imports PerfectRigidity, RestrainedFifteen, RestrainedEighteen

A special prime q > 7 of exponent 1 does not send back to a prime of exponent 2 that sends to it; every prime factor is reached from any other along the relation "sends to"; in the restrained family with special exponent 1, some prime factor is more than 3 steps from 3.

Proof idea. Say that p sends to t when t | σ(pvp(N)). Let U be a nonempty proper set of prime factors. The unitary divisor of N carried by the complement of U has a forced prime (exists_forced_prime of PerfectRigidity); it lies in U and divides the divisor sum of a component of the complement, so some prime factor outside U sends to a member of U (exists_sends_into). Hence the balls around a prime factor exhaust the prime factors. If every prime of a layer has exponent at most 2, the product of the next layer is at most twice the square of the product of this layer (prod_layer_succ_le). In the restrained family this bounds the product of all prime factors within distance d of 3, and so the exponent of 3; the landed bound 288482 then rules out distance 3.

OddPerfect.not_dvd_phi3_of_dvd_succ

theorem not_dvd_phi3_of_dvd_succ {q t : ℕ} (h7 : 7 < q) (htd : t ∣ q + 1) :
  ¬ q ∣ t ^ 2 + t + 1

Forbidden return. For q > 7 (in particular a prime q > 7) and a divisor t of q + 1, q does not divide t² + t + 1. With q + 1 = t h, q ∣ t² + t + 1 gives q ∣ h² + h + 1; for z = min(t, h) this forces z² + z + 1 = q and z ∣ 2, so q ∈ {3, 7}. The primality of q and the positivity of t are not needed. The statement also follows from eq_one_or_two_or_four_of_dvd_phi3_of_dvd_succ in OddPerfect/LargePrimes.lean, which gives t ∈ {1, 2, 4}. Restricted result; novelty not verified.

  (hqs : q ∣ σ 1 (s ^ N.factorization s)) : ¬ s ∣ σ 1 (q ^ N.factorization q)

No return to a square prime. Let the prime q > 7 have exponent 1 in N (for an odd perfect number: the special prime with exponent 1), and let the prime s have exponent 2 and send to q, that is q ∣ σ(s ^ 2) = s² + s + 1. Then q does not send to s: s ∤ σ(q) = q + 1. The hypothesis that N is odd perfect is not needed. It also follows from prime_dvd_phi3_dvd_succ in OddPerfect/LargePrimes.lean, which forces (s, q) = (2, 7). Restricted result; novelty not verified.

OddPerfect.LedgerPrime

OddPerfect/LedgerPrime.lean · 294 lines · 8 public theorems · imports Valuation, SpecialPrime, Reciprocity

A conditional statement: if the divisor sum σ(p^e) of every ordinary prime power component of an odd perfect number is prime, then at least five distinct ordinary exponents occur. The hypothesis is a case and is not known to hold. Whether the result is new was not checked.

Proof idea. If σ(p^e) is a prime s, then p has order e + 1 modulo s, so s ≡ 1 modulo e + 1. A prime receives at most one unit from each exponent, and none from a sender with its own exponent, because then e + 1 would divide its own divisor sum. With at most four exponents the special prime has exponent 1, its sender has exponent 2, and a sender into that one has exponent 2 as well, which is the forbidden same exponent pattern.

OddPerfect.LedgerPrimeTwo

OddPerfect/LedgerPrimeTwo.lean · 415 lines · 6 public theorems · imports LedgerPrime, EulerIndexPrimePower, Counting

Under the case hypothesis that the divisor sum of every ordinary component is prime: at least eleven distinct ordinary exponents occur (before: five); there is a forced collision of two distinct ordinary primes with the same prime divisor sum s, where σ of the component of s is the special prime; and N has at least 12 distinct prime factors and at least 185 prime factors with multiplicity. The hypothesis is not known to hold. Whether the results are new was not verified.

Proof idea. With at most ten exponent values the special exponent is 1, 5 or 9 and a prime that receives nothing from the special component has exponent 2, 4 or 6. Residues of q + 1 along a chain of senders (6, 8, 4, then 32 or 58) show that too few senders are available. For the collision: not every sender into q can divide a + 1, and a sender that does not must receive from at least two ordinary primes.

If the full divisor sum σ(p ^ e_p) is prime for every prime factor p ≠ q, then at least eleven distinct values occur among the exponents e_p, p ≠ q. A forced collision among prime full divisor sums. Let N be an odd perfect number and q its special prime. If the full divisor sum σ(p ^ e_p) is prime for every prime factor p ≠ q, then there are an ordinary prime s with σ(s ^ e_s) = q and s ∤ σ(q ^ a), whose exponent is even and at least 2, and two distinct ordinary primes p ≠ r with σ(p ^ e_p) = σ(r ^ e_r) = s and e_p ≠ e_r. Counting consequences of eleven exponents. Let N be an odd perfect number and q its special prime. If the full divisor sum σ(p ^ e_p) is prime for every prime factor p ≠ q, then ω N ≥ 12, Ω N ≥ 185 and Ω N ≥ 2 ω N + 161. The eleven distinct ordinary exponents all have prime index e + 1 (an odd prime), so they are at least 2, 4, 6, 10, 12, 16, 18, 22, 28, 30, 36. OddPerfect.LedgerPrimeThree

OddPerfect/LedgerPrimeThree.lean · 358 lines · 11 public theorems · imports LedgerPrimeTwo, LedgerOrdersTwo

Structure of the forced collision in the case where every ordinary divisor sum is prime (a hypothesis not known to hold): congruences and size brackets for the three primes involved, which make the collision a solution of the Goormaghtigh equation with odd prime bases and a prime common value. Conditional corollary, with the open statement as an explicit hypothesis: if that equation has no such solution, some ordinary divisor sum of an odd perfect number is composite. Also a capacity bound for prime factors whose index is divisible by a fixed d. Whether these statements are in the literature was not verified.

Proof idea. With σ(pe) = s and e + 1 = m prime, the order of p modulo s is m, so m divides s − 1; the same for the second sender and for s against q. Residues modulo 4 of a geometric sum with an even exponent give the alternative on the exponent of s.

Structure of the forced collision. Let N be an odd perfect number and q its special prime. If the full divisor sum σ(p ^ e_p) is prime for every prime factor p ≠ q, there are ordinary primes s, p ≠ r with σ(s ^ g) = q, s ∤ σ(q ^ a), σ(p ^ e) = σ(r ^ f) = s, e < f (e = e_p, f = e_r, g = e_s, all even, e, g ≥ 2), prime indices m = e + 1, n = f + 1, k = g + 1, and moreover: 2 m n ∣ s - 1, 2 k ∣ q - 1, q ≡ k (mod 2 m n), g ≡ 0 (mod 4) or (p ≡ r ≡ 1 (mod 4) and e ≡ f ≡ 2 (mod 4)), s ≥ 2 m n + 1, r < p, p ^ e < s < p ^ m, r ^ f < s < r ^ n, s ^ g < q < s ^ k, and p ≢ 1 (mod m), r ≢ 1 (mod n), s ≢ 1 (mod k). The primality of all ordinary full divisor sums is a case hypothesis, not known to hold for a hypothetical odd perfect number. Whether this result is in the literature was not verified.

OddPerfect.LedgerOrders

OddPerfect/LedgerOrders.lean · 162 lines · 5 public theorems · imports Zsigmondy, ValuationBounds

A counting inequality: for a set A of prime factors, the number of pairs (p, d) with p in A and d a divisor of e_p + 1 divisible by 3 is at most the sum over the prime factors t ≡ 1 (mod 3) of min(e_t, |A|). In particular the number of ordinary primes with 9 dividing e + 1 is at most the sum of the exponents of the ordinary primes that are 1 modulo 3. Whether the result is new was not checked.

Proof idea. For each such divisor d, a prime t of exact order d modulo p divides σ(p^e) (Bang and Zsigmondy), and t ≡ 1 modulo d, hence modulo 3. Different d give different t for the same p, and each pair (p, t) uses one unit of the exponent of t in N.

OddPerfect.LedgerThreeFree

OddPerfect/LedgerThreeFree.lean · 1079 lines · 2 public theorems · imports Abundancy, SpecialPrime, ExponentCap, Phi3, Valuation, Seed.Example

If at most 31 ordinary primes of an odd perfect number have an exponent e with 3 not dividing e + 1, and each of them is 2 modulo 3, then 3 divides N. There is no restriction on the special prime, and the other primes need only satisfy 3 ∣ e + 1. Whether the result is new was not checked.

Proof idea. Assume 3 does not divide N. Every non exceptional prime p has p² + p + 1 equal to an odd power of the special prime q, so these primes are far apart and contribute little to the abundancy; with the 31 smallest primes that are 2 modulo 3 the total stays below 2 unless q = 109. For q = 109 every prime is exceptional, 5 divides N with exponent at least 4, and a count of the factors 5 supplied by the divisor sums, with a finite check of fifteen small primes and a congruence argument for the 125th cyclotomic value, gives fewer than needed.

OddPerfect/LedgerReceiver.lean · 167 lines · 5 public theorems · imports LedgerOrders, LedgerThreeFree, Counting, SpecialPrime

Conditional family: every prime factor that is 1 modulo 3 is one number q. Then 3 dividing e + 1 forces exponent 2; and if 3 does not divide N and q is the special prime, at least 32 ordinary primes have 3 not dividing e + 1, ω ≥ 33 and Ω ≥ 2ω + 63. Proof idea. The orders 3 and e + 1 of p need two different receiver primes, both 1 modulo 3; only q is available. Then every ordinary prime is 2 modulo 3 and the 31 exception theorem applies.

OddPerfect.LedgerOrdersTwo

OddPerfect/LedgerOrdersTwo.lean · 137 lines · 3 public theorems · imports Zsigmondy, ValuationBounds, SpecialPrime

For every odd perfect number: choose for each prime p of a set A some orders d ≥ 3 dividing ep + 1. The number of chosen orders is at most the sum, over all prime factors t, of the smaller of the exponent of t and the number of sources compatible with t. A tool for case analyses.

Proof idea. Each chosen order needs its own receiver prime within one source (Bang's theorem), and each use of a receiver t spends one unit of the exponent of t.

OddPerfect.LedgerParity

OddPerfect/LedgerParity.lean · 200 lines · 6 public theorems · imports Network, Phi3, SpecialPrime

A parity count on the graph of which prime divides which divisor sum: with m the number of pairs (p, r) of prime factors such that r divides σ(p^e), s₂ the number of ordinary primes with exponent 2 and D the number of senders into the special prime, s₂ + D + 2ω(N) ≤ 2m + 2. Whether the result is new was not checked.

Proof idea. For exponent 2 the divisor sum p² + p + 1 is not a square, so it has a prime factor with odd valuation. An ordinary prime has even exponent in N, so a receiver with one odd incoming valuation has a second sender. Counting senders per receiver gives the inequality.

OddPerfect.SquareRow

OddPerfect/SquareRow.lean · 441 lines · 2 public theorems

For an odd prime p and an even exponent e > 0, σ(pe) is a perfect square only for p = 3, e = 4 (σ(34) = 112). Known mathematics: a case of the equation (xn − 1)/(x − 1) = y2 treated in classical work of Nagell and Ljunggren.

Proof idea. A square value gives a solution of p U2 − (p − 1) V2 = 1 with U a power of p. Through the Pell equation for d = p(p − 1), whose fundamental solution is (2p − 1, 2), U is the coefficient of an odd power m of p + √d. The binomial expansion shows that the power of p dividing U is at most the power dividing m (one more for p = 3), while U grows exponentially in m; only p = 3, m = 3 survives.

  (he0 : e ≠ 0) : IsSquare (σ 1 (p ^ e)) ↔ p = 3 ∧ e = 4

Square rows. For an odd prime p and an even exponent e > 0, the divisor sum σ(p ^ e) = 1 + p + ⋯ + p ^ e is a perfect square exactly when p = 3 and e = 4 (σ(3 ^ 4) = 121 = 11 ^ 2). This is a special case of classical results on (x ^ n - 1) / (x - 1) = y ^ 2 (see Nagell and Ljunggren); the proof here goes through the Pell equation x ^ 2 - p (p - 1) y ^ 2 = 1 and a p-adic valuation count.

OddPerfect.SignedRepunit

OddPerfect/SignedRepunit.lean · 551 lines · 2 public theorems

For a prime q ≥ 5, u = qh and odd n ≥ 3: the sum 1 + u + ⋯ + un − 1 is not a square when h is odd, and (un + 1)/(u + 1) is not a square when u ≡ 1 (mod 4). Reported to be special cases of the classical theorem of Ljunggren on (xn − 1)/(x − 1) = y2; the case of a negative base was not page checked. Nothing new is claimed.

Proof idea. The proof follows SquareRow, which treats a prime base. A square value gives a solution of a Pell type equation whose solutions are the odd powers of P + √d. The binomial expansion bounds the power of q in one coordinate by the power of q in the index of the power, while the coordinate grows exponentially in that index.

Prime power repunits are not squares. For a prime q ≥ 5, an odd h and an odd n ≥ 3, the sum 1 + q ^ h + ⋯ + (q ^ h) ^ (n - 1) is not a perfect square. The proof goes through the Pell equation x ^ 2 - u (u - 1) y ^ 2 = 1 with u = q ^ h and a q-adic valuation count.

For a prime q ≥ 5, an exponent h ≥ 1 with q ^ h ≡ 1 (mod 4) and an odd n ≥ 3, the number ((q ^ h) ^ n + 1) / (q ^ h + 1) is not a perfect square: (q ^ h) ^ n + 1 ≠ (q ^ h + 1) y ^ 2. The proof goes through the Pell equation x ^ 2 - (u + 1) u y ^ 2 = 1 with u = q ^ h and a q-adic valuation count.

OddPerfect.SignedRepunitJacobi

OddPerfect/SignedRepunitJacobi.lean · 269 lines · 3 public theorems

For X ≡ 1 (mod 4) write An = (Xn + 1)/(X + 1), n odd. For coprime odd n, m the Jacobi symbol of An over Am is 1. For an odd prime p, Ap is not p times a square. The condition on X is needed: for X = 23, A3 = 3·132. No published source was checked for these two statements. Novelty not verified.

Proof idea. Am is 1 modulo 4 and 1 modulo X, so X is a square in the Jacobi sense modulo Am. Since Xm ≡ −1 modulo Am, the index n reduces modulo 2m to an odd r < m; reciprocity swaps the two entries and a Euclidean descent ends at A1 = 1. If Ap = p·y2 then p divides X + 1 and Ac ≡ c modulo p; an odd c that is not a square modulo p gives the symbol −1, a contradiction.

The parity count of LedgerParity without any condition on the exponents: with k = ω(N) and m the number of pairs (p, r) of prime factors such that r divides σ of the component of p, every odd perfect number has 3k ≤ 2m + 3, and 3k ≤ 2m + 2 when the exponent of 3 is not 4. Proof idea. By SquareRow every ordinary row other than 34 has a prime factor with odd valuation. An ordinary prime has even exponent in N, so a receiver with one odd incoming valuation has a second sender; counting senders per receiver gives the inequality. Every even perfect number satisfies it too, so it excludes nothing by itself.

OddPerfect.PureRows

OddPerfect/PureRows.lean · 227 lines · 8 public theorems · imports LedgerPrime, LedgerParityTwo, Zsigmondy

Rows whose σ value is a power rw of one prime (pure rows). For an odd prime p and an even exponent e > 0: the index e + 1 is prime, r ≡ 1 (mod e + 1), and w is odd except for σ(34) = 112. In an odd perfect number the full components grow along pure rows, so pure rows form no cycle. If every ordinary row is pure, the special component must feed about half of the prime factors.

Proof idea. A composite odd index would give two prime factors of different orders by Bang's theorem, but a pure row has one prime factor. An even weight makes the σ value a square, which happens only for 34. Growth: pe < σ(pe) = rw and w ≤ e_r by the exact count at r. The fan-out inequality |R| + D_q ≤ 2d_q comes from the parity count of LedgerParityTwo, because every pure ordinary row has exactly one receiver. The module excludes nothing: a path of pure rows can end at a row with two receivers.

OddPerfect.PureCommonIndex

OddPerfect/PureCommonIndex.lean · 144 lines · 2 public theorems · imports PureRows, EulerPart, EqualExponents

No odd perfect number has every ordinary row a prime power together with one odd prime dividing every ordinary index.

Proof idea. A pure row has prime index, so all indices equal the common prime l, and each receiver is 1 modulo l. No ordinary prime is 1 modulo l, so every receiver is the special prime: every ordinary row is a power of q. Then every prime factor of the Euler index would be q, which does not divide m.

OddPerfect.PureCoverPacking

OddPerfect/PureCoverPacking.lean · 330 lines · 5 public theorems · imports PureRows, KanoldGeneral, AbundancyTail

A statement on finite sets of primes; no odd perfect number appears. Let S be a set of odd primes and X a set of at most K numbers such that every p in S outside X has 1 + p + ⋯ + pl−1 equal to a power of a prime in X. Then at most K centers in S contain every p in S that is not 1 modulo l and is at most 3l−1, and the product of p/(p − 1) over the rest of S is at most the product over the first K numbers that are 1 modulo 2l times an explicit tail factor. No published source was checked; novelty not verified.

Proof idea. Primes with the same receiver grow at least like a power l − 1, so each block between powers of 3l−1 holds at most one per receiver; the receivers are distinct and 1 modulo 2l.

Packing for pure covers. Let l be an odd prime, S a finite set of odd primes and X a set of at most K numbers, K + 1 < 3 ^ (l - 1), such that every p ∈ S outside X has ∑ i < l, p ^ i = r ^ w for a prime r ∈ X. Then some C ⊆ S with at most K elements contains every p ∈ S with p % l ≠ 1 and p ≤ 3 ^ (l - 1), and the product of p / (p - 1) over S \ C is at most ∏ j < K, H(2 (j + 1) l + 1) times (3 ^ (l - 1) - 1) / (3 ^ (l - 1) - 1 - K). Restricted result; no published source was checked; novelty not verified.

Setting: N odd perfect with special prime q, and one prime l divides the index ep + 1 of every ordinary prime p. A row σ(pe) is impure when it is not a prime power. Proof idea. The set X is the special prime together with the primes that have an impure row; the prime l is a center because l divides N.

If every prime factor p ∉ X has l ∣ e_p + 1 and a pure row σ(p ^ e_p) = r ^ w, then for every such p the row equals ∑ i < l, p ^ i and is a power of a prime in X.

theorem impureRowT_le {l L m K : ℕ} (hL : 0 < L) (hLl : L ≤ l) (hm : m ≤ l - 1)

      (((3 : ℚ) ^ m - 1) / ((3 : ℚ) ^ m - 1 - (K : ℚ)))

**Monotonicity of impureRowT.** For L ≤ l and m ≤ l - 1 with K < 3 ^ m - 1, the factor impureRowT l K is at most the same expression with l replaced by L in the product and 3 ^ (l - 1) replaced by 3 ^ m in the last factor.

OddPerfect.impureRow_core_of

theorem impureRow_core_of (hpack : PackingStatement) {N q l : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N)
  (hq : q.Prime) (hodd : Odd (N.factorization q)) (hl : l.Prime) (hl2 : l ≠ 2)
  {X : Finset ℕ} (hqX : q ∈ X)
  (hidx : ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ∉ X → l ∣ N.factorization p + 1)
  (hpure : ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ∉ X →
    ∃ r w, r.Prime ∧ σ 1 (p ^ N.factorization p) = r ^ w)
  {K : ℕ} (hX : X.card ≤ K) (hK : K + 1 < 3 ^ (l - 1)) :
  ∃ C : Finset ℕ, C ⊆ N.primeFactors ∧ C.card ≤ K ∧
    (∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p % l ≠ 1 → p ≤ 3 ^ (l - 1) → p ∈ C) ∧
    ∏ p ∈ N.primeFactors, ((p : ℚ) / ((p : ℚ) - 1)) ≤
      (∏ p ∈ C, ((p : ℚ) / ((p : ℚ) - 1))) * impureRowT l K

Core bound, assuming the packing statement. Let N be an odd perfect number with special prime q, l an odd prime and X ∋ q a finite set with at most K elements, where K + 1 < 3 ^ (l - 1). If every prime factor p ∉ X has l ∣ e_p + 1 and a pure row, there is a set C of at most K prime factors of N, containing every prime factor p with p % l ≠ 1 and p ≤ 3 ^ (l - 1), such that ∏ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p/(p-1) ≤ (∏ p ∈ C, p/(p-1)) * impureRowT l K.

  (hq : q.Prime) (hodd : Odd (N.factorization q)) (hl : l.Prime) (hl2 : l ≠ 2)

  (hM : ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ≠ q → p ∉ M →
    ∃ r w, r.Prime ∧ σ 1 (p ^ N.factorization p) = r ^ w)

OddPerfect.ImpureRowFourBase

Setting: N odd perfect with special prime q, and one prime l divides the index ep + 1 of every ordinary prime p. A row σ(pe) is impure when it is not a prime power. This notion is not the mixed index family of other modules. The count of four for l ≥ 523 with the packing statement as a hypothesis, and two lemmas for the case that 3, 5 and 11 or 13 divide N. Proof idea. The centers other than l are at most three odd primes. The worst sets are {3, 5, 7}, excluded because 105 does not divide N, and {3, 5, 11}, {3, 5, 13}, which force q = 5 with exponent 1 and then a factor 6/5 in place of 5/4.

OddPerfect.ImpureRowCount

OddPerfect/ImpureRowCount.lean · 92 lines · 4 public theorems · imports ImpureRowBase, PureCoverPacking

Setting: N odd perfect with special prime q, and one prime l divides the index ep + 1 of every ordinary prime p. A row σ(pe) is impure when it is not a prime power. This notion is not the mixed index family of other modules. Any finite set M that contains every ordinary prime with an impure row has at least 2 elements for l ≥ 7 and at least 3 for l ≥ 31. For l ≥ 13 it is impossible that every ordinary prime but one has index divisible by l and a pure row. Restricted results: smaller l is not covered, and nothing is said when no odd prime divides every ordinary index. No published source was checked; novelty not verified.

Proof idea. The packing lemma bounds the product of p/(p − 1) outside the centers; exact rational bounds on the centers keep the whole product below 2.

OddPerfect.two_le_card_of_pure_outside

theorem two_le_card_of_pure_outside {N q l : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N) (hq : q.Prime)
  (hodd : Odd (N.factorization q)) (hl : l.Prime) (hl7 : 7 ≤ l)
  (hidx : ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ≠ q → l ∣ N.factorization p + 1) (M : Finset ℕ)
  (hM : ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ≠ q → p ∉ M →
    ∃ r w, r.Prime ∧ σ 1 (p ^ N.factorization p) = r ^ w) : 2 ≤ M.card

(A) At least two impure rows. Let N be an odd perfect number with special prime q and l ≥ 7 a prime dividing e_p + 1 for every prime factor p ≠ q. If M is a finite set such that every prime factor p ≠ q outside M has a row σ(p ^ e_p) that is a prime power, then M has at least two elements; so at least two ordinary rows are not prime powers. Restricted result (one odd prime divides every ordinary index); no published source was checked; novelty not verified. The cases l < 7 are not covered, and nothing is said when no odd prime divides every ordinary index. The odd perfect number conjecture remains open.

OddPerfect.ImpureRowTreeCheck

OddPerfect/ImpureRowTreeCheck.lean · 614 lines · 21 public theorems · imports EqualExponentCount, PureRows, KanoldGeneral

Setting: N odd perfect with special prime q, and one prime l divides the index ep + 1 of every ordinary prime p. A row σ(pe) is impure when it is not a prime power. A checker for finite trees and its soundness theorem for a general prime l: if the trees for a prime l are accepted and 3 or 5 divides N, then at least four ordinary primes have an impure row. A conditional tool: the data modules supply the trees. No published source was checked; novelty not verified.

Proof idea. A node adds a proved prime factor of N as a parent or branches on the special prime. A leaf counts pairwise coprime divisors of rows of the parents: each holds a prime that is 1 modulo l, and an ordinary prime that is 1 modulo l has an impure row. The special prime is subtracted when it may be among the counted primes.

theorem leafOK_sound (H : Hyp N q l M) {pc : List (ℕ × ℕ × List ℕ)}
  (hpc : Pratt.check pc = true) {qs : Option ℕ} {par : List ℕ} (hI : Inv N q qs par)
  {imps : List (ℕ × List Item)} {items : List Item}
  (hc : leafOK l pc qs par imps items = true) : 4 ≤ M.card

OddPerfect.ImpTree.dvdR_sound

theorem dvdR_sound (H : Hyp N q l M) {qs : Option ℕ} {par : List ℕ} (hI : Inv N q qs par)
  {t : ℕ} (ht : t.Prime) (hd : dvdR l qs par t = true) : t ∣ N

OddPerfect.ImpTree.neR_sound

theorem neR_sound (H : Hyp N q l M) {qs : Option ℕ} (hI : ∀ Q, qs = some Q → Q = q) {t : ℕ}
  (hn : neR qs t = true) : t ≠ q

OddPerfect.ImpTree.chk_sound

theorem chk_sound (H : Hyp N q l M) {pc : List (ℕ × ℕ × List ℕ)}
  (hpc : Pratt.check pc = true) (tr : Tree) :
  ∀ (qs : Option ℕ) (par : List ℕ), Inv N q qs par → chk l pc qs par tr = true →
    4 ≤ M.card

OddPerfect.ImpTree.checkTree_sound

theorem checkTree_sound {l s : ℕ} {pc : List (ℕ × ℕ × List ℕ)} {tr : Tree}
  (hc : checkTree l pc s tr = true) {N q : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N) (hq : q.Prime)
  (hodd : Odd (N.factorization q)) (hl : l.Prime) (hl2 : l ≠ 2)
  (hidx : ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ≠ q → l ∣ N.factorization p + 1) (M : Finset ℕ)
  (hM : ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ≠ q → p ∉ M →
    ∃ r w, r.Prime ∧ σ 1 (p ^ N.factorization p) = r ^ w)
  (hs : s.Prime) (hsN : s ∣ N) (hsq : s ≠ q) : 4 ≤ M.card

Soundness of a tree certificate. Let N be an odd perfect number with special prime q, l an odd prime dividing e_p + 1 for every prime factor p ≠ q, M a finite set such that every prime factor p ≠ q outside M has a row that is a prime power, and s an ordinary prime factor of N. An accepted certificate for (l, s) gives 4 ≤ M.card.

OddPerfect.ImpTree.tableOK_nil

theorem tableOK_nil (pc : List (ℕ × ℕ × List ℕ)) : tableOK pc [] = true

OddPerfect.ImpTree.tableOK_cons

theorem tableOK_cons {pc : List (ℕ × ℕ × List ℕ)} {e : ℕ × Tree × Tree}
  {tab : List (ℕ × Tree × Tree)} (h1 : tableOK pc [e] = true) (h2 : tableOK pc tab = true) :
  tableOK pc (e :: tab) = true

OddPerfect.ImpTree.tableOK_sound

theorem tableOK_sound {pc : List (ℕ × ℕ × List ℕ)} {tab : List (ℕ × Tree × Tree)}
  (htab : tableOK pc tab = true) {l : ℕ} (hmem : l ∈ tab.map Prod.fst) {N q : ℕ}
  (h : OddPerfect N) (hq : q.Prime) (hodd : Odd (N.factorization q)) (hl : l.Prime)
  (hl2 : l ≠ 2) (hidx : ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ≠ q → l ∣ N.factorization p + 1)
  (M : Finset ℕ)
  (hM : ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ≠ q → p ∉ M →
    ∃ r w, r.Prime ∧ σ 1 (p ^ N.factorization p) = r ^ w)
  (hseed : 3 ∣ N ∨ (5 ∣ N ∧ 5 ≠ q)) : 4 ≤ M.card

Soundness of a table. For a length l listed in an accepted table, 4 ≤ M.card whenever 3 ∣ N, or 5 ∣ N with 5 ≠ q.

OddPerfect.ImpureRowCountSmall

OddPerfect/ImpureRowCountSmall.lean · 236 lines · 6 public theorems · imports ImpureRowTreeD01, ImpureRowTreeD02, ImpureRowTreeD03, ImpureRowTreeD04, ImpureRowTreeD05, ImpureRowTreeD06, ImpureRowTreeD07, ImpureRowTreeD08, ImpureRowTreeD09, ImpureRowTreeD10, ImpureRowCount

Setting: N odd perfect with special prime q, and one prime l divides the index ep + 1 of every ordinary prime p. A row σ(pe) is impure when it is not a prime power. For every prime l from 5 to 521, any finite set M that contains every ordinary prime with an impure row has at least 4 elements. Restricted result: the common index family is not excluded. No published source was checked; novelty not verified.

Proof idea. Assume at most three impure rows. The packing lemma then forces 3 or 5 to divide N, and the tree for l starting from that prime counts four impure rows: a contradiction.

Public theorems

OddPerfect.impureRowTree_prod_H_step

theorem impureRowTree_prod_H_step {C : Finset ℕ} {a b k : ℕ} {B : ℚ} (ha : 2 ≤ a)
  (hB : 1 ≤ B) (hC : ∀ x ∈ C, x.Prime ∧ a ≤ x) (hcard : C.card ≤ k + 1)
  (hab : ∀ x, x.Prime → a < x → b ≤ x)
  (hrest : ∀ D : Finset ℕ, D.card ≤ k → (∀ x ∈ D, x.Prime ∧ b ≤ x) →
    ∏ x ∈ D, ((x : ℚ) / ((x : ℚ) - 1)) ≤ B) :
  ∏ x ∈ C, ((x : ℚ) / ((x : ℚ) - 1)) ≤ (a : ℚ) / ((a : ℚ) - 1) * B

One step of a bound for a product of p / (p - 1) over distinct primes: the least element is at least a, the others are primes above it, hence at least b.

OddPerfect.impureRowTree_prod_H_seven

theorem impureRowTree_prod_H_seven {C : Finset ℕ} (hC : ∀ x ∈ C, x.Prime ∧ 7 ≤ x)
  (hcard : C.card ≤ 4) :
  ∏ x ∈ C, ((x : ℚ) / ((x : ℚ) - 1)) ≤
    ((7 : ℕ) : ℚ) / (((7 : ℕ) : ℚ) - 1) * (((11 : ℕ) : ℚ) / (((11 : ℕ) : ℚ) - 1) *
      (((13 : ℕ) : ℚ) / (((13 : ℕ) : ℚ) - 1) *
        (((17 : ℕ) : ℚ) / (((17 : ℕ) : ℚ) - 1) * 1)))

The product of p / (p - 1) over at most four distinct primes, each at least 7, is at most H(7) H(11) H(13) H(17).

theorem impureRowTree_seed {N q l : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N) (hq : q.Prime)

OddPerfect.ImpureRowCountAll

OddPerfect/ImpureRowCountAll.lean · 54 lines · 1 public theorem · imports ImpureRowCountSmall, ImpureRowCountFour, McDaniel

Setting: N odd perfect with special prime q, and one prime l divides the index ep + 1 of every ordinary prime p. A row σ(pe) is impure when it is not a prime power. For every odd prime l, any finite set M that contains every ordinary prime with an impure row has at least 4 elements. Restricted result: the count is four, not more, and the common index family is not excluded. No published source was checked; novelty not verified.

Proof idea. Three ranges: l = 3 is contradictory by McDaniel's theorem, the primes from 5 to 521 have tree certificates, and larger primes follow from the packing bound.

OddPerfect.AbundancyGap

OddPerfect/AbundancyGap.lean · 534 lines · 27 public theorems · imports Abundancy

A statement on finite sets of odd prime powers; no odd perfect number appears. For every K there are a bound B and a rational ε > 0 such that the product of σ(ce)/ce over at most K odd primes, with every exponent at least B (one prime that is 1 modulo 4 with an exponent that is 1 modulo 4 is exempt), is either above 2 or below 2 − ε. The values B and ε are not explicit. No published source was checked; novelty not verified.

Proof idea. Induction on the number of primes not yet fixed. A fixed finite set of odd primes has a limit value that is never 2, by parity. If the limit is above 2, large exponents push the product above 2. If it is below 2, the least new prime is either large, and the product stays away from 2, or one of finitely many small primes, which joins the fixed set.

OddPerfect.ImpureRowUnboundedBase

OddPerfect/ImpureRowUnboundedBase.lean · 194 lines · 1 public theorem · imports ImpureRowCount, Abundancy, Valuation

Setting: N odd perfect with special prime q, and one prime l divides the index ep + 1 of every ordinary prime p. A row σ(pe) is impure when it is not a prime power. The reduction: with the gap statement of AbundancyGap as a hypothesis (AbundancyGapStatement, a definition), for every K there is a bound L such that l ≥ L forces at least K impure rows. A conditional statement; ImpureRowUnbounded removes the hypothesis. No published source was checked; novelty not verified.

Proof idea. With fewer than K impure rows the packing lemma leaves at most K centers. Their exponents are at least l − 1, so the gap applies, and the rest of the product tends to 1 as l grows.

OddPerfect.ImpureRowLog

OddPerfect/ImpureRowLog.lean · 277 lines · 5 public theorems · imports ImpureRowBase, UpperBound, OmegaSevenFinal, TwoExceptionsUniform

Setting: N odd perfect with special prime q, and one prime l divides the index ep + 1 of every ordinary prime p. A row σ(pe) is impure when it is not a prime power. If every ordinary row outside a finite set M is a prime power, then l − 1 is below 16 to the power card M + 1. So at least K ordinary rows are impure once 16K < l: an explicit form of the theorem of ImpureRowUnbounded. Restricted result: the common index family is not excluded. The counting method is published: Lemmas 3.1 to 3.3 of T. Yamada, On finiteness of odd superperfect numbers (arXiv 0803.0437v7). That paper does not state this result; no other source was checked; novelty not verified.

Proof idea. Primes with a pure row and the same receiver form a chain in which each is above a power of the one before. A long chain makes N very large, a short one leaves N with few prime factors, and the landed upper bound for N in terms of its number of prime factors contradicts both.

OddPerfect.IndexColumnLower

OddPerfect/IndexColumnLower.lean · 332 lines · 10 public theorems · imports KanoldFive, SpecialIndexWitness, PrimePowerIndexBound

Setting: N odd perfect with special prime q, and one prime l divides the index ep + 1 of every ordinary prime p. Let B be the number of ordinary prime factors that are 1 modulo l. If l is odd, is not q, and no prime factor outside the class 1 modulo l has a row divisible by l, then 2(l − 1) ≤ 2B2 + B. That hypothesis holds when every ordinary index is a power of l, and when l is a Fermat prime that does not divide q + 1. For equal exponents l − 1: 2(l − 1) ≤ 3B and 2l + 4 ≤ 3ω(N). Restricted results: lower bounds for a count; no family is excluded. No published source was checked; novelty not verified.

Proof idea. The exponent of l in N is at least l − 1. It is paid by the rows of the primes that are 1 modulo l: an ordinary row pays at most B, the special row at most half of B.

  (hfeed : ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p % l ≠ 1 → ¬ l ∣ σ 1 (p ^ N.factorization p)) :
  2 * (l - 1) ≤ 2 * (N.primeFactors.filter fun p => p ≠ q ∧ p % l = 1).card ^ 2 +
    (N.primeFactors.filter fun p => p ≠ q ∧ p % l = 1).card

The column of a common index prime with no outside feeder. Let q be the special prime of the odd perfect number N and l ≠ q an odd prime with l ∣ e_p + 1 for every ordinary prime factor p. If no prime factor that is not 1 modulo l feeds l (that is, l ∤ σ(p ^ e_p) for every prime factor p with p ≢ 1 (mod l)), then the number B of ordinary prime factors that are 1 modulo l satisfies 2 (l - 1) ≤ 2 B ^ 2 + B. Restricted result (a lower bound for B; it excludes no family); no published source was checked; novelty not verified. The conjecture remains open.

OddPerfect.TwoExceptionThree

OddPerfect/TwoExceptionThree.lean · 569 lines · 7 public theorems · imports ThreeFreeTwo, SpecialPrime, Phi3

Special prime 5 and at most two further primes with an exponent different from 2: then the exponent of 3 is not 4, so it is 2 or at least 6. For exponent 2 the module proves partial results that describe every surviving configuration; that case is closed in TwoExceptionThreeA and TwoExceptionThreeB. Whether these statements are new was not verified.

Proof idea. If the exponent of 3 is 4, then σ(34) = 112 forces 11, and 11 must be the second exception, since exponent 2 at 11 would force 7 and 105 does not divide N. The factor 5 of σ(N) can then only come from σ(11e), so 5 divides e + 1 and σ(114) = 5 · 3221 starts a chain of exact squares 3221, 10378063, 769, 31. The divisor 34 · 5 · 114 · 312 of N is abundant, a contradiction.

Let N be an odd perfect number with special prime 5 in which every prime factor other than 5, r₁ and r₂ has exponent exactly 2. Then the exponent of 3 in N is not 4.

OddPerfect.TwoExceptionThree.five_sender_mod

theorem five_sender_mod {p e : ℕ} (hp : p.Prime) (hp5 : p ≠ 5) (he : Even e)
  (hd : 5 ∣ σ 1 (p ^ e)) : p % 5 = 1 ∧ 5 ∣ e + 1

If 5 ∣ σ(p^e) with p ≠ 5 prime and e even, then p ≡ 1 (mod 5) and 5 ∣ e + 1.

OddPerfect.two_exceptions_five_three_sq_sixty_one

theorem two_exceptions_five_three_sq_sixty_one {N r₁ r₂ : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N)
  (hodd : Odd (N.factorization 5))
  (hsq : ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ≠ 5 → p ≠ r₁ → p ≠ r₂ → N.factorization p = 2)
  (h32 : N.factorization 3 = 2) :
  ¬ 5 ∣ σ 1 (61 ^ N.factorization 61)

Let N be an odd perfect number with special prime 5 in which every prime factor other than 5, r₁ and r₂ has exponent exactly 2, and suppose e₃ = 2. Then the component of 61 does not send the prime 5: 5 ∤ σ(61^{e₆₁}). If 5 ∣ σ(61^e) then 5 ∣ e + 1, so σ(61^4) = 5 · 131 · 21491 divides 2N, and 61 is exceptional. The prime 13 (from σ(3^2)), 17293 = σ(131^2) and 421 ∣ σ(21491^2) are 1 (mod 3); at most one of the chains 13, 131 → 17293, 21491 → 421 can be cut by the second exception, so two of these exact squares send a factor 3, and with 5 this gives three senders against e₃ = 2.

OddPerfect.two_exceptions_five_three_sq_thirteen_sq

theorem two_exceptions_five_three_sq_thirteen_sq {N r₁ r₂ : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N)
  (hodd : Odd (N.factorization 5))
  (hsq : ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ≠ 5 → p ≠ r₁ → p ≠ r₂ → N.factorization p = 2)
  (h32 : N.factorization 3 = 2) (h132 : N.factorization 13 = 2) :
  6 ≤ N.factorization 61 ∧ ¬ 3 ∣ N.factorization 61 + 1 ∧ ¬ 5 ∣ N.factorization 61 + 1

With special prime 5, at most two exceptional exponents and e₃ = 2: if e₁₃ = 2, then 61 is exceptional with e₆₁ ≥ 6, 3 ∤ e₆₁ + 1 and 5 ∤ e₆₁ + 1.

OddPerfect.two_exceptions_five_three_sq_thirteen

theorem two_exceptions_five_three_sq_thirteen {N r₁ r₂ : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N)
  (hodd : Odd (N.factorization 5))
  (hsq : ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ≠ 5 → p ≠ r₁ → p ≠ r₂ → N.factorization p = 2)
  (h32 : N.factorization 3 = 2) :
  N.factorization 13 = 2 ∨ ¬ 3 ∣ N.factorization 13 + 1

With special prime 5, at most two exceptional exponents and e₃ = 2: either e₁₃ = 2 or 3 ∤ e₁₃ + 1.

OddPerfect.two_exceptions_five_three_sq_shape

theorem two_exceptions_five_three_sq_shape {N r₁ r₂ : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N)
  (hodd : Odd (N.factorization 5))
  (hsq : ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ≠ 5 → p ≠ r₁ → p ≠ r₂ → N.factorization p = 2)
  (h32 : N.factorization 3 = 2) :
  ∃ s, s.Prime ∧ s ∣ N ∧ s % 5 = 1 ∧ 5 ∣ N.factorization s + 1 ∧ s ≠ 61 ∧
    ((N.factorization 13 = 2 ∧
        ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ≠ 5 → p ≠ 61 → p ≠ s → N.factorization p = 2) ∨
      (N.factorization 13 ≠ 2 ∧ ¬ 3 ∣ N.factorization 13 + 1 ∧
        ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ≠ 5 → p ≠ 13 → p ≠ s → N.factorization p = 2))

The shape of every configuration that survives for e₃ = 2: with special prime 5 and at most two exceptional exponents, e₃ = 2 forces a prime s ≠ 61, s ≡ 1 (mod 5), dividing N with 5 ∣ e_s + 1, and either e₁₃ = 2 and every prime factor other than 5, 61, s has exponent 2, or e₁₃ ≠ 2, 3 ∤ e₁₃ + 1 and every prime factor other than 5, 13, s has exponent 2.

OddPerfect.TwoExceptionThreeA

OddPerfect/TwoExceptionThreeA.lean · 397 lines · 4 public theorems · imports TwoExceptionThreeAData, TwoExceptionThree, RestrainedFour

Special prime 5, at most two further primes with an exponent different from 2, exponent 2 at 3: the exponent of 13 is not 2. What remains of this case is one branch: the index of 13 is not divisible by 3 and one further prime s that is 1 modulo 5 has index divisible by 5. That branch is closed in TwoExceptionThreeB. Whether these statements are new was not verified.

Proof idea. If 132 exactly divides N the exceptions are 61 and a prime x that is 1 modulo 5. Below 116281 the table gives a third prime sending a factor 3, against exponent 2 at 3; above it the abundancy stays below 2 by the Rankin tail bound.

OddPerfect.two_exceptions_five_three_sq_thirteen_ne_two

theorem two_exceptions_five_three_sq_thirteen_ne_two {N r₁ r₂ : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N)
  (hodd : Odd (N.factorization 5))
  (hsq : ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ≠ 5 → p ≠ r₁ → p ≠ r₂ → N.factorization p = 2)
  (h32 : N.factorization 3 = 2) : N.factorization 13 ≠ 2

Let N be an odd perfect number with special prime 5 in which every prime factor other than 5, r₁ and r₂ has exponent exactly 2, and let e₃ = 2. Then e₁₃ ≠ 2.

OddPerfect.two_exceptions_five_three_sq_branch_b

theorem two_exceptions_five_three_sq_branch_b {N r₁ r₂ : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N)
  (hodd : Odd (N.factorization 5))
  (hsq : ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ≠ 5 → p ≠ r₁ → p ≠ r₂ → N.factorization p = 2)
  (h32 : N.factorization 3 = 2) :
  N.factorization 13 ≠ 2 ∧ ¬ 3 ∣ N.factorization 13 + 1 ∧
    ∃ s, s.Prime ∧ s ∣ N ∧ s % 5 = 1 ∧ 5 ∣ N.factorization s + 1 ∧ s ≠ 61 ∧
      ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ≠ 5 → p ≠ 13 → p ≠ s → N.factorization p = 2

The corollary: with special prime 5, at most two exceptional exponents and e₃ = 2, the configuration is branch B: e₁₃ ≠ 2, 3 ∤ e₁₃ + 1, and there is a prime s ≠ 61, s ≡ 1 (mod 5), dividing N with 5 ∣ e_s + 1 such that every prime factor other than 5, 13, s has exponent 2.

OddPerfect.TwoExceptionThreeBCheck

OddPerfect/TwoExceptionThreeBCheck.lean · 240 lines · 6 public theorems · imports TwoExceptionThreeACheck

Checker for the two walks behind TwoExceptionThreeB, and the structure of the branch as a set of rules (Ctx): which primes are forced into N, and which pairs of primes cannot both divide N.

Proof idea. A forcing chain starts at a prime known to divide N and follows prime factors of p2 + p + 1 until it reaches 7 or two primes that are 1 modulo 3; both are impossible in this branch.

OddPerfect.TwoExceptionThreeB

OddPerfect/TwoExceptionThreeB.lean · 468 lines · 6 public theorems · imports TwoExceptionThreeBData, TwoExceptionThreeA

Special prime 5 and at most two further primes with an exponent different from 2: the exponent of 3 is at least 6. This closes the case of exponent 2 at 3 that the earlier modules left open. Whether these statements are new was not verified.

Proof idea. In the last branch the exceptions are 13 and a prime s that is 1 modulo 5. At most one further prime t that is 1 modulo 3 divides N, and 7 does not. Small s are closed by forcing chains; for large s the prime t satisfies t2 + t + 1 = 3 · 13a · sb, which a second walk excludes for small t, and beyond that the abundancy stays below 2.

OddPerfect.branch_b_ctx

theorem branch_b_ctx {N s : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N) (hodd : Odd (N.factorization 5))
  (h32 : N.factorization 3 = 2) (hs : s.Prime) (hse : 5 ∣ N.factorization s + 1)
  (hsq : ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ≠ 5 → p ≠ 13 → p ≠ s → N.factorization p = 2) :
  Ctx N s

The structure of branch B. Let N be an odd perfect number with special prime 5 and e₃ = 2, let s be a prime with 5 ∣ e_s + 1, and let every prime factor other than 5, 13 and s have exponent 2. Then Ctx N s holds: every prime factor of Φ₅(s) other than 2 divides N, every prime factor other than 2 of σ(v^2) for a prime factor v ∉ {5, 13, s} divides N, two distinct prime factors ≡ 1 (mod 3) outside {13, s} do not exist, and 7 ∤ N.

OddPerfect.TwoExceptionFiveIndex

OddPerfect/TwoExceptionFiveIndex.lean · 310 lines · 15 public theorems · imports TwoExceptionThreeB, MixedIndexThree, Network, SpecialPrime, Phi3

Special prime 5 with at most two exceptional primes: the exceptions are 3 and a prime s ≡ 1 (mod 5) whose index is divisible by 5; the index of 3 is prime to 105 and has no prime factor up to 31; the exponent of 3 is at least 36.

Proof idea. The exact count of the factors 5 in σ(N) gives a sender s ≡ 1 (mod 5) with index divisible by 5; it is not an exponent 2 row, so it is an exception, and 3 is the other one by the earlier modules. The mixed index theorem then gives a row whose index is prime to 105, and it can only be the row of 3. For each prime l from 11 to 31 dividing the index of 3, a prime factor of σ(3l−1) divides N and starts a short chain of forced primes through rows of exponent 2 and the row of s; every chain reaches 7, which cannot divide N when 3 and 5 do. The exponent of 3 stays unbounded.

OddPerfect.TwoExceptionFour

OddPerfect/TwoExceptionFour.lean · 768 lines · 4 public theorems · imports TwoExceptionFourCheck, TwoExceptionThreeB

Two exceptional exponents with any special prime q. If q ≡ 2 (mod 3) and 9 divides σ of the special component (for example q ≡ 8 (mod 9)), the exponent of 3 is not 2. If the exponent of 3 is 4 and q ≠ 5, then 11 divides N with an even exponent e ≥ 6 such that neither 3 nor 5 divides e + 1, and the two exceptions are 3 and 11. Whether these statements are new has not been checked.

Proof idea. With exponent 2 at the prime 3 and 9 dividing σ of the special component, the ledger of 3 has no room left, so 13 = σ(32) is an exception and every squared prime t has t2 + t + 1 supported on 13 and the other exception. The abundancy then stays below 2 by a tail estimate, a finite table, or an abundant divisor in the few remaining cases.

OddPerfect.TwoExceptionFourMod

OddPerfect/TwoExceptionFourMod.lean · 299 lines · 5 public theorems · imports TwoExceptionFour, TwoExceptionThree

Two exceptional primes and exponent 4 at the prime 3: the special prime q satisfies q ≡ 1 (mod 12).

Proof idea. The exceptions are 3 and 11 by TwoExceptionFour, and the exponent e of 11 is even. Suppose q ≡ 2 (mod 3). A prime that is 2 modulo 3 divides no σ(p2), so no row of exponent 2 feeds q, and 11 is fed by rows of exponent 2 not at all beyond σ(34) = 112. The exact counts of the factors q and 11 give σ(11e) = A·qα and σ(qα) = 2·11e−2·B. Abundancy bounds give 67 ≤ AB ≤ 70, and congruences modulo 3 give A = 23 and B = 3. The closed forms of the two geometric sums then have no common solution. For q ≡ 1 (mod 12) rows of exponent 2 can feed q and the argument stops.

OddPerfect.TwoExceptionFourChains

OddPerfect/TwoExceptionFourChains.lean · 463 lines · 27 public theorems · imports TwoExceptionFourMod, Phi3

Two exceptional primes and exponent 4 at the prime 3: no prime below 79 other than 3 and 11 divides N.

Proof idea. The exceptions are 3 and 11 and q ≡ 1 (mod 12). A prime p of exponent 2 forces the prime factors of p2 + p + 1; those other than 3 are 1 modulo 3, so each is q or a prime of exponent 2 that is 1 modulo 3. At most four such primes exist, because each sends a factor 3 and the exponent of 3 is 4. The special prime forces the odd prime factors of q + 1. Forcing chains exclude each prime from 5 to 73 other than 11, in increasing order: a chain ends at a prime excluded before or at a fifth prime of exponent 2 that is 1 modulo 3. A forced prime that is 1 modulo 12 is split into the cases equal to q and different from q.

OddPerfect.TwoExceptionFourEmpty

OddPerfect/TwoExceptionFourEmpty.lean · 269 lines · 3 public theorems · imports TwoExceptionFourChains, Abundancy, EqualExponentsBound

With two exceptional primes the exponent of 3 is not 4: no odd perfect number has exponent 4 at 3 and exponent 2 at every other prime except the special prime and two more.

Proof idea. After TwoExceptionFourChains every prime factor other than 3 and 11 is at least 79. At most 13 of them have a row that is not a pure power of q: q itself, at most four primes of exponent 2 that are 1 modulo 3, and at most two senders into each of those. The rows that are pure powers of q have distinct exponents, so their primes grow by a factor above 8 and together add at most the factor 401/395 to the abundancy. Then σ(N)/N ≤ (121/81)·(11/10)·(79/78)13·(401/395) < 1.97, which contradicts σ(N) = 2N.

OddPerfect.ThreeSquareCapacity

OddPerfect/ThreeSquareCapacity.lean · 178 lines · 3 public theorems · imports Network, Phi3, SpecialPrime, ForcingClosed

If 32 exactly divides an odd perfect number N, then p4 divides N for some p in {7, 13, 19, 31, 61, 97, 127, 331}.

Proof idea. Call a prime factor p good when it is not the special prime, p ≡ 1 (mod 3) and 3 divides its exponent plus 1. Then p2 + p + 1 divides the divisor sum of the p component, so p sends a factor 3 and every prime factor of p2 + p + 1 divides N. The factors 3 received add up to the exponent of 3, which is 2, so three good primes cannot exist. Now σ(32) = 13 divides N, 13 forces 61 and 61 forces 97. If none of them is the special prime q, that makes three good primes. If q is 13, 61 or 97, the odd part of q + 1 forces 7 or 31 and their rows supply the third prime (19 and 127, or 331). So one of the eight primes, not q, has an exponent e with 3 not dividing e + 1; that exponent is even and not 2, hence at least 4.

OddPerfect.TwoExcEngineCode

OddPerfect/TwoExcEngineCode.lean · 685 lines · 0 public theorems · imports Pratt

The computable checker for certificates of the family with a bounded number of exceptional primes and a fixed exponent at 3 (2 by default): states, certificate trees and the functions check and checkV. Definitions only.

Proof idea. A state lists decided prime factors of N with a role (exponent 2, or a free exponent with recorded divisibility data, either the special prime or an exception) and the factors each one receives from the rows of other decided primes, plus a bound x below which every prime factor is decided. A certificate is a tree of rule applications. The checker derives every state, value and budget itself; the certificate carries only choices and witnesses. The hot paths use the arithmetic that the kernel evaluates fast.

OddPerfect.TwoExcEngineState

OddPerfect/TwoExcEngineState.lean · 162 lines · 3 public theorems · imports TwoExcEngineCode, SpecialPrime

The meaning of a checker state (Holds), the family predicate with a parameter for the number of exceptions, and the root lemma.

Proof idea. Holds says: N is an odd perfect number of the family, every listed key is a prime factor with the stated role, every recorded contribution pw divides the divisor sum of the named component, and every prime factor below x is listed. The family gives the root state, where only 3 is listed, with exponent 2 or, for the entry point checkV, with the exponent fixed by the parameters.

OddPerfect.TwoExcEngineCheck

OddPerfect/TwoExcEngineCheck.lean · 1715 lines · 32 public theorems · imports TwoExcEngineState, Network, ThreeSquareCapacity, TwoExceptionFour, TwoExceptionThreeB, Cyclotomic

Soundness of the checker: an accepted certificate refutes the family (check_sound, and checkV_sound for a fixed exponent at 3), for every rule except the deficiency leaf, which enters as a hypothesis.

Proof idea. One lemma per rule. Rows: the divisor sum of a decided component sends its prime factors, with weights checked by one modular power. Budgets: the weights a prime receives from distinct components add up to at most its exponent. Forcing: a forced prime gets one of an exhaustive list of roles. Receipt: a prime that is 2 modulo 3 must divide the divisor sum of the special prime's or an exception's component, which fixes a multiplicative order condition on the exponent. Abundancy: the decided components already give a ratio above 2. Capacity: the counting rule at 3 from ThreeSquareCapacity. The module also proves the bridge from named exceptions to the family predicate and the table of primes below 4096.

OddPerfect.TwoExcEngineTail

OddPerfect/TwoExcEngineTail.lean · 1374 lines · 1 public theorem · imports TwoExcEngineState, RankinTailPade

Soundness of the deficiency leaf (defSound): when the checker's upper bound for σ(N)/N is below 2, the state is contradictory.

Proof idea. The decided primes contribute a known product. An undecided prime factor is at least x and is one of: the special prime; a new exception; a square prime that is 1 modulo 3, of which the budget of 3 allows at most its exponent minus those already counted; a square prime that is 2 modulo 3 whose row contains a prime with a bounded remaining budget; or a square prime that is 2 modulo 3 whose row is built from finitely many generators. The first four classes have bounded size, so they contribute a bounded factor. For the last class the rows below a limit are enumerated exactly and the rest are bounded by rankin_tail_general.

OddPerfect.TwoExceptionTwo

OddPerfect/TwoExceptionTwo.lean · 131 lines · 4 public theorems · imports TwoExceptionTwoData1, TwoExceptionTwoData2, TwoExceptionTwoData3, TwoExceptionTwoData4, TwoExceptionTwoData5, TwoExceptionTwoData6, TwoExceptionTwoData7, TwoExceptionTwoData8, TwoExceptionFourEmpty

With at most two exceptional primes, the exponent of 3 in an odd perfect number is not 2, and therefore at least 6.

Proof idea. The top of the certificate tree reaches the 162 subtrees of the data modules, and check_sound turns the accepted certificate into the theorem. The certificate has 12,273 records: 7,341 contradiction leaves, 209 abundant leaves, 3 capacity leaves and 707 deficiency leaves. The certificate uses three earlier theorems on the special prime in this family. The bound 6 follows because 3 divides N, its exponent is even, and exponent 4 was excluded before.

OddPerfect.two_exceptions_three_ne_two

theorem two_exceptions_three_ne_two {N q r₁ r₂ : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N) (hq : q.Prime)
  (hodd : Odd (N.factorization q))
  (hsq : ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ≠ q → p ≠ r₁ → p ≠ r₂ → N.factorization p = 2) :
  N.factorization 3 ≠ 2

Let N be an odd perfect number with special prime q in which every prime factor other than q, r₁ and r₂ has exponent exactly 2 (a restricted family with two exceptional exponents). Then the exponent of 3 in N is not 2. This concerns only this restricted family, not odd perfect numbers in general.

OddPerfect.two_exceptions_six_le_three

theorem two_exceptions_six_le_three {N q r₁ r₂ : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N) (hq : q.Prime)
  (hodd : Odd (N.factorization q))
  (hsq : ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ≠ q → p ≠ r₁ → p ≠ r₂ → N.factorization p = 2) :
  6 ≤ N.factorization 3

In the same family the exponent of 3 is at least 6. The prime 3 divides N (three_dvd_of_two_exceptions) and is not the special prime (that one is 1 modulo 4), so its exponent is even and positive, and it is neither 2 (two_exceptions_three_ne_two) nor 4 (two_exceptions_three_ne_four).

OddPerfect.TwoExceptionTwoThree

OddPerfect/TwoExceptionTwoThree.lean · 39 lines · 1 public theorem · imports TwoExceptionTwo

With at most two exceptional primes, one of them is 3.

Proof idea. The prime 3 divides N, it is not the special prime, and its exponent is at least 6 by two_exceptions_six_le_three. So 3 is not among the primes of exponent 2, and it must be one of the two named exceptions. For one exceptional prime the corresponding statement is restrained_exception_eq_three.

OddPerfect.SpecialIndexWitness

OddPerfect/SpecialIndexWitness.lean · 289 lines · 7 public theorems · imports Zsigmondy, EqualExponents

A budget inequality that ties the exponent of the special prime to the exponent of any odd prime l.

Proof idea. Let a be the exponent of the special prime q and v the exponent of l in a + 1. For each j from 1 to v, both lj and 2lj divide a + 1, and a primitive prime factor of σ(qa) exists for each of these orders (module Zsigmondy). These 2v primes are distinct prime factors of N, different from q and 1 modulo l. Each one whose exponent e has l dividing e + 1 sends a factor l into σ(N) = 2N, and σ(qa) itself contributes its own factors l. Counting the factors l gives special_index_witnesses. For l = 3 the remaining witnesses have exponent at least 4.

OddPerfect.two_mul_special_index_le_card

theorem two_mul_special_index_le_card {N q l : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N) (hq : q.Prime)
  (hodd : Odd (N.factorization q)) (hl : l.Prime) (hl2 : l ≠ 2) :
  2 * padicValNat l (N.factorization q + 1) ≤
    (N.primeFactors.filter fun p => p ≠ q ∧ p % l = 1).card

The witness step: an odd perfect number has at least 2 v_l(a + 1) prime factors other than the special prime q (of exponent a) that are 1 modulo the odd prime l.

OddPerfect.special_index_budget

theorem special_index_budget {N q l : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N) (hq : q.Prime)
  (hodd : Odd (N.factorization q)) (hl : l.Prime) (hl2 : l ≠ 2) :
  padicValNat l (σ 1 (q ^ N.factorization q)) +
      (N.primeFactors.filter fun p =>
        p ≠ q ∧ p % l = 1 ∧ l ∣ N.factorization p + 1).card ≤
    N.factorization l

The budget of an odd prime l: the special prime q pays v_l(σ(q ^ a)), and every prime factor p ≠ q with p ≡ 1 (mod l) and l ∣ v_p(N) + 1 pays at least one factor l.

OddPerfect.special_index_witnesses

theorem special_index_witnesses {N q l : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N) (hq : q.Prime)
  (hodd : Odd (N.factorization q)) (hl : l.Prime) (hl2 : l ≠ 2) :
  2 * padicValNat l (N.factorization q + 1) +
      padicValNat l (σ 1 (q ^ N.factorization q)) ≤
    N.factorization l + (N.primeFactors.filter fun p =>
      p ≠ q ∧ p % l = 1 ∧ ¬ l ∣ N.factorization p + 1).card

The special index inequality: 2 v_l(a + 1) + v_l(σ(q ^ a)) ≤ v_l(N) + #{p} over the prime factors p ≠ q of N with p ≡ 1 (mod l) and l ∤ v_p(N) + 1, for every odd prime l.

OddPerfect.three_mul_special_index_le

theorem three_mul_special_index_le {N q : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N) (hq : q.Prime)

OddPerfect.four_exceptions_of_three_sq_of_nine_dvd

theorem four_exceptions_of_three_sq_of_nine_dvd {N q : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N) (hq : q.Prime)

  (h9 : 9 ∣ N.factorization q + 1) :
  4 ≤ (N.primeFactors.filter fun p => p ≠ q ∧ p % 3 = 1 ∧ 4 ≤ N.factorization p).card

If 3 ^ 2 exactly divides the odd perfect number N and 9 ∣ a + 1 for the exponent a of the special prime q, then at least four prime factors p ≠ q with p ≡ 1 (mod 3) have exponent at least 4.

OddPerfect.SpecialIndexDivisors

OddPerfect/SpecialIndexDivisors.lean · 210 lines · 5 public theorems · imports LedgerOrders, SpecialIndexWitness

If 3 divides the special index a + 1, then a + 1 has at most 4T divisors, T the total excess.

Proof idea. Every divisor of a + 1 that is a multiple of 3 is the order of q modulo a different prime factor of the special row, and these primes are 1 modulo 3. Those with index divisible by 3 use the exponent of 3; the others have exponent at least 4 and use the excess.

Public theorems

OddPerfect.card_divisors_filter_three_le_card

theorem card_divisors_filter_three_le_card {N q : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N) (hq : q.Prime)
  (hodd : Odd (N.factorization q)) :
  ((N.factorization q + 1).divisors.filter (3 ∣ ·)).card ≤
    (N.primeFactors.filter fun p => p ≠ q ∧ p % 3 = 1).card

The divisors d of a + 1 with 3 ∣ d are at most as many as the prime factors p ≠ q of N with p ≡ 1 (mod 3), where a is the exponent of the special prime q.

OddPerfect.factorization_three_add_card_le_excess

theorem factorization_three_add_card_le_excess {N q : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N) (hq : q.Prime)
  (hodd : Odd (N.factorization q)) :
  N.factorization 3 + (N.primeFactors.filter fun p =>
      p ≠ q ∧ p % 3 = 1 ∧ ¬ 3 ∣ N.factorization p + 1).card ≤
    2 * (∑ p ∈ N.primeFactors.erase q, (N.factorization p / 2 - 1)) + 2

The excess bridge: v_3(N) + b₀ ≤ 2 T + 2, where b₀ counts the prime factors p ≠ q with p ≡ 1 (mod 3) and 3 ∤ v_p(N) + 1, and T is the total excess.

OddPerfect.card_divisors_filter_three_add_le

theorem card_divisors_filter_three_add_le {N q : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N) (hq : q.Prime)
  (hodd : Odd (N.factorization q)) :
  ((N.factorization q + 1).divisors.filter (3 ∣ ·)).card +
      padicValNat 3 (N.factorization q + 1) ≤
    2 * (∑ p ∈ N.primeFactors.erase q, (N.factorization p / 2 - 1)) + 2

Orders of the special row and the excess. For an odd perfect number N with special prime q of exponent a, the number of divisors d of a + 1 with 3 ∣ d, plus v_3(a + 1), is at most 2 T + 2, where T = ∑_{p ∣ N, p ≠ q} (v_p(N) / 2 - 1) is the total excess. Whether this inequality is in the literature was not verified.

OddPerfect.card_divisors_le_four_mul_of_card_filter_three

theorem card_divisors_le_four_mul_of_card_filter_three {n T : ℕ} (hn4 : n % 4 = 2)
  (h3 : 3 ∣ n) (hD : (n.divisors.filter (3 ∣ ·)).card + padicValNat 3 n ≤ 2 * T + 2) :
  n.divisors.card ≤ 4 * T

Divisor count step: if n ≡ 2 (mod 4), 3 ∣ n and the divisors d of n with 3 ∣ d together with v_3(n) number at most 2 T + 2, then τ(n) ≤ 4 T.

OddPerfect.card_divisors_special_index_le_four_mul_excess

theorem card_divisors_special_index_le_four_mul_excess {N q : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N)
  (hq : q.Prime) (hodd : Odd (N.factorization q)) (h3 : 3 ∣ N.factorization q + 1) :
  (N.factorization q + 1).divisors.card ≤
    4 * (∑ p ∈ N.primeFactors.erase q, (N.factorization p / 2 - 1))

Divisors of the special index. For an odd perfect number N with special prime q of exponent a, if 3 ∣ a + 1, then τ(a + 1) ≤ 4 T, where T = ∑_{p ∣ N, p ≠ q} (v_p(N) / 2 - 1) is the total excess. This removes no unbounded family outright. For each fixed total excess T it bounds the number of divisors of the special index a + 1 on the branch 3 ∣ a + 1; the primes dividing a + 1 stay unbounded, and the branch 3 ∤ a + 1 is untouched. Whether this inequality is in the literature was not verified.

OddPerfect.SevenModTwelve

OddPerfect/SevenModTwelve.lean · 214 lines · 8 public theorems · imports Phi3, SpecialPrime, ForcingClosed, MixedIndexCheck

Primes that are 7 modulo 12 cannot feed each other; a chain argument for a small exponent of 3.

Proof idea. For a prime p that is 5 or 7 modulo 12, p² + p + 1 has a prime factor that is 7 modulo 12. If r divides p² + p + 1 then p³ is 1 modulo r, so p is a square modulo r. For two primes that are 3 modulo 4, quadratic reciprocity says they cannot both be squares modulo each other, so two such primes never divide each other's value. A chain of primes that are 7 modulo 12, each with 3 dividing its exponent plus 1 and each feeding the next, therefore has three distinct members, and each sends a factor 3. With the exponent of 3 at most 2 the chain must stop at a prime of exponent at least 4.

OddPerfect.ThreeCycleSpill

OddPerfect/ThreeCycleSpill.lean · 191 lines · 7 public theorems · imports SevenModTwelve, Seed.Starter

A cycle of three square rows on primes that are 7 modulo 12 forces an exponent of at least 4 or a prime outside the cycle.

Proof idea. With all three exponents 2 and no outside prime, each row is 3 times a power of the next prime; modulo 4 the power is odd, hence 1, so each prime is smaller than the next around the cycle.

Public theorems

OddPerfect.ThreeCycleSpill.row_lt

theorem row_lt {N r s t : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N)
  (hr : r ∈ N.primeFactors) (hs : s ∈ N.primeFactors) (htp : t.Prime) (htr : t ≠ r)
  (hr12 : r % 12 = 7) (hs12 : s % 12 = 7) (ht12 : t % 12 = 7)
  (h1 : s ∣ phi3 r) (h3 : r ∣ phi3 t)
  (hvr : N.factorization r < 4) (hvs : N.factorization s < 4)
  (hno : ∀ u, u.Prime → u ∣ phi3 r → u = 3 ∨ u = r ∨ u = s ∨ u = t) :
  r < s

One row of the cycle. Let r, s, t be prime factors of an odd perfect number N, all 7 modulo 12, with r ≠ t, s ∣ phi3 r and r ∣ phi3 t. If v_r(N) < 4, v_s(N) < 4 and every prime factor of phi3 r is one of 3, r, s, t, then r < s (the proof shows phi3 r = 3 * s).

OddPerfect.three_cycle_excess_or_outside

theorem three_cycle_excess_or_outside {N r s t : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N)
  (hr : r ∈ N.primeFactors) (hs : s ∈ N.primeFactors) (ht : t ∈ N.primeFactors)
  (hrs : r ≠ s) (hst : s ≠ t) (htr : t ≠ r)
  (hr12 : r % 12 = 7) (hs12 : s % 12 = 7) (ht12 : t % 12 = 7)
  (h1 : s ∣ phi3 r) (h2 : t ∣ phi3 s) (h3 : r ∣ phi3 t) :
  (4 ≤ N.factorization r ∨ 4 ≤ N.factorization s ∨ 4 ≤ N.factorization t) ∨
    ∃ u, u.Prime ∧ u ≠ 3 ∧ u ≠ r ∧ u ≠ s ∧ u ≠ t ∧ (u ∣ phi3 r ∨ u ∣ phi3 s ∨ u ∣ phi3 t)

Let N be an odd perfect number and r, s, t three distinct prime factors of N, all 7 modulo 12, forming a cycle of square rows: s ∣ phi3 r, t ∣ phi3 s, r ∣ phi3 t. Then one of v_r(N), v_s(N), v_t(N) is at least 4, or some prime other than 3, r, s, t divides one of phi3 r, phi3 s, phi3 t. This disjunction does not bound anything alone: different cycles may spill into the same outside prime.

OddPerfect.ThreeFourthCapacity

OddPerfect/ThreeFourthCapacity.lean · 132 lines · 2 public theorems · imports Phi3, SpecialPrime, ForcingClosed, Spoof, MixedIndexCheck

Exponent 4 at 3 forces the fourth power of one of six named primes.

Proof idea. σ(3⁴) = 11², so 11 divides N. If every prime among 7, 11, 19, 31, 127, 5419 that divides N had an exponent e with 3 dividing e + 1, then 11 would force 7 and 19, then 19 forces 127, 127 forces 5419, and 5419 forces 31. The five primes 7, 19, 31, 127, 5419 are 1 modulo 3 and each would send a factor 3, but only four are available. All six primes are 3 modulo 4, so none is the special prime and no condition on it is needed.

    3 ∣ N.factorization p + 1) : False

Core form. Let N be an odd perfect number with v_3(N) = 4. If every prime p among 7, 11, 19, 31, 127, 5419 that divides N has 3 ∣ v_p(N) + 1, a contradiction follows: the primes 7, 19, 31, 127, 5419 all divide N and each sends a factor 3, but only four are available.

Headline. An odd perfect number with 3 ^ 4 exactly dividing it is divisible by p ^ 4 for some p among 7, 11, 19, 31, 127, 5419 with 3 ∤ v_p(N) + 1.

OddPerfect.ExcessFourReduction

OddPerfect/ExcessFourReduction.lean · 218 lines · 2 public theorems · imports RestrainedEight, TwoExceptionTwoThree, ThreeFreeThree, Steuerwald

Reduces the bound Ω(m) − ω(m) ≥ 4 to three families with fixed exponents.

Proof idea. Write N = qam² with q the special prime. Each prime factor p of m has an even exponent e in N; call e/2 − 1 its excess. If the total excess is at most 3, at most three primes have a positive excess. With at most one such prime, the landed theorem on one exceptional prime gives exponent at least 12 at 3, an excess of 5. With two, the landed theorems say one of them is 3 with exponent at least 6, which leaves exponent 6 at 3 and one prime of exponent 4. With three, each has exponent 4 and 3 divides N, so the exponent of 3 is 4 or 2. The three families that remain are hypotheses of this module; the next three modules exclude them.

  4 ≤ ∑ p ∈ N.primeFactors.erase q, (N.factorization p / 2 - 1)

Under the three exclusions, the total excess ∑ (v_p(N) / 2 - 1) over the prime factors p ≠ q of an odd perfect number is at least 4. The exclusions are unproved hypotheses.

OddPerfect.ExcessFourS1

OddPerfect/ExcessFourS1.lean · 128 lines · 4 public theorems · imports ExcessFourReduction, TwoExcEngineTail

Excludes exponent 6 at 3 with at most one further prime of exponent 4 and squares elsewhere.

Proof idea. σ(3⁶) = 1093, so 1093 divides N, and each forced prime forces more. An exact search follows these chains, branching on the role of each new prime (special prime, exponent 2, exponent 4), and closes every branch by a contradiction, by abundance, or, in one branch, by a bound showing the abundancy index stays below 2. The search output is a certificate of 398 lines; the kernel checks it through the checker engine. In this family Ω(N) − 2ω(N) is at most a + 4 with a the special exponent, so for a at most 45 the exclusion also follows from the published inequality Ω(N) ≥ 2ω(N) + 51 of Ochem and Rao (2014). Whether the case of a larger special exponent is new has not been verified.

OddPerfect/ExcessFour.lean · 100 lines · 4 public theorems · imports ExcessFourS1, ExcessFourS2a, ExcessFourS2b

For N = qam², ω(m) + 4 ≤ Ω(m): the total excess of the exponents over 2 is at least 4.

Proof idea. Combines the reduction with the three exclusions. Steuerwald's theorem (m is not squarefree) is the bound 1.
