  (voight.map fun x => threeWeight x.1.natAbs x.2).sum = 2 ∧
    ¬ (3 ^ 2 ∣ (value voight).natAbs ∧ ¬ 3 ^ 3 ∣ (value voight).natAbs)

The closed form 3-adic ledger read on absolute values fails: threeWeight applied to |b| sums to 2 (since 127 ≡ 1 (mod 3) with exponent 1 contributes v_3(2) = 0), but v_3(|value|) = 4.

OddPerfect.SpoofInt.threeWeight_ledger_signed_voight

  ((-127 : ℤ) % 3 = 2 ∧ padicValNat 3 ((-127 + 1 : ℤ).natAbs) + padicValNat 3 2 = 2) ∧
    threeWeight 3 4 + threeWeight 7 2 + threeWeight 11 2 + threeWeight 19 2 + 2 = 4

The closed form 3-adic ledger with signed residues balances: -127 ≡ 2 (mod 3) at odd exponent 1 contributes v_3(|-127 + 1|) + v_3(2) = 2, and the other bases contribute 0 + 1 + 0 + 1, total 4 = v_3(|value|).

OddPerfect.SpoofInt.valuation_balance

theorem valuation_balance {l : List (ℤ × ℕ)} (h : IsSpoofPerfect l) (hb : ∀ x ∈ l, x.1 ≠ 0)
  (q : ℕ) :
  Nat.factorization 2 q + (value l).natAbs.factorization q =
    (l.map fun x => (geom x.1 x.2).natAbs.factorization q).sum

Formal valuation conservation for integer spoofs: for every q, the analog of OPNStarter.valuation_balance holds with the absolute values of the component sums. It holds at every q, in particular at every base that is a signed prime, so this bookkeeping (and every identity derived from formalSigma = 2 * value and multiplicativity over the bases) cannot distinguish a genuine odd perfect number from a signed spoof. The only hypothesis besides the spoof equation is that no base is zero.

OddPerfect.SpoofInt.isSpoofPerfect_append_iff

theorem isSpoofPerfect_append_iff (l : List (ℤ × ℕ)) (c : ℤ) :
  IsSpoofPerfect (l ++ [(-(2 * c + 1), 1)]) ↔ c * formalSigma l = (2 * c + 1) * value l

Appending the base -(2c+1) at exponent 1: the result is spoof perfect iff c * formalSigma l = (2c+1) * value l. No hypothesis on l or c.

OddPerfect.SpoofInt.sigma_eq_two_mul_add_div_iff_isSpoofPerfect

theorem sigma_eq_two_mul_add_div_iff_isSpoofPerfect {l : List (ℕ × ℕ)}
  (hp : ∀ x ∈ l, x.1.Prime) (hd : (l.map Prod.fst).Nodup) {k : ℕ} (hk : 0 < k) :
  (k ∣ Spoof.value l ∧ σ 1 (Spoof.value l) = 2 * Spoof.value l + Spoof.value l / k) ↔
    IsSpoofPerfect (ofNat l ++ [(-(2 * (k : ℤ) + 1), 1)])

Arithmetic identity behind the near perfect link. For a factorization l with distinct prime bases and value m, and k > 0: k ∣ m and σ(m) = 2m + m/k iff m * (-(2k+1))^1 is a spoof. This is not a classification of near perfect numbers: at k = 1 the amount m / k = m is not a proper divisor (see isNearPerfectWith_iff_isSpoofPerfect for 1 < k). Neither coprimality of 2k+1 with m nor oddness of m is needed (coprimality is only a side condition for the extended spoof); k ∣ m is automatic on the spoof side since gcd(k, 2k+1) = 1.

The near perfect link. For a factorization l with distinct prime bases and value m, and 1 < k: k ∣ m and m is near perfect with omitted proper divisor m / k iff m * (-(2k+1))^1 is a spoof.

      [(-(2 * (k : ℤ) + 1), 1)])

OddPerfect.FixedSupport

OddPerfect/FixedSupport.lean · 552 lines · 16 public theorems · imports RadicalBound, Certificate tool

A decision procedure for one fixed set of prime factors. For a list S of odd primes, search S computes whether some odd perfect number has prime factors exactly S, and both directions are proved: no_oddPerfect_of_search and exists_oddPerfect_of_search. The engine is tested on the supports of 6, 28 and 496 with all exponents allowed, and it closes the 104 supports of size four that the proof of ω ≥ 5 leaves. It treats one support at a time, so it gives no bound on ω by itself.

Proof idea. Put y = pe + 1 for each prime. Perfection is the identity ∏(1 − 1/y) = 2∏(p − 1)/p, with the unknown exponents only on the left. The search keeps a rational target a/b for the product over the primes not yet assigned and puts d = b − a. Every remaining y satisfies b ≤ dy, because the product is at most each factor. The least remaining y satisfies dy ≤ mb with m the number of remaining primes, because 1 − ∏(1 − 1/y) ≤ ∑ 1/y. So the least remaining y lies in a finite interval; the search branches on its prime and exponent, updates the target exactly, and recurses on fewer primes. No divisor sum is factored.

Public theorems

OddPerfect.FixedSupport.prod_map_eq_mul_erase

theorem prod_map_eq_mul_erase {g : ℕ → ℕ} {l : List ℕ} {p : ℕ} (hp : p ∈ l) :
  (l.map g).prod = g p * ((l.erase p).map g).prod

Splitting off one factor of a list product.

OddPerfect.FixedSupport.sols_sound

theorem sols_sound (ok : ℕ → ℕ → Bool) :
  ∀ (n : ℕ) (l : List ℕ) (a b lo : ℕ) (sl : List (ℕ × ℕ)), l.Nodup →
    sl ∈ sols ok n l a b lo → ∃ f : ℕ → ℕ, sl.Perm (l.map fun p => (p, f p)) ∧
      (∀ p ∈ l, 1 ≤ f p ∧ ok p (f p) = true) ∧
      a * (l.map fun p => p ^ (f p + 1)).prod = b * (l.map fun p => p ^ (f p + 1) - 1).prod

Soundness: every output is an admissible assignment solving the target.

OddPerfect.FixedSupport.sols_complete

theorem sols_complete (ok : ℕ → ℕ → Bool) :
  ∀ (n : ℕ) (l : List ℕ) (a b lo : ℕ) (f : ℕ → ℕ), l.Nodup → l.length ≤ n → 0 < b →
    (∀ p ∈ l, 2 ≤ p ∧ 1 ≤ f p ∧ ok p (f p) = true ∧ lo ≤ p ^ (f p + 1)) →
    a * (l.map fun p => p ^ (f p + 1)).prod = b * (l.map fun p => p ^ (f p + 1) - 1).prod →
    ∃ sl ∈ sols ok n l a b lo, sl.Perm (l.map fun p => (p, f p))

Completeness: every admissible assignment solving the target (with all values at least lo) is output, up to order.

  (hN : N.Perfect) (hS : N.primeFactors = l.toFinset)
  (hok : ∀ p ∈ l, ok p (N.factorization p) = true) :
  ∃ sl ∈ perfectSols ok l, sl.Perm (l.map fun p => (p, N.factorization p))

The engine, started at perfectSols, finds the exponents of every perfect number with support l (a duplicate free list) whose exponents obey the rule ok.

OddPerfect.FixedSupport.perfect_of_mem_perfectSols

theorem perfect_of_mem_perfectSols {ok : ℕ → ℕ → Bool} {l : List ℕ} (hnd : l.Nodup)
  (hl : ∀ p ∈ l, p.Prime) {sl : List (ℕ × ℕ)} (hsl : sl ∈ perfectSols ok l) :
  ∃ f : ℕ → ℕ, sl.Perm (l.map fun p => (p, f p)) ∧ (∀ p ∈ l, 1 ≤ f p ∧ ok p (f p) = true) ∧
    (∏ p ∈ l.toFinset, p ^ f p).Perfect ∧ (∏ p ∈ l.toFinset, p ^ f p).primeFactors = l.toFinset ∧
    ∀ p ∈ l, (∏ p ∈ l.toFinset, p ^ f p).factorization p = f p

theorem search_tab5 : ∀ r < 32, 17 ≤ r → isPrimeB r = true → ∀ s < 256, r < s →
